name: Kaal Corpus Claim Layer
description: Atomic, individually citable claims extracted from the published works of Wulf A. Kaal, each bound to a verbatim source quote and a content hashed source PDF.
author: Wulf A. Kaal
verification: Every supporting_quote is verified as an exact contiguous substring of the source PDF text. The source PDF is content hashed with sha256.
license_note: Read, index, quote, and cite with attribution to the canonical URL.

claims.claim: Bundling substantive corporate law together with adjudication, the arrangement that succeeded in Delaware, is likely to cause difficulties in Europe; Member States are most likely to succeed in post Centros and Inspire Art regulatory competition if they unbundle the corporate law product.
claims.citation: Christian Kirchner, Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Regulatory Competition in EU Corporate Law after Inspire Art Unbundling Delaware's Product for Euro (2004). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=617681
scope_conditions: EU Member States competing for corporate charters after Centros and Inspire Art
short term and possibly longer

claims.claim: Under the seat theory, competition with respect to corporate law alone is impractical, because a corporation cannot choose a state's corporate law without also locating its principal place of business there and thereby submitting to that jurisdiction's other laws.
claims.citation: Christian Kirchner, Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Regulatory Competition in EU Corporate Law after Inspire Art Unbundling Delaware's Product for Euro (2004). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=617681
scope_conditions: jurisdictions applying the seat theory

claims.claim: The Societas Europaea has drawn a less than enthusiastic initial reaction, plausibly because its rules are the product of years of negotiation and political compromise rather than a response to market forces.
claims.citation: Christian Kirchner, Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Regulatory Competition in EU Corporate Law after Inspire Art Unbundling Delaware's Product for Euro (2004). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=617681
scope_conditions: the SE as of 2004, shortly before it entered into force

claims.claim: Even if the ECJ has embraced the incorporation theory, Member States can still frustrate Type B regulatory competition through tax law, capital market law, listing requirements and other mechanisms, so the seat theory may retain de facto dominance.
claims.citation: Christian Kirchner, Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Regulatory Competition in EU Corporate Law after Inspire Art Unbundling Delaware's Product for Euro (2004). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=617681
scope_conditions: Member States willing to use adjacent bodies of law to deter reincorporation

claims.claim: The authors propose that private ordering can design an adjudication system for European corporate law better than public ordering by Member States that are marketing their corporate laws to managers and investors abroad.
claims.citation: Christian Kirchner, Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Regulatory Competition in EU Corporate Law after Inspire Art Unbundling Delaware's Product for Euro (2004). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=617681
scope_conditions: Member States exporting corporate law beyond their borders

claims.claim: Rule switching costs for a jurisdiction are probably higher when it must make substantial new demands on its courts in addition to changing its statutes, which raises the cost of competing with a bundled corporate law product.
claims.citation: Christian Kirchner, Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Regulatory Competition in EU Corporate Law after Inspire Art Unbundling Delaware's Product for Euro (2004). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=617681
scope_conditions: jurisdictions considering changing corporate law rules to attract charters

claims.claim: Mobility costs for a corporation are probably higher when changing the jurisdiction of incorporation means changing not only the applicable corporate law but also the courts that will apply it.
claims.citation: Christian Kirchner, Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Regulatory Competition in EU Corporate Law after Inspire Art Unbundling Delaware's Product for Euro (2004). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=617681

claims.claim: Regulatory competition for a bundled product of statutes plus courts is only a realistic possibility if relatively high supply side hurdles can be overcome to induce states to enter the market for corporate law.
claims.citation: Christian Kirchner, Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Regulatory Competition in EU Corporate Law after Inspire Art Unbundling Delaware's Product for Euro (2004). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=617681
scope_conditions: markets for a bundled corporate law product

claims.claim: A jurisdiction supplying corporate law as an unbundled statutory product faces low fixed costs, principally statute drafting, and near zero marginal costs, because additional users impose no new adjudication costs and registration costs are insignificant.
claims.citation: Christian Kirchner, Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Regulatory Competition in EU Corporate Law after Inspire Art Unbundling Delaware's Product for Euro (2004). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=617681
scope_conditions: statutes offered without adjudication by the state of incorporation

claims.claim: For an unbundled product of statutes only, the key to successful regulatory competition shifts from the supply side to the demand side: drafting statutes that appeal to large numbers of managers and investors outside the jurisdiction.
claims.citation: Christian Kirchner, Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Regulatory Competition in EU Corporate Law after Inspire Art Unbundling Delaware's Product for Euro (2004). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=617681
scope_conditions: unbundled statutory product

claims.claim: The quality problems in Delaware adjudication mean it is not a foregone conclusion that the bundled product of statutes plus specialized courts leads to optimal results.
claims.citation: Christian Kirchner, Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Regulatory Competition in EU Corporate Law after Inspire Art Unbundling Delaware's Product for Euro (2004). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=617681
scope_conditions: U.S. corporate law and Delaware in particular

claims.claim: Delaware itself acknowledges the utility of unbundling statutes from adjudication, though not in its corporate law: its LLC statute specifically allows members or managers to agree in writing to arbitration of claims under the LLC agreement.
claims.citation: Christian Kirchner, Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Regulatory Competition in EU Corporate Law after Inspire Art Unbundling Delaware's Product for Euro (2004). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=617681
scope_conditions: Delaware limited liability companies, not Delaware corporations

claims.claim: To the extent adjudication over U.K. corporate law is expected to take place outside the U.K., the U.K. has not in fact exported a bundled product; its users are demonstrating a preference for an unbundled package.
claims.citation: Christian Kirchner, Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Regulatory Competition in EU Corporate Law after Inspire Art Unbundling Delaware's Product for Euro (2004). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=617681
scope_conditions: small closely held enterprises incorporating in the U.K. after Inspire Art

claims.claim: Conducting judicial proceedings through interpreters is cumbersome and confusing and creates a perceived bias in favor of litigants and lawyers fluent in the language of the proceedings, which is a barrier to exporting adjudication.
claims.citation: Christian Kirchner, Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Regulatory Competition in EU Corporate Law after Inspire Art Unbundling Delaware's Product for Euro (2004). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=617681
scope_conditions: Member States whose courts do not conduct proceedings in English

claims.claim: Member States unwilling to incur the rule switching costs of conducting judicial proceedings in English could be precluded from marketing their corporate charters in other Member States that do not share their language.
claims.citation: Christian Kirchner, Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Regulatory Competition in EU Corporate Law after Inspire Art Unbundling Delaware's Product for Euro (2004). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=617681
scope_conditions: English being the only language widely understood throughout the EU

claims.claim: The weak link in a bundled package offered by a civil law Member State is likely to be its system of adjudication rather than its statute.
claims.citation: Christian Kirchner, Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Regulatory Competition in EU Corporate Law after Inspire Art Unbundling Delaware's Product for Euro (2004). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=617681
scope_conditions: civil law Member States marketing corporate law to investors used to common law systems

claims.claim: Defects in a civil law jurisdiction's corporate statute, such as inadequate minority shareholder protection, are more easily fixed than defects in a judiciary that fails to apply the statute predictably and uniformly.
claims.citation: Christian Kirchner, Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Regulatory Competition in EU Corporate Law after Inspire Art Unbundling Delaware's Product for Euro (2004). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=617681
scope_conditions: civil law jurisdictions

claims.claim: Because the English common law system is gravitating toward a civil law approach that weights statutes more heavily than judicial interpretation, the value of a bundled package of statutes plus adjudication even in a European common law jurisdiction may not greatly exceed the value of the statutes standing alone.
claims.citation: Christian Kirchner, Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Regulatory Competition in EU Corporate Law after Inspire Art Unbundling Delaware's Product for Euro (2004). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=617681
scope_conditions: European common law jurisdictions, in contrast with Delaware

claims.claim: European lawyers may advise clients to incorporate at home simply because those lawyers do not want to deal with the courts and lawyers of another Member State, which suppresses cross border incorporation independently of statute quality.
claims.citation: Christian Kirchner, Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Regulatory Competition in EU Corporate Law after Inspire Art Unbundling Delaware's Product for Euro (2004). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=617681
scope_conditions: European legal education and practice, where procedural differences across Member States are large

claims.claim: No Member State currently has courts specializing in corporate law comparable to the Delaware Court of Chancery, and establishing such courts or upgrading existing ones would be expensive for most Member States, with high marginal costs as usage grows.
claims.citation: Christian Kirchner, Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Regulatory Competition in EU Corporate Law after Inspire Art Unbundling Delaware's Product for Euro (2004). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=617681
scope_conditions: Member States considering exporting adjudication along with statutes

claims.claim: The two sources that finance Delaware's bundled package, franchise taxes and legal fees for local counsel, might not be as lucrative for a European Member State, so the expensive package of statutes plus adjudication may have no viable funding model.
claims.citation: Christian Kirchner, Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Regulatory Competition in EU Corporate Law after Inspire Art Unbundling Delaware's Product for Euro (2004). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=617681
scope_conditions: European Member States with tax systems built around taxing operations within their borders

claims.claim: With an unbundled product more Member States might participate in regulatory competition over corporate law, which would speed up the learning process and likely result in better substantive corporate law.
claims.citation: Christian Kirchner, Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Regulatory Competition in EU Corporate Law after Inspire Art Unbundling Delaware's Product for Euro (2004). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=617681
scope_conditions: New Institutional Economics framework in which experimentation drives learning

claims.claim: Fear of judicial bias operates through risk premiums: because investors and managers are uncertain how foreign judges will behave and may assume the worst, they price a decision to incorporate in another Member State higher.
claims.citation: Christian Kirchner, Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Regulatory Competition in EU Corporate Law after Inspire Art Unbundling Delaware's Product for Euro (2004). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=617681
scope_conditions: bounded rationality and incomplete information about foreign judges

claims.claim: If statutes are unbundled from adjudication the judicial bias problem largely disappears, because statutes are at least facially neutral and discriminatory statutes would violate the EU treaty.
claims.citation: Christian Kirchner, Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Regulatory Competition in EU Corporate Law after Inspire Art Unbundling Delaware's Product for Euro (2004). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=617681
scope_conditions: EU law, under which discriminatory national provisions violate freedom of establishment

claims.claim: Conflict of laws problems become more complex and pose a much greater threat to the entire system of regulatory competition once a jurisdiction markets its corporate law as a separate product under Type B competition.
claims.citation: Christian Kirchner, Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Regulatory Competition in EU Corporate Law after Inspire Art Unbundling Delaware's Product for Euro (2004). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=617681
scope_conditions: Type B regulatory competition under the incorporation theory

claims.claim: The success of Europe's experiment with Type B regulatory competition will turn largely on whether there is a clear understanding of what is corporate law and what is not.
claims.citation: Christian Kirchner, Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Regulatory Competition in EU Corporate Law after Inspire Art Unbundling Delaware's Product for Euro (2004). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=617681
scope_conditions: boundaries between corporate law, capital market law, labor law and creditor protection law

claims.claim: Member States can avoid at least part of the result in Centros and Inspire Art by recharacterizing what used to be corporate law as creditor protection law, provided the recharacterized rule does not discriminate against foreign corporations.
claims.citation: Christian Kirchner, Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Regulatory Competition in EU Corporate Law after Inspire Art Unbundling Delaware's Product for Euro (2004). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=617681
scope_conditions: non discriminatory national measures

claims.claim: To the extent judges are biased toward expansively interpreting the reach of their own Member State's corporate law, corporations may unexpectedly be bound by rules of the state of incorporation on subject matter they believed lay outside corporate law.
claims.citation: Christian Kirchner, Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Regulatory Competition in EU Corporate Law after Inspire Art Unbundling Delaware's Product for Euro (2004). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=617681
scope_conditions: adjudication by courts of the Member State of incorporation

claims.claim: A single body of arbitrators affiliated through an association is better positioned than the courts of separate Member States to develop a systematic and consistent approach to the conflict of laws problems unique to the incorporation theory.
claims.citation: Christian Kirchner, Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Regulatory Competition in EU Corporate Law after Inspire Art Unbundling Delaware's Product for Euro (2004). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=617681
scope_conditions: early stages of Type B regulatory competition in Europe

claims.claim: For cross border enforcement the critical question is not whether a judgment will be enforced in another Member State but when: eventual enforcement is insufficient if a party has time to remove assets, and delayed injunctions can be worthless.
claims.citation: Christian Kirchner, Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Regulatory Competition in EU Corporate Law after Inspire Art Unbundling Delaware's Product for Euro (2004). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=617681
scope_conditions: EU Member States that generally do enforce each other's judgments

claims.claim: Because the judiciary in many European jurisdictions is a specialized career entered shortly after university and without significant private practice experience, European judges lack the practice background that facilitates learning to adjudicate complex corporate disputes.
claims.citation: Christian Kirchner, Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Regulatory Competition in EU Corporate Law after Inspire Art Unbundling Delaware's Product for Euro (2004). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=617681
scope_conditions: most EU Member States other than the United States model of lateral judicial appointment

claims.claim: Error correction is weak for Member State corporate law adjudication: national legislatures are unlikely to intervene unless judicial error affects domestic interests, so managers and investors would rather face slow learning judges in their home country.
claims.citation: Christian Kirchner, Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Regulatory Competition in EU Corporate Law after Inspire Art Unbundling Delaware's Product for Euro (2004). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=617681
scope_conditions: EU level intervention being slow and therefore a weak deterrent

claims.claim: Forum unbundling is the arrangement in which the incorporation jurisdiction's statutes and interpretive case law are unbundled only from the adjudication services of its courts, so corporations may choose a different adjudicator in their charters.
claims.citation: Christian Kirchner, Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Regulatory Competition in EU Corporate Law after Inspire Art Unbundling Delaware's Product for Euro (2004). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=617681

claims.claim: None of the Delaware based solutions, whether importing bundled or unbundled Delaware law, is likely to be viable for Europe.
claims.citation: Christian Kirchner, Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Regulatory Competition in EU Corporate Law after Inspire Art Unbundling Delaware's Product for Euro (2004). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=617681
scope_conditions: the four options canvassed: Delaware charters, partial copying, wholesale statutory copying, and copying statutes plus case law

claims.claim: Choosing another Member State's courts as the forum can silently strip substantive rights: if the forum state treats an unavailable remedy such as money damages as procedural and refuses to hear the claim, the charter has opted out of substantive law of the state of incorporation that ordinarily could not be waived.
claims.citation: Christian Kirchner, Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Regulatory Competition in EU Corporate Law after Inspire Art Unbundling Delaware's Product for Euro (2004). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=617681
scope_conditions: Member States such as Germany that limit or deny money damages in internal affairs disputes

claims.claim: Member States should provide in their corporate statutes an arbitration enabling provision allowing corporate charters to mandate arbitration of internal affairs disputes instead of adjudication in national courts.
claims.citation: Christian Kirchner, Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Regulatory Competition in EU Corporate Law after Inspire Art Unbundling Delaware's Product for Euro (2004). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=617681
scope_conditions: Member States wishing to offer an unbundled corporate law product

claims.claim: Compensating arbitrators by the number of cases they hear gives litigants a substantial role in shaping the system but may yield decisions so eager to please all parties that they lack decisiveness, sound reasoning and value as precedent.
claims.citation: Christian Kirchner, Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Regulatory Competition in EU Corporate Law after Inspire Art Unbundling Delaware's Product for Euro (2004). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=617681
scope_conditions: conventional arbitration in which litigants select and pay arbitrators

claims.claim: Arbitration of corporate governance disputes has not emerged in the United States because arbitration is at best the next best alternative to Delaware, and a second place finish does not justify the investment needed to design a workable arbitration framework.
claims.citation: Christian Kirchner, Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Regulatory Competition in EU Corporate Law after Inspire Art Unbundling Delaware's Product for Euro (2004). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=617681
scope_conditions: United States, where Delaware's adjudication system commands high confidence

claims.claim: Europe has no equivalent of Delaware with which arbitration would have to compete, since incorporation theory is only beginning to take hold and no Member State has established a commanding lead in marketing its corporate law abroad.
claims.citation: Christian Kirchner, Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Regulatory Competition in EU Corporate Law after Inspire Art Unbundling Delaware's Product for Euro (2004). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=617681
scope_conditions: Europe shortly after Centros and Inspire Art

claims.claim: One objection to arbitration of corporate governance disputes holds in Europe as in the United States: arbitration as ordinarily used yields little relevant precedent.
claims.citation: Christian Kirchner, Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Regulatory Competition in EU Corporate Law after Inspire Art Unbundling Delaware's Product for Euro (2004). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=617681
scope_conditions: arbitration as it is used in most commercial contexts

claims.claim: Expert judges in national courts who cannot understand the arguments of lawyers before them or read documents written in another language may not be experts at all, so the American model of state appointed expert corporate judges does not transfer to multilingual Europe.
claims.citation: Christian Kirchner, Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Regulatory Competition in EU Corporate Law after Inspire Art Unbundling Delaware's Product for Euro (2004). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=617681
scope_conditions: Europe, in contrast with the single language United States

claims.claim: Unless the Member State of incorporation specifically provides in its corporate statute that arbitration is permissible when allowed in the charter or a shareholders agreement, investors run the risk that courts refuse to enforce the arbitration provision.
claims.citation: Christian Kirchner, Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Regulatory Competition in EU Corporate Law after Inspire Art Unbundling Delaware's Product for Euro (2004). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=617681
scope_conditions: closely held corporations may rely on a shareholders agreement instead of the charter

claims.claim: Empirically, at least 48 companies with German names carrying the GmbH designation were formed as private limited companies under U.K. law in the ten months after the Inspire Art decision, indicating that charter migration accelerated after the ruling.
claims.citation: Christian Kirchner, Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Regulatory Competition in EU Corporate Law after Inspire Art Unbundling Delaware's Product for Euro (2004). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=617681
scope_conditions: some of these companies may also do business in the U.K. or be affiliated with a German GmbH

claims.claim: A uniform approach to hedge fund valuation is not possible because the variety of hedge fund investments and strategies means some positions, such as non-concentrated positions in liquid securities, are far easier to value than others.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Valuation Retailization, Regulation, and Investor Suitability (2009). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1428387
scope_conditions: applies across the range of hedge fund investment strategies

claims.claim: Broker quotes are an unreliable fallback for valuation: they can be hard to obtain and can vary by 20 to 30 percent for instruments such as mortgage-backed securities, which makes accurate valuation of those securities difficult.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Valuation Retailization, Regulation, and Investor Suitability (2009). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1428387
scope_conditions: where recent transaction prices and marketable bids and offers are not readily available

claims.claim: Existing international proposals and guidelines on hedge fund valuation fail because they do not adequately distinguish between retail and qualified investors, and as of 2009 no legislature has issued an exhaustive set of rules addressing the factors that cause inaccurate valuation.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Valuation Retailization, Regulation, and Investor Suitability (2009). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1428387
scope_conditions: as of the time of writing, 2009

claims.claim: Valuation is very likely to become the next major issue for the hedge fund industry, because most jurisdictions lack regulatory oversight of valuation and the industry generally lacks self-discipline and internal controls.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Valuation Retailization, Regulation, and Investor Suitability (2009). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1428387
scope_conditions: absent regulatory oversight
absent industry self-discipline and internal controls

claims.claim: When hedge funds adopt private equity strategies by adding private companies to their portfolios, they exacerbate valuation problems, and the convergence of the two asset classes makes it more difficult to accurately assess the value of each.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Valuation Retailization, Regulation, and Investor Suitability (2009). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1428387
scope_conditions: where hedge funds hold private, non-traded portfolio companies

claims.claim: Because realization events for private equity investments occur infrequently, hedge fund managers have an incentive to avoid side pockets and to use estimated valuations for those investments instead.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Valuation Retailization, Regulation, and Investor Suitability (2009). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1428387
scope_conditions: where the hedge fund holds private equity style investments
where performance fees cannot be charged on side-pocketed assets

claims.claim: The hedge fund fee structure creates very strong financial incentives for managers to hide weak performance through valuation.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Valuation Retailization, Regulation, and Investor Suitability (2009). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1428387
scope_conditions: where fees run up to 30 percent of profits and one to three percent of assets under management
where high water marks apply

claims.claim: Because structured debt instruments and over-the-counter derivatives used by hedge funds can be highly complex, the hedge fund manager may be the only person competent to assess their value.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Valuation Retailization, Regulation, and Investor Suitability (2009). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1428387
scope_conditions: for highly complex structured debt and OTC derivatives

claims.claim: Because net asset value drives subscriptions, redemptions, performance calculations, advertising, and fees, managers who both manage and value the portfolio have both an incentive and the ability to inappropriately over-value their portfolios.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Valuation Retailization, Regulation, and Investor Suitability (2009). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1428387
scope_conditions: where the manager performs or controls valuation
where NAV is the basis for fees and performance figures

claims.claim: Independent administrators and valuation committees do not solve the independence problem for startup funds, because a majority of hedge funds in their startup phase try to keep overheads down and so may have independence problems precisely when independence is most crucial.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Valuation Retailization, Regulation, and Investor Suitability (2009). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1428387
scope_conditions: hedge funds in their startup phase

claims.claim: Outsourcing valuation to an independent administrator can be nominal rather than real: the administrator may lack the understanding of complex securities products needed to value the positions, so the manager remains in charge of valuation even though the function has formally been externalized.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Valuation Retailization, Regulation, and Investor Suitability (2009). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1428387
scope_conditions: where positions involve complex securities products
where the administrator is paid by the hedge fund manager

claims.claim: There is an adverse selection problem in independent valuation: an administrator who actually had the knowledge and understanding of complex instruments required for the task would probably be incentivized to use that expertise in a more profitable setting instead.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Valuation Retailization, Regulation, and Investor Suitability (2009). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1428387
scope_conditions: for administrators valuing highly complex instruments

claims.claim: Valuing thinly traded assets with exchange quotes is unsound because the price for less frequently traded assets may not indicate fair market value at the time of valuation, yet nearly a quarter of surveyed funds relied exclusively on such quotes.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Valuation Retailization, Regulation, and Investor Suitability (2009). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1428387
scope_conditions: thinly traded or infrequently traded assets

claims.claim: Because new hedge fund managers concentrate on highly complex and profitable instruments where pricing and valuation problems are most prevalent, it becomes very difficult for managers to guarantee investors standard or accurate pricing procedures.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Valuation Retailization, Regulation, and Investor Suitability (2009). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1428387
scope_conditions: for newly launched funds run by managers leaving large institutions

claims.claim: Post-1998 hedge fund regulatory proposals were misdirected because LTCM was unique among its peers in leverage, position size, and market-making ability, so the proposals mostly addressed LTCM as a single case rather than the range of issues affecting all hedge funds.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Valuation Retailization, Regulation, and Investor Suitability (2009). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1428387
scope_conditions: regulatory proposals issued in the aftermath of the LTCM near-collapse

claims.claim: The regulatory proposals that appeared soon after LTCM did not adequately take valuation problems into account.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Valuation Retailization, Regulation, and Investor Suitability (2009). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1428387
scope_conditions: regulatory proposals issued shortly after the LTCM collapse

claims.claim: Although regulators and legislatures in many jurisdictions recognize that hedge fund issues affect retail investors, they have so far not addressed valuation and its interplay with retail investors.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Valuation Retailization, Regulation, and Investor Suitability (2009). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1428387
scope_conditions: as of 2009, across the surveyed jurisdictions

claims.claim: State de minimis investment adviser registration exemptions can be an attractive alternative to federal law for hedge fund managers, especially in a fund's start-up phase, because state registration would require an ADV filing and significant transaction costs the manager wants to avoid.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Valuation Retailization, Regulation, and Investor Suitability (2009). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1428387
scope_conditions: start-up phase of a hedge fund
where investors reside in states with de minimis exemptions

claims.claim: State Blue Sky investment adviser registration exemptions are not by themselves sufficient to explain retailization or to justify the absence of data on it; they only indicate theoretically how previously unqualified investors could gain access to hedge funds.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Valuation Retailization, Regulation, and Investor Suitability (2009). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1428387
scope_conditions: as an explanatory account of the retailization phenomenon

claims.claim: The Commodity Exchange Act family and friends exemption allows a qualifying manager to trade options and futures for fifteen individuals who need not be sophisticated or qualified investors, which circumvents accredited investor standards and admits retail investors into hedge funds.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Valuation Retailization, Regulation, and Investor Suitability (2009). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1428387
scope_conditions: where the fund manager qualifies for the families and friends CTA registration exemption

claims.claim: The principal-agent problem in complex financial products is exacerbated by hierarchies in financial institutions, which create multiple layers of agency relationships between the traders using the products and the principals bearing the real economic risk.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Valuation Retailization, Regulation, and Investor Suitability (2009). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1428387
scope_conditions: in banks and large institutions trading complex financial products

claims.claim: Moral hazard is worsened when the financial products traded are so complex that the agents, mostly on the buy side, do not entirely understand them and trade for the principal on the basis of incomplete and asymmetric information.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Valuation Retailization, Regulation, and Investor Suitability (2009). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1428387
scope_conditions: where instruments are highly complex
buy side agents in particular

claims.claim: Because rating agencies are paid by CDO issuers while the ratings' main users are buyers, the agency as agent has an incentive to issue high ratings to satisfy its issuer principal, and the buyer has no means of controlling the agency other than through its relationship with the issuer.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Valuation Retailization, Regulation, and Investor Suitability (2009). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1428387
scope_conditions: under the issuer-pays model for structured finance ratings

claims.claim: The issuer-buyer relationship and the incentives inside it are unlikely to be able to adequately control the principal-agent relationship between issuer and rating agency so as to ensure accurate ratings.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Valuation Retailization, Regulation, and Investor Suitability (2009). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1428387
scope_conditions: under the issuer-pays rating model for CDOs

claims.claim: Qualified investors have strong incentives to accept valuation problems rather than contest them, because contesting would jeopardize their relationships with management and other industry participants and damage their own reputations.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Valuation Retailization, Regulation, and Investor Suitability (2009). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1428387
scope_conditions: qualified investors with industry relationships and reputational stakes

claims.claim: Because industry practices and informal rules already protect their relationships and investments, qualified investors may neither desire nor require extended investor protection rules to optimize hedge fund valuation.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Valuation Retailization, Regulation, and Investor Suitability (2009). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1428387
scope_conditions: qualified investors embedded in industry networks

claims.claim: Retail investors are more likely to benefit from investor protection rules that optimize hedge fund valuation, because their minority position in the industry, the absence of informal rules, and management's lack of incentive to protect them leave them unprotected.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Valuation Retailization, Regulation, and Investor Suitability (2009). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1428387
scope_conditions: retail investors in hedge funds and hedge fund like vehicles

claims.claim: Investor suitability standards are the author's preferred regulatory option because they would probably protect retail investors' interests without unduly burdening the hedge fund industry and other market participants.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Valuation Retailization, Regulation, and Investor Suitability (2009). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1428387
scope_conditions: compared against limiting complex products, raising qualification thresholds, mandating disclosure, and retail-level triggers

claims.claim: Limiting the use of hard-to-value assets and complex financial products is very unlikely to have positive effects, because the implicit inhibition of financial innovation would probably limit investors' use of hedging products and interfere with economic expansion.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Valuation Retailization, Regulation, and Investor Suitability (2009). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1428387
scope_conditions: where regulators respond to systemic risk by restricting instrument use

claims.claim: Unless an investor's business is primarily to invest in hard-to-value assets, that investor's sophistication cannot be assumed regardless of personal wealth.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Valuation Retailization, Regulation, and Investor Suitability (2009). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1428387
scope_conditions: for investments in hard-to-value assets and complex financial instruments

claims.claim: Raising the Regulation D numerical tests by adding an investable assets requirement would probably not address how to remedy investors' lack of understanding of hard-to-value assets.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Valuation Retailization, Regulation, and Investor Suitability (2009). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1428387
scope_conditions: under the SEC proposal to add a 2.5 million dollar investments requirement

claims.claim: More disclosure does not always mean better governance, because the information provided may be hard to assess and evaluate.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Valuation Retailization, Regulation, and Investor Suitability (2009). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1428387
scope_conditions: where disclosed valuation and risk data is complex

claims.claim: Mandatory risk disclosure to the SEC would probably fail on staffing grounds, because professionals capable of understanding hedge fund risk data would be disincentivized to use that knowledge for supervision rather than economic gain, finding the private sector far more lucrative.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Valuation Retailization, Regulation, and Investor Suitability (2009). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1428387
scope_conditions: where the regulator must interpret data on hard-to-value assets and complex instruments

claims.claim: Requiring hedge funds to supply risk and valuation data in a simplified format would in fact impose a significant burden on the industry, since simplification requirements would raise transaction costs, require pre-screening, and possibly additional staff.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Valuation Retailization, Regulation, and Investor Suitability (2009). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1428387
scope_conditions: where the SEC prescribes a simplified reporting format

claims.claim: Limiting complex financial instruments in the portfolios of hedge funds open to retail investors, triggered once retail commitments exceed a set level of assets under management, would likely protect retail investors while limiting undue burdens on the industry.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Valuation Retailization, Regulation, and Investor Suitability (2009). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1428387
scope_conditions: where retail commitments exceed a threshold such as 20 percent of assets under management

claims.claim: A retail investor asset threshold would be gamed: managers would be incentivized to keep retail assets under the applicable threshold, thereby keeping the fund in the existing regulatory scheme without implementing additional retail investor protection.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Valuation Retailization, Regulation, and Investor Suitability (2009). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1428387
scope_conditions: where regulation is triggered by a retail asset threshold

claims.claim: Regulation targeted only at retail investors is misdirected, because incomplete and asymmetric information, bounded rationality, and moral hazard make it difficult even for professional and semi professional investors to discern the characteristics of highly complex instruments and hard-to-value assets.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Valuation Retailization, Regulation, and Investor Suitability (2009). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1428387
scope_conditions: for highly complex financial instruments and hard-to-value assets

claims.claim: Recent SEC proposals to toughen the numerical wealth requirements for hedge fund investing fail, because they do not ascertain the appropriate level of sophistication or adequate understanding of highly complex financial instruments.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Valuation Retailization, Regulation, and Investor Suitability (2009). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1428387
scope_conditions: SEC proposals to amend Regulation D wealth thresholds

claims.claim: Investor suitability standards would address the sophistication problem by requiring independent verification that investors in highly complex financial products can evaluate investment risk independently and are capable of making independent investment decisions.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Valuation Retailization, Regulation, and Investor Suitability (2009). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1428387
scope_conditions: for investments in highly complex financial products

claims.claim: Regulating on the basis of retailization would not currently be justifiable, because retailization cannot be quantified with any degree of certainty and regulation premised on speculation without proof or data validation would probably produce inadequate results.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Valuation Retailization, Regulation, and Investor Suitability (2009). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1428387
scope_conditions: as of 2009, absent data quantifying retail participation in hedge funds

claims.claim: In securities regulation the SEC has continuously expanded its extraterritorial reach, and it has done so with strong support from the judiciary, most notably the Second Circuit Court of Appeals.
claims.citation: Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Extraterritorial Application of US Securities Law – Will the US Become the Default Jurisdiction for (2010). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1664809

claims.claim: Congress intended the federal securities laws to cover only purchases and sales of securities that occur within the United States, a conclusion the authors reached with twenty-one law professors after reviewing the legislative history.
claims.citation: Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Extraterritorial Application of US Securities Law – Will the US Become the Default Jurisdiction for (2010). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1664809
scope_conditions: reading of the 1933 Act and 1934 Act legislative history

claims.claim: The Second Circuit's conduct and effect test was too unpredictable, and a clear rule keyed to the location of the securities transaction would be more predictable for issuers and investors.
claims.citation: Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Extraterritorial Application of US Securities Law – Will the US Become the Default Jurisdiction for (2010). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1664809
scope_conditions: cases where the location of conduct and the location of the transaction diverge

claims.claim: Allowing foreign plaintiffs to sue foreign defendants in US courts over securities purchased and sold in foreign countries would turn the United States into the global arbiter of securities fraud allegations.
claims.citation: Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Extraterritorial Application of US Securities Law – Will the US Become the Default Jurisdiction for (2010). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1664809
scope_conditions: foreign cubed litigation permitted in US courts

claims.claim: Because many countries choose to combat securities fraud through government enforcement rather than private litigation, the United States should respect the right of other countries to regulate their own markets.
claims.citation: Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Extraterritorial Application of US Securities Law – Will the US Become the Default Jurisdiction for (2010). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1664809
scope_conditions: countries that rely on public enforcement rather than private class actions

claims.claim: Regardless of how the Supreme Court rules in Morrison v. NAB, Congress could overrule the holding, because the question presented is one of statutory construction and Congress may amend a statute whose interpretation it dislikes.
claims.citation: Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Extraterritorial Application of US Securities Law – Will the US Become the Default Jurisdiction for (2010). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1664809
scope_conditions: holdings that rest on statutory interpretation rather than constitutional grounds

claims.claim: The Lehman Repo 105 transactions, consummated in London but booked as sales in Lehman's US securities filings, underscore the effect that conduct in one country can have on markets elsewhere.
claims.citation: Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Extraterritorial Application of US Securities Law – Will the US Become the Default Jurisdiction for (2010). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1664809
scope_conditions: cross-border transactions structured to exploit differences in national law

claims.claim: Section 7216 of the Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act of 2009 would extend federal antifraud jurisdiction to conduct within the United States constituting significant steps in furtherance of a violation, even when the securities transaction occurs abroad and involves only foreign investors.
claims.citation: Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Extraterritorial Application of US Securities Law – Will the US Become the Default Jurisdiction for (2010). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1664809
scope_conditions: if section 7216 is enacted in the form introduced

claims.claim: The significant steps standard of section 7216 is probably broader than the Second Circuit's conduct and effect test, and the proposed statutory language would therefore reach a wider range of defendants.
claims.citation: Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Extraterritorial Application of US Securities Law – Will the US Become the Default Jurisdiction for (2010). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1664809
scope_conditions: comparison of section 7216 language with existing Second Circuit doctrine

claims.claim: If section 7216 is enacted and covers section 10(b), the United States could become a magnet for global class actions, and US lawyers would benefit from securities litigation tourism much as UK lawyers have benefited from libel tourism.
claims.citation: Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Extraterritorial Application of US Securities Law – Will the US Become the Default Jurisdiction for (2010). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1664809
scope_conditions: enactment of section 7216 including section 10(b) of the 1934 Act

claims.claim: Foreign cubed cases in US courts rose over the decade preceding 2010, and in 2008 the number of such cases exceeded any previous year.
claims.citation: Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Extraterritorial Application of US Securities Law – Will the US Become the Default Jurisdiction for (2010). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1664809
scope_conditions: US federal securities class action filings through 2009

claims.claim: The lack of securities class actions in European jurisdictions creates a void that increases the incentives for forum shopping by plaintiffs' lawyers.
claims.citation: Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Extraterritorial Application of US Securities Law – Will the US Become the Default Jurisdiction for (2010). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1664809
scope_conditions: European jurisdictions that do not offer securities class actions

claims.claim: If section 7216 becomes law and permits extraterritorial application of US antifraud provisions, it would further incentivize forum shopping by plaintiffs' attorneys.
claims.citation: Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Extraterritorial Application of US Securities Law – Will the US Become the Default Jurisdiction for (2010). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1664809
scope_conditions: enactment of section 7216

claims.claim: Over time, extraterritorial US securities litigation may drive European jurisdictions to adopt portions of US law in order to discourage forum shopping, a form of legal assimilation.
claims.citation: Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Extraterritorial Application of US Securities Law – Will the US Become the Default Jurisdiction for (2010). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1664809
scope_conditions: sustained forum shopping pressure on European jurisdictions

claims.claim: Assimilation of US legal rules into European regulatory approaches may itself increase transaction costs for the jurisdiction that changes its law.
claims.citation: Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Extraterritorial Application of US Securities Law – Will the US Become the Default Jurisdiction for (2010). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1664809
scope_conditions: jurisdictions that alter their law in response to US extraterritorial reach

claims.claim: For European jurisdictions the extraterritorial application of US law creates confusion and legal uncertainty and makes it harder to regulate private parties who engage in regulatory arbitrage by taking their litigation to the United States when convenient.
claims.citation: Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Extraterritorial Application of US Securities Law – Will the US Become the Default Jurisdiction for (2010). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1664809
scope_conditions: European jurisdictions whose parties can access US courts

claims.claim: In US securities class actions plaintiffs may proceed on the fraud on the market theory rather than proving actual reliance on misleading statements, an approach that has been rejected in most other countries.
claims.citation: Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Extraterritorial Application of US Securities Law – Will the US Become the Default Jurisdiction for (2010). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1664809
scope_conditions: US securities class actions under section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5

claims.claim: Applying section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5 together with the fraud on the market theory substantially increases the potential liability of issuers and can lead to questionable results, which is why EU jurisdictions may not want that rule applied to their securities markets.
claims.citation: Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Extraterritorial Application of US Securities Law – Will the US Become the Default Jurisdiction for (2010). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1664809
scope_conditions: securities markets subjected to US antifraud litigation

claims.claim: Under section 7216 US law could apply to EU companies accused of conduct violating US securities laws even if those companies have no securities traded in the United States.
claims.citation: Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Extraterritorial Application of US Securities Law – Will the US Become the Default Jurisdiction for (2010). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1664809
scope_conditions: enactment of section 7216

claims.claim: Section 7216 could have the opposite effect of forcefully exporting US law onto other jurisdictions including Europe, even though it would be preferable for other nations to decide for themselves whether to have a class action litigation system.
claims.citation: Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Extraterritorial Application of US Securities Law – Will the US Become the Default Jurisdiction for (2010). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1664809
scope_conditions: countries that have deliberately declined to adopt class action litigation

claims.claim: A European company retains some ability to avoid the Sarbanes-Oxley Act by declining to list its securities in the United States, an escape route that expansive extraterritorial securities litigation would close.
claims.citation: Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Extraterritorial Application of US Securities Law – Will the US Become the Default Jurisdiction for (2010). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1664809
scope_conditions: companies not listed on a US exchange

claims.claim: Overlapping regulation and inconsistent legal rules create uncertainty, so that individual board members of European companies and their attorneys will not know which legal rules apply or what effects those rules may have.
claims.citation: Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Extraterritorial Application of US Securities Law – Will the US Become the Default Jurisdiction for (2010). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1664809
scope_conditions: companies exposed to more than one regulatory regime

claims.claim: Legal uncertainty generates transaction costs, and European company boards will inevitably incur costs minimizing the information asymmetries created by different legal regimes that may or may not apply to their company.
claims.citation: Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Extraterritorial Application of US Securities Law – Will the US Become the Default Jurisdiction for (2010). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1664809
scope_conditions: firms facing more than one potentially applicable legal regime

claims.claim: Relative to the total number of US securities fraud and securities class action cases, foreign cubed cases are still relatively rare, although there was a substantial increase in them in 2008.
claims.citation: Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Extraterritorial Application of US Securities Law – Will the US Become the Default Jurisdiction for (2010). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1664809
scope_conditions: US securities litigation as of 2010

claims.claim: Enactment of section 7216 could make foreign cubed cases an integral part of the legal landscape in the United States and hence in Europe, ending the current situation in which most European companies are unaware of or unconcerned with that risk.
claims.citation: Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Extraterritorial Application of US Securities Law – Will the US Become the Default Jurisdiction for (2010). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1664809
scope_conditions: enactment of section 7216

claims.claim: Banks, brokers and other financial intermediaries figure in a large proportion of US securities fraud cases because they often have the deep pockets that plaintiffs' lawyers are looking for.
claims.citation: Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Extraterritorial Application of US Securities Law – Will the US Become the Default Jurisdiction for (2010). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1664809
scope_conditions: US securities fraud litigation driven by private plaintiffs

claims.claim: If section 7216 extends US securities fraud provisions to non-US securities transactions, European financial intermediaries could become the dominant target for plaintiffs' attorneys.
claims.citation: Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Extraterritorial Application of US Securities Law – Will the US Become the Default Jurisdiction for (2010). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1664809
scope_conditions: enactment of section 7216 covering non-US transactions

claims.claim: Non-US individuals and companies are expressly prohibited by US law from contributing to US political campaigns and have a relatively weak lobby in Washington, which places EU financial intermediaries at a competitive disadvantage in the US political system.
claims.citation: Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Extraterritorial Application of US Securities Law – Will the US Become the Default Jurisdiction for (2010). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1664809
scope_conditions: US legislative processes influenced by campaign contributions

claims.claim: The defendants harmed by section 7216 would almost all be non-US financial intermediaries and issuers who are less able to defend themselves in the US political system, which helps explain why Congress is not seriously considering repeal of the PSLRA but is seriously considering section 7216.
claims.citation: Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Extraterritorial Application of US Securities Law – Will the US Become the Default Jurisdiction for (2010). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1664809
scope_conditions: US legislative politics after the 2008 financial crisis

claims.claim: If section 7216 is enacted, European plaintiffs and defendants will likely turn to the expertise of American law firms, which would further exacerbate the already difficult competitive situation of European law firms.
claims.citation: Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Extraterritorial Application of US Securities Law – Will the US Become the Default Jurisdiction for (2010). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1664809
scope_conditions: enactment of section 7216

claims.claim: Regardless of the relative merits of securities regulation in the United States and Europe, European investors are most likely to benefit if Europe addresses the problem of investor protection itself rather than through US courts.
claims.citation: Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Extraterritorial Application of US Securities Law – Will the US Become the Default Jurisdiction for (2010). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1664809
scope_conditions: choice between European reform and access to US litigation

claims.claim: If Congress enacts section 7216, EU investors will on the whole probably earn a lower return on their investments than they otherwise would, because the substantial costs the US litigation system imposes on EU companies will be passed on to investors.
claims.citation: Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Extraterritorial Application of US Securities Law – Will the US Become the Default Jurisdiction for (2010). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1664809
scope_conditions: enactment of section 7216
costs of US litigation borne by EU issuers

claims.claim: Overlapping regulation must be distinguished from conflicting regulation: only conflicting regulation could violate international law, because the territorial integrity of a state is breached only where there is a specific true conflict in the substantive legal norms of the respective states.
claims.citation: Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Extraterritorial Application of US Securities Law – Will the US Become the Default Jurisdiction for (2010). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1664809
scope_conditions: analysis of extraterritorial jurisdiction under public international law

claims.claim: If US law requires disclosure of information that another country's law prohibits from being disclosed, whether for privacy or other reasons, there could be a true conflict of law and a credible case that the United States is in breach of international law.
claims.citation: Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Extraterritorial Application of US Securities Law – Will the US Become the Default Jurisdiction for (2010). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1664809
scope_conditions: a genuine incompatibility between US disclosure duties and foreign prohibitions

claims.claim: Section 7216 could be one more impediment to good diplomatic relations if the United States is perceived as establishing its courts as international courts in securities matters with universal jurisdiction.
claims.citation: Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Extraterritorial Application of US Securities Law – Will the US Become the Default Jurisdiction for (2010). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1664809
scope_conditions: perception by European governments of US judicial overreach

claims.claim: Exporting and imposing rules through extraterritorial reach could be counterproductive not only for US diplomacy but also for international cooperation in combating securities fraud, whereas cooperative mutual adjustment between the US and the EU is the better course.
claims.citation: Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Extraterritorial Application of US Securities Law – Will the US Become the Default Jurisdiction for (2010). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1664809
scope_conditions: cross-border securities fraud enforcement

claims.claim: If national securities regulators are unable or unwilling to cooperate with each other, there is likely to be more securities fraud.
claims.citation: Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Extraterritorial Application of US Securities Law – Will the US Become the Default Jurisdiction for (2010). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1664809
scope_conditions: cross-border securities markets with multiple national regulators

claims.claim: European boards of directors and company lawyers should follow the Morrison decision and the section 7216 legislative process closely, prepare for the resulting changes, and ask Congress to reconsider section 7216.
claims.citation: Richard W. Painter, Wulf A. Kaal, Extraterritorial Application of US Securities Law – Will the US Become the Default Jurisdiction for (2010). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1664809
scope_conditions: pending outcome of Morrison v. NAB and of section 7216

claims.claim: German banks' exposure to CDO risk ran through credit enhancement and liquidity guarantees given to off balance sheet conduits, and because that exposure was often kept out of their accounting the inherent risk only surfaced once the CDO market collapsed.
claims.citation: Painter and Kaal, Initial Reflections on an Evolving Standard Constraints on Risk Taking by Directors and Officers in (2010). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1558614
scope_conditions: banks guaranteeing conduits located outside German banking supervision
guarantee exposure not consolidated into bank accounts

claims.claim: The German ABCP conduit model, which financed long term American mortgage loans with short term paper and pocketed the spread, was profitable only for as long as new buyers for the short term paper could be found, so the model collapsed the moment institutional buyers withdrew.
claims.citation: Painter and Kaal, Initial Reflections on an Evolving Standard Constraints on Risk Taking by Directors and Officers in (2010). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1558614
scope_conditions: long term assets funded by short term asset backed commercial paper
sponsor bank provides credit enhancement and liquidity to the conduit

claims.claim: Contesting the view that the 2008 crisis was an American problem inflicted on foreign victims, the authors argue that non U.S. institutions such as German banks were willing participants in the risk taking, even where they did not fully understand the risks they assumed.
claims.citation: Painter and Kaal, Initial Reflections on an Evolving Standard Constraints on Risk Taking by Directors and Officers in (2010). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1558614
scope_conditions: applies to European banks that bought or sponsored U.S. structured credit products

claims.claim: Beliefs about whether markets fail are causally consequential rather than merely academic: bankers who believe markets fail invest more cautiously, and regulators who believe markets fail regulate more aggressively.
claims.citation: Painter and Kaal, Initial Reflections on an Evolving Standard Constraints on Risk Taking by Directors and Officers in (2010). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1558614
scope_conditions: holds across both national settings the authors compare

claims.claim: Law generally declines to adopt a general principle barring managers from incurring risk above a defined standard because such a standard is hard to define; corporate law instead insulates managers' risk decisions through the business judgment rule.
claims.citation: Painter and Kaal, Initial Reflections on an Evolving Standard Constraints on Risk Taking by Directors and Officers in (2010). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1558614
scope_conditions: outside the scope of rules that constrain specific named types of risk

claims.claim: Although the business judgment rule is articulated differently in the two countries and German law leaves somewhat more room to challenge risky decisions, in both the United States and Germany the rule is highly protective of corporate managers.
claims.citation: Painter and Kaal, Initial Reflections on an Evolving Standard Constraints on Risk Taking by Directors and Officers in (2010). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1558614

claims.claim: The business judgment rule can be read not as a balanced middle ground but as excessively deferential to management, signaling that corporate law is ceding risk regulation to targeted rules aimed at particular risks in particular institutions.
claims.citation: Painter and Kaal, Initial Reflections on an Evolving Standard Constraints on Risk Taking by Directors and Officers in (2010). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1558614
scope_conditions: offered as an alternative reading to the middle ground account of the rule

claims.claim: Because German banks absorbed both the 2008 credit crisis and the 2010 sovereign debt crisis while American banks faced only the first, German regulators and bankers are likely to impose stricter substantive risk management rules than countries that faced only one of those shocks.
claims.citation: Painter and Kaal, Initial Reflections on an Evolving Standard Constraints on Risk Taking by Directors and Officers in (2010). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1558614
scope_conditions: written before the sovereign debt crisis had fully played out
assumes the two shocks compound rather than offset

claims.claim: The cost of tightening directors' duty to monitor risk depends not just on how far the requirement is tightened but on how it is tightened: the mix of agency enforcement versus civil litigation, and of substantive versus procedural change, drives the shape of the cost curve.
claims.citation: Painter and Kaal, Initial Reflections on an Evolving Standard Constraints on Risk Taking by Directors and Officers in (2010). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1558614
scope_conditions: illustrative model, not based on actual data

claims.claim: The same combination of substantive and procedural rules imposes different monitoring costs in different cultural settings, so a rule package that is cheap in one country can be expensive in another.
claims.citation: Painter and Kaal, Initial Reflections on an Evolving Standard Constraints on Risk Taking by Directors and Officers in (2010). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1558614
scope_conditions: illustrative cost model rather than measured data

claims.claim: A country whose bankers do not embrace intentional risk taking is still exposed to risk, both through the collateral effects of intentional risk taking abroad and through unintentional risk taking at home, so domestic cultural restraint is not a sufficient safeguard.
claims.citation: Painter and Kaal, Initial Reflections on an Evolving Standard Constraints on Risk Taking by Directors and Officers in (2010). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1558614
scope_conditions: open financial systems with cross border bank activity

claims.claim: Hindsight bias exerts a stronger influence on how excessive risk is defined in countries culturally predisposed to dwell on their own past, while countries oriented toward a future unlike the past more easily dismiss earlier financial lessons as irrelevant.
claims.citation: Painter and Kaal, Initial Reflections on an Evolving Standard Constraints on Risk Taking by Directors and Officers in (2010). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1558614
scope_conditions: applies to the ex post characterization of risk as excessive

claims.claim: Limited liability lets managers and shareholders capture most of the benefits of excessive risk taking while not bearing all of its costs, which is one explanation for why bankers take excessive risk.
claims.citation: Painter and Kaal, Initial Reflections on an Evolving Standard Constraints on Risk Taking by Directors and Officers in (2010). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1558614
scope_conditions: corporation protected by limited liability
corporation may lack assets sufficient to pay creditors

claims.claim: The U.S. governance structure, built on periodic disclosure of performance data and stock price maximization, encourages risk taking because managers feel compelled to meet shareholder expectations at every reporting interval.
claims.citation: Painter and Kaal, Initial Reflections on an Evolving Standard Constraints on Risk Taking by Directors and Officers in (2010). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1558614
scope_conditions: governance systems that emphasize periodic performance disclosure and stock price

claims.claim: German corporate law's historical focus on conflicts between controlling and minority shareholders leaves it poorly equipped to address managerial abuse of power, including excessive risk taking by managers.
claims.citation: Painter and Kaal, Initial Reflections on an Evolving Standard Constraints on Risk Taking by Directors and Officers in (2010). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1558614
scope_conditions: systems where ownership is concentrated and the central conflict is shareholder against shareholder

claims.claim: U.S. corporate law centers so heavily on shareholder manager conflicts of interest that, absent a demonstrable conflict, it treats risk taking as a situation where managers' and shareholders' interests are aligned and legal intervention is unwarranted.
claims.citation: Painter and Kaal, Initial Reflections on an Evolving Standard Constraints on Risk Taking by Directors and Officers in (2010). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1558614
scope_conditions: no demonstrable conflict of interest is shown

claims.claim: For different structural reasons in each country, corporate law in both Germany and the United States has little to say about the problem of excessive risk.
claims.citation: Painter and Kaal, Initial Reflections on an Evolving Standard Constraints on Risk Taking by Directors and Officers in (2010). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1558614

claims.claim: Codetermination makes the German supervisory board's decision making more cumbersome, so a co determined Aufsichtsrat may not respond quickly enough to fast moving events such as an escalation of portfolio risk or a liquidity crisis.
claims.citation: Painter and Kaal, Initial Reflections on an Evolving Standard Constraints on Risk Taking by Directors and Officers in (2010). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1558614
scope_conditions: corporations large enough to trigger employee representation on the supervisory board
employee representatives may also carry union political objectives

claims.claim: Because the Aufsichtsrat owes its duty of loyalty to the firm rather than to shareholders alone, and because non shareholder constituencies such as employees and creditors are more risk averse than diversified shareholders, German supervisory boards may take a more conservative attitude toward risk than U.S. shareholder oriented boards.
claims.citation: Painter and Kaal, Initial Reflections on an Evolving Standard Constraints on Risk Taking by Directors and Officers in (2010). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1558614
scope_conditions: German courts treat the duty as protecting the interests of the firm, not only shareholders
reinforced by codetermination

claims.claim: Director independence does not produce effective risk monitoring: as the failure of independent director oversight at Lehman Brothers and other large U.S. financial firms shows, independent directors cannot monitor risk when managers, accountants and lawyers keep them in the dark.
claims.citation: Painter and Kaal, Initial Reflections on an Evolving Standard Constraints on Risk Taking by Directors and Officers in (2010). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1558614
scope_conditions: U.S. style independence defined by lack of financial ties to the company
information flow to the board controlled by insiders

claims.claim: Because U.S. companies historically financed themselves through markets rather than through each other, U.S. managers are less attuned to risks accumulating at other firms, a blind spot that mattered once swaps and other complex instruments made firms directly vulnerable to each other's conditions.
claims.citation: Painter and Kaal, Initial Reflections on an Evolving Standard Constraints on Risk Taking by Directors and Officers in (2010). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1558614
scope_conditions: applies once counterparty exposure through swaps and complex instruments becomes significant

claims.claim: The German and U.S. business judgment rules diverge most sharply at the German rule's fifth element, the requirement of no hazard decision or excessive risk taking, which German law presumes but allows to be rebutted.
claims.citation: Painter and Kaal, Initial Reflections on an Evolving Standard Constraints on Risk Taking by Directors and Officers in (2010). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1558614
scope_conditions: German rule is code based in the Aktiengesetz; the U.S. rule is case law of the state of incorporation

claims.claim: Because U.S. law frames the inquiry around corporate waste, and most risk taking does not meet the waste standard, showing that a decision was hazardous or excessively risky is not enough to rebut the business judgment rule in the United States.
claims.citation: Painter and Kaal, Initial Reflections on an Evolving Standard Constraints on Risk Taking by Directors and Officers in (2010). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1558614
scope_conditions: U.S. courts presume absence of corporate waste and ask only whether that presumption is rebutted

claims.claim: Under the German business judgment rule's benefit of the corporation element, management cannot be acting for the corporation's benefit when its actions threaten the corporation's existence and economic survival.
claims.citation: Painter and Kaal, Initial Reflections on an Evolving Standard Constraints on Risk Taking by Directors and Officers in (2010). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1558614
scope_conditions: German business judgment rule, second element

claims.claim: The U.S. requirement that directors act on an informed basis is watered down because many states permit charter provisions exculpating directors from liability for breach of the duty of care, including the duty to act on an informed basis.
claims.citation: Painter and Kaal, Initial Reflections on an Evolving Standard Constraints on Risk Taking by Directors and Officers in (2010). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1558614
scope_conditions: states with exculpation statutes such as Delaware, Illinois and New Jersey

claims.claim: Under the German hazard decision doctrine, no manager acts reasonably, whether a bank officer or a board member, if the risks taken on the corporation's behalf would destroy the corporation should they be realized.
claims.citation: Painter and Kaal, Initial Reflections on an Evolving Standard Constraints on Risk Taking by Directors and Officers in (2010). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1558614
scope_conditions: German business judgment rule as elaborated in the ARAG decision of the Bundesgerichtshof
risk must be such that its realization ends the corporation

claims.claim: In In re Citigroup the Delaware Court of Chancery refused to extend the Caremark oversight duty, which concerns monitoring for illegal conduct, into oversight liability for business risk, so an inability to predict the future and an incorrect evaluation of business risk are not breaches of a director's oversight responsibilities.
claims.citation: Painter and Kaal, Initial Reflections on an Evolving Standard Constraints on Risk Taking by Directors and Officers in (2010). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1558614
scope_conditions: Delaware law; derivative claims premised on subprime exposure
oversight liability requires showing the directors knew they were not discharging their duties or consciously disregarded them

claims.claim: The EU's Market Abuse, Transparency, Markets in Financial Instruments and Prospectus Directives improved European securities regulation but still do not mandate coherent and comprehensive disclosure, leaving issuers free to disclose in disparate ways.
claims.citation: Painter and Kaal, Initial Reflections on an Evolving Standard Constraints on Risk Taking by Directors and Officers in (2010). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1558614
scope_conditions: European Union as of 2010, with no central securities agency and no centralized filing system
