claims.claim: Routine engagement in highly complex transactions lets public companies conceal risky transactions from investors and even from their own directors, which is a structural weakness in the supposedly rigorous U.S. disclosure regime.
claims.citation: Painter and Kaal, Initial Reflections on an Evolving Standard Constraints on Risk Taking by Directors and Officers in (2010). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1558614
scope_conditions: companies whose ordinary business consists of highly complex transactions

claims.claim: The more a country leads in financial innovation, the more exposed its disclosure regime is to misrepresentation and fraud, which makes the U.S. regime more vulnerable than Germany's despite being formally stricter.
claims.citation: Painter and Kaal, Initial Reflections on an Evolving Standard Constraints on Risk Taking by Directors and Officers in (2010). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1558614
scope_conditions: assumes U.S. financial innovation runs ahead of German financial innovation

claims.claim: The United States compensates for its lenient corporate law treatment of risk taking under the business judgment rule with a comparatively strict disclosure regime and a robust securities class action litigation regime; substantive corporate law pushes the monitoring requirement toward leniency while securities enforcement pushes it back toward stringency.
claims.citation: Painter and Kaal, Initial Reflections on an Evolving Standard Constraints on Risk Taking by Directors and Officers in (2010). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1558614

claims.claim: In the United States the duty to disclose risk indirectly generates risk monitoring, because directors who know they are responsible for disclosing risk have reason to monitor it even though corporate law imposes no explicit duty to monitor.
claims.citation: Painter and Kaal, Initial Reflections on an Evolving Standard Constraints on Risk Taking by Directors and Officers in (2010). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1558614
scope_conditions: risk must be of a kind that securities law requires to be disclosed

claims.claim: U.S. courts applying the business judgment rule give little or no weight to the overall health of the company or to whether the risk jeopardizes the company's very existence, so managers are permitted to incur most of the risks they wish to incur.
claims.citation: Painter and Kaal, Initial Reflections on an Evolving Standard Constraints on Risk Taking by Directors and Officers in (2010). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1558614

claims.claim: The U.S. approach left both of its risk controls ineffective: the securities disclosure regime failed to prevent the 2008 financial crisis, while the expansive business judgment rule that permitted the risk taking in the first place survived the crisis unchanged.
claims.citation: Painter and Kaal, Initial Reflections on an Evolving Standard Constraints on Risk Taking by Directors and Officers in (2010). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1558614

claims.claim: Germany's 2005 introduction of the derivative suit tightened the standard of care only partially, because section 148(1) of the AktG conditions shareholder standing on holding shares worth roughly 100,000 euros, a threshold with no U.S. counterpart.
claims.citation: Painter and Kaal, Initial Reflections on an Evolving Standard Constraints on Risk Taking by Directors and Officers in (2010). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1558614
scope_conditions: German derivative suits under section 148(1) AktG as amended by the UMAG
partly counterbalanced by VorstAG liability and compensation reduction provisions

claims.claim: The German legislature enacted the VorstAG on the premise that managers who emphasize short term parameters lose sight of the corporation's long term benefit and are thereby incentivized to take irresponsible risks, and it accordingly required compensation reduction in a corporate crisis, a D&O deductible, and deferred payout of performance based pay.
claims.citation: Painter and Kaal, Initial Reflections on an Evolving Standard Constraints on Risk Taking by Directors and Officers in (2010). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1558614
scope_conditions: German stock corporations subject to the VorstAG of August 2009

claims.claim: The Dodd-Frank Act is notable for what it omits: it does not break up the largest banks, does little to help smaller and regional banks compete, and because compliance is burdensome and expensive may actually have raised the barrier to entry into financial services.
claims.citation: Painter and Kaal, Initial Reflections on an Evolving Standard Constraints on Risk Taking by Directors and Officers in (2010). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1558614

claims.claim: Dodd-Frank's mandatory risk committee is a significant change because most boards then delegated risk oversight to the audit committee, and it may generate new litigation if committee composition or alleged committee failure becomes a basis for shareholder suits.
claims.citation: Painter and Kaal, Initial Reflections on an Evolving Standard Constraints on Risk Taking by Directors and Officers in (2010). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1558614
scope_conditions: publicly traded non bank financial companies supervised by the Federal Reserve and bank holding companies with more than $10 billion in assets

claims.claim: Delaware courts have not explicitly imposed a duty to monitor risk, but that omission may be moot: because failing to disclose risk violates federal securities law, unmonitored risk is likely to become undisclosed risk and therefore actionable.
claims.citation: Painter and Kaal, Initial Reflections on an Evolving Standard Constraints on Risk Taking by Directors and Officers in (2010). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1558614
scope_conditions: risk of a kind that federal securities law requires to be disclosed

claims.claim: Because of the political climate and concern about the social externalities of business failure, monitoring requirements and their enforcement procedures are likely to become more severe regardless of whether the increased monitoring costs are offset by fewer bad business decisions.
claims.citation: Painter and Kaal, Initial Reflections on an Evolving Standard Constraints on Risk Taking by Directors and Officers in (2010). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1558614
scope_conditions: post crisis political climate in both Germany and the United States
the company's own cost perspective may not govern

claims.claim: Contingent capital is defined as the predefined conversion of a financial institution's debt securities into equity securities upon a triggering event, and this stipulated definition governs the whole analysis.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Christoph Henkel, Contingent Capital with Sequential Triggers (2011). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1908473

claims.claim: Contrary to proposals that would replace Chapter 11 with contingent capital, the authors argue Chapter 11 needs no replacement; contingent capital should instead stabilize large financial firms for which Chapter 11 reorganization is not ideal or not legally available.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Christoph Henkel, Contingent Capital with Sequential Triggers (2011). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1908473
scope_conditions: Applies to banks and other financial institutions ineligible for or poorly served by Chapter 11
Particularly relevant from the European perspective

claims.claim: If conversion of contingent capital securities is triggered too early, before a real financial need for an equity injection exists, the expected financial impact of that injection may dissipate.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Christoph Henkel, Contingent Capital with Sequential Triggers (2011). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1908473
scope_conditions: Trigger fires absent genuine need for equity capital and additional voting shareholders

claims.claim: If conversion from debt to equity is triggered too late, the institution may already be in the resolution stage, and conversion at that point may not supply enough equity to produce the intended financial improvement.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Christoph Henkel, Contingent Capital with Sequential Triggers (2011). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1908473
scope_conditions: Institution has already entered the resolution stage when conversion occurs

claims.claim: Because policymakers may adopt a suboptimal single trigger design, and because contingent capital has uses at several points in a firm's life cycle, contingent capital securities should be built with sequential triggers rather than one.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Christoph Henkel, Contingent Capital with Sequential Triggers (2011). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1908473
scope_conditions: Assumes mandatory issuance of contingent capital securities

claims.claim: The second trigger, which increases voting rights before resolution, should fire on evidence that conversion into equity was unsuccessful, that conversion came too early or too late, or that the firm's financial performance keeps trending downward.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Christoph Henkel, Contingent Capital with Sequential Triggers (2011). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1908473
scope_conditions: Applies after the first trigger has already converted debt into equity
Applies before authorities initiate resolution

claims.claim: Beyond super-voting rights and dilution, the second trigger functions as a reorganization tool that operates independently of management decisions and of corrective action by regulators.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Christoph Henkel, Contingent Capital with Sequential Triggers (2011). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1908473

claims.claim: The first trigger should be based on a threshold in market value rather than accounting measures, because a market value trigger avoids total reliance on accounting methods that are open to manipulation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Christoph Henkel, Contingent Capital with Sequential Triggers (2011). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1908473
scope_conditions: The authors decline to take a general position in the first trigger debate

claims.claim: The volume of contingent capital issuance should be large enough that conversion produces sufficient dilution, and the trigger timeframe should be roughly ninety days.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Christoph Henkel, Contingent Capital with Sequential Triggers (2011). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1908473
scope_conditions: Stated as a probable rather than settled design choice

claims.claim: Contingent capital offers only limited protection against information asymmetries, principal and agent conflicts, and collective action problems, so it cannot by itself prevent economic failure.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Christoph Henkel, Contingent Capital with Sequential Triggers (2011). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1908473

claims.claim: Existing proposals for implementing contingent capital do not explain how they would address the information asymmetries and principal and agent problems that may lie at the core of the credit crisis.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Christoph Henkel, Contingent Capital with Sequential Triggers (2011). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1908473
scope_conditions: Assumes information asymmetries and principal agent problems were central causes of the crisis

claims.claim: Because contingent capital is a hybrid instrument that pays fixed returns while bearing equity like risk, it may receive low or no ratings, attract a much smaller investor base, and carry higher funding costs.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Christoph Henkel, Contingent Capital with Sequential Triggers (2011). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1908473
scope_conditions: Holds while rating methodologies for hybrid contingent instruments remain unsettled

claims.claim: Letting national regulators keep their existing Tier 1 capital definitions creates a collective action problem: countries with stricter definitions appear to have less capital and thinner cushions than countries with broader ones.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Christoph Henkel, Contingent Capital with Sequential Triggers (2011). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1908473
scope_conditions: Applies where EU wide harmonization of the Tier 1 definition is absent

claims.claim: The incentive effects of corporate governance controls may not operate in systemically important financial institutions, because managers and owners who anticipate a bailout commitment adjust their risk preferences upward.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Christoph Henkel, Contingent Capital with Sequential Triggers (2011). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1908473
scope_conditions: Applies to institutions considered too big to fail

claims.claim: Switching to contingent capital financing may reinforce rather than reduce risk incentives, and whether the risk incentives generated by contingent capital outweigh its risk reduction potential remains unresolved.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Christoph Henkel, Contingent Capital with Sequential Triggers (2011). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1908473
scope_conditions: Turns on the design features of the securities and on how much control equity holders retain after conversion

claims.claim: By internalizing the costs of bank failure, contingent capital can reduce moral hazard, and because a contingent debt security with a conversion trigger would presumably not default, it helps avoid contagion and systemic spillovers.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Christoph Henkel, Contingent Capital with Sequential Triggers (2011). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1908473
scope_conditions: Assumes the conversion trigger operates as designed

claims.claim: Contingent capital securities are likely to be more efficient than raising capital requirements, because the capital arrives only when it is needed.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Christoph Henkel, Contingent Capital with Sequential Triggers (2011). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1908473

claims.claim: The threat of loss on conversion and the implicit dilution of existing stock holdings reduce shareholders' incentive to press management for higher risk in pursuit of higher returns.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Christoph Henkel, Contingent Capital with Sequential Triggers (2011). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1908473

claims.claim: Mandatory contingent capital issuance requires the creation of a new market, and market creation takes time: the European hybrid market established in 1997 needed five years to reach critical mass.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Christoph Henkel, Contingent Capital with Sequential Triggers (2011). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1908473

claims.claim: Requiring financial institutions to sell high volumes of contingent capital securities, on the order of four to nineteen percent of risk weighted assets, could raise pricing pressure and increase their cost of funding.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Christoph Henkel, Contingent Capital with Sequential Triggers (2011). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1908473
scope_conditions: Applies at the issuance volumes contemplated by the EU Commission working document

claims.claim: Without a degree of international convergence in contingent capital rules, regulatory arbitrage could undermine the establishment of contingent capital as an integral part of financial markets.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Christoph Henkel, Contingent Capital with Sequential Triggers (2011). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1908473
scope_conditions: Assumes jurisdictions legislate contingent capital independently of one another

claims.claim: Although the EU debt write-down proposal gives regulators certainty and discretion, it could produce greater market uncertainty, raise costs, and have the unintended effect of increasing the size of financial institutions.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Christoph Henkel, Contingent Capital with Sequential Triggers (2011). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1908473
scope_conditions: Applies to the debt write-down element of the EU Commission proposal

claims.claim: A dual trigger that relies on a financial institution index gains from its use of market prices but is vulnerable to index manipulation and to bondholders attempting to force the institution into bankruptcy.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Christoph Henkel, Contingent Capital with Sequential Triggers (2011). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1908473
scope_conditions: Applies to dual price trigger designs that include a sector or system index component

claims.claim: Departing from Coffee's design, super-voting rights should be allocated to contingent capital holders only if the first trigger failed to improve the institution's financial health; at the first trigger the new shareholder gets one vote per share.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Christoph Henkel, Contingent Capital with Sequential Triggers (2011). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1908473
scope_conditions: Voting rights escalate only on a continuing downward trend after the first conversion

claims.claim: To balance constituent incentives and prevent abuse, the voting rights increase should be calibrated so that contingent capital holders obtain a majority stake only in combination with the largest institutional shareholder.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Christoph Henkel, Contingent Capital with Sequential Triggers (2011). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1908473
scope_conditions: Change of control limited to the case where the first trigger failed

claims.claim: Sequential triggers invite manipulation of the triggering events and abusive practices such as asset stripping near bankruptcy, a risk the contract or corporate charter can counter by imposing a mandatory holding period on contingent capital securities.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Christoph Henkel, Contingent Capital with Sequential Triggers (2011). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1908473
scope_conditions: Holding period could be extended until after bankruptcy

claims.claim: Conversion at the first trigger under this proposal lacks the finality of Coffee's design, because it does not necessarily hand the institution to creditors unless the firm deteriorates further.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Christoph Henkel, Contingent Capital with Sequential Triggers (2011). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1908473

claims.claim: The second trigger should be an objective, automatic, institution specific trigger, with improvement measured through a combination of debt to equity ratio improvement and credit default swap spread narrowing after conversion.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Christoph Henkel, Contingent Capital with Sequential Triggers (2011). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1908473
scope_conditions: The precise arithmetic must be institution specific

claims.claim: Information asymmetries between market participants and a systemically important institution's management before default can be reduced if a financial weakening after conversion of contingent capital triggers a voting rights increase.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Christoph Henkel, Contingent Capital with Sequential Triggers (2011). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1908473
scope_conditions: Requires that the weakening occur after contingent capital has converted into equity

claims.claim: The second trigger voting rights increase should never actually be triggered; its function is to level the playing field between constituents, incentivize negotiation, and provide an alternative to reorganization.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Christoph Henkel, Contingent Capital with Sequential Triggers (2011). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1908473

claims.claim: German corporate law permits increases in voting rights only in very limited circumstances, such as grandfathered multiple voting shares, so the proposed voting rights increase would require statutory reform in Germany.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Christoph Henkel, Contingent Capital with Sequential Triggers (2011). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1908473
scope_conditions: Höchststimmrechte were banned for listed German corporations in 1998
France and the United Kingdom by contrast permit multiple votes per share

claims.claim: Allocating super-voting stock to contingent capital holders satisfies Delaware's legitimate business purpose requirement, because the allocation serves to avoid insolvency and dissolution of the institution.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Christoph Henkel, Contingent Capital with Sequential Triggers (2011). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1908473
scope_conditions: Delaware permits alternative voting arrangements if the charter provides for them or is amended
Increases are limited if inequitable or in breach of fiduciary duty

claims.claim: Exchange uniform voting rights policies should not be applied to contingent capital securities, and the NYSE and Nasdaq would themselves benefit from an exemption because it could increase marketability and trading on each exchange.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Christoph Henkel, Contingent Capital with Sequential Triggers (2011). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1908473
scope_conditions: Exchange policies allow dual class capitalization but bar midstream dilutive changes in voting rights

claims.claim: A substantial voting rights increase at the second trigger could raise the cost of contingent capital securities, with issuers demanding premiums that push primary issuance toward institutional investors interested in the change of control possibility.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Christoph Henkel, Contingent Capital with Sequential Triggers (2011). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1908473
scope_conditions: Especially where the voting rights increase can reach the level of change of control

claims.claim: Contingent capital holders, as former creditors whose main interest is realizing their claims, have a natural interest in continuity and are therefore likely to support incumbent management after conversion.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Christoph Henkel, Contingent Capital with Sequential Triggers (2011). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1908473
scope_conditions: Analogy to the debtor in possession concept under Chapter 11

claims.claim: Contingent capital with increased voting rights delivers a more flexible and efficient outcome than Chapter 11, because it requires neither court involvement nor a threshold of creditor approval.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Christoph Henkel, Contingent Capital with Sequential Triggers (2011). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1908473
scope_conditions: Contingent capital holders with increased voting rights hold powers comparable to a creditors' committee

claims.claim: Reorganization through contingent capital eliminates the holdout problem, because the majority of contingent capital holders, or those holders together with shareholders, determine governance after conversion, so a lone dissenter cannot collect more than other creditors.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Christoph Henkel, Contingent Capital with Sequential Triggers (2011). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1908473
scope_conditions: Applies after conversion and before resolution
The holdout who becomes a shareholder shares losses proportionate to equity ownership

claims.claim: Because the Bankruptcy Code does not define adequate information, prepackaged plans risk inadequate disclosure, creditor challenge, and unusable prepetition votes that force the case into the longer ordinary Chapter 11 confirmation procedure.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Christoph Henkel, Contingent Capital with Sequential Triggers (2011). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1908473

claims.claim: Contingent capital is more efficient than prepackaged plans or preplan sales because it provides a resolution mechanism outside formal proceedings and free of their restrictions, since the Bankruptcy Code does not regulate conversion or the use of increased voting rights.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Christoph Henkel, Contingent Capital with Sequential Triggers (2011). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1908473
scope_conditions: Contingent capital securities are for the most part privately negotiated contracts

claims.claim: Strategic maneuvering by creditors before a bankruptcy filing or during plan negotiations could distort the incentive structure the sequential trigger proposal depends on.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Christoph Henkel, Contingent Capital with Sequential Triggers (2011). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1908473
scope_conditions: Strategic behavior can arise equally at the conversion stage and at the voting rights increase

claims.claim: Contrary to critics who blame the Basel Accords, harmonization through Basel II is not what made banks hold similar assets; banks held similar assets because those assets were profitable.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Regulation Via Basel III (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1806252

claims.claim: Because hedge funds play a large role in the credit derivatives market and that market recently failed, an increased regulatory emphasis on banks' lending exposure to hedge funds is justified.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Regulation Via Basel III (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1806252
scope_conditions: credit derivatives market experienced recent failure
hedge funds are major users of credit default swaps

claims.claim: Building on the increase in capital requirements for counterparty risk already suggested in Basel III, Basel III could add a charge on banks' assets based on their lending exposure to hedge funds.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Regulation Via Basel III (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1806252
scope_conditions: Basel Committee adopts the proposal

claims.claim: Asymmetric hedge fund regulation, in which Dodd-Frank and the AIFM Directive regulate banks and hedge funds separately and differently, is counterproductive.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Regulation Via Basel III (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1806252
scope_conditions: US and EU hedge funds operate in the same markets with similar strategies

claims.claim: The AIFM Directive could create incentives for regulatory arbitrage and could provoke retaliatory action by countries outside the European Union.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Regulation Via Basel III (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1806252
scope_conditions: non-EU funds and managers face restricted access to EU markets

claims.claim: Regulating entities that operate in the same markets under asymmetric rules creates legal uncertainty and significant transaction costs.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Regulation Via Basel III (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1806252
scope_conditions: entities compete in the same markets

claims.claim: Hedge fund managers subjected to stricter rules in one jurisdiction while competing with funds in less restrictive jurisdictions could be placed at a comparative disadvantage.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Regulation Via Basel III (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1806252
scope_conditions: managers compete for the same clients and profit margins across jurisdictions

claims.claim: If regulators lack the resources to protect against systemic risk, hedge fund regulation could be futile.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Regulation Via Basel III (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1806252
scope_conditions: regulators are given a systemic risk mandate they lack capacity to execute

claims.claim: Regulators who obtain hedge funds' proprietary information could inadvertently pass it to third parties, and because that information is highly valuable to competitors in the same markets, such leakage could undermine trading strategies and the long-term viability of hedge funds.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Regulation Via Basel III (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1806252
scope_conditions: mandatory disclosure of trading positions and strategies to regulators

claims.claim: Because hedge fund trading strategies depend on confidentiality, required disclosures that let other market participants trade along or anticipate a fund's transactions can negatively affect the fund's absolute returns.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Regulation Via Basel III (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1806252
scope_conditions: strategies rely on interpreting market environments not yet priced in by others

claims.claim: Banks' lending practices and counterparty credit risk management can curtail hedge funds' excessive risk taking because banks can use the threat of cutting off future lending to change a fund's behavior.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Regulation Via Basel III (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1806252
scope_conditions: the bank has an ongoing lending relationship with the fund

claims.claim: Banks are ideally positioned to deal with asymmetric information, moral hazard, and systemic issues pertaining to hedge funds, which is why hedge fund regulation should run through bank regulation.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Regulation Via Basel III (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1806252

claims.claim: Because banks expect to be bailed out with taxpayer funds, they may have less incentive to monitor their hedge fund lending activities, even though hedge funds are not themselves counterparties in government bailouts.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Regulation Via Basel III (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1806252
scope_conditions: governments are presumed willing to bail out banks

claims.claim: Systemic risk and financial market stability are public goods, so individual banks free ride on other banks' hedge fund credit risk management and are not incentivized to adequately monitor or limit their own hedge fund risk exposure.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Regulation Via Basel III (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1806252

claims.claim: An institution or a country creates externalities when it manages its own hedge fund generated systemic risk without considering how its actions or inactions affect risk in the system as a whole.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Regulation Via Basel III (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1806252

claims.claim: Even if hedge fund investing does have systemic implications, systemic risk is multifaceted enough that addressing it could require more than one regulator in a single jurisdiction, so the SEC alone may be unable to accomplish the task.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Regulation Via Basel III (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1806252
scope_conditions: systemic risk is difficult to measure and the required information is widely dispersed

claims.claim: The SEC would be better advised to interpret the rulemaking authority it received from Congress than to increase requirements on hedge funds in order to address concerns over potential systemic risk.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Regulation Via Basel III (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1806252
scope_conditions: indicia suggest hedge funds may not pose systemic risk

claims.claim: A lack of regulatory guidance creates legal uncertainty, and legal uncertainty in turn generates transaction costs.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Regulation Via Basel III (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1806252
scope_conditions: regulator relies on no-action letters rather than rules

claims.claim: Because the AIFM Directive exposes depositaries to strict liability in certain circumstances, depositaries must weigh the risks and benefits of serving EU alternative investment funds, and a negative assessment would harm the depository business and, implicitly, hedge funds.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Regulation Via Basel III (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1806252
scope_conditions: AIFM Directive retains elements of strict depositary liability
depositaries reassess whether to serve alternative investment funds in the European Union

claims.claim: Discrimination against non-EU jurisdictions under the AIFM Directive could provoke retaliatory action, and retaliation combined with a lack of intra-European cooperation could damage the European financial services industry and the whole European economy.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Regulation Via Basel III (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1806252
scope_conditions: obstacles to EU market access for non-EU funds and managers persist

claims.claim: Market failure in complex financial instruments, rather than hedge fund activity as such, could have been a contributing factor in the recent credit crisis.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Regulation Via Basel III (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1806252
scope_conditions: evidence drawn from the 2007 collapse of the CDO and CDS markets

claims.claim: Although hedge funds manage only a small proportion of the investment universe compared with banks, they do manage a proportionally large part of complex financial instruments such as CDOs and other derivatives.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Regulation Via Basel III (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1806252

claims.claim: British Bankers' Association data show that since 2000 hedge funds steadily increased their share of the credit derivatives market while banks' role in that market progressively declined.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Regulation Via Basel III (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1806252
scope_conditions: data cover 2000 to 2006; the BBA discontinued the series in 2007

claims.claim: Legislators had disincentives to impose harsher requirements on the hedge fund industry before the crisis, because harsher regulation could have driven franchise taxes and other business to offshore centers.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Regulation Via Basel III (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1806252
scope_conditions: a significant number of hedge funds operate through offshore centers

claims.claim: Basel III capital charges based on a bank's lending exposure to hedge funds could help address the threat of regulatory arbitrage.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Regulation Via Basel III (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1806252
scope_conditions: banks participating in the Basel framework lend to the funds

claims.claim: Implementing the hedge fund lending charge through Basel III would require no separate national implementation, because compliance falls on banks that have already joined the framework, so transaction costs for national regulators would be avoided.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Regulation Via Basel III (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1806252
scope_conditions: the bank has joined the Basel framework

claims.claim: Even combining hedge fund regulation via Basel III rules with the de minimis investment rules in Dodd-Frank could leave some issues open, and calibrating such a regulatory combination requires time and experience.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Regulation Via Basel III (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1806252

claims.claim: A standard objection to indirect regulation is that counterparty credit risk management will not work effectively unless the lending bank has an exclusive relationship with the hedge fund that lets it control the relationship.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Regulation Via Basel III (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1806252
scope_conditions: a hedge fund borrows from more than one bank, so no single bank sees its overall risk exposure

claims.claim: Contesting the exclusivity objection, exclusivity of a banking relationship is not the only effective way to exercise control and manage risk: the intensity, endurance, and quality of the relationship also influence how much control a bank can exercise over a hedge fund.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Regulation Via Basel III (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1806252
scope_conditions: most hedge funds maintain more than one banking relationship

claims.claim: Because some hedge fund trading strategies depend on the immediate availability of capital and will not work without sufficient lines of credit, banks may retain enough influence over hedge funds even where funds use multiple lenders.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Regulation Via Basel III (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1806252
scope_conditions: fund uses dynamic trading strategies requiring additional capital on short notice

claims.claim: Banks' role in monitoring hedge funds is not easily comparable to the principal agent problem between securities buyers and credit rating agencies, because banks have more influence over hedge funds than securities buyers have over rating agencies and their ratings.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Regulation Via Basel III (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1806252

claims.claim: The numerical wealth requirements used to define qualified hedge fund investors fail as a regulatory device, because investors who meet the wealth thresholds do not always have the knowledge, understanding, and sophistication needed to invest in highly complex financial instruments.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Regulation Via Basel III (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1806252
scope_conditions: accredited investor standards under Regulation D and PFIARA

claims.claim: Requiring advisers to adopt written policies to prevent and detect securities law violations presumes those violations are foreseeable, yet because Dodd-Frank substantially changed securities law, the foreseeability of potential violations is itself further curtailed.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Regulation Via Basel III (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1806252
scope_conditions: PFIARA requires written compliance policies just after Dodd-Frank changed the underlying law

claims.claim: Without the threat of systemic risk and without a clear delineation of the social externalities that hedge funds cause, the purpose of direct hedge fund regulation is unclear.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Regulation Via Basel III (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1806252
scope_conditions: hedge funds have fewer assets and less leverage than banks
collapses such as Amaranth in 2006 and large redemptions did not cause systemic problems

claims.claim: Registering hedge funds with regulators and requiring disclosure of pertinent information could help minimize the moral hazard, social externalities, and systemic risk generated by the hedge fund industry.
claims.citation: Kaal, Hedge Fund Regulation Via Basel III (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1806252
scope_conditions: extent of hedge fund involvement in the 2008 to 2009 credit crisis remains unclear

claims.claim: Because Morrison ties Section 10(b) to the location of the securities transaction rather than to the place where the deception originated, the logic of the holding implies that the SEC likewise has no enforcement rights over securities transactions occurring outside the United States.
claims.citation: Kaal and Painter, The Aftermath of Morrison v. National Australia Bank and Elliott Associates v. Porsche (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1765901
scope_conditions: Section 10(b) claims
transactions executed outside the United States

claims.claim: Before Morrison, U.S. courts refused to adopt a bright line rule for the extraterritorial reach of Section 10(b), and the resulting case by case conduct and effects analysis was applied inconsistently.
claims.citation: Kaal and Painter, The Aftermath of Morrison v. National Australia Bank and Elliott Associates v. Porsche (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1765901
scope_conditions: pre-Morrison case law
foreign-cubed securities litigation

claims.claim: The plaintiffs' reading that Section 10(b) covers transactions anywhere in any security of a class listed on a U.S. exchange is inconsistent with Morrison, because the opinion turns on the location of the transaction and on the holding that Section 10(b) has no extraterritorial application.
claims.citation: Kaal and Painter, The Aftermath of Morrison v. National Australia Bank and Elliott Associates v. Porsche (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1765901
scope_conditions: dually listed securities
transactions executed on a foreign exchange

claims.claim: Morrison itself refutes a listing based reading of Section 10(b): the Court knew that National Australia Bank had registered and listed shares in New York, yet held that Section 10(b) did not reach trades in those ordinary shares in Australia.
claims.citation: Kaal and Painter, The Aftermath of Morrison v. National Australia Bank and Elliott Associates v. Porsche (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1765901
scope_conditions: foreign issuers with U.S. registered ADRs or listed shares

claims.claim: There is no substantive difference between a foreign issuer listing ADRs on a U.S. exchange and listing its ordinary shares there, so Section 10(b) coverage of foreign transactions should not turn on which arrangement the issuer chose.
claims.citation: Kaal and Painter, The Aftermath of Morrison v. National Australia Bank and Elliott Associates v. Porsche (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1765901
scope_conditions: foreign issuers accessing U.S. markets through ADRs

claims.claim: Section 30 of the Exchange Act is Congress's only articulation of the extraterritorial reach of Section 10(b), and Congress did not intend the Exchange Act to have extraterritorial effect beyond that provision.
claims.citation: Kaal and Painter, The Aftermath of Morrison v. National Australia Bank and Elliott Associates v. Porsche (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1765901
scope_conditions: Exchange Act antifraud provisions

claims.claim: The Supreme Court should have summarized its Morrison holding in language matching the opinion's logic, namely that Section 10(b) applies only to securities bought or sold in the United States; the Court's summary language instead invited confusion.
claims.citation: Kaal and Painter, The Aftermath of Morrison v. National Australia Bank and Elliott Associates v. Porsche (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1765901
scope_conditions: judicial opinion drafting
summary language of Morrison

claims.claim: Permitting Section 10(b) suits over dually listed securities traded outside the United States would undermine Morrison's own policy rationale, because it would interfere with the laws of other countries and turn the United States into a haven for plaintiffs' lawyers suing over foreign exchange purchases.
claims.citation: Kaal and Painter, The Aftermath of Morrison v. National Australia Bank and Elliott Associates v. Porsche (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1765901
scope_conditions: dually listed securities
purchases on foreign exchanges

claims.claim: Judge Baer's dismissal of the Porsche complaint reaches the correct result under Morrison, but parts of his reasoning require further refinement.
claims.citation: Kaal and Painter, The Aftermath of Morrison v. National Australia Bank and Elliott Associates v. Porsche (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1765901
scope_conditions: security-based swap agreements referencing foreign traded stock

claims.claim: The Porsche swap transactions were not the functional equivalent of a transaction on a U.S. securities exchange, but neither were they the functional equivalent of a transaction on a German exchange, contrary to the implication of Judge Baer's opinion.
claims.citation: Kaal and Painter, The Aftermath of Morrison v. National Australia Bank and Elliott Associates v. Porsche (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1765901
scope_conditions: over-the-counter security-based swap agreements

claims.claim: The economic reality of swap agreements does not justify fixing the location of the transaction in every case solely by reference to the market where the reference security trades, even though Judge Baer was right that the Porsche swaps were not U.S. transactions.
claims.citation: Kaal and Painter, The Aftermath of Morrison v. National Australia Bank and Elliott Associates v. Porsche (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1765901
scope_conditions: privately negotiated swap agreements
application of Morrison to derivatives

claims.claim: Morrison provides no clear parameters for classifying privately negotiated transactions as domestic or foreign, because the case involved publicly traded securities and never reached the question.
claims.citation: Kaal and Painter, The Aftermath of Morrison v. National Australia Bank and Elliott Associates v. Porsche (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1765901
scope_conditions: privately negotiated securities and derivative transactions

claims.claim: If the presence of a single U.S. party sufficed to locate a privately negotiated derivative transaction in the United States, U.S. parties could sue in U.S. courts regardless of other factors such as where the counterparties were located.
claims.citation: Kaal and Painter, The Aftermath of Morrison v. National Australia Bank and Elliott Associates v. Porsche (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1765901
scope_conditions: privately negotiated derivative transactions
a one party location test

claims.claim: Locating a private transaction by the location of the parties is often unworkable, because the parties are frequently institutions simultaneously present in the United States and abroad, and individual parties are often in transit.
claims.citation: Kaal and Painter, The Aftermath of Morrison v. National Australia Bank and Elliott Associates v. Porsche (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1765901
scope_conditions: private transactions in conventional securities
institutional and mobile parties

claims.claim: Given the defects of a party location analysis, courts should de-emphasize where the parties are and instead use a totality of the circumstances approach to determine where a privately negotiated derivative transaction took place.
claims.citation: Kaal and Painter, The Aftermath of Morrison v. National Australia Bank and Elliott Associates v. Porsche (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1765901
scope_conditions: privately negotiated derivative transactions under Morrison

claims.claim: Treating the U.S. location of a broker as making the securities purchase domestic would circumvent most of the Morrison holding, since a foreign buyer of foreign securities could invoke U.S. law simply by routing the order through a U.S. broker.
claims.citation: Kaal and Painter, The Aftermath of Morrison v. National Australia Bank and Elliott Associates v. Porsche (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1765901
scope_conditions: orders placed through U.S. brokers for execution on foreign exchanges

claims.claim: Non-U.S. investors have a strong incentive to route foreign trades through U.S. brokers if that preserves a U.S. cause of action, because their home jurisdictions rarely offer the attractive features of the U.S. system such as broad discovery, higher damages, class actions, and no exposure to defendants' costs.
claims.citation: Kaal and Painter, The Aftermath of Morrison v. National Australia Bank and Elliott Associates v. Porsche (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1765901
scope_conditions: a broker location theory accepted by U.S. courts
non-U.S. clients trading non-U.S. securities

claims.claim: For exchange traded securities, the location of the exchange rather than the location of the plaintiff's broker should be the controlling factor under Morrison, although it is uncertain whether all courts will adopt this bright line test.
claims.citation: Kaal and Painter, The Aftermath of Morrison v. National Australia Bank and Elliott Associates v. Porsche (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1765901
scope_conditions: exchange traded securities
claims analyzed under Morrison

claims.claim: Porsche could be exposed to substantial U.S. sanctions even though neither its own common stock nor Volkswagen's traded in the United States, solely because of swap agreements to which Porsche was not a party.
claims.citation: Kaal and Painter, The Aftermath of Morrison v. National Australia Bank and Elliott Associates v. Porsche (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1765901
scope_conditions: derivative contracts referencing foreign traded shares
foreign issuers with no U.S. listing

claims.claim: If Section 10(b) were held to reach swap agreements based on stocks traded outside the United States, plaintiffs' attorneys would use that holding as precedent to limit Morrison broadly, and other courts might create a general exception for U.S. derivative contracts referencing non-U.S. securities.
claims.citation: Kaal and Painter, The Aftermath of Morrison v. National Australia Bank and Elliott Associates v. Porsche (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1765901
scope_conditions: appellate reversal of the Porsche dismissal
U.S. derivative contracts referencing foreign securities

claims.claim: Unless courts can construe Morrison for swap agreements and other derivatives consistently with both the logic and the language of the opinion, Congress will have to enact new clarifying legislation.
claims.citation: Kaal and Painter, The Aftermath of Morrison v. National Australia Bank and Elliott Associates v. Porsche (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1765901
scope_conditions: derivative transactions with extraterritorial components

claims.claim: The Second Circuit should uphold Judge Baer's ruling on a totality of the circumstances basis and explain more fully how those circumstances determine the location of a swap agreement under Morrison.
claims.citation: Kaal and Painter, The Aftermath of Morrison v. National Australia Bank and Elliott Associates v. Porsche (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1765901
scope_conditions: appeal of the Porsche dismissal

claims.claim: On its face Section 929P(b) of the Dodd-Frank Act addresses only the jurisdiction of the district courts and does not expand the geographic scope of the substantive provisions of U.S. securities law.
claims.citation: Kaal and Painter, The Aftermath of Morrison v. National Australia Bank and Elliott Associates v. Porsche (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1765901
scope_conditions: suits brought by the SEC or the Department of Justice
the enacted text as distinct from legislative history

claims.claim: There is a substantial likelihood that U.S. courts will read the Dodd-Frank Act as giving some extraterritorial effect to SEC and DOJ suits, so Morrison cannot be expected to survive intact in actions brought under Section 929P(b).
claims.citation: Kaal and Painter, The Aftermath of Morrison v. National Australia Bank and Elliott Associates v. Porsche (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1765901
scope_conditions: enforcement suits brought by the SEC or DOJ

claims.claim: Section 929P(b) may not have been necessary, because Section 10(b) already gives the SEC enforcement authority whenever a single U.S. securities transaction is affected by the alleged fraud.
claims.citation: Kaal and Painter, The Aftermath of Morrison v. National Australia Bank and Elliott Associates v. Porsche (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1765901
scope_conditions: SEC enforcement authority after Morrison

claims.claim: Foreign-cubed rulings such as Morrison determined the size of the plaintiff class in private suits, but were irrelevant to the SEC's ability to enforce wherever a U.S. securities transaction is connected to the alleged fraud.
claims.citation: Kaal and Painter, The Aftermath of Morrison v. National Australia Bank and Elliott Associates v. Porsche (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1765901
scope_conditions: private class actions compared with SEC enforcement

claims.claim: Read as more than a jurisdictional grant, the Dodd-Frank provision becomes an open-ended statute rather than the targeted authority the SEC already held under Section 10(b) and Section 30, and it is undesirable for the SEC to use such powers unilaterally without consulting foreign regulators and the U.S. foreign policy establishment.
claims.citation: Kaal and Painter, The Aftermath of Morrison v. National Australia Bank and Elliott Associates v. Porsche (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1765901
scope_conditions: if Section 929P(b) is construed to confer substantive powers

claims.claim: Section 929P(b) risks complications where the SEC proceeds unilaterally in situations in which coordinated enforcement with foreign regulators would be more effective, for example insider trading cases involving exchanges whose home regimes do not recognize comparable insider trading rules.
claims.citation: Kaal and Painter, The Aftermath of Morrison v. National Australia Bank and Elliott Associates v. Porsche (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1765901
scope_conditions: unilateral SEC enforcement over foreign exchange transactions

claims.claim: Expanded SEC enforcement under the Dodd-Frank provision runs a serious risk of being perceived as an encroachment on the corporate governance of foreign companies.
claims.citation: Kaal and Painter, The Aftermath of Morrison v. National Australia Bank and Elliott Associates v. Porsche (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1765901
scope_conditions: expanded extraterritorial enforcement by the SEC or DOJ

claims.claim: Overuse of the Dodd-Frank extraterritorial enforcement provision by the SEC or the DOJ could deter foreign companies from having U.S. operations.
claims.citation: Kaal and Painter, The Aftermath of Morrison v. National Australia Bank and Elliott Associates v. Porsche (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1765901
scope_conditions: frequent extraterritorial enforcement under Section 929P(b)

claims.claim: Extending private rights of action extraterritorially would expose non-U.S. companies to Section 10(b) liability based on any U.S. conduct, including conduct inside U.S. business operations alleged to have produced securities fraud abroad, and much of global securities litigation would migrate to the United States.
claims.citation: Kaal and Painter, The Aftermath of Morrison v. National Australia Bank and Elliott Associates v. Porsche (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1765901
scope_conditions: if Congress legislatively overrules Morrison for private plaintiffs

claims.claim: A private right of action in foreign-cubed cases would compel EU companies to modify U.S. business operations that expose them to Section 10(b) litigation, including operations unrelated to U.S. securities markets or U.S. investors.
claims.citation: Kaal and Painter, The Aftermath of Morrison v. National Australia Bank and Elliott Associates v. Porsche (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1765901
scope_conditions: if Congress imposes a private right of action in foreign-cubed cases
EU companies with U.S. operations

claims.claim: Changing national rules in a spirit of cooperation among states and regulators is more productive for preventing securities fraud than imposing U.S. rules on foreign nations through extraterritorial imperialism.
claims.citation: Kaal and Painter, The Aftermath of Morrison v. National Australia Bank and Elliott Associates v. Porsche (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1765901
scope_conditions: cross border securities fraud enforcement

claims.claim: Regardless of what the SEC study concludes, Congress should decline to reinstate private rights of action in foreign-cubed cases.
claims.citation: Kaal and Painter, The Aftermath of Morrison v. National Australia Bank and Elliott Associates v. Porsche (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1765901
scope_conditions: the Section 929Y study of private rights of action

claims.claim: The SEC study is very unlikely to produce an extraterritorial extension of private rights of action so long as Republicans control the House of Representatives.
claims.citation: Kaal and Painter, The Aftermath of Morrison v. National Australia Bank and Elliott Associates v. Porsche (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1765901
scope_conditions: U.S. political control of the House of Representatives

claims.claim: Because of the ambiguities in Morrison and Dodd-Frank and the consequences of a broad reading for persons and companies in European and other jurisdictions, Congress should clarify its intent in Section 929P(b) with respect to SEC and DOJ suits over securities transactions outside the United States.
claims.citation: Kaal and Painter, The Aftermath of Morrison v. National Australia Bank and Elliott Associates v. Porsche (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1765901
scope_conditions: SEC and DOJ suits over securities transactions outside the United States

claims.claim: A clear and restrained U.S. approach to extraterritoriality will bring predictability to global securities markets and avoid a downturn in international economic cooperation.
claims.citation: Kaal and Painter, The Aftermath of Morrison v. National Australia Bank and Elliott Associates v. Porsche (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1765901
scope_conditions: restraint and clarification of U.S. extraterritorial securities law

claims.claim: Where bank resolution regimes are not coordinated across jurisdictions, the same systemically important financial institution can be handled in opposite ways: it might petition for reorganization under German law and emerge leaner and more competitive, while its United States operations are liquidated under the Boxer Amendment of the Dodd-Frank Act.
claims.citation: Christoph K. Henkel, Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in European Union Bank Restructuring (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2061166
scope_conditions: SIFIs with operations in multiple countries
absent coordination and convergence of resolution regimes

claims.claim: The authors contend that the European Commission's goal of maximum harmonization through a global single rule book may not be achievable, and that a legal framework for private ordering of contingent capital is the more realistic route to an adequate level of convergence.
claims.citation: Christoph K. Henkel, Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in European Union Bank Restructuring (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2061166
scope_conditions: European Union bank resolution and restructuring regimes

claims.claim: Contingent capital is stipulated as the predefined conversion of a financial institution's debt securities into equity securities, and on that definition it supplies an option for the efficient restructuring and resolution of failing financial institutions.
claims.citation: Christoph K. Henkel, Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in European Union Bank Restructuring (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2061166

claims.claim: Purely national crisis measures proved ineffective during the financial crisis because they could not reach cross-border banking operations or contain contagion, as the failures of Lehman Brothers, Fortis, the Icelandic banks, Northern Rock and Hypo Real Estate Holding demonstrated.
claims.citation: Christoph K. Henkel, Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in European Union Bank Restructuring (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2061166
scope_conditions: bank failures with cross-border operations
2007 to 2009 financial crisis

claims.claim: Because most national crisis responses took the form of public bail-outs adopted without broad international consensus, they increased the threat of international regulatory arbitrage and damaged the global competitiveness of national financial markets.
claims.citation: Christoph K. Henkel, Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in European Union Bank Restructuring (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2061166
scope_conditions: crisis-era emergency measures adopted without international coordination

claims.claim: Mutual recognition of countercyclical capital buffers hollows out the national discretion the Commission proposal appears to grant: the financially strongest Member States with the largest financial sectors will effectively set the buffer size for smaller Member States whose institutions do business there.
claims.citation: Christoph K. Henkel, Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in European Union Bank Restructuring (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2061166
scope_conditions: countercyclical buffers up to the 2.5 percent mutual recognition ceiling
institutions with branches or subsidiaries in the buffer-setting Member State

claims.claim: Even the residual national discretion to set countercyclical buffers between 2.5 and 5 percent is misleading, because a Member State such as the United Kingdom is unlikely to sustain a 5 percent buffer while Germany requires only 2.5 percent and thereby hands German banks a competitive advantage.
claims.citation: Christoph K. Henkel, Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in European Union Bank Restructuring (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2061166
scope_conditions: buffers set above the 2.5 percent mutual recognition ceiling
competing national banking sectors, especially where the state holds bank ownership stakes

claims.claim: The authors identify a drafting defect in the proposed CRD IV Regulation: the distinction drawn by financial institution in Article 51(a) is ambiguous and the cross reference to the institution referred to in point (a) of Article 87 is unclear and indeterminate, so the provision requires clarification or amendment.
claims.citation: Christoph K. Henkel, Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in European Union Bank Restructuring (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2061166
scope_conditions: Article 51 of the proposed CRD IV Regulation as drafted

claims.claim: Placing bank reorganization in the hands of an administrative supervisory authority rather than a bankruptcy court, as Swiss law does, trades better sector knowledge and a faster procedure against the cost of very broad agency discretion.
claims.citation: Christoph K. Henkel, Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in European Union Bank Restructuring (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2061166
scope_conditions: civil law jurisdictions where the supervisor is also the resolution authority
Swiss Federal Law on Banks and Savings and Loans

claims.claim: Reliance on public bail-outs, unaccompanied by any threat that management, shareholders and creditors would share significant losses, created an asymmetric incentive for excessive risk taking by financial institutions.
claims.citation: Christoph K. Henkel, Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in European Union Bank Restructuring (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2061166
scope_conditions: Germany and the United States during the height of the financial crisis
where insolvency was not a credible threat

claims.claim: Before the 2010 reform, the German regulatory intervention regime for financial institutions contained no procedure that would have reliably permitted a bank to be operated as a going concern during the financial crisis.
claims.citation: Christoph K. Henkel, Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in European Union Bank Restructuring (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2061166
scope_conditions: German law prior to the Financial Institution Reorganization Act entering into force on January 1, 2011

claims.claim: The German provision allowing appropriate compensation of shareholders whose rights are impaired can defeat the statute's own purpose, because time is of the essence in bank reorganization and the appointment of a court-appointed expert to value shareholder claims may significantly slow the procedure.
claims.citation: Christoph K. Henkel, Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in European Union Bank Restructuring (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2061166
scope_conditions: reorganization procedure under the German Financial Institution Reorganization Act
where shareholders' rights are permanently impaired by the plan

claims.claim: The German voluntary reorganization procedure has a structural gap: groups of financial institutions, financial holding groups and conglomerates cannot petition for protection under it, even though these are precisely the entities that qualify as systemically important and pose the highest risk to market stability on failure.
claims.citation: Christoph K. Henkel, Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in European Union Bank Restructuring (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2061166
scope_conditions: voluntary reorganization procedure under the German Financial Institution Reorganization Act
not applicable to the involuntary procedure initiated by the supervisor under the German Banking Act

claims.claim: Because German law fixes no threshold conditions or determining factors for market reception or market confidence, the systemic relevance and contagion determinations that turn on those factors can never be made in a reliable and objective manner.
claims.citation: Christoph K. Henkel, Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in European Union Bank Restructuring (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2061166
scope_conditions: determination of systemic threat under the German Banking Act

claims.claim: Because the amendments to the German Banking Act sharply increase the supervisor's intervention powers, the prospect that any systemically important bank would voluntarily petition under the German stabilization or reorganization procedure is remote at best.
claims.citation: Christoph K. Henkel, Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in European Union Bank Restructuring (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2061166
scope_conditions: systemically important banks in Germany
after the increase of BaFin intervention powers, which also reach groups, financial holdings and conglomerates

claims.claim: The supervisor's discretion to set a deadline for a recovery plan before issuing a transfer order is unlikely ever to be exercised in practice, because in a crisis time will be of the essence to prevent contagion.
claims.citation: Christoph K. Henkel, Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in European Union Bank Restructuring (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2061166
scope_conditions: asset transfer to a bridge bank under the German Banking Act
crisis conditions with contagion risk

claims.claim: Requiring only that consideration be commensurate with the value of transferred assets invites frequent and significant disputes over valuation, a problem compounded when the consideration consists of shares in the bridge bank, whose own value must then also be assessed.
claims.citation: Christoph K. Henkel, Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in European Union Bank Restructuring (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2061166
scope_conditions: asset transfers to a bridge bank under the German Banking Act
consideration paid in shares of the transferee entity

claims.claim: The German bank levy is internally inconsistent because financial institutions without systemic relevance must contribute to the reorganization fund yet are ineligible to receive support payments from it.
claims.citation: Christoph K. Henkel, Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in European Union Bank Restructuring (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2061166
scope_conditions: German reorganization fund financed by a levy on all German banks

claims.claim: The German reorganization fund's maximum volume of 70 billion euros may not suffice in a financial crisis, and the availability of those funds and the time needed to raise them are an even greater concern than the ceiling itself.
claims.citation: Christoph K. Henkel, Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in European Union Bank Restructuring (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2061166
scope_conditions: German reorganization fund under the Restructuring Fund Law

claims.claim: The German Banking Act requirement that a bridge bank have its head office inside Germany is of highly questionable compatibility with European Union law, specifically the principle of free movement of capital under Article 63 TFEU.
claims.citation: Christoph K. Henkel, Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in European Union Bank Restructuring (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2061166
scope_conditions: bridge bank transferee requirements under the German Banking Act

claims.claim: Contingent capital supports general risk control and reduces moral hazard by holding shareholders responsible and internalizing the costs of bank failure rather than externalizing them onto taxpayers.
claims.citation: Christoph K. Henkel, Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in European Union Bank Restructuring (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2061166

claims.claim: Because conversion carries a threat of loss and implicit dilution of stock holdings, contingent capital reduces shareholders' incentive to push management toward higher risk in pursuit of higher returns.
claims.citation: Christoph K. Henkel, Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in European Union Bank Restructuring (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2061166
scope_conditions: conversion terms that dilute existing equity holders

claims.claim: The authors contend that the European Commission's suggested floor of 4 to 19 percent of risk-weighted assets in pre-qualified bail-inable debt under the targeted approach is unrealistically high.
claims.citation: Christoph K. Henkel, Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in European Union Bank Restructuring (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2061166
scope_conditions: targeted approach in the DG Internal Market working document

claims.claim: Implementing the European Commission's debt write-down proposal has the potential to increase funding costs for financial institutions and to make their funding more volatile.
claims.citation: Christoph K. Henkel, Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in European Union Bank Restructuring (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2061166
scope_conditions: statutory bail-in regime as proposed by the Commission

claims.claim: Article 13 of the Swiss Banking Act, which authorizes boards of systemically important banks to issue mandatory convertible bonds subject to disclosure of the conversion triggering event and permits tranches with multiple triggers, could serve as a model for other European legislators and for the United States legislator.
claims.citation: Christoph K. Henkel, Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in European Union Bank Restructuring (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2061166
scope_conditions: systemically important banks
issuance within the scope of the articles of incorporation with disclosed trigger events

claims.claim: Enacting the proposed German Corporation Act amendments that would give contingent capital securities a statutory basis would require substantial changes across other areas of German law, and is unlikely to be achieved unless European Union law requires it and the standards are internationally recognized.
claims.citation: Christoph K. Henkel, Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in European Union Bank Restructuring (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2061166
scope_conditions: proposed amendments to Sections 192, 194 and 221 of the German Corporation Act

claims.claim: Efficient calibration of the triggering event is the central design problem for contingent capital, and the optimal design of a trigger that converts debt into equity remains unclear.
claims.citation: Christoph K. Henkel, Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in European Union Bank Restructuring (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2061166

claims.claim: Mandating the issuance of contingent capital does not guarantee that a viable market in contingent capital securities will develop.
claims.citation: Christoph K. Henkel, Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in European Union Bank Restructuring (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2061166
scope_conditions: mandatory minimum issuance requirements imposed by regulators

claims.claim: Building critical mass in the contingent capital securities market could require banks and other financial institutions to buy their competitors' contingent capital securities, which would raise ethical, antitrust and incentive concerns.
claims.citation: Christoph K. Henkel, Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in European Union Bank Restructuring (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2061166
scope_conditions: where non-bank demand is insufficient to absorb issuance volumes

claims.claim: The authors posit an inverse relationship between trigger uncertainty and market development: as the uncertainty generated by trigger designs increases, issuance volume of contingent capital securities falls, while the risk and the pre-conversion interest rate on those securities rises.
claims.citation: Christoph K. Henkel, Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in European Union Bank Restructuring (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2061166
scope_conditions: the interplay of trigger structure, uncertainty and market development has not been systematically studied

claims.claim: A trigger that fires too early wastes the equity injection: conversion occurs without a real need for capital or additional voting shareholders, and the effect of the injection may have dissipated by the time it is actually needed.
claims.citation: Christoph K. Henkel, Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in European Union Bank Restructuring (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2061166
scope_conditions: contingent capital converting on a trigger set too far from distress

claims.claim: A trigger that fires too late is equally useless: by then the financial institution may already be in the resolution stage, and conversion at that point will not supply enough equity to turn the company around.
claims.citation: Christoph K. Henkel, Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in European Union Bank Restructuring (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2061166
scope_conditions: contingent capital converting only at or near the point of non-viability

claims.claim: Dual trigger proposals draw their central strength from reliance on market prices, but the index leg is a major disadvantage because it can create incentives to manipulate the index or to force an entity into bankruptcy before conversion occurs.
claims.citation: Christoph K. Henkel, Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in European Union Bank Restructuring (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2061166
scope_conditions: dual trigger designs combining a firm stock price trigger with a financial institutions index trigger

claims.claim: A second, sequential trigger placed before reorganization or resolution cushions the risk that policy makers misstructure the first trigger, absorbing the negative effects of inadequate or untimely conversion at the moment the institution needs capital.
claims.citation: Christoph K. Henkel, Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in European Union Bank Restructuring (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2061166
scope_conditions: contingent capital with sequential triggers spanning going and gone concern
where the first trigger proves unsuccessful

claims.claim: Conversion of contingent capital securities from debt to equity should be timed to occur once problems are first detected but before the early intervention powers of regulatory authorities are triggered.
claims.citation: Christoph K. Henkel, Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in European Union Bank Restructuring (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2061166
scope_conditions: European Union bank resolution framework with early intervention powers

claims.claim: Using contingent capital as a preventative tool does not foreclose the statutory core power or the debt write-down tool within resolution; if early contractual write-down and conversion fail, authorities remain free to intervene and impose a haircut on shareholders, debt investors and other private parties.
claims.citation: Christoph K. Henkel, Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in European Union Bank Restructuring (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2061166
scope_conditions: contractual conversion at an early stage that does not achieve the desired result

claims.claim: Convergence of contingent capital standards is impeded by a first mover problem: single jurisdictions hesitate to impose contingent capital requirements before they know how competing jurisdictions and their financial institutions will structure their own rules.
claims.citation: Christoph K. Henkel, Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in European Union Bank Restructuring (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2061166
scope_conditions: jurisdictions whose banks compete internationally

claims.claim: Without a degree of similarity and convergence in bank resolution and contingent capital rules, regulatory arbitrage will work against establishing contingent capital as an integral part of financial markets.
claims.citation: Christoph K. Henkel, Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in European Union Bank Restructuring (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2061166
scope_conditions: absent international convergence of resolution and contingent capital rules

claims.claim: Given the European initiatives on contingent capital and the nascent European market in contingent capital securities, the Board of Governors of the United States Federal Reserve would be well advised to consider implementing contingent capital standards.
claims.citation: Christoph K. Henkel, Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in European Union Bank Restructuring (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2061166
scope_conditions: United States regulators acting under Dodd-Frank authority contingent on the mandated feasibility study
