claims.claim: The Basel Committee rejected European Union Member State requests to allow contingent capital to satisfy the new capital buffer requirements under Basel III, deciding instead that systemically important institutions must meet heightened capital requirements with retained earnings and ordinary shares.
claims.citation: Christoph K. Henkel, Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in European Union Bank Restructuring (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2061166
scope_conditions: Basel III capital buffer requirements for systemically important financial institutions

claims.claim: Early European initiatives to put contingent convertible bonds into executive pay lack governance-improving designs; contingent convertible bonds with an early conversion trigger should be used in executive compensation instead.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in Executive Compensation (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2097160
scope_conditions: systemically important financial institutions
executive compensation packages

claims.claim: The methodological assumptions of incomplete contract theory improve the analysis of executive compensation arrangements relative to the classical and spot contract models normally used.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in Executive Compensation (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2097160

claims.claim: Contingent convertible bonds placed in executive compensation serve a different purpose than those sold to investors: the point is not capital infusion during a crisis but governance-improving design that optimizes management incentives.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in Executive Compensation (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2097160
scope_conditions: contingent convertible bonds held by executives rather than outside investors

claims.claim: The conversion feature of contingent convertible bonds affects corporate governance in a SIFI only if issuance volumes are sufficient and design features are adequate, because the governance effect runs through the threat of dilution of existing equity positions.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in Executive Compensation (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2097160
scope_conditions: sufficient volume of contingent convertible bond issuance
adequate design features

claims.claim: Market solutions and private ordering alone are unlikely to produce contingent capital designs that improve corporate governance in SIFIs, because privately negotiated sales so far have not produced governance-sensitive designs.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in Executive Compensation (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2097160
scope_conditions: market for contingent convertible bonds still in its infancy

claims.claim: Analyzing executive compensation as a single contract between an executive agent and a corporate principal fails, because it ignores the informal relational element of the principal agent relationship that often overshadows the legal terms of the agreement.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in Executive Compensation (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2097160
scope_conditions: executive compensation contracts
classical contract model or spot contract model

claims.claim: Control rights in executive compensation contracts cannot sufficiently constrain ex post opportunism by executives, because of incomplete information, information asymmetry, bounded rationality, limited foresight, and transaction costs.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in Executive Compensation (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2097160
scope_conditions: principal agent relationship under incomplete contracting

claims.claim: Adding contingent convertible bonds with an early trigger to executive compensation packages creates a corporate governance mechanism that addresses the inability of contractual control rights to constrain executive opportunism.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in Executive Compensation (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2097160

claims.claim: Barclays's Contingent Capital Plan uses synthetic CoCos that simply lapse when the Group Core Tier 1 capital ratio falls below seven percent, rather than converting into equity.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in Executive Compensation (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2097160
scope_conditions: Barclays Contingent Capital Plan as of the 2010 annual report

claims.claim: Because the Barclays award falls away rather than converting, it does not create a fixed claim giving managers a stake in the firm's liquidation value, and therefore it does not lower agency cost.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in Executive Compensation (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2097160
scope_conditions: contingent capital awards that lapse instead of converting

claims.claim: A contingent capital award to executives without a conversion feature yields only limited governance improvement and only limited incentive to lower risk-taking; in its current form it operates as a mere compensation supplement.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in Executive Compensation (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2097160
scope_conditions: contingent capital awards without conversion into equity

claims.claim: Contingent convertible bonds issued to executives are typically too small in volume to dilute investors' equity holdings or to supply a meaningful equity infusion during a crisis, so copying investor CoCo designs for executive pay produces suboptimal outcomes.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in Executive Compensation (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2097160
scope_conditions: contingent convertible bonds issued only to executives
volumes smaller than investor issuances

claims.claim: The early trigger converts only the executives' portion of debt into equity, ahead of investors' contingent convertible bonds and while the entity is still sound on a micro-prudential basis, which is what makes it an early warning system rather than a recapitalization device.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in Executive Compensation (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2097160
scope_conditions: entity still sound on a micro-prudential basis at the time of conversion

claims.claim: Regulatory triggers generate the highest level of uncertainty and can produce ad hoc regulatory decisions and adverse market responses, so they are not the best option for contingent convertible bonds in executive compensation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in Executive Compensation (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2097160
scope_conditions: triggers left to regulatory discretion

claims.claim: Regulatory triggers insufficiently incentivize executives to lower risk, because executives would not have to self-monitor and adjust their own risk-taking preferences in order to avoid the trigger.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in Executive Compensation (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2097160
scope_conditions: conversion decided by regulators rather than by an automatic institution-specific term

claims.claim: Market-based trigger measures are vulnerable to market manipulation and bank runs, while accounting-based measures are updated too infrequently to respond adequately in a financial crisis.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in Executive Compensation (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2097160
scope_conditions: institution-specific automatic triggers keyed to market or accounting metrics

claims.claim: Institution-specific automatic triggers are the preferred basis for early trigger designs because they are flexible and independent of regulatory discretion.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in Executive Compensation (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2097160

claims.claim: To be effective, early triggers must be set well above the Basel III capital requirement threshold, and capital-ratio early triggers should be independent of regulatory demands about capitalization levels.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in Executive Compensation (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2097160
scope_conditions: early triggers expressed as capital ratios
Basel III capital regime

claims.claim: Because conversion damages both the debt portion and the surviving equity portion of an executive's package at the moment equity matters most for total pay, the combined effect is a strong incentive for executives to lower risk in order to avoid the triggering event.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in Executive Compensation (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2097160
scope_conditions: executive package combines contingent convertible bonds with equity-based compensation

claims.claim: Ordinary SIFI creditors have suboptimal incentives to monitor management because they implicitly expect that the government will provide bailout funding given the nature of the entity.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in Executive Compensation (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2097160
scope_conditions: systemically important financial institutions carrying implicit government guarantees

claims.claim: The impending threat of dilution from a possible conversion of investor-held contingent convertible bonds can motivate existing shareholders to become actively involved in the governance of the entity.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in Executive Compensation (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2097160
scope_conditions: investors also hold contingent convertible bonds subject to a later trigger

claims.claim: Early triggers in executive compensation improve the signaling of default risk by producing the signal while default risk is present but still somewhat remote.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in Executive Compensation (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2097160

claims.claim: Existing default risk signals were inadequate: CAMEL ratings and credit default swap pricing did not suffice to signal default risk at Lehman Brothers, Bear Stearns, or Merrill Lynch.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in Executive Compensation (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2097160
scope_conditions: the 2008 to 2009 financial crisis

claims.claim: Before conversion, executives holding securities with long-term maturities and coupon payments have incentives to manage the company with debt-holders' interests in mind.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in Executive Compensation (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2097160
scope_conditions: before any conversion into equity
strength depends on the proportion of debt in the package

claims.claim: Replacing stock options with contingent convertible bonds both lowers total executive compensation and disincentivizes short-termism and the executive focus on quarterly stock price performance.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in Executive Compensation (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2097160
scope_conditions: contingent convertible bonds substitute for equity-based compensation rather than adding to it

claims.claim: Path dependencies in United States executive compensation culture could make it difficult to lower overall executive pay or to add new design elements such as contingent convertible bonds.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in Executive Compensation (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2097160
scope_conditions: United States executive compensation practice

claims.claim: Executives paid in contingent convertible bonds have an opportunistic reason to manipulate the triggering event, because conversion at a depressed price before or during a crisis hands them cheap stock.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in Executive Compensation (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2097160
scope_conditions: executives compensated with contingent convertible bond instruments
payoff from conversion is substantial

claims.claim: Where rules and regulatory guidance are absent, fiduciary duties are the only constraint on executives, and existing fiduciary duties could prove insufficient to limit opportunism and abuse when the payoff is substantial.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in Executive Compensation (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2097160
scope_conditions: no rules or regulatory guidance on contingent convertible bond design and issuance
substantial payoff to executives

claims.claim: A mandatory holding period covering all equity securities executives hold in the entity they manage, applied after their contingent convertible bonds convert, would limit abuse of the trigger.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in Executive Compensation (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2097160
scope_conditions: after conversion of the executives' contingent convertible bonds into equity

claims.claim: If executives influence the drafting of their own trigger, opportunism within the bounds of fiduciary duty will produce suboptimal early triggers and increase the potential for abuse, because executives can use the trigger to obtain cheap stock during a crisis.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in Executive Compensation (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2097160
scope_conditions: executives involved in the executive compensation and trigger design process

claims.claim: Regulatory guidance on contingent capital design and issuance may be needed to curtail executive involvement in designing these instruments and to produce socially optimal designs.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in Executive Compensation (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2097160
scope_conditions: regulators unlikely to supply rules or best practice guidance in the near term

claims.claim: The governance benefits of traditional inside debt, incentive optimization and reduced agency costs, all depend on the entity remaining solvent, and inside debt supplies no mechanism of its own to ensure that solvency.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in Executive Compensation (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2097160
scope_conditions: inside debt without a conversion feature, such as pensions and deferred compensation

claims.claim: Contingent convertible bonds with a conversion feature add what plain inside debt lacks: an early warning system and a buffer before insolvency that can help the entity avoid default.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in Executive Compensation (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2097160
scope_conditions: conversion feature rather than write-down
trigger set before insolvency

claims.claim: Unlike the liquidation value backing traditional inside debt, equity received by executives on early conversion can still appreciate, because the early trigger creates a substantial buffer before insolvency.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in Executive Compensation (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2097160
scope_conditions: conversion occurs early, before bankruptcy

claims.claim: Before conversion, contingent convertible bonds incentivize executives to lower risk-taking because their prices are sensitive to the downside risks of SIFIs, including default risk.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in Executive Compensation (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2097160
scope_conditions: before conversion into equity
market prices for the instrument are observable

claims.claim: Against the critique that long-term debt in pay does not deter short-run risky bets because expected short-term gains exceed the discounted value of the debt, adding early-trigger contingent convertible bonds changes managers' incentives by forcing them to weigh the effects of triggering events rather than only the debt to equity mix of their portfolio.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in Executive Compensation (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2097160
scope_conditions: early trigger attached to a substantial portion of the executive's debt holdings

claims.claim: Contrary to Gordon's view that contingent convertible bonds do not address the Fuld Problem, if executive packages do not include a large equity portion, managers have no incentive to block an equity infusion in order to preserve the value of their own equity.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in Executive Compensation (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2097160
scope_conditions: a large part of equity-based executive compensation is replaced with contingent convertible bonds

claims.claim: Trigger designs that work well in institutions with the traditional mix of debt-holders and shareholders may be suboptimal once executives themselves hold contingent convertible bonds.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in Executive Compensation (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2097160
scope_conditions: executives hold debt instruments in the form of contingent convertible bonds

claims.claim: Who owns the contingent convertible bonds affects the efficiency, effectiveness, and corporate governance results of a trigger design, so ownership characteristics belong in the design analysis.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in Executive Compensation (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2097160

claims.claim: An early trigger design for contingent convertible bonds in executive compensation enables earlier signaling of default risk, increases incentives for creditors and shareholders to monitor, and increases executives' incentives to lower risk-taking.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Contingent Capital in Executive Compensation (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2097160

claims.claim: After Morrison, parties to securities transactions can be confident that U.S. law will not apply in private suits so long as their transactions are definitively located outside the United States, a certainty that did not exist under the prior conduct and effects tests.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Richard W. Painter, Forum Competition and Choice of Law Competition in Securities Law after Morrison v. National Austral (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2029983
scope_conditions: private lawsuits, not SEC or DOJ enforcement
transaction location is unambiguous

claims.claim: The authors stipulate that Choice of Law Competition is a subcategory of jurisdictional competition in which jurisdictions compete on substantive legal rules to attract contracting parties ex ante, with adjudication of disputes a secondary consideration.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Richard W. Painter, Forum Competition and Choice of Law Competition in Securities Law after Morrison v. National Austral (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2029983

claims.claim: The authors stipulate that jurisdictions which take steps only to expand the jurisdiction of their courts as venues for litigation, rather than to attract transactions, engage in Forum Competition.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Richard W. Painter, Forum Competition and Choice of Law Competition in Securities Law after Morrison v. National Austral (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2029983

claims.claim: Most Forum Competition turns on a jurisdiction's attractiveness to lawyers ex post: such jurisdictions ignore the preferences of transacting parties at the time of contracting and appeal only to the preferences of some parties and their lawyers after a dispute has arisen.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Richard W. Painter, Forum Competition and Choice of Law Competition in Securities Law after Morrison v. National Austral (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2029983
scope_conditions: applies to the ex post variant of Forum Competition, not to ex ante forum selection clauses

claims.claim: Because Morrison limits U.S. securities law to transactions inside the United States, plaintiffs' attorneys are predicted to look increasingly to European countries and other venues in which to file securities class actions and similar suits.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Richard W. Painter, Forum Competition and Choice of Law Competition in Securities Law after Morrison v. National Austral (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2029983
scope_conditions: holds for private securities class actions after Morrison

claims.claim: Jurisdictional competition adapts legal rules to changed economic circumstances faster than harmonization does, because a single jurisdiction can change its rule unilaterally whereas harmonized regimes require all jurisdictions to agree on a rule before it can change.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Richard W. Painter, Forum Competition and Choice of Law Competition in Securities Law after Morrison v. National Austral (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2029983
scope_conditions: underlying market conditions are changing
actors have imperfect information about optimal rules

claims.claim: Harmonization can fail on the merits: the harmonious rule may be the wrong rule for the problem it addresses, or it may become the wrong rule later as circumstances change.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Richard W. Painter, Forum Competition and Choice of Law Competition in Securities Law after Morrison v. National Austral (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2029983
scope_conditions: most acute in fast evolving areas such as financial regulation

claims.claim: Harmonization is politically unattainable absent either a central authority able to preempt the law of many jurisdictions or a single jurisdiction with enough economic clout to impose its rules on others, which makes harmonization especially difficult beyond national borders.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Richard W. Painter, Forum Competition and Choice of Law Competition in Securities Law after Morrison v. National Austral (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2029983
scope_conditions: cross border harmonization
no supranational preemptive authority exists

claims.claim: Harmonization invites its own defeat by creating an incentive for rogue jurisdictions to attract, into their legal systems, the private actors who do not agree with the harmonized rule.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Richard W. Painter, Forum Competition and Choice of Law Competition in Securities Law after Morrison v. National Austral (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2029983
scope_conditions: applies even within organized communities of jurisdictions such as the European Union

claims.claim: Defined geographic borders for securities transactions, the overarching assumption behind Morrison, are an unstable basis for limiting the extraterritorial reach of either private litigation or government regulation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Richard W. Painter, Forum Competition and Choice of Law Competition in Securities Law after Morrison v. National Austral (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2029983
scope_conditions: securities transactions whose location is contestable
applies to both private suits and regulatory enforcement

claims.claim: Jurisdictional competition in global securities litigation after Morrison will be bifurcated, because some jurisdictions recognize private rights of action while others do not, and some, including the United States, extend government enforcement extraterritorially where private suits are barred.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Richard W. Painter, Forum Competition and Choice of Law Competition in Securities Law after Morrison v. National Austral (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2029983
scope_conditions: post-Morrison global securities litigation

claims.claim: Bifurcation lets a party to a disputed offshore transaction reintroduce U.S. law into the civil liability regime by threatening to involve the SEC or DOJ unless the other party offers an attractive settlement.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Richard W. Painter, Forum Competition and Choice of Law Competition in Securities Law after Morrison v. National Austral (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2029983
scope_conditions: transaction located outside the United States
Section 929P enforcement remains available

claims.claim: Because Section 929P did not restore private rights of action, the most powerful weapon in plaintiffs' arsenal, the fraud-on-the-market theory in class actions, is thwarted wherever the transaction took place outside the United States.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Richard W. Painter, Forum Competition and Choice of Law Competition in Securities Law after Morrison v. National Austral (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2029983
scope_conditions: private class actions over non-U.S. transactions
SEC and DOJ actions remain possible

claims.claim: Government enforcement acts as a backstop that makes the case for choice of law freedom stronger: allowing parties to choose their legal regime is more defensible when bad choices, such as moving transactions to regimes with little regulation, do not thwart government enforcement.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Richard W. Painter, Forum Competition and Choice of Law Competition in Securities Law after Morrison v. National Austral (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2029983
scope_conditions: SEC and DOJ retain extraterritorial enforcement power under Section 929P

claims.claim: Geographic tests create the risk of a no man's land transaction: defendants may persuade the courts of every jurisdiction that the transaction took place outside their borders, leaving the transaction governed by no law and with no available forum.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Richard W. Painter, Forum Competition and Choice of Law Competition in Securities Law after Morrison v. National Austral (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2029983
scope_conditions: transactions whose geographic location is ambiguous
courts in all candidate jurisdictions apply geographic tests

claims.claim: Without an opt-out mechanism, European class sizes will likely be substantially smaller than their U.S. counterparts, which in turn depresses settlement amounts and damages awards.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Richard W. Painter, Forum Competition and Choice of Law Competition in Securities Law after Morrison v. National Austral (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2029983
scope_conditions: European collective procedures that require plaintiffs to opt in

claims.claim: The requirement that each plaintiff show individual reliance, followed in most jurisdictions outside the United States, is not merely a substantive difference: it undermines collective litigation because class procedures work only when plaintiffs share common questions of law and fact.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Richard W. Painter, Forum Competition and Choice of Law Competition in Securities Law after Morrison v. National Austral (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2029983
scope_conditions: jurisdictions that reject the fraud-on-the-market theory

claims.claim: Despite signs of movement in that direction, there is as yet no genuine European substitute for the U.S. securities class action brought under the fraud-on-the-market theory.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Richard W. Painter, Forum Competition and Choice of Law Competition in Securities Law after Morrison v. National Austral (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2029983
scope_conditions: as of the article's 2012 assessment of European collective procedures

claims.claim: The German KapMuG does not relieve trial judges of deciding the legal issues in every individual case, so it remains administratively burdensome even though its model case judgment binds the trial courts.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Richard W. Painter, Forum Competition and Choice of Law Competition in Securities Law after Morrison v. National Austral (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2029983
scope_conditions: German model case proceedings for capital markets claims

claims.claim: The WCAM's requirement that a court evaluate procedural and substantive fairness and the efficiency of the settlement lets the Dutch system avoid blackmail settlements, where a defendant pays simply to escape endless proceedings and reputational loss.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Richard W. Painter, Forum Competition and Choice of Law Competition in Securities Law after Morrison v. National Austral (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2029983
scope_conditions: Dutch collective settlements certified by the Amsterdam Court of Appeal

claims.claim: The Dutch unfair trade practice and misrepresentation provisions invoked in Fortis, taken together, approximate the legal protections available in the United States under Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5, which makes the Dutch legal system a possible avenue for circumventing the restrictions imposed by Morrison.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Richard W. Painter, Forum Competition and Choice of Law Competition in Securities Law after Morrison v. National Austral (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2029983
scope_conditions: claims brought under Dutch civil law and the Dutch Financial Supervision Act

claims.claim: In Converium the Amsterdam Court of Appeal declared an international collective settlement binding on the parties even though the class members had only tenuous connections to the Netherlands.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Richard W. Painter, Forum Competition and Choice of Law Competition in Securities Law after Morrison v. National Austral (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2029983
scope_conditions: WCAM collective settlement proceedings
none of the defendants and only a few plaintiffs were domiciled in the Netherlands
alleged wrongdoing occurred outside the Netherlands and claims were not brought under Dutch law

claims.claim: By approving U.S.-style fee arrangements, the Converium decision adds an important incentive for plaintiffs' attorneys to bring claims in the Netherlands.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Richard W. Painter, Forum Competition and Choice of Law Competition in Securities Law after Morrison v. National Austral (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2029983
scope_conditions: attorney fees of about twenty percent of the settlement payment

claims.claim: The Converium fee holding is a weak predictor of Dutch practice because lead counsel's work in that case was performed largely within the American legal system and by U.S. law firms, so it remains to be seen whether a case litigated in Dutch courts without U.S. exposure would yield a comparable fee structure.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Richard W. Painter, Forum Competition and Choice of Law Competition in Securities Law after Morrison v. National Austral (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2029983
scope_conditions: cases litigated in Dutch courts without exposure to the U.S. legal system

claims.claim: The Netherlands is already Europe's most attractive venue for collective settlements because it is the only European country that allows a collective settlement in mass litigation to bind all class members who do not opt out.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Richard W. Painter, Forum Competition and Choice of Law Competition in Securities Law after Morrison v. National Austral (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2029983
scope_conditions: European jurisdictions as of 2012

claims.claim: Given the Fortis and Converium decisions, it is conceivable that Dutch courts will expand their extraterritorial reach beyond the enforcement of settlements to cases litigated as class actions.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Richard W. Painter, Forum Competition and Choice of Law Competition in Securities Law after Morrison v. National Austral (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2029983
scope_conditions: continuation of the trend visible in Fortis and Converium

claims.claim: Because the Dutch Supreme Court's World Online presumption of reliance can be extended to ad hoc disclosure violations and misleading periodic reports, the Dutch legal system could compete effectively with the United States by lowering the crucial reliance threshold in securities actions.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Richard W. Painter, Forum Competition and Choice of Law Competition in Securities Law after Morrison v. National Austral (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2029983
scope_conditions: Dutch courts extend World Online beyond prospectus liability

claims.claim: The WCAM requirement that a court approved foundation pursue the action makes the Dutch regime more burdensome than the U.S. system, which requires only a lead plaintiff and class approval.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Richard W. Painter, Forum Competition and Choice of Law Competition in Securities Law after Morrison v. National Austral (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2029983
scope_conditions: Dutch collective proceedings under the WCAM

claims.claim: The WCAM's structural limits could reduce the number of successful settlements: while the largest cases such as Shell and Fortis give plaintiffs enough leverage to force large settlements, smaller cases may not be successfully settled in Dutch courts.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Richard W. Painter, Forum Competition and Choice of Law Competition in Securities Law after Morrison v. National Austral (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2029983
scope_conditions: smaller claims with limited settlement leverage

claims.claim: Canada could engage in Forum Competition with the United States if its courts allow suits under Canadian law over all transactions in securities listed for trading in Canada, even transactions executed in the United States, assembling a class of Canadian and U.S. investors that Morrison forbids in U.S. courts.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Richard W. Painter, Forum Competition and Choice of Law Competition in Securities Law after Morrison v. National Austral (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2029983
scope_conditions: Canadian courts adopt a posture different from U.S. courts applying Morrison

claims.claim: Morrison's transactional test could prove relatively short lived because it is rooted in geography while an increasing number of securities transactions defy geographical boundaries.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Richard W. Painter, Forum Competition and Choice of Law Competition in Securities Law after Morrison v. National Austral (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2029983
scope_conditions: transactions off organized exchanges and on exchanges that cross borders

claims.claim: The Second Circuit's Absolute Activist test, locating a transaction where title transfers or irrevocable liability is incurred, is easy to manipulate: parties can arrange for irrevocable liability to arise outside the United States, for example by conditioning liability on approval by an agent located abroad.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Richard W. Painter, Forum Competition and Choice of Law Competition in Securities Law after Morrison v. National Austral (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2029983
scope_conditions: private securities transactions off organized exchanges

claims.claim: The authors propose a rule under which, unless a transaction is unambiguously inside the United States, the transaction is not inside the United States if the parties have expressly stated that intent; this can be harmonized with both Morrison and the existing statutory framework.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Richard W. Painter, Forum Competition and Choice of Law Competition in Securities Law after Morrison v. National Austral (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2029983
scope_conditions: geographically ambiguous transactions only
does not apply to transactions unequivocally inside the United States

claims.claim: The race to the bottom objection to a contract based approach is weaker than assumed because a race to the bottom requires the consent of both buyers and sellers, and the objection assumes that buyers will simply accept whatever securities law sellers choose.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Richard W. Painter, Forum Competition and Choice of Law Competition in Securities Law after Morrison v. National Austral (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2029983
scope_conditions: private transactions where geography is ambiguous and buyers are sophisticated
weaker as an objection for exchange traded securities

claims.claim: The SEC, rather than the courts or Congress, is the institution positioned to implement a choice of law regime for securities transactions, through rulemaking.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Richard W. Painter, Forum Competition and Choice of Law Competition in Securities Law after Morrison v. National Austral (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2029983
scope_conditions: Chevron deference to agency interpretation of statutes it administers

claims.claim: U.S. courts have only a limited capacity to integrate parties' choice of law into a post-Morrison regime for defining transaction location, and adding variables raises the risk of inconsistent case law across districts and circuits.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Richard W. Painter, Forum Competition and Choice of Law Competition in Securities Law after Morrison v. National Austral (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2029983
scope_conditions: absent a clear mandate in Morrison and given the statutory bar on opting out

claims.claim: A contract selecting non-U.S. securities law can fail entirely: if the chosen jurisdiction's courts decline jurisdiction because the transaction did not clear there or the parties lack a local presence, the contract may as a practical matter mean that no law applies.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Richard W. Painter, Forum Competition and Choice of Law Competition in Securities Law after Morrison v. National Austral (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2029983
scope_conditions: the chosen foreign jurisdiction must actually accept jurisdiction and apply its law
one party may be better informed about this risk than the other

claims.claim: Choice of law should replace the geographically based transactional test in those circumstances where geography is ambiguous.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Richard W. Painter, Forum Competition and Choice of Law Competition in Securities Law after Morrison v. National Austral (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2029983
scope_conditions: limited to transactions whose geographic location is ambiguous

claims.claim: If Forum Competition between the United States and Europe expands, the acceptable outer bounds of jurisdictional competition may eventually have to be defined by treaty or other multilateral agreement.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Richard W. Painter, Forum Competition and Choice of Law Competition in Securities Law after Morrison v. National Austral (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2029983
scope_conditions: depends on future expansion of Dutch and other non-U.S. jurisdiction

claims.claim: Although many jurisdictions may protect investors less well than the United States, it is not at all certain that U.S. law does a better job of deterring securities fraud.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Richard W. Painter, Forum Competition and Choice of Law Competition in Securities Law after Morrison v. National Austral (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2029983
scope_conditions: comparison of deterrence, not of investor protection generally

claims.claim: Freedom from supervision and disclosure obligations was functional rather than incidental for hedge funds: it enabled successful fund launches, helped generate higher returns, and attracted investors, which is why manager registration is contested.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Fund Manager Registration Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2150377
scope_conditions: hedge funds operating before the Dodd-Frank Act
funds investing in global markets

claims.claim: The immediate deregistration of hedge fund advisers following Goldstein v. SEC is revealed-preference evidence of the industry's opposition to registration and disclosure requirements, not merely a technical response to the vacatur.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Fund Manager Registration Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2150377
scope_conditions: advisers who had registered under the SEC's 2004 rule
2006, immediately after the Goldstein decision

claims.claim: The client counting safe harbor, which let an adviser count a pooled entity rather than each investor as a single client, allowed advisers to manage large amounts of securities indirectly for several hundreds of investors across multiple hedge funds while remaining outside registration and supervision.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Fund Manager Registration Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2150377
scope_conditions: under the 1985 safe harbor as broadened in 1997
before the Dodd-Frank Act repealed the private adviser exemption

claims.claim: Before Dodd-Frank the perimeter of hedge fund regulation was set by SEC no-action letters on client counting and by courts that gave very limited and sometimes contradictory guidance, so compliance rested on an unstable and uncertain base rather than on rules.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Fund Manager Registration Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2150377
scope_conditions: the period between the 1968 Merrill Lynch action and the 1985 safe harbor rule
advisers seeking to stay exempt from securities regulation

claims.claim: Losing the private adviser exemption imposed a bundle of obligations, disclosure duties and code of ethics requirements on top of inspections and record keeping, and the direct consequence was significantly higher legal fees for hedge funds.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Fund Manager Registration Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2150377
scope_conditions: advisers subject to the SEC's 2004 registration rule

claims.claim: The SEC's 2004 attempt to reach hedge fund advisers failed as a matter of administrative law: in July 2006 the D.C. Circuit vacated the hedge fund rule in Goldstein v. SEC as an instance of arbitrary rulemaking, because the SEC had no authority to define a term the Advisers Act left undefined.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Fund Manager Registration Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2150377
scope_conditions: SEC rulemaking under the Investment Advisers Act
where the statutory term client is not otherwise defined

claims.claim: Under the Private Fund Investment Advisers Registration Act, hedge funds with more than $150 million in assets under management must register as investment advisers and disclose information about their trades and portfolios to the SEC, making assets under management the operative trigger for the regime.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Fund Manager Registration Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2150377
scope_conditions: advisers acting solely as advisers to private funds
assets under management measured in the United States

claims.claim: Because Title IV's registration exemptions are broad enough to threaten the rule they qualify, the Dodd-Frank Act deliberately gives the SEC rulemaking authority to keep the exemptions from swallowing the rules.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Fund Manager Registration Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2150377
scope_conditions: exemptions for private fund advisers, venture capital advisers, and foreign private advisers under Title IV

claims.claim: Revised Form ADV requires advisers to report gross rather than net regulatory assets under management and narrows their discretion to include or exclude assets, so the registration threshold becomes harder to manage down through reporting choices.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Fund Manager Registration Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2150377
scope_conditions: advisers filing the November 2011 revised Form ADV

claims.claim: Form PF reporting achieves broad coverage of systemic exposure with narrow coverage of firms: the SEC expects the small set of large filers to account for eighty percent of total hedge fund assets under management in the United States.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Fund Manager Registration Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2150377
scope_conditions: advisers with at least $1.5 billion in RAUM attributable to hedge funds
SEC estimates at the time of Form PF adoption

claims.claim: Quarterly rather than annual Form PF updating for large hedge fund advisers is designed for timeliness: its purpose is to give the Financial Stability Oversight Council data current enough to identify emerging trends in systemic risk.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Fund Manager Registration Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2150377
scope_conditions: advisers with at least $1.5 billion RAUM attributable to hedge funds

claims.claim: This Article reports the first survey study of hedge fund advisers conducted after the SEC's registration effective date, drawing on a population of 1267 private fund advisers who registered before March 30, 2012.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Fund Manager Registration Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2150377
scope_conditions: United States private fund advisers
registration effective date of March 30, 2012

claims.claim: The hedge fund industry's concern with confidentiality and privacy is itself an obstacle to empirical research: it made obtaining a substantial effective sample size for this study difficult, independent of the survey design.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Fund Manager Registration Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2150377
scope_conditions: surveys of hedge fund managers
questions touching firm or client financial status

claims.claim: Persistent multi-channel follow-up, by fax, e-mail, and telephone, yielded ninety-four completed surveys, a 7.42% response rate from a population of 1267, which is substantially higher than response rates in prior surveys of this industry.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Fund Manager Registration Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2150377
scope_conditions: population of 1267 registered private fund advisers
data collected within three months of March 30, 2012

claims.claim: Mandated disclosure does not automatically produce usable public data: although Form ADV requires advisers to disclose chief compliance officer contact information, the SEC dataset omitted it and contained no e-mail addresses, so researchers could not reach the officers responsible for compliance.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Fund Manager Registration Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2150377
scope_conditions: the IARD dataset and filed Form ADVs as of 2012

claims.claim: The standard remedies for selection bias are not reliably corrective: simulation studies show that many techniques used to prevent selection bias problems have mixed success rates, can worsen rather than improve estimates, and may skew results under ordinary circumstances.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Fund Manager Registration Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2150377
scope_conditions: statistical corrections for sample selection bias in social research

claims.claim: A treatment and control design is unavailable for studying registration effects, because managers who did not have to register have no exposure to the treatment and therefore cannot generate informative responses about its effects.

scope_conditions: survey research on the effects of mandatory registration
where the treatment is exposure to the registration requirement itself

claims.claim: Managers who avoided registration by restructuring, for example by changing organizational form or assets under management, are practically and administratively very difficult to identify, so the population that adapted away from the rule remains largely unobservable to researchers.

scope_conditions: identification of advisers who altered structure or AUM to avoid registration

claims.claim: Comparison of the responding sample against the full registered population on Form ADV parameters shows the sample is not biased toward any particular subgroup of hedge fund advisers, and gives no indication that respondents differ from nonrespondents.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Fund Manager Registration Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2150377
scope_conditions: parameters reported on Form ADV such as organizational form, client numbers, adviser type, region, AUM, and advisory services

claims.claim: Advisers responded to Dodd-Frank registration mainly through administrative and advisory adjustments: the most common actions were outsourcing compliance work, hiring additional counsel, instituting new record keeping policies, hiring additional staff, changing marketing materials, and changing investor communications.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Fund Manager Registration Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2150377
scope_conditions: survey respondents, n=94
within three months of the March 30, 2012 registration effective date

claims.claim: Structural and portfolio level responses to registration were rare: only a minority of respondents severed an advising relationship, changed a fund's legal structure, liquidated positions, changed investment styles, changed portfolio structure, or closed funds to new investors.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Fund Manager Registration Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2150377
scope_conditions: survey respondents, n=94
measured shortly after the registration effective date

claims.claim: A majority of surveyed advisers, 72.09%, do not plan any strategic response to the Dodd-Frank Act registration and reporting requirements.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Fund Manager Registration Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2150377
scope_conditions: survey respondents to Question 3
shortly after the registration effective date

claims.claim: Compliance with the registration and disclosure requirements cost a majority of surveyed advisers between $50,000 and $200,000, while a significant minority estimated total compliance cost from $200,000 to over $400,000.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Fund Manager Registration Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2150377
scope_conditions: survey respondents estimating cost of compliance with Dodd-Frank registration and disclosure rules

claims.claim: The time burden of complying with all federal rules applicable to hedge fund advisers has a median of 500 hours per year, with three quarters of respondents at 750 hours or less and a quarter above that, so the burden distribution is skewed rather than uniform.

scope_conditions: respondents to survey Question 6.a.ii
compliance with all federal rules including Treasury, SEC, and CFTC

claims.claim: Among the minority of advisers who do factor regulation into fund sizing, the pressure runs in both directions: about 25% would go smaller to avoid regulatory hassle while about 50% would grow or need a certain size to cover the increased expenses.
