scope_conditions: respondents who answered yes to survey Question 7.b

claims.claim: The Form PF quarterly reporting threshold of $1.5 billion in assets under management is not a binding sizing constraint for most advisers: 80.46% would not take it into account in determining fund size, while 19.54% would.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Fund Manager Registration Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2150377
scope_conditions: respondents to survey Question 10
measured shortly after the registration effective date

claims.claim: Where the Form PF quarterly reporting threshold does influence behavior, it distorts fund size downward: a majority of the advisers who take the threshold into account plan to stay under $1.5 billion in assets under management, and some would close funds to new investors to do so.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Fund Manager Registration Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2150377
scope_conditions: the 19.54% of respondents who would take the Form PF threshold into account

claims.claim: Registration and disclosure costs had not reached investors at the time of the survey: 76.09% of respondents reported that their investors' rate of return was not affected, while 23.91% believed investors would be affected.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Fund Manager Registration Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2150377
scope_conditions: respondents to survey Questions 11a and 11b
measured within three months of the registration effective date

claims.claim: The incidence of Dodd-Frank compliance cost falls on the management company rather than the fund: the responses indicate that the management company bears the brunt of registration and disclosure costs, and whether and how those expenses will be passed to investors over time is unclear.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Fund Manager Registration Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2150377
scope_conditions: the pool of respondents in this study
short run, within months of the registration effective date

claims.claim: Of the respondents reporting an effect on management company profits, 87.50% attributed it specifically to increased costs and decreased profits caused by the registration and reporting requirements.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Fund Manager Registration Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2150377
scope_conditions: the 78.26% of respondents who reported that management company profits were affected

claims.claim: Registration and disclosure did not push advisers to change what they invest in: only 2.44% of respondents said they would have to change strategy significantly over five years, while 4.88% expressly reported no strategy change.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Fund Manager Registration Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2150377
scope_conditions: respondents to survey Question 4 on effects over the next five years

claims.claim: Respondents identified the creation of barriers to entry as an industry level effect of the registration and disclosure requirements, because the rules make the market environment for private funds less attractive to new entrants.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Fund Manager Registration Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2150377
scope_conditions: respondent projections for the private fund industry over five years
survey Question 5 response clusters

claims.claim: The compliance burden has raised the minimum viable scale for launching a hedge fund: an adviser reports that the capital needed to start a fund in New York rose from roughly $25 to $50 million to at least $100 million because of the increased cost of compliance with the registration and disclosure requirements.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Fund Manager Registration Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2150377
scope_conditions: startup hedge funds in New York
single respondent account highlighted by the Author

claims.claim: Prior surveys of hedge fund manager expectations left the central questions unanswered because they were fielded before the registration effective date and used substantially smaller samples, so they measured anticipation rather than experience.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Fund Manager Registration Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2150377
scope_conditions: surveys conducted before March 30, 2012
including the EisnerAmper and Rothstein Kass studies

claims.claim: Despite documented cost concerns, the hedge fund industry appears to be only modestly affected by the Dodd-Frank reporting and disclosure requirements and is adapting well to the new regulatory environment.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Fund Manager Registration Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2150377
scope_conditions: the first months after the March 30, 2012 registration effective date
survey respondents, n=94

claims.claim: Strategic adjustment to registration is a function of firm size: firms that planned a strategic response to Dodd-Frank were smaller than firms that did not.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Fund Manager Registration Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2150377
scope_conditions: survey respondents, n=94, comparing the twenty-four advisers planning a strategic response with the sixty-two who did not

claims.claim: Quick absorption of registration costs does not settle the policy question: even if advisers absorb the reported cost implications relatively quickly after registration, the long-term cost implications of registration and reporting obligations could still affect the private fund industry.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Fund Manager Registration Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2150377
scope_conditions: private fund industry beyond the short observation window of this study

claims.claim: Mandatory reporting does not guarantee informative reporting: anecdotal evidence indicates that advisers can present the information required in Forms ADV and PF in ways that in effect flatten out and sanitize the disclosures.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Fund Manager Registration Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2150377
scope_conditions: anecdotal evidence, the level of sanitizing cannot be verified

claims.claim: If advisers sanitize their Form ADV and Form PF filings, the disclosures become less useful for FSOC and SEC evaluation and undermine the very determination of systemic risk posed by private funds that the reporting regime was built to enable.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Fund Manager Registration Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2150377
scope_conditions: to the extent disclosures are in fact sanitized, which the Author states cannot be verified

claims.claim: The study's findings are bounded in time: because the data was collected within three months of the registration effective date, the study shows trends and perceptions but does not provide insights on the long-term implications of the registration and disclosure requirements.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Fund Manager Registration Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2150377
scope_conditions: data collected within three months of March 30, 2012

claims.claim: Government bailouts of systemically important financial institutions create strong incentives for those institutions to externalize the cost of their risk taking onto taxpayers.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Initial Reflections on the Possible Application of Contingent Capital in Corporate Governance (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1998455
scope_conditions: where governments provide bailout funding to systemically important financial institutions

claims.claim: The implicit guarantees contained in a bailout multiply the incentives for systemically important financial institutions to increase leverage, because those guarantees make debt cheaper than equity.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Initial Reflections on the Possible Application of Contingent Capital in Corporate Governance (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1998455
scope_conditions: where market participants expect governments to bail out systemically important firms

claims.claim: Because governments prioritize the rescue of systemically important financial institutions over other entities, those institutions are incentivized to adopt similar risk profiles and to correlate their risks.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Initial Reflections on the Possible Application of Contingent Capital in Corporate Governance (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1998455
scope_conditions: where governments visibly prioritize SIFI bailouts because of systemic implications

claims.claim: Because both European regulatory initiatives and the United States academic debate concentrate on the technical design features of contingent capital securities, the possible corporate governance applications of those securities are mostly ignored.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Initial Reflections on the Possible Application of Contingent Capital in Corporate Governance (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1998455
scope_conditions: state of the debate as of 2012 in Europe and the United States

claims.claim: Combined with other corporate governance mechanisms, contingent capital securities function as an internal, institution specific mechanism that could fill the void left by regulators' apparent inability to supervise financial institutions effectively.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Initial Reflections on the Possible Application of Contingent Capital in Corporate Governance (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1998455
scope_conditions: where CCS are used alongside, not instead of, other corporate governance mechanisms

claims.claim: The anecdotal record of ethically questionable conduct by leaders of systemically important financial institutions is not dispositive and does not establish an underlying trend, but it does show that some of the most pervasive cases of unethical conduct involved such institutions.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Initial Reflections on the Possible Application of Contingent Capital in Corporate Governance (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1998455
scope_conditions: based on the high profile cases surveyed: Citigroup, Bear Stearns, AIG, Merrill Lynch, Lehman Brothers

claims.claim: For purposes of this Article contingent capital is stipulated to be the predefined conversion of a certain percentage of a financial institution's debt securities into equity securities.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Initial Reflections on the Possible Application of Contingent Capital in Corporate Governance (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1998455
scope_conditions: stipulated definition used throughout the Article

claims.claim: Contingent capital contributes to minimizing moral hazard by internalizing bank failure costs, that is, by placing those costs on the institution's own security holders rather than on the public.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Initial Reflections on the Possible Application of Contingent Capital in Corporate Governance (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1998455
scope_conditions: where the conversion feature actually shifts failure costs to CCS holders and shareholders

claims.claim: Installing contingent capital can be more efficient than raising capital requirements, because the capital injection becomes available only when it is needed and only enough securities convert to recapitalize the firm.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Initial Reflections on the Possible Application of Contingent Capital in Corporate Governance (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1998455
scope_conditions: assumes a functioning trigger that fires at the right time
assumes incremental or calibrated conversion

claims.claim: The threat of dilution of stock holdings, combined with the threat of loss on conversion, reduces the pressure shareholders place on the management of systemically important financial institutions to take higher risks.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Initial Reflections on the Possible Application of Contingent Capital in Corporate Governance (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1998455
scope_conditions: where conversion dilutes existing common shareholders

claims.claim: Trigger designs can be ranked by the certainty they give market participants: institution specific triggers presumably grant the most certainty, while regulatory trigger designs provide lower levels of certainty.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Initial Reflections on the Possible Application of Contingent Capital in Corporate Governance (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1998455
scope_conditions: comparing institution specific triggers against regulatory or systemic triggers

claims.claim: Converting contingent capital securities prematurely, while the institution can still operate without an equity injection, dissipates the benefit: the injection is no longer available at the later moment when the institution cannot obtain other funding.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Initial Reflections on the Possible Application of Contingent Capital in Corporate Governance (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1998455
scope_conditions: where the trigger fires before the institution has exhausted other funding sources

claims.claim: Converting contingent capital securities too late makes the capital injection superfluous, because by that stage the institution may face unresolvable difficulties that a capital injection can only marginally soften, and conversion may not suffice once the institution has entered resolution.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Initial Reflections on the Possible Application of Contingent Capital in Corporate Governance (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1998455
scope_conditions: where the trigger fires after the institution's difficulties have become unresolvable
especially once the institution has entered the resolution stage

claims.claim: Contingent capital by itself, without additional measures and supplemental corporate governance improvements, may not prevent firm failure; its real potential unfolds only when it supplements other corporate governance improvements.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Initial Reflections on the Possible Application of Contingent Capital in Corporate Governance (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1998455
scope_conditions: where contingent capital is deployed as a standalone regulatory tool

claims.claim: Divergent national definitions of Tier 1 capital produce a distortion: financial institutions in countries with stricter definitions that exclude contingent capital appear to hold less capital and thinner capital cushions than institutions in countries with broader definitions, and investors may read that appearance as a negative attribute.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Initial Reflections on the Possible Application of Contingent Capital in Corporate Governance (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1998455
scope_conditions: absent harmonized EU wide or international standards for Tier 1 capital

claims.claim: If a market evolves in which contingent capital designs appear to provide sufficient protection against systemic risk and contagion, decision makers may come to rely on the design of those securities and neglect their own role as monitors.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Initial Reflections on the Possible Application of Contingent Capital in Corporate Governance (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1998455
scope_conditions: theoretical possibility flagged by the author
presupposes CCS designs that appear protective

claims.claim: Contingent capital rules could contribute to overriding the moral reasoning of decision makers, in which case contingent capital would actually increase, not reduce, risk incentives for institutions that are too big to fail.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Initial Reflections on the Possible Application of Contingent Capital in Corporate Governance (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1998455
scope_conditions: where decision makers operate under an illusion of heightened protection
where the underlying contingent capital design is flawed

claims.claim: Regular corporate governance controls may not work in systemically important financial institutions, because those institutions are considered too big to fail and their leaders, anticipating a bailout commitment, are incentivized to shift their risk preferences upwards.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Initial Reflections on the Possible Application of Contingent Capital in Corporate Governance (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1998455
scope_conditions: where the institution is treated as too big to fail and a bailout is anticipated

claims.claim: Switching to contingent capital financing could reinforce rather than dampen risk incentives, and these distorted risk incentives are a drawback of contingent capital issuances.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Initial Reflections on the Possible Application of Contingent Capital in Corporate Governance (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1998455
scope_conditions: where the issuing institution is already treated as too big to fail
the author notes these drawbacks are unlikely to materialize in the near term given the nascent market

claims.claim: A mandatory contingent capital issuance regime induces institutions to buy their competitors' securities to satisfy regulatory obligations rather than for economic reasons, and the resulting cross holdings among systemically important institutions undermine the ability of contingent capital to limit systemic risk and contagion.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Initial Reflections on the Possible Application of Contingent Capital in Corporate Governance (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1998455
scope_conditions: under a regime requiring mandatory CCS issuance
where SIFIs are permitted to purchase each other's CCS

claims.claim: Where institutions hold each other's contingent capital and share similar risk profiles, they will be hesitant after conversion to vote for necessary organizational changes at a competitor or otherwise exercise their voting rights, because they are similarly exposed and may face reciprocal voting power.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Initial Reflections on the Possible Application of Contingent Capital in Corporate Governance (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1998455
scope_conditions: where SIFIs hold similar risk profiles and CCS positions in similarly exposed entities
especially where cross holdings are reciprocal

claims.claim: Absent cross holdings, the opposite conflict arises: institutions holding a competitor's converted contingent capital could be tempted to exercise their voting rights against the interests of that competitor.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Initial Reflections on the Possible Application of Contingent Capital in Corporate Governance (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1998455
scope_conditions: where a SIFI holds a competitor's CCS without a reciprocal position
after a conversion to equity has been triggered

claims.claim: Coupon rates between seven and nine and a half percent attracted sufficient investor interest in European contingent capital securities to establish what appears to be a sustainable market in those securities.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Initial Reflections on the Possible Application of Contingent Capital in Corporate Governance (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1998455
scope_conditions: European CCS issuances through 2011
based on the Lloyds, Credit Suisse and Bank of Cyprus offerings and industry interviews

claims.claim: The combination of demonstrated investor interest and an underdeveloped regulatory structure in the United States presents a unique opportunity to experiment with contingent capital designs and with their application to the corporate governance of systemically important financial institutions.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Initial Reflections on the Possible Application of Contingent Capital in Corporate Governance (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1998455
scope_conditions: United States market conditions as of 2012
structurally different debt and equity markets from Europe

claims.claim: The political economy of financial regulation ensures that the expansion of regulatory oversight induced by Dodd-Frank will be followed by a phase of relaxation, since historically the introduction of regulatory regimes after a crisis is followed by a gradual easing of regulatory strictures.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Initial Reflections on the Possible Application of Contingent Capital in Corporate Governance (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1998455
scope_conditions: post crisis regulatory regimes generally
based on historical patterns of financial regulation

claims.claim: Harmonization and coordination can facilitate experimentation and learning, but experimentation is most effective when several different approaches are tried simultaneously in different jurisdictions.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Initial Reflections on the Possible Application of Contingent Capital in Corporate Governance (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1998455
scope_conditions: where multiple jurisdictions are free to adopt divergent rules

claims.claim: Where jurisdictions are not compelled to agree on the same rule, some jurisdiction will try a different rule, and will do so more quickly, when changed economic circumstances make a different rule optimal.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Initial Reflections on the Possible Application of Contingent Capital in Corporate Governance (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1998455
scope_conditions: where jurisdictions are not compelled to converge on a single rule
where underlying economic circumstances change so that a different rule would be optimal

claims.claim: Contingent capital securities approximate the characteristics of a quasi-public good: just as ships cannot readily be excluded from a lighthouse, systemically important institutions benefit from the issuance of contingent capital by other such institutions whenever the design minimizes systemic risk and contagion.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Initial Reflections on the Possible Application of Contingent Capital in Corporate Governance (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1998455
scope_conditions: only if the CCS design actually minimizes systemic risk and contagion

claims.claim: The social welfare maximization potential of contingent capital securities is lower if their design features are left entirely to private ordering, because private parties do not necessarily structure those features with a view toward the common good, the avoidance of future bailouts, or the limitation of systemic risk and contagion.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Initial Reflections on the Possible Application of Contingent Capital in Corporate Governance (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1998455
scope_conditions: where regulators leave CCS design features entirely to industry groups and private parties

claims.claim: Under strong institutional and cultural forces, decision makers in financial institutions tend to compartmentalize their lives and disconnect their moral reasoning from their conduct in the workplace, so that even a leader with strong personal values can engage in questionable conduct.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Initial Reflections on the Possible Application of Contingent Capital in Corporate Governance (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1998455
scope_conditions: where industry, institutional and peer pressure shape decision making

claims.claim: Issuing contingent capital securities with a conversion feature is a way for a banking entity to signal to its market that it will adhere to stricter standards, ethical or otherwise.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Initial Reflections on the Possible Application of Contingent Capital in Corporate Governance (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1998455
scope_conditions: where the market can observe and interpret the issuance as a commitment
the author notes the signaling effect of any particular issuance is difficult to ascertain

claims.claim: A contingent capital design that increases voting rights on conversion allows systemically important institutions to lower risk taking implicitly and to achieve an indirect, institution specific form of corporate governance reform through increased checks and balances.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Initial Reflections on the Possible Application of Contingent Capital in Corporate Governance (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1998455
scope_conditions: where CCS are issued with a voting rights increase upon conversion
issuance may be voluntary or mandatory

claims.claim: Because the threat of a change of control leads leaders to take fewer risks in order to avoid triggering conversion, a contingent capital design with increased voting rights allows those leaders to act more in accordance with their moral convictions and conscience.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Initial Reflections on the Possible Application of Contingent Capital in Corporate Governance (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1998455
scope_conditions: where conversion carries a credible threat of change of control
where shareholders respond by allowing management more discretion over risk taking

claims.claim: Management incentives for risk control are heightened upon conversion, especially where management knows that holders of converted contingent capital would command a majority vote, with or without institutional shareholders.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Initial Reflections on the Possible Application of Contingent Capital in Corporate Governance (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1998455
scope_conditions: depends on the volume of CCS issuance, which determines the influence of CCS holders

claims.claim: Treating the price of contingent capital securities as an indicator of how much people care about market integrity and moral hazard would require altruistic motives on the part of purchasers, and the author doubts this: the nascent market appears to have been built on investors' expectation of above average returns.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Initial Reflections on the Possible Application of Contingent Capital in Corporate Governance (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1998455
scope_conditions: based on the observed nascent market in CCS

claims.claim: If central banks were to purchase contingent capital securities issued by systemically important institutions in the primary or secondary market as part of monetary policy, the prospect of internalizing bank failure costs would be undermined, and primary market purchases could also undermine market participants' confidence in these instruments.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Initial Reflections on the Possible Application of Contingent Capital in Corporate Governance (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1998455
scope_conditions: where central banks are permitted to purchase CCS issued by SIFIs

claims.claim: Combining the existing prioritization of bailouts for systemically important institutions with central bank purchases of their contingent capital in a given jurisdiction would further incentivize those institutions to adopt similar risk profiles and correlate their risks.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Initial Reflections on the Possible Application of Contingent Capital in Corporate Governance (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1998455
scope_conditions: in a jurisdiction where both bailout prioritization and central bank CCS purchases occur

claims.claim: Rather than banning purchases by systemically important institutions of each other's contingent capital, which could be detrimental to market evolution, the design should require disclosure of the purchaser's identity and approval by the issuer.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Initial Reflections on the Possible Application of Contingent Capital in Corporate Governance (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1998455
scope_conditions: where the concern is competitors acquiring voting rights as equity holders upon conversion

claims.claim: An outright retroactive charge for government subsidies or for actions taken by regulators could backfire, because it would legitimize the bailout and perpetuate its socially suboptimal consequences.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Initial Reflections on the Possible Application of Contingent Capital in Corporate Governance (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1998455
scope_conditions: where the counter-subsidy takes the form of a retroactive charge on bailout recipients

claims.claim: Contingent capital can facilitate an incentive structure that lets regulators rely partially on private party contracting for the design of these securities while still accounting for systemic risk.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Initial Reflections on the Possible Application of Contingent Capital in Corporate Governance (2012). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=1998455
scope_conditions: where a general regulatory framework enables rather than displaces private ordering

claims.claim: The nearly insurmountable standard for liability in oversight cases in the United States undermines the signalling of the expected standard of conduct, and this could have long-term implications for American corporate law.
claims.citation: Kaal, A Comparative Perspective on the Limitations of the Duty of Oversight – A Comment on Lisa Fairfax (2013)
scope_conditions: United States, Delaware corporate law
oversight or duty to monitor claims

claims.claim: Stable rules may not suffice to make directors' oversight role more robust, so contractual and quasi law forms of dynamic governance are a promising supplement for improving the duty of oversight.
claims.citation: Kaal, A Comparative Perspective on the Limitations of the Duty of Oversight – A Comment on Lisa Fairfax (2013)
scope_conditions: United States corporate governance
duty of oversight

claims.claim: Without a workable duty of oversight, corporate directors who seek to comply with the oversight duty lack meaningful guidance about the conduct expected of them.
claims.citation: Kaal, A Comparative Perspective on the Limitations of the Duty of Oversight – A Comment on Lisa Fairfax (2013)
scope_conditions: doctrine of oversight remains immature and incoherent

claims.claim: Because directors serve part-time as outsiders, it is unreasonable to expect them to have the knowledge, capacity, and expertise needed to monitor effectively the business affairs of large and increasingly complex corporations.
claims.citation: Kaal, A Comparative Perspective on the Limitations of the Duty of Oversight – A Comment on Lisa Fairfax (2013)
scope_conditions: large and complex modern corporations
outside directors serving part time

claims.claim: Under Delaware law as applied in In re Citigroup, directors' incorrect evaluation of business risk and their inability to predict the future do not violate the duty of oversight, so the Caremark duty to monitor is not extended to business risk.
claims.citation: Kaal, A Comparative Perspective on the Limitations of the Duty of Oversight – A Comment on Lisa Fairfax (2013)
scope_conditions: Delaware law
claims framed as failures to monitor business risk

claims.claim: Losses alone are not sufficient to hold directors personally liable for taking risks that lead to those losses, because risk is inherent in maximizing shareholder value.
claims.citation: Kaal, A Comparative Perspective on the Limitations of the Duty of Oversight – A Comment on Lisa Fairfax (2013)
scope_conditions: Delaware law
risk taking that produces corporate losses

claims.claim: Oversight liability in Delaware can be established only on a showing that the directors knew they were not discharging their fiduciary duties or consciously disregarded their responsibilities.
claims.citation: Kaal, A Comparative Perspective on the Limitations of the Duty of Oversight – A Comment on Lisa Fairfax (2013)
scope_conditions: Delaware oversight litigation

claims.claim: Delaware's signalling of expected conduct is undermined when the state simultaneously imposes a near insurmountable standard for liability in cases involving breaches of the duty of oversight.
claims.citation: Kaal, A Comparative Perspective on the Limitations of the Duty of Oversight – A Comment on Lisa Fairfax (2013)
scope_conditions: Delaware as the signalling jurisdiction
oversight breach claims

claims.claim: Courts often provide very specific language about the standard of conduct expected of directors, but lawyers do not sufficiently communicate that expected conduct to directors.
claims.citation: Kaal, A Comparative Perspective on the Limitations of the Duty of Oversight – A Comment on Lisa Fairfax (2013)
scope_conditions: United States corporate officers and directors

claims.claim: Directors who are inadequately informed about the expected standard of conduct will underestimate their personal liability exposure and engage in riskier behavior than is desirable for the company itself.
claims.citation: Kaal, A Comparative Perspective on the Limitations of the Duty of Oversight – A Comment on Lisa Fairfax (2013)
scope_conditions: directors depend on counsel for fiduciary duty guidance

claims.claim: Germany has taken a much stricter approach than the United States to cases involving a breach of the duty of oversight, even though the German business judgment rule formally requires a showing of the same elements as the American one.
claims.citation: Kaal, A Comparative Perspective on the Limitations of the Duty of Oversight – A Comment on Lisa Fairfax (2013)
scope_conditions: comparison of German and Delaware corporate law

claims.claim: Under German law, directors' business decisions lose the protection of the business judgment rule where the business risk taken was inappropriately excessive, a standard German courts announced in ARAG/Garmenbeck.
claims.citation: Kaal, A Comparative Perspective on the Limitations of the Duty of Oversight – A Comment on Lisa Fairfax (2013)
scope_conditions: German stock corporation law
Section 93 AktG business judgment rule

claims.claim: German commentators, whose expertise German courts rely on heavily, concluded after the financial crisis that managers do not act reasonably under the German business judgment rule if the risks they take on behalf of the corporation result in the demise of the corporation.
claims.citation: Kaal, A Comparative Perspective on the Limitations of the Duty of Oversight – A Comment on Lisa Fairfax (2013)
scope_conditions: Germany
post financial crisis evaluation of liability rules

claims.claim: The German ARAG/Garmenbeck holding is diametrically opposed to In re Citigroup, where the Delaware Chancery Court declared that directors' incorrect evaluation of business risk did not violate the duty of oversight.
claims.citation: Kaal, A Comparative Perspective on the Limitations of the Duty of Oversight – A Comment on Lisa Fairfax (2013)
scope_conditions: comparison of German and Delaware case law on business risk

claims.claim: The German Federal Court of Justice held in Mannesmann that directors breached their fiduciary duty by awarding a bonus of roughly seventeen million dollars to a chief executive whose tenure had substantially increased shareholder value, whereas Delaware courts imposed no liability for the far larger Ovitz payout in Disney.
claims.citation: Kaal, A Comparative Perspective on the Limitations of the Duty of Oversight – A Comment on Lisa Fairfax (2013)
scope_conditions: executive compensation decisions
German versus Delaware adjudication

claims.claim: Comparative corporate law research is challenging and may include inaccuracies because countries differ in legal history, legal origins, and legal cultures.
claims.citation: Kaal, A Comparative Perspective on the Limitations of the Duty of Oversight – A Comment on Lisa Fairfax (2013)
scope_conditions: cross country comparison of adjudicated cases

claims.claim: Despite the limits of the comparison, had In re Citigroup and Disney been decided in Germany the allocation of liability would have been different, because German courts are generally more willing than Delaware courts to second-guess directors' decisions.
claims.citation: Kaal, A Comparative Perspective on the Limitations of the Duty of Oversight – A Comment on Lisa Fairfax (2013)
scope_conditions: cases involving extreme facts at the cusp of culpable conduct

claims.claim: The different legal standards for allocating liability in Germany and the United States illustrate rather different legal and societal attitudes toward managers' risk-taking.
claims.citation: Kaal, A Comparative Perspective on the Limitations of the Duty of Oversight – A Comment on Lisa Fairfax (2013)

claims.claim: Delaware's signalling of expected conduct could be dramatically improved by adopting a moderate rather than near insurmountable standard for liability in cases involving breaches of the duty of oversight.
claims.citation: Kaal, A Comparative Perspective on the Limitations of the Duty of Oversight – A Comment on Lisa Fairfax (2013)
scope_conditions: United States, Delaware corporate law
breaches of the duty of oversight

claims.claim: If the liability standard were lowered, directors and officers would take their increased personal liability exposure into account and could be incentivized to engage in less risky behavior.
claims.citation: Kaal, A Comparative Perspective on the Limitations of the Duty of Oversight – A Comment on Lisa Fairfax (2013)
scope_conditions: a moderate liability standard for oversight breaches is adopted

claims.claim: Increasing oversight liability would give courts an opportunity to clarify the oversight doctrine, so that it could evolve into a mature and coherent doctrine rather than remaining immature and incoherent.
claims.citation: Kaal, A Comparative Perspective on the Limitations of the Duty of Oversight – A Comment on Lisa Fairfax (2013)
scope_conditions: more oversight suits reach the merits

claims.claim: Increased liability is no panacea and cannot alone adequately address the central shortcomings of the duty of oversight and of corporate governance in the United States, because heightened liability does not give part-time outside directors the capacity to monitor complex corporations.

scope_conditions: large and increasingly complex corporations
directors serving part time as outsiders

claims.claim: Cost increases and path dependencies may make it nearly impossible to relax the close to insurmountable standard for liability in oversight cases.
claims.citation: Kaal, A Comparative Perspective on the Limitations of the Duty of Oversight – A Comment on Lisa Fairfax (2013)
scope_conditions: United States corporate law
existing liability regime already entrenched

claims.claim: The author endorses the conclusion that attempts to enhance oversight in the United States may fail and that emphasizing improved oversight as a means of enhancing corporate governance could be ill-advised.
claims.citation: Kaal, A Comparative Perspective on the Limitations of the Duty of Oversight – A Comment on Lisa Fairfax (2013)
scope_conditions: United States corporate governance

claims.claim: The common denominator between the Sarbanes-Oxley Act, the Dodd-Frank Act, and other reform proposals is a top down regulatory approach of direct regulatory intervention with stable and supposedly optimal rules.
claims.citation: Kaal, A Comparative Perspective on the Limitations of the Duty of Oversight – A Comment on Lisa Fairfax (2013)
scope_conditions: United States corporate governance reform since 2002

claims.claim: Governance adjustments made through stable rules in reaction to a systemic shock can result in suboptimal governance outcomes, market volatility, and economic loss.
claims.citation: Kaal, A Comparative Perspective on the Limitations of the Duty of Oversight – A Comment on Lisa Fairfax (2013)
scope_conditions: reforms enacted in the immediate aftermath of a crisis

claims.claim: Governance adjustments are often enacted merely to address the problem perceived in the given market environment and the then existing economic conditions, without regard to possible future developments.
claims.citation: Kaal, A Comparative Perspective on the Limitations of the Duty of Oversight – A Comment on Lisa Fairfax (2013)

claims.claim: Following enactment, governance adjustments are often later repealed or diluted, and anticipation of future developments plays no significant role in the top down approach to regulation.
claims.citation: Kaal, A Comparative Perspective on the Limitations of the Duty of Oversight – A Comment on Lisa Fairfax (2013)
scope_conditions: top down regulatory approach

claims.claim: The economic conditions and the corresponding requirements for optimal and stable rules are constantly evolving, so rules fixed at one moment lose their fit over time.
claims.citation: Kaal, A Comparative Perspective on the Limitations of the Duty of Oversight – A Comment on Lisa Fairfax (2013)
scope_conditions: evolving market environments

claims.claim: Financial innovation, the globalization of markets, transnationalism, ethical challenges, and the bounded rationality of humans are likely to create and increase future challenges that require additional and more extensive governance adjustments.
claims.citation: Kaal, A Comparative Perspective on the Limitations of the Duty of Oversight – A Comment on Lisa Fairfax (2013)
scope_conditions: continuing financial innovation and globalization

claims.claim: The shortcomings of stable rules, especially the perpetual need for rule enactment and revision, justify a supplemental dynamic approach to regulating the financial industry that enhances and extends the established regulatory framework rather than replacing it.
claims.citation: Kaal, A Comparative Perspective on the Limitations of the Duty of Oversight – A Comment on Lisa Fairfax (2013)
scope_conditions: financial industry regulation

claims.claim: Dynamic Regulation is defined as an adapting governance mechanism that is constantly evolving and adjusting to the given market environment, financial innovation, and regulatory environment.
claims.citation: Kaal, A Comparative Perspective on the Limitations of the Duty of Oversight – A Comment on Lisa Fairfax (2013)

claims.claim: Dynamic Regulation could help avoid the regulatory sine curve and its negative and costly consequences, and could provide a self enforcement mechanism independent of the existing regulatory structure and agency enforcement.
claims.citation: Kaal, A Comparative Perspective on the Limitations of the Duty of Oversight – A Comment on Lisa Fairfax (2013)
scope_conditions: dynamic regulation deployed as a supplement to stable rules

claims.claim: Dynamic Regulation may enable regulators to anticipate future changes and challenges and to adapt stable rules accordingly.
claims.citation: Kaal, A Comparative Perspective on the Limitations of the Duty of Oversight – A Comment on Lisa Fairfax (2013)
scope_conditions: dynamic regulation supplements the existing framework

claims.claim: Using court decisions and stable rules to make the oversight role more robust could be insufficient, whereas contractual and quasi law forms of dynamic governance could help improve the duty of oversight.
claims.citation: Kaal, A Comparative Perspective on the Limitations of the Duty of Oversight – A Comment on Lisa Fairfax (2013)
scope_conditions: directors are outsiders working part time
increasing complexity of modern corporations

claims.claim: Corporate Integrity Agreements are one form of dynamic governance that may be able to temporarily increase fiduciary duties as a form of quasi law.
claims.citation: Kaal, A Comparative Perspective on the Limitations of the Duty of Oversight – A Comment on Lisa Fairfax (2013)
scope_conditions: corporations subject to a Corporate Integrity Agreement

claims.claim: More research is needed to understand how dynamic forms of governance could help improve fiduciary duties and corporate governance.
claims.citation: Kaal, A Comparative Perspective on the Limitations of the Duty of Oversight – A Comment on Lisa Fairfax (2013)

claims.claim: Governance adjustments enacted via stable rules in reaction to financial crises are inevitably followed by relaxation, revision, and retraction of those rules.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857
scope_conditions: applies to rules enacted as a reaction to financial crises

claims.claim: Because economic conditions and the corresponding requirements for optimal and stable rules are constantly evolving, a rule set that is optimal at enactment ceases to be optimal over time.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857
scope_conditions: economic and market conditions continue to evolve after enactment

claims.claim: Dynamic regulation could dampen the volatility of both the cosine curve describing common elements of financial crises and the regulatory sine curve, by creating an anticipatory rather than reactive regulatory response.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857
scope_conditions: dynamic elements are actually implemented in the regulatory framework

claims.claim: Financial regulation is characteristically enacted only in the aftermath of financial crises rather than in advance of them.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857

claims.claim: Since 2002 United States corporate governance has been substantially upgraded twice in response to crises, following more than seventy years of comparative regulatory inactivity, a concentration of regulatory activity in a short timespan that is itself striking.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857
scope_conditions: United States corporate governance regime
period since 2002

claims.claim: The existing literature on financial regulation has not adequately addressed the underlying causes and consequences of cyclical regulation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857

claims.claim: Initiatives for sustainable financial regulation are largely missing, because anticipation of unknown future contingencies and preemption of possible future crises play no significant role either in the current regulatory framework or in the literature on financial regulation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857

claims.claim: Congress, financial regulators, and the financial regulation literature rely almost exclusively on rules presumed to be stable and optimal, which is the common denominator of regulatory responses to crises.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857
scope_conditions: United States rulemaking institutions

claims.claim: Rulemakers discount or willingly accept unknown future contingencies and the inevitable need for later revision, amendment, and retraction, because they are pursuing certainty and predictability in the rules they enact.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857
scope_conditions: rulemakers prioritize certainty and predictability

claims.claim: A regulatory framework that relies exclusively on stable and presumptively optimal rules cannot adequately address future challenges, and the amendments, revisions, and retractions such a framework generates create substantial transaction costs and uncertainty.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857
scope_conditions: framework relies exclusively on stable rules

claims.claim: Rules established in reaction to financial crises inevitably fail to soften, curtail, or preempt the effects of financial crises, because reactive rules are tailored to the economic and regulatory issues existing at the time of enactment and ignore possible future contingencies.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857
scope_conditions: rules enacted reactively after a crisis

claims.claim: Dynamic elements built into the regulatory structure would allow regulators to continually adapt to new market environments, to financial innovation, and to changes in financial markets that are themselves caused by financial regulation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857
scope_conditions: dynamic elements are incorporated into the regulatory structure

claims.claim: Although implementing dynamic elements in regulatory structures remains uncertain, promising regulatory tools with dynamic elements already exist, including contingent capital securities, corporate integrity agreements, and deferred prosecution agreements.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857
scope_conditions: existing instruments serve as building blocks rather than new institutions

claims.claim: The regulatory sine curve itself may be inevitable, but its costly and suboptimal regulatory effects can nonetheless be limited.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857

claims.claim: Financial rulemaking is most needed ex-ante before financial crises, not ex-post after crises have already imposed steep costs on the economy, markets, and financial institutions and have distorted the rulemaking process itself.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857

claims.claim: The aftermath of a financial crisis creates shock conditions that constitute a suboptimal environment for rulemaking.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857
scope_conditions: period immediately following a financial crisis

claims.claim: Post-crisis rulemaking occurs in an economic, political, and legal environment whose sense of urgency prevents a full evaluation of the consequences of new rules for all affected constituencies.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857
scope_conditions: rulemaking under post-crisis urgency

claims.claim: The shock conditions that trigger calls for rulemaking have typically not been analyzed or absorbed systematically, so rulemaking under those conditions is associated with high levels of incomplete information.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857
scope_conditions: rulemaking triggered by an unabsorbed shock

claims.claim: The bounded rationality of public rulemakers aggravates shock conditions during rulemaking, because rulemakers satisfy their own constituencies rather than all affected parties and are therefore more willing to act on incomplete information.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857
scope_conditions: public rulemakers accountable to particular constituencies

claims.claim: Financial regulation is characterized and controlled by a classic collective action problem, and as a consequence regulatory oversight is never constant.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857

claims.claim: In the competition to shape financial policy through rulemaking, small and well organized special interest groups such as the financial industry dominate latent groups such as dispersed investors.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857
scope_conditions: ordinary, non-crisis periods

claims.claim: During and after crises, political entrepreneurs assume the transaction costs of organizing otherwise disinterested latent groups, which temporarily overcomes the predominance of special interest groups in rulemaking.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857
scope_conditions: during and immediately after a crisis

claims.claim: Once crises recede, regulatory oversight diminishes as societies and markets return to their prior equilibrium, and this dichotomy causes reform legislation and deregulatory legislation to be enacted in quick succession.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857
scope_conditions: after markets return to normalcy

claims.claim: Bank crises share four core common elements: an exogenous shock, a favorable response to that shock, the dissipation of favorable conditions, and a systemic rise in bank failures.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857
scope_conditions: banking crises generally

claims.claim: An exogenous shock, often a fundamental technological advancement, starts the crisis sequence by creating conditions for optimism in the real and financial sectors of the economy.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857
scope_conditions: historical pattern of banking crises

claims.claim: The cyclical nature of public rulemaking under incomplete information and bounded rationality is costly and produces suboptimal regulatory outcomes with long-term implications for financial markets and the economy.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857
scope_conditions: rulemaking conducted cyclically under incomplete information

claims.claim: Regulatory cycles make it nearly impossible to address financial regulatory concerns adequately, and systemic risk in particular is difficult to address if rules are enacted in a cyclical and reactive format.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857
scope_conditions: rules enacted cyclically and reactively

claims.claim: The regulatory sine curve is the pattern of governance adjustments made in reaction to financial crises together with the inevitable relaxation, revision, and retraction of the rules enacted as part of that adjustment.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857

claims.claim: Regulatory intensity is never constant: it increases after a market crash and then wanes as society and the market return to normalcy.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857
scope_conditions: following a market crash

claims.claim: In the absence of crises the intensity of regulation diminishes, because regulators cannot commit to long-term regulatory strategies and instead fall back on private strategies such as self-regulation to overcome resource constraints.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857
scope_conditions: non-crisis periods
regulators facing resource constraints

claims.claim: The regulatory expansion that follows crises inevitably leads to amendments, revisions, and retractions of the previously established rules.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857
scope_conditions: rules created during post-crisis regulatory expansion

claims.claim: Both the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and the Dodd-Frank Act were amended and revised, and some of their most controversial provisions were never enforced.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857
scope_conditions: United States federal securities and financial regulation

claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857

claims.claim: The partial repeal of Section 404 of Sarbanes-Oxley through the Dodd-Frank Act illustrates that broad rules enacted during times of political expediency are often later retracted.

scope_conditions: broad rules enacted under political expediency

claims.claim: Foreign issuers began delisting from United States exchanges after the enactment of Section 404 of Sarbanes-Oxley and identified that section as a leading cause of their decision to delist.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857
scope_conditions: foreign issuers listed on U.S. exchanges after 2002

claims.claim: The Jumpstart Our Business Startups Act exemptions for emerging growth companies from Section 404(b), from say-on-pay, and from pay ratio disclosure illustrate the post-crisis easing of constraints imposed on the financial services industry.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857
scope_conditions: emerging growth companies under the JOBS Act

claims.claim: In the current regulatory environment the relationship between the regulatory sine curve and the common elements of banking and financial crises is suboptimal, because regulatory activity only begins its ascent once bank failures are already increasing.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857
scope_conditions: current regulatory framework without dynamic elements

claims.claim: Future financial crises may be inevitable, because globalization, financial innovation, ethical challenges, suboptimal institutional designs, and the bounded rationality of decision makers create conditions that produce crises.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857

claims.claim: Business and regulatory cycles will persist, but optimizing the relationship between indicators of financial crises and the regulatory sine curve, especially the timing of regulatory responses, could soften some of the effects of crises.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857
scope_conditions: cycles themselves are taken as given

claims.claim: Increasing the availability of relevant information for rulemaking through a countercyclical and dynamic process is a starting point for improved rulemaking.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857

claims.claim: Dynamic regulation is the antithesis of static, stable, and presumptively optimal regulation, and it is intended to counterbalance the effects of stable and presumptively optimal rules rather than replace them.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857

claims.claim: The increasing volatility of financial markets combined with financial innovation parallels the pace of technological development in telecommunications, the industry where dynamic regulation has predominantly been applied.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857
scope_conditions: comparison drawn between financial and telecommunications markets

claims.claim: Although some regulators use the term dynamic regulation in the context of SEC exemptive powers, the literature on financial regulation mostly ignores dynamic elements for regulation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857

claims.claim: Regulatory cycles would benefit from supplementing, rather than replacing, the existing regulatory framework with dynamic elements.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857
scope_conditions: dynamic elements operate as a supplement to stable rules

claims.claim: Dynamic financial regulation is the study of financial regulatory phenomena in relation to both preceding and succeeding events, by analogy to economic dynamics.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857

claims.claim: In a dynamic framework rulemaking ceases to be a merely reactive process driven by the collective action problem, and instead increasingly uses institution specific and decentralized information that both reflects preceding events and anticipates future contingencies.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857
scope_conditions: dynamic elements are incorporated into the rulemaking process

claims.claim: Rulemaking with dynamic elements increases the adaptive capabilities of financial regulation through the increasing use of institution specific information, including information on how financial institutions and their decision makers actually act and are expected to react to unforeseen contingencies.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857
scope_conditions: institution specific information is actually generated and available

claims.claim: The social and mental properties of decision makers in financial institutions, combined with the incentive structure of the respective institutional setup, determine a financial institution's adaptive capability.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857

claims.claim: Experimentation with different combinations of regulatory approaches is effective when several different approaches can be tried simultaneously in different jurisdictions.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857
scope_conditions: multiple jurisdictions available for parallel experimentation

claims.claim: Dynamic elements can help anticipate and preempt financial crises by changing the timing of regulation, the availability and quality of information, and the emphasis of regulation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857
scope_conditions: dynamic elements actually change timing and information flows

claims.claim: The core problem for financial regulation is timing: governance improvements are not enacted before crises when they are most needed, because the collective action problem makes financial regulation mostly reactive and tied to business cycles.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857

claims.claim: Financial rulemaking often relies on centralized rather than decentralized information, which is a further defect of the existing framework.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857

claims.claim: Including dynamic elements converts the sine curve of financial regulation into an anticipatory sine curve in relation to the phase-shifted first derivative, the cosine curve, that describes the common elements of financial crises.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857
scope_conditions: dynamic elements are appropriately implemented

claims.claim: Depending on their design, contingent capital securities can function as an early warning system that helps preempt financial crises.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857
scope_conditions: CoCo trigger design is institution specific and automatic

claims.claim: Institution specific automatic triggers in contingent capital securities are flexible and can be tailored to the parties' needs precisely because they operate independently of regulatory discretion.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857
scope_conditions: triggers are privately negotiated and automatic

claims.claim: Managers are incentivized to manage their institutions so as to avoid contingent capital triggers, and that incentive itself can optimize the governance of financial institutions.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857
scope_conditions: CoCos are outstanding with credible trigger terms

claims.claim: A contingent capital triggering event signals that management was unable to manage the entity so as to avoid the trigger, and therefore signals to rulemakers that regulatory action may be needed, information regulators cannot obtain by monitoring debt to equity and capital adequacy ratios alone.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857
scope_conditions: a CoCo trigger is actually reached in a specific institution

claims.claim: Contingent capital triggers have significant design limitations: accounting based triggers may not respond adequately in financial crises because they are updated too infrequently, while market based triggers are susceptible to market manipulation and bank runs.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857
scope_conditions: accounting based institution specific triggers
market based institution specific triggers

claims.claim: Prosecutors negotiating deferred prosecution agreements may lack the expertise needed to negotiate high level corporate governance changes such as personnel changes and internal corporate and compliance procedures.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857
scope_conditions: deferred prosecution agreements negotiated by prosecutors

claims.claim: The institution specific and decentralized information generated by deferred prosecution agreements allows regulators to better understand shortcomings in a particular market segment or industry, so that rulemaking can be more narrowly tailored.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857
scope_conditions: DPAs are applied broadly across financial institutions

claims.claim: Almost 300 deferred prosecution agreements have been executed since 2003, whereas before 2003 they were rarely used.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857
scope_conditions: United States federal prosecution practice

claims.claim: Corporate integrity agreements improve corporate governance because the ease of reopened prosecution, increased government scrutiny, and the potential for crippling penalties improve boards' and managements' knowledge of pertinent issues in the institution and its monitoring.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857
scope_conditions: institution operating under a corporate integrity agreement

claims.claim: The threat of heightened scrutiny under a deferred prosecution or corporate integrity agreement optimizes incentives because increased government monitoring attaches only after a first time offense, giving institutions a reason to comply and self-regulate in order to avoid it.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857
scope_conditions: DPAs and CIAs applied broadly to financial institutions

claims.claim: A mixture of mandatory rules, market solutions, and private ordering would increase the adaptive capabilities of rulemaking, curtail the effects of the collective action problem of rulemaking, and dampen regulatory cycles.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857
scope_conditions: mixed regime combining mandatory and private mechanisms

claims.claim: Adding dynamic elements to financial regulation would cause the sine curve of financial regulation to start its upward slope before the occurrence of financial crises, thereby dampening regulatory cycles.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation of the Financial Services Industry (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2273857
scope_conditions: dynamic elements are implemented in the regulatory framework

claims.claim: Dynamic regulation is an optimization process for the learning experience in the New Institutional Economics framework, describing intra- and inter-jurisdictional feedback effects between different public rulemakers and between private and public rulemakers.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560

claims.claim: Dynamic elements in the rulemaking process increase the availability of relevant information for rulemaking and thereby improve institutional design.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560

claims.claim: Dynamic regulation as part of institutional design in the evolution of law has not been systematically analyzed, despite an existing economics literature applying dynamic regulation to telecommunications, learning by doing, and principal-agent problems.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560

claims.claim: The institutional infrastructure for rulemaking was designed for a relatively stable society and stable economic and market environments, and it therefore fails to keep pace with rapidly evolving and increasingly complex modern markets.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560
scope_conditions: rapid societal, market, and financial innovation

claims.claim: Rulemaking conducted under conditions of incomplete information and bounded rationality produces suboptimal outcomes that require costly rule revisions, retractions, and additional rulemaking.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560
scope_conditions: information is systematically incomplete
actors are boundedly rational

claims.claim: Trial-and-error rulemaking is suboptimal because participating actors acquire the necessary information ex-post, only after rules have turned out to be suboptimal, rather than increasing the availability of relevant information ex-ante.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560

claims.claim: The feedback effect between different public rulemakers and between private and public rulemakers reduces incomplete information, which in turn enables the rulemaker to modify the next action in the rulemaking process.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560

claims.claim: Supplementing the rulemaking process with dynamic elements increases the public rulemaker's ability to adapt public rules to unknown future states, and thereby curtails public trial-and-error rulemaking.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560

claims.claim: Rules with suboptimal characteristics are themselves the product of institutional arrangements and reinforce those suboptimal institutional arrangements and rulemaking processes, creating a self-perpetuating feedback loop.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560

claims.claim: Even institutional arrangements that produce optimal governance solutions generate solutions that become suboptimal over time, necessitating rule revision, updating, and revocation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560
scope_conditions: passage of time and changing circumstances

claims.claim: Rules that lack adaptability to future states of the world reinforce the very institutions and processes that produce suboptimal outcomes.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560

claims.claim: Rules can be adaptable only if the institutions and rulemaking processes that produce them integrate dynamic elements that generate timely, relevant, and decentralized information for rulemaking.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560

claims.claim: Dynamic regulation is a form of Popper's piecemeal social engineering rather than holistic or utopian social engineering, because it is a piecemeal optimization process for institutional design with a largely private character.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560

claims.claim: The centralized planning of the holistic social engineer forces him to fall back on piecemeal improvisation and to engage in unintended actions, producing the phenomenon of unplanned planning.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560
scope_conditions: holistic or utopian approach to regulatory reform

claims.claim: Under dynamic regulation a presumption of reform feasibility is unnecessary because the feedback effect makes ad-hoc decisions obsolete, curtailing centralized planning and minimizing unintended actions.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560

claims.claim: Because feedback effects increase the availability of relevant, decentralized, and timely information, rulemakers can predict unforeseen contingencies and adjust their actions ex-ante to avoid complex reforms and unwanted consequences.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560

claims.claim: Rules should be promulgated only after the particularized need for the rule has been identified and possible effects on society at large have been evaluated.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560

claims.claim: Private rulemakers have a comparative advantage over public rulemakers in the dynamic regulation framework because public rulemakers lack comparable access to timely and institution-specific information.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560

claims.claim: NIE acknowledges that transaction costs, imperfect information, and bounded rationality influence the rulemaking process, with the consequence that even optimal solutions to regulatory problems become unstable and suboptimal over time.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560

claims.claim: In the conventional NIE learning process, the requirements for rules and their adaptability to future states become clear only after stable and presumptively optimal rules have already emerged as suboptimal, so anticipation of future developments plays no role and learning is confined to learning from mistakes.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560
scope_conditions: conventional, non-dynamic learning process

claims.claim: Opportunities for integrating dynamic elements into the rulemaking process include intra-jurisdictional feedback processes, feedback effects between private and public rulemakers, inter-jurisdictional feedback processes, informal rules, and organizational culture.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560

claims.claim: Parties subject to informal rules signal their preferences and efficient solutions to the public rulemaker, so informal rules and practices supply additional information that modifies rulemakers' actions and improves rulemaking.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560
