claims.claim: Unenforceable rules are irrelevant for purposes of economic analysis because they provide neither incentives nor sanctions, and legal rules without enforcement mechanisms do not qualify as institutions in the NIE framework.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560
scope_conditions: economic analysis within the NIE framework

claims.claim: Unlike ordinary private ordering, where formalization of informal rules can be a lengthy process that is never finalized, formalization of informal rules in the dynamic process happens sooner and is more likely to succeed if those informal rules provide relevant information for public rulemaking.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560
scope_conditions: informal rules provide relevant information for the public rulemaking process

claims.claim: Public rulemakers rely on stable and presumptively optimal rules because they lack necessary, comparable, decentralized, and institution-specific information.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560

claims.claim: Congressional studies do not remedy regulators' informational disadvantage because they mostly follow after Congress has already identified concerns and may not provide real-time relevant information before regulatory action is necessary.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560

claims.claim: Private rulemakers can work with and utilize decentralized information continuously, which enables them to react in a timely fashion to emerging, decentralized, and institution-specific information, while public rulemakers are limited in the information they can obtain.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560

claims.claim: The feedback process between public and private rulemakers increases the availability, timeliness, and quality of information available to the public rulemaker, which induces and supports a learning process and creates incentives for that learning.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560

claims.claim: Competition between legislators does not necessarily provide a feedback process in the sense of cooperation, but it nevertheless provides incentives for public rulemakers to consider regulatory solutions from other jurisdictions.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560

claims.claim: Because competition between legislators requires public rulemakers to meet consumers' and legal addressees' quality expectations and preferences, it adds a dynamic and market-driven element with a feedback effect to the rulemaking process.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560

claims.claim: Consumer opt-out from existing rules creates a feedback effect for the public rulemaker: when a critical mass of opt-outs signals that a different rule may be optimal, it triggers a modification of the rulemaker's next action.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560
scope_conditions: a critical mass of consumer opt-outs occurs

claims.claim: Information exchange between agents of public rulemakers, such as regulators, will not necessarily involve decentralized information, unlike feedback effects between private and public rulemakers.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560

claims.claim: Opportunistic behavior, transaction costs, and bounded rationality undermine comprehensive contracting, so contracting parties do not specify all of their respective obligations ex-ante because anticipating all contingencies is too costly.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560

claims.claim: Contractual incompleteness can be lowered through dynamic processes within the rulemaking process, because dynamic elements improve the availability, timeliness, and quality of information via the feedback process.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560

claims.claim: The learning process in incomplete contract theory can be improved because experimentation with different rules, rule revision, and additional rulemaking create significant transaction costs, and postponing rulemaking until sufficient information is available may not always be possible or desirable.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560

claims.claim: Rules, especially in financial regulation, are mostly enacted when it is politically opportune rather than when appropriate information for rulemaking is available.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560
scope_conditions: financial regulation in particular

claims.claim: A classic collective action problem controls rulemaking: smaller and better organized special interest groups usually dominate latent groups such as dispersed investors in the competition to shape rules.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560

claims.claim: During and after crises, political entrepreneurs assume the transaction costs of organizing otherwise disinterested latent groups, temporarily overcoming the predominance of special interest groups in the rulemaking process.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560
scope_conditions: during and after crises

claims.claim: The collective action problem and the cyclical nature of rulemaking are likely to persist, which makes alternatives and supplements to existing institutional designs for rulemaking more relevant.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560

claims.claim: Dynamic regulation should supplement existing institutional designs for rulemaking in order to counteract the negative consequences of cyclical rulemaking and improve corresponding institutional designs.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560

claims.claim: Contracting parties need to postpone the specification of obligations only if the feedback process in the dynamic framework did not generate sufficient information; where sufficient information is available, contractual incompleteness can be lowered.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560
scope_conditions: sufficient information is generated by the feedback process

claims.claim: Assessing the sufficiency of information by rulemakers alone can lead to suboptimal results because path dependencies may lead decision-makers to believe they control sufficient information for rulemaking when in fact they do not.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560
scope_conditions: sufficiency of information assessed by rulemakers alone

claims.claim: The availability of information generated through the dynamic feedback process cannot be optimized at any given point in time, because the feedback effect is intended to perpetually reinforce itself.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560

claims.claim: Parties in the incomplete contract model cannot adapt to unforeseen contingencies because they cannot specify ex-ante how those contingencies will be met, and transactions may be foregone or become too expensive if participants cannot rely on efficient and equitable adaptation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560

claims.claim: Dynamic regulation takes issue with the broad scope of contractual incompleteness and delayed decision-making assumed by the incomplete contract model, contesting the view that such incompleteness and delay are always necessary.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560

claims.claim: Dynamic regulation helps rulemakers anticipate how institutions will react to circumstances as they arise, because the feedback process provides decentralized, timely, and institution-specific information, allowing rules to be adjusted ex-ante in anticipation of future contingencies.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560

claims.claim: The broad scope for contractual incompleteness and delayed decision-making stipulated by the incomplete contract model are necessary only if the feedback effect did not produce sufficient information for rulemaking.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560
scope_conditions: feedback effect fails to produce sufficient information

claims.claim: The feedback process in dynamic regulation may be viewed as a focal point or principle for rulemaking, enabling rulemakers to provide for contingencies ex-ante and to adopt rules that are applicable and adaptable to future states of the world.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560

claims.claim: Because dynamic regulation supplies information ex-ante via a feedback process before rules are finalized, certainty for involved parties is not affected ex-post after rules become effective, so contractual incompleteness is lowered while certainty in rulemaking is maintained.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560

claims.claim: The feedback effect in dynamic regulation, as part of the organizational culture of rulemaking, may allow cooperation and coordination not only among private actors but also among public rulemakers and between private and public rulemakers.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560

claims.claim: The combination of multiple feedback processes results in a sequence of mutually-reinforcing, information-enhancing events that minimizes ex-post trial-and-error experimentation with stable rules after those rules have already emerged as failures.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560

claims.claim: Under dynamic regulation, ex-ante experimentation before the enactment of rules becomes the focal point of rulemaking, and anticipation of and adaptability to future contingencies become part of the rulemaking process.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Evolution of Law Dynamic Regulation in a New Institutional Economics Framework (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2267560

claims.claim: There is a substantial overlap between the systemic risk disclosure requirements imposed on hedge fund advisers under Title IV of the Dodd-Frank Act and the disclosure requirements under the fully revised version of Bankruptcy Rule 2019.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Funds’ Systemic Risk Disclosures in Bankruptcy (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2348463
scope_conditions: hedge fund advisers subject to Title IV reporting
creditors and groups covered by Revised Rule 2019 in chapter 9 and chapter 11 cases

claims.claim: Under the regulatory framework in place at the time of writing, the threat that hedge funds' systemic risk filings could be publicly disclosed through the bankruptcy process will affect hedge funds' tactics and their role in distressed investing only marginally.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Funds’ Systemic Risk Disclosures in Bankruptcy (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2348463
scope_conditions: current regulatory framework as of 2013 to 2014
Form PF disclosures not yet standardized by the SEC

claims.claim: Hedge funds' distressed and default debt investments in the United States grew dramatically over two decades, rising from roughly $70 billion in 1998 to roughly $867 billion in 2007.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Funds’ Systemic Risk Disclosures in Bankruptcy (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2348463
scope_conditions: United States distressed and defaulted debt market

claims.claim: The proliferation of distressed-focused hedge funds gave hedge funds roughly one quarter of the total distressed-debt market and made the distressed-focused approach the fifth-largest hedge fund strategy.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Funds’ Systemic Risk Disclosures in Bankruptcy (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2348463
scope_conditions: United States distressed-debt market
period through 2007

claims.claim: Under Revised Rule 2019, parties acting in concert must disclose not only equity holdings and claims but also derivative instruments such as swaps, options, and short positions.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Funds’ Systemic Risk Disclosures in Bankruptcy (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2348463
scope_conditions: groups, committees, and entities acting in concert in chapter 9 and chapter 11 cases

claims.claim: The threat of systemic risk disclosure, combined with rising competition in the distressed-debt market, could further incentivize hedge fund managers to cooperate in the bankruptcy process.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Funds’ Systemic Risk Disclosures in Bankruptcy (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2348463
scope_conditions: increasing competition in the distressed-debt market
credible prospect that systemic risk filings become visible in bankruptcy

claims.claim: The SEC has not standardized the disclosures required in Form PF, and there is evidence that Form PF requirements rest on an inconsistent use of industry terms, which can in turn produce inconsistent and contradictory data reporting.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Funds’ Systemic Risk Disclosures in Bankruptcy (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2348463
scope_conditions: Form PF as promulgated and in effect at the time of writing

claims.claim: Creditors and shareholders in bankruptcy, unlike debtors, are typically not required to disclose their interests until they participate in the case by filing a proof of interest or claim and seeking to be heard by a judge.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Funds’ Systemic Risk Disclosures in Bankruptcy (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2348463
scope_conditions: United States bankruptcy cases
parties other than the debtor

claims.claim: Because creditor disclosure obligations in bankruptcy are minimal and a general statement of the type of claim often suffices, hedge funds' penchant for secrecy carries over into the bankruptcy process even when they participate as debt holders.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Funds’ Systemic Risk Disclosures in Bankruptcy (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2348463
scope_conditions: hedge funds participating as debt holders rather than as debtors

claims.claim: Old Bankruptcy Rule 2019 was applied inconsistently in practice, with courts interpreting it with a high degree of variability both across and within jurisdictions.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Funds’ Systemic Risk Disclosures in Bankruptcy (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2348463
scope_conditions: period before the 2011 revision of Rule 2019

claims.claim: The growing number of conflicting decisions under old Rule 2019, and the confusion and uncertainty they produced, is what precipitated the concerted effort by bankruptcy practitioners and the federal bankruptcy bench to revise the rule.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Funds’ Systemic Risk Disclosures in Bankruptcy (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2348463
scope_conditions: United States bankruptcy practice in the late 2000s

claims.claim: Revised Rule 2019 clarifies some of the ambiguities of the old rule, but uncertainty and confusion about its application remain inevitable.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Funds’ Systemic Risk Disclosures in Bankruptcy (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2348463
scope_conditions: Revised Rule 2019 as effective December 1, 2011

claims.claim: The scope of Revised Rule 2019 is broader than that of the old rule because it triggers disclosure for committees, entities, and groups that are acting in concert to advance common interests and that are not composed entirely of affiliates or insiders of one another.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Funds’ Systemic Risk Disclosures in Bankruptcy (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2348463
scope_conditions: chapter 9 and chapter 11 cases

claims.claim: The definition of representation in Revised Rule 2019 leaves it unclear whether attorneys who merely monitor a bankruptcy case for a client, without soliciting or advocating a position before the court, represent those clients for disclosure purposes.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Funds’ Systemic Risk Disclosures in Bankruptcy (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2348463
scope_conditions: attorneys retained to monitor rather than advocate
Revised Rule 2019 definitions of represents and disclosable economic interest

claims.claim: The central compromise in Revised Rule 2019 is that parties need not disclose the price or the date of acquisition of disclosable economic interests, which is precisely the outcome the hedge fund industry lobbied for.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Funds’ Systemic Risk Disclosures in Bankruptcy (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2348463
scope_conditions: Revised Rule 2019 as adopted
subject to a court ordering such discovery under authority outside the rule

claims.claim: Systemic risk reports filed by registered investment advisers are confidential and are not publicly available, so any effect of these filings on bankruptcy practice depends on the prospect of disclosure rather than on actual public access.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Funds’ Systemic Risk Disclosures in Bankruptcy (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2348463
scope_conditions: reports filed with the SEC under Title IV
framework as of the time of writing

claims.claim: Mandatory quarterly Form PF reporting for large hedge fund advisers is designed to give the Financial Stability Oversight Council timely data for identifying emerging systemic risk trends and to align United States practice with international trends.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Funds’ Systemic Risk Disclosures in Bankruptcy (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2348463
scope_conditions: advisers with at least $1.5 billion regulatory assets under management attributable to hedge funds

claims.claim: Bankruptcy and systemic risk disclosure obligations for hedge funds have different origins and serve different purposes: bankruptcy disclosure is meant to level the playing field in the restructuring process, while systemic risk disclosure is meant to help regulators detect and prevent systemic consequences.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Funds’ Systemic Risk Disclosures in Bankruptcy (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2348463

claims.claim: Under both the bankruptcy and the systemic risk disclosure regimes, filed data carries a serious risk of being out of date and less accurate at the time it is analyzed than when it was disclosed, partly because of the lag needed to collect data before filing.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Funds’ Systemic Risk Disclosures in Bankruptcy (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2348463
scope_conditions: any analysis of data filed under Revised Rule 2019 or Form PF

claims.claim: Data staleness degrades systemic risk evaluation more than it degrades evaluation of bankruptcy disclosures, because many distressed investment strategies depend on the outcome of the restructuring process and creditors are therefore incentivized to hold their positions until it completes.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Funds’ Systemic Risk Disclosures in Bankruptcy (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2348463
scope_conditions: distressed investment strategies tied to restructuring outcomes

claims.claim: Form PF's required disclosure of a reporting fund's strategies includes a separate subcategory for event driven, distressed and restructuring strategies, which is what makes the form potentially relevant to bankruptcy proceedings.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Funds’ Systemic Risk Disclosures in Bankruptcy (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2348463
scope_conditions: Form PF section 1c, item B.20

claims.claim: Form PF disclosures have not been standardized, and anecdotal evidence indicates that the SEC and the FSOC may be working with contradictory, misleading, inaccurate, and incomplete systemic risk data.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Funds’ Systemic Risk Disclosures in Bankruptcy (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2348463
scope_conditions: Form PF filings made under the initial implementation stages

claims.claim: Because the SEC is still working out the appropriate use of Form PF and still improving the form and its instructions, its enforcement division is unlikely to open investigations into alleged misreporting or failures to report.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Funds’ Systemic Risk Disclosures in Bankruptcy (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2348463
scope_conditions: period while Form PF remains unstandardized

claims.claim: Form PF's systemic risk disclosure obligations were created, in a non-bankruptcy context, precisely to counteract the kind of shadow activity that is now resurfacing in bankruptcy under Revised Rule 2019.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Funds’ Systemic Risk Disclosures in Bankruptcy (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2348463

claims.claim: Revised Rule 2019 may in effect produce less overall disclosure of creditor activities in the bankruptcy process and push bankruptcy creditors into the shadows, the opposite of the transparency the revision sought.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Funds’ Systemic Risk Disclosures in Bankruptcy (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2348463
scope_conditions: if the rule reaches only parties who appear publicly in court or serve on official committees
groups that negotiate a plan without appearing in court

claims.claim: Hedge fund adviser registration and disclosure requirements under Title IV and the SEC implementation rules were instituted for the opposite reason: to stop hedge funds from operating in the shadows of financial markets.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Funds’ Systemic Risk Disclosures in Bankruptcy (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2348463

claims.claim: The overlap between hedge fund adviser disclosures under Revised Rule 2019 and systemic risk disclosures under Form PF, combined with the uncertainties Revised Rule 2019 created, points to a possible future role for systemic risk disclosures in bankruptcy.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Funds’ Systemic Risk Disclosures in Bankruptcy (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2348463
scope_conditions: contingent on Revised Rule 2019 producing less overall disclosure by distressed hedge fund investors

claims.claim: Form PF disclosures in their existing format are too generic to be appropriately applied in bankruptcy, but accumulated experience with the form and standardization of its items could yield less generic disclosures that become increasingly relevant to bankruptcy over time.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Funds’ Systemic Risk Disclosures in Bankruptcy (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2348463
scope_conditions: Form PF as designed at the time of writing
assumes future SEC standardization

claims.claim: If Form PF systemic risk data became publicly available, or even only available to the presiding bankruptcy judge in a chapter 9 or chapter 11 case, the hedge fund industry's strong preference for secrecy could itself precipitate a change in distressed investment practices.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Funds’ Systemic Risk Disclosures in Bankruptcy (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2348463
scope_conditions: public access or judge-only access to Form PF data
hedge fund industry retains its emphasis on secrecy

claims.claim: The threat that hedge fund managers' systemic risk filings could be publicly disclosed could help incentivize hedge fund investors to abstain from trading while serving on a creditors' committee and to avoid holding multiple offsetting positions in distressed entities.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Funds’ Systemic Risk Disclosures in Bankruptcy (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2348463
scope_conditions: hedge funds serving on committees in bankruptcy cases

claims.claim: Disclosing otherwise private and proprietary Form PF systemic risk data exclusively to bankruptcy judges could alleviate the hedge fund industry's concerns about privacy and about the reverse engineering of its strategies and positions.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Funds’ Systemic Risk Disclosures in Bankruptcy (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2348463
scope_conditions: judge-only access, with no disclosure to debtors or other creditors

claims.claim: Restricting Form PF data to the eyes of the bankruptcy judge alone would create problems in the litigation process, because opposing parties may demand access to the same information.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Funds’ Systemic Risk Disclosures in Bankruptcy (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2348463
scope_conditions: judge-only access design

claims.claim: Because systemic risk disclosures are far more generic and are not tailored to any specific distressed investment, importing them into bankruptcy would improve only marginally the information available about the motives of distressed securities investors.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Funds’ Systemic Risk Disclosures in Bankruptcy (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2348463
scope_conditions: Form PF disclosures in their current generic form

claims.claim: Systemic risk disclosures in the bankruptcy process would also not significantly change or limit hedge funds' influence in that process, nor would they protect against the misuse of confidential information.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Funds’ Systemic Risk Disclosures in Bankruptcy (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2348463
scope_conditions: Form PF disclosures in their current form

claims.claim: Increased disclosure obligations let so-called pilot fish emulate hedge funds' investment strategies and positions, which makes those positions more expensive to build and strips systematic bargaining strength from the negotiation process.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Funds’ Systemic Risk Disclosures in Bankruptcy (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2348463
scope_conditions: markets where competitors can observe and copy disclosed positions
illiquid distressed debt markets

claims.claim: There is a real risk that increased disclosure through Form PF would destroy the balance of power in the restructuring process.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Funds’ Systemic Risk Disclosures in Bankruptcy (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2348463
scope_conditions: if Form PF data were introduced into the bankruptcy process

claims.claim: Bankruptcy judges and the parties to a bankruptcy case may be unable to adequately evaluate Form PF data pertaining to a creditor, which limits the usefulness of that data in bankruptcy.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Funds’ Systemic Risk Disclosures in Bankruptcy (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2348463
scope_conditions: Form PF data as currently structured
SEC and FSOC themselves have not established how to evaluate the data

claims.claim: Using generic and possibly outdated systemic risk data in the bankruptcy process would not improve hedge funds' bankruptcy practices in the near term.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Funds’ Systemic Risk Disclosures in Bankruptcy (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2348463
scope_conditions: near term, before standardization of Form PF
Form PF information can be out of date immediately after filing

claims.claim: Public access to hedge fund managers' systemic risk disclosures under the Dodd-Frank Act and the SEC implementation rules could improve hedge funds' distressed investments and their bankruptcy practices.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hedge Funds’ Systemic Risk Disclosures in Bankruptcy (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2348463
scope_conditions: assumes public access to filings that are currently confidential

claims.claim: The Investment Advisers Act prohibits contingent fee arrangements between investment advisers and their clients because such arrangements could induce inappropriate risk taking by the adviser.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Investment Adviser Regulation (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2337268
scope_conditions: advisory contracts governed by the IAA
outside the post 1985 exemption for certain qualifying large advisory contracts

claims.claim: The IAA restricts the assignment of advisory contracts without client consent in order to protect investors against changes in the character or quality of the advisory services they contracted for.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Investment Adviser Regulation (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2337268
scope_conditions: contracts between investment advisers and their clients

claims.claim: Exemption from registration under the IAA does not exempt an adviser from the antifraud provision, which reaches both negligent misstatements and misstatements made with intent to defraud.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Investment Adviser Regulation (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2337268
scope_conditions: advisers exempt from SEC registration

claims.claim: Investment adviser status under the IAA requires that the advice concern a security; without a security in the dealings between adviser and client the statutory definition does not apply.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Investment Adviser Regulation (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2337268
scope_conditions: classification of a person as an investment adviser under the IAA

claims.claim: Providing investment advice without compensation makes a person less likely to fall within the IAA definition of investment adviser, but the SEC construes compensation for advisory services broadly, which narrows the practical value of that limit.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Investment Adviser Regulation (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2337268
scope_conditions: determining whether a person is in the business of rendering advice

claims.claim: The frequency of advice helps determine adviser status: advice rendered occasionally, rarely, and in a non-periodic fashion makes classification as an investment adviser less likely.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Investment Adviser Regulation (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2337268
scope_conditions: determining whether a person is in the business of rendering investment advice

claims.claim: A broker dealer who holds himself or herself out as a financial planner does not thereby trigger registration obligations under the IAA.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Investment Adviser Regulation (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2337268
scope_conditions: broker dealers holding out as financial planners

claims.claim: Proof of special compensation is a necessary condition for classifying a broker dealer as an investment adviser, and the burden of proving both special compensation and that the advice exceeded the incidental is on the plaintiff.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Investment Adviser Regulation (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2337268
scope_conditions: broker dealers whose advisory services are solely incidental to brokerage

claims.claim: Congress created distinct hedge fund adviser categories in Title IV of the Dodd-Frank Act because it recognized that not all hedge fund advisers pose the same systemic risks and therefore do not all require the same level of oversight.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Investment Adviser Regulation (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2337268
scope_conditions: hedge fund advisers under Title IV of the Dodd-Frank Act

claims.claim: Title IV and the SEC forms use assets under management as a proxy for systemic threat, so that disclosure obligations scale upward with the size of the hedge fund adviser.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Investment Adviser Regulation (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2337268
scope_conditions: hedge fund advisers categorized by AUM under Title IV

claims.claim: Mid-sized investment advisers, those with between $25 and $100 million AUM, fall to state authorities rather than the SEC, though they may still have to register with the state agency where their principal place of business is located.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Investment Adviser Regulation (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2337268
scope_conditions: advisers with between $25 and $100 million AUM
under Title IV of the Dodd-Frank Act

claims.claim: Where a state does not provide sufficient regulation of mid-sized investment advisers, oversight reverts to the SEC, so state level regulatory gaps trigger a federal backstop rather than leaving advisers unsupervised.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Investment Adviser Regulation (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2337268
scope_conditions: mid-sized investment advisers
states whose regulation is deemed insufficient

claims.claim: Advisers with more than $150 million in regulatory assets under management are defined as large private fund advisers and must register with the SEC.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Investment Adviser Regulation (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2337268
scope_conditions: advisers to one or more private funds
RAUM above $150 million

claims.claim: Registering large private fund advisers works by increasing the volume of data available to regulators, which in turn may help protect against systemic risk.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Investment Adviser Regulation (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2337268
scope_conditions: large private fund advisers registered with the SEC

claims.claim: The pre Dodd-Frank exemption for advisers with fewer than fifteen clients failed as a regulatory boundary because most hedge fund advisers deliberately designed their operations and legal structures to fit within it and thereby escape SEC registration and supervision.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Investment Adviser Regulation (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2337268
scope_conditions: hedge fund advisers before the enactment of Title IV in 2010

claims.claim: The foreign private adviser exemption that replaced the fewer than fifteen clients exemption is conjunctive: it requires fewer than fifteen U.S. clients and investors, no U.S. place of business, no holding out to the U.S. public, and less than $25 million AUM attributable to U.S. clients and investors.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Investment Adviser Regulation (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2337268
scope_conditions: advisers claiming the foreign private adviser exemption after 2010

claims.claim: The Title IV threshold registration requirement pulls a majority of the hedge fund advisers who had previously relied on the fewer than fifteen clients exemption into SEC registration.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Investment Adviser Regulation (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2337268
scope_conditions: private fund advisers managing more than $150 million AUM

claims.claim: Registration is the gateway that makes data collection and enhanced disclosure by hedge fund managers possible, and the Dodd-Frank Act raised disclosure requirements for registered advisers specifically to address systemic risk concerns.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Investment Adviser Regulation (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2337268
scope_conditions: registered investment advisers after the Dodd-Frank Act

claims.claim: Part 2 of Form ADV requires a plain English narrative brochure for prospective advisory customers, making the brochure the primary disclosure document delivered to an adviser's clients.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Investment Adviser Regulation (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2337268
scope_conditions: investment advisers registering with the SEC

claims.claim: Mandatory disclosure of referral compensation, related person status of brokers and dealers, and soft dollar benefits is designed to defuse conflicts of interest arising when an adviser runs several types of business and services.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Investment Adviser Regulation (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2337268
scope_conditions: advisers filing Form ADV Part 1A

claims.claim: Form PF was created to improve SEC and CFTC investigations and examinations and to enable the Financial Stability Oversight Council to monitor systemic risk in U.S. financial markets.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Investment Adviser Regulation (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2337268
scope_conditions: private fund advisers required to file Form PF after October 2011

claims.claim: Form PF filings, unlike Form ADV filings, are confidential and not publicly available, so the systemic risk disclosure regime is built for regulators rather than for market or investor scrutiny.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Investment Adviser Regulation (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2337268
scope_conditions: Form PF filings by private fund advisers

claims.claim: The frequency of Form PF reporting is keyed to size: advisers with at least $1.5 billion RAUM attributable to hedge funds must update quarterly, while advisers below that level file only annually.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Investment Adviser Regulation (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2337268
scope_conditions: SEC registered advisers managing at least $150 million AUM

claims.claim: Quarterly rather than annual reporting by large private fund advisers is intended to give the FSOC data timely enough to identify emerging systemic risk trends.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Investment Adviser Regulation (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2337268
scope_conditions: large private fund advisers filing Form PF quarterly

claims.claim: Form PF requires disclosure of the reporting fund's positions and how long it would take to liquidate them, because the SEC needs a view of portfolio liquidity rather than positions alone.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Investment Adviser Regulation (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2337268
scope_conditions: private fund advisers filing Form PF

claims.claim: The division of labor in adviser regulation dates to the 1996 National Securities Markets Improvement Act, under which Congress assigned larger investment advisers to the SEC and smaller advisers to the states.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Investment Adviser Regulation (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2337268
scope_conditions: federal and state allocation of adviser oversight after 1996

claims.claim: An adviser that would otherwise have to register in fifteen or more states because of the $100 million AUM threshold may register directly with the SEC instead, so multi-state registration burden operates as an escape hatch to federal oversight.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Investment Adviser Regulation (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2337268
scope_conditions: advisers whose state registrations would reach fifteen or more states

claims.claim: Investment advisers that provide advice exclusively through the Internet may register with the SEC regardless of how much they have under management, so the delivery channel rather than size determines the forum.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Investment Adviser Regulation (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2337268
scope_conditions: advisers providing investment advice exclusively through the Internet

claims.claim: The Dodd-Frank Act added an inflation adjustment to the qualified client standard, requiring the SEC to adjust any dollar amount test within one year of enactment and every five years thereafter.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Investment Adviser Regulation (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2337268
scope_conditions: SEC use of a net asset or dollar amount test for qualified client status

claims.claim: The SEC excludes the value of a primary residence and related debts from the qualified client net-worth test because persons who clear the threshold only by counting their home are less able to bear the risk of performance fee arrangements.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Investment Adviser Regulation (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2337268
scope_conditions: net-worth test for qualified client status under the IAA

claims.claim: Excluding the primary residence from the net-worth test removed a large population from qualified client status: SEC estimates suggest roughly 1.3 million households no longer qualify under the revised test.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Investment Adviser Regulation (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2337268
scope_conditions: households assessed under the revised net-worth test

claims.claim: The Dodd-Frank Act tightened custodial practice by requiring safeguards for client assets and verification by independent accountants, a response to concerns over theft and client exposure to Ponzi schemes.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Investment Adviser Regulation (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2337268
scope_conditions: investment advisers with custody of client assets after 2010

claims.claim: The custodian requirements work by cutting off the operational mechanics of Ponzi finance: they curtail an adviser's ability to pay existing investors with money invested by new investors, and custodians may execute client trades but cannot remit sales proceeds to the adviser or to third parties.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Investment Adviser Regulation (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2337268
scope_conditions: client assets held through qualified custodians under the Dodd-Frank custody rules

claims.claim: A person who provides investment advice over the Internet escapes registration only if the advice is impersonal; personalized advice delivered through chat rooms and websites can trigger the registration requirement.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Investment Adviser Regulation (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2337268
scope_conditions: persons providing investment advice via Internet chat rooms and websites

claims.claim: The passive electronic bulletin board exemption holds only so long as the provider gives no advice on the merits of any particular trade and stays out of securities purchases and sale negotiations.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Investment Adviser Regulation (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2337268
scope_conditions: providers of electronic bulletin boards posting securities information

claims.claim: Because investment advisers owe a duty to obtain best execution for customer orders, they ought to evaluate the executions carried out on their clients' behalf on a periodic basis.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Investment Adviser Regulation (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2337268
scope_conditions: advisers placing or directing client orders

claims.claim: Mandatory ethics codes, disclosures, and client consents are effective instruments for curtailing fraudulent practices by investment advisers.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Investment Adviser Regulation (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2337268
scope_conditions: registered investment advisers subject to IAA compliance rules

claims.claim: The SEC mandated written compliance policies and procedures for investment advisers as a reaction to mutual fund industry scandals and in an effort to curb IAA violations.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Investment Adviser Regulation (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2337268
scope_conditions: registered investment advisers

claims.claim: A chief compliance officer is effective only if he or she combines sufficient knowledge of IAA obligations with adequate authority to develop and enforce policies and procedures; knowledge without authority is insufficient.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Investment Adviser Regulation (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2337268
scope_conditions: registered investment advisers required to designate a chief compliance officer

claims.claim: Enforcement of the IAA's prohibited transactions provision is limited because the Supreme Court in Transamerica Mortgage Advisors, Inc. v. Lewis held that a violation of that provision does not support an implied private right of action.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Investment Adviser Regulation (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2337268
scope_conditions: violations of the IAA prohibited transactions provision

claims.claim: With private enforcement foreclosed, enforcement of the IAA's prohibited transactions provision depends entirely on injunctive relief, administrative sanctions, and criminal prosecution, all of which require public actors to move.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Investment Adviser Regulation (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2337268
scope_conditions: enforcement against violations of the prohibited transactions provision

claims.claim: The IAA bars compensation tied to the performance of the client's account but permits compensation tied to the average value of the client's assets, so fee regulation targets performance linkage rather than asset based fees.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Investment Adviser Regulation (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2337268
scope_conditions: fee arrangements in advisory contracts under the IAA

claims.claim: Referral fees to third parties are permitted only if the recipients are bona fide persons under securities laws, the fees are disclosed to the adviser's clients, and the fees are paid under a written agreement.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Investment Adviser Regulation (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2337268
scope_conditions: referral fees paid by investment advisers to third parties

claims.claim: The traditional fiduciary duty doctrine is one of the most amorphous concepts in the law, and its indeterminacy produces confusion, inconsistency, and cases with problematic outcomes.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Elizabeth R. Malay, The Role of Corporate Integrity Agreements in the Expansion of Fiduciary Duties (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2317580
scope_conditions: traditional judicially developed fiduciary duty doctrine

claims.claim: The liability standard for breach of fiduciary duty is set so high that courts rarely find directors in violation, because only a board's sustained or systematic failure to exercise oversight can produce liability.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Elizabeth R. Malay, The Role of Corporate Integrity Agreements in the Expansion of Fiduciary Duties (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2317580
scope_conditions: director oversight liability under Caremark and its progeny

claims.claim: The decades long academic debate over improving fiduciary duty doctrine has overlooked Corporate Integrity Agreements entirely, even though the debate is otherwise framed as a choice between expanding and curtailing the doctrine.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Elizabeth R. Malay, The Role of Corporate Integrity Agreements in the Expansion of Fiduciary Duties (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2317580

claims.claim: Corporate Integrity Agreements are a hybrid instrument: they are compliance programs funded by health care companies but administratively enforced by the government, that is, contracts between health care companies and the federal government carrying costly mandatory compliance measures and penalties.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Elizabeth R. Malay, The Role of Corporate Integrity Agreements in the Expansion of Fiduciary Duties (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2317580
scope_conditions: health care companies settling federal health care program investigations

claims.claim: Because directors contractually agree to increase compliance through an open door policy for the government, CIAs substantially raise the liability risk for companies whose directors did not act in accordance with their fiduciary responsibilities.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Elizabeth R. Malay, The Role of Corporate Integrity Agreements in the Expansion of Fiduciary Duties (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2317580
scope_conditions: a CIA has been executed
directors granted the government access, including site visits

claims.claim: Although CIAs sit outside the formal legal framework that defines fiduciary duties, they belong to the penumbra of extra legal forces that clarifies what is expected of directors.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Elizabeth R. Malay, The Role of Corporate Integrity Agreements in the Expansion of Fiduciary Duties (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2317580
scope_conditions: fiduciary duty law understood as supplemented by extra legal forces

claims.claim: The contractual obligations contained in CIAs can enhance directors' default fiduciary duties, expanding the duty of care for directors of health care corporations beyond the legal standard set by Caremark and Stone v. Ritter.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Elizabeth R. Malay, The Role of Corporate Integrity Agreements in the Expansion of Fiduciary Duties (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2317580
scope_conditions: directors of health care corporations operating under an executed CIA

claims.claim: Sarbanes-Oxley and the Dodd-Frank Act have influenced and shaped fiduciary duties, but they have not necessarily improved or clarified them.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Elizabeth R. Malay, The Role of Corporate Integrity Agreements in the Expansion of Fiduciary Duties (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2317580
scope_conditions: federal legislative responses to financial crises

claims.claim: Because state fiduciary duty law is permissive rather than regulatory, fiduciary standards can legitimately develop from non-legislative sources, which makes extra legal forces a proper source for shaping fiduciary duties.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Elizabeth R. Malay, The Role of Corporate Integrity Agreements in the Expansion of Fiduciary Duties (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2317580
scope_conditions: state law fiduciary duties
fiduciary responsibilities understood as largely aspirational best practices

claims.claim: The OIG leverages providers' participation in federal health care programs, and the revenues that participation generates, to extract substantive CIA provisions that increase compliance with expected conduct and overall welfare.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Elizabeth R. Malay, The Role of Corporate Integrity Agreements in the Expansion of Fiduciary Duties (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2317580
scope_conditions: OIG settlements of false claims investigations
providers dependent on Medicare and Medicaid revenue

claims.claim: Noncompliance with a CIA carries serious penalties, because the OIG may prosecute the company or seek its exclusion from federal health care programs.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Elizabeth R. Malay, The Role of Corporate Integrity Agreements in the Expansion of Fiduciary Duties (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2317580
scope_conditions: term of an executed CIA

claims.claim: CIA penalties reach individuals as well as entities: firms supervised by the FDA may not employ persons dismissed for CIA violations, and the careers of pharmaceutical directors and officers prosecuted over CIA violations can be severely damaged.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Elizabeth R. Malay, The Role of Corporate Integrity Agreements in the Expansion of Fiduciary Duties (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2317580
scope_conditions: FDA regulated companies
pharmaceutical industry directors and officers

claims.claim: Certification requirements that compel directors and officers to certify compliance with a CIA's provisions lower the procedural and enforcement hurdles for pursuing increased sanctions against noncompliant companies.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Elizabeth R. Malay, The Role of Corporate Integrity Agreements in the Expansion of Fiduciary Duties (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2317580
scope_conditions: CIAs containing board and officer certification requirements

claims.claim: As the number of individuals required to certify compliance under CIAs grows, so does the potential for false certifications and the corresponding liability, including False Claims Act and criminal false statement exposure.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Elizabeth R. Malay, The Role of Corporate Integrity Agreements in the Expansion of Fiduciary Duties (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2317580
scope_conditions: expanded certification requirements going beyond the chief compliance officer

claims.claim: CIAs often become the benchmark for expected conduct in a subsequent civil or criminal trial, which distinguishes them from ordinary contractual arrangements between companies and the government.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Elizabeth R. Malay, The Role of Corporate Integrity Agreements in the Expansion of Fiduciary Duties (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2317580
scope_conditions: litigation following execution of a CIA

claims.claim: Once a CIA has been executed it is much easier for the government to reopen a case than to pursue a new one, and this ease of further prosecution, combined with increased OIG scrutiny and the threat of crippling penalties, substantially affects board knowledge, monitoring, and management.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Elizabeth R. Malay, The Role of Corporate Integrity Agreements in the Expansion of Fiduciary Duties (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2317580
scope_conditions: companies operating under an executed CIA

claims.claim: A CIA raises the stakes for directors who would otherwise neglect their governance responsibilities, because the agreement puts the company effectively on parole and gives the government direct access that facilitates detection of compliance failures.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Elizabeth R. Malay, The Role of Corporate Integrity Agreements in the Expansion of Fiduciary Duties (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2317580
scope_conditions: companies operating under an executed CIA
OIG inspection and site visit rights

claims.claim: If the government finds problems on inspection it can escalate beyond the CIA's own substantive provisions to criminal prosecution, fines, additional CIAs, and exclusion from federally funded health care programs.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Elizabeth R. Malay, The Role of Corporate Integrity Agreements in the Expansion of Fiduciary Duties (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2317580
scope_conditions: government inspection of a company operating under a CIA

claims.claim: CIAs reach into the day to day compliance operations of corporations by elevating the chief compliance officer, typically mandating the appointment of a CCO who reports directly to the CEO rather than to the general counsel or chief financial officer and who has direct access to the board.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Elizabeth R. Malay, The Role of Corporate Integrity Agreements in the Expansion of Fiduciary Duties (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2317580
scope_conditions: regulated entities operating under a comprehensive CIA

claims.claim: By prescribing the number of board meetings devoted to compliance review and requiring specific board resolutions, CIA provisions let the government contractually determine how and when a board will interact.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Elizabeth R. Malay, The Role of Corporate Integrity Agreements in the Expansion of Fiduciary Duties (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2317580
scope_conditions: CIAs containing board specific provisions, as in the Allergan, Pfizer, and AstraZeneca agreements

claims.claim: Certification requirements push directors to demand more detailed reports from corporate officers and to take a greater role in overseeing compliance with both the CIA and federal regulations.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Elizabeth R. Malay, The Role of Corporate Integrity Agreements in the Expansion of Fiduciary Duties (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2317580
scope_conditions: boards subject to CIA certification requirements

claims.claim: Codes of conduct adopted under a CIA should encourage disclosure of compliance issues and protect whistle blowers from retaliation by maintaining the anonymity of disclosures.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Elizabeth R. Malay, The Role of Corporate Integrity Agreements in the Expansion of Fiduciary Duties (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2317580
scope_conditions: codes of conduct implemented under a CIA

claims.claim: The additional CIA requirements, and especially the self-reporting provisions, force companies to spend additional resources and at times to alter their day to day operations after signing.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Elizabeth R. Malay, The Role of Corporate Integrity Agreements in the Expansion of Fiduciary Duties (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2317580
scope_conditions: companies operating under a CIA

claims.claim: Although CIAs are not laws, they go beyond aspirational governance standards because they set forth concrete governance rules that more clearly define the duties to be informed, to exercise oversight, and to maintain effective reporting systems, thereby requiring a higher standard of care.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Elizabeth R. Malay, The Role of Corporate Integrity Agreements in the Expansion of Fiduciary Duties (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2317580
scope_conditions: directors of companies operating under a CIA

claims.claim: Unlike private contracts, CIAs are not the product of genuine bargaining choice: companies execute them to avoid further prosecution and exclusion from Medicaid and Medicare, so that once the government decides a CIA is warranted, a company that wishes to remain in its industry has its hands tied.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Elizabeth R. Malay, The Role of Corporate Integrity Agreements in the Expansion of Fiduciary Duties (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2317580
scope_conditions: health care companies dependent on federal health care program participation

claims.claim: Because CIAs combine contractual and public enforcement, with the OIG enforcing them and private rights of action also available, they are more than contractual arrangements, and a breach of a CIA may be treated like a breach of law for purposes of the duty of care.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Elizabeth R. Malay, The Role of Corporate Integrity Agreements in the Expansion of Fiduciary Duties (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2317580
scope_conditions: CIAs enforceable by the OIG and, under Delaware law, by courts via derivative suit

claims.claim: Boards are consistently held not liable for their companies' illegal marketing efforts even though federal law prohibits off-label marketing, but a board that certifies compliance with a CIA is certifying that the company properly monitors its sales teams' promotional activities, so CIAs contractually expand the applicable legal standard.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Elizabeth R. Malay, The Role of Corporate Integrity Agreements in the Expansion of Fiduciary Duties (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2317580
scope_conditions: off-label marketing cases
boards subject to CIA certification requirements

claims.claim: Because CIAs mandate a chief compliance officer and dictate how that officer interacts with the board, they increase the board's knowledge and monitoring of compliance, and a board possessing such knowledge should play a bigger role in ensuring that the company meets federal and state standards.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Elizabeth R. Malay, The Role of Corporate Integrity Agreements in the Expansion of Fiduciary Duties (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2317580
scope_conditions: CIAs that mandate a CCO and prescribe CCO to board reporting

claims.claim: CIA provisions create economic incentives that affect directors' diligence, because stipulated daily noncompliance penalties stacked on top of monetary penalties under federal health laws expose companies that executed CIAs to significant financial ramifications.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Elizabeth R. Malay, The Role of Corporate Integrity Agreements in the Expansion of Fiduciary Duties (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2317580
scope_conditions: companies with self-reporting obligations under a CIA
exposure under the False Claims Act, Sunshine, Stark, AKS, and HIPAA

claims.claim: Outside the CIA context, oversight claims are the most difficult theory in corporation law on which to win judgment, and courts dismiss duty of care cases routinely at the pleading stage.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Elizabeth R. Malay, The Role of Corporate Integrity Agreements in the Expansion of Fiduciary Duties (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2317580
scope_conditions: derivative suits alleging lack of oversight
demand futility pleading requirements

claims.claim: Courts treat companies that executed a CIA differently from other companies, and are increasingly recognizing the role of CIAs and their implications for directors' fiduciary duties.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Elizabeth R. Malay, The Role of Corporate Integrity Agreements in the Expansion of Fiduciary Duties (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2317580
scope_conditions: derivative litigation involving companies operating under a CIA

claims.claim: When a company operates under a CIA, the judicial distinction between the law and aspirational corporate governance becomes less clear.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Elizabeth R. Malay, The Role of Corporate Integrity Agreements in the Expansion of Fiduciary Duties (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2317580
scope_conditions: companies operating under a CIA

claims.claim: In re Pfizer stipulates that for a company that executed a CIA the court will allow an assumption that the directors were fully informed and therefore willing participants in the corporate malfeasance, so that the CIAs themselves became the court's proof that the directors could have breached their fiduciary duties.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Elizabeth R. Malay, The Role of Corporate Integrity Agreements in the Expansion of Fiduciary Duties (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2317580
scope_conditions: In re Pfizer, 722 F. Supp. 2d 453 (S.D.N.Y. 2010)
boards obligated by prior CIAs to monitor the very conduct alleged

claims.claim: Abbott Labs set the stage for the Pfizer holding: although Abbott's Voluntary Compliance Plan was not a CIA, the Seventh Circuit used it as evidence that the directors knew of and should have stopped noncompliant activities.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Elizabeth R. Malay, The Role of Corporate Integrity Agreements in the Expansion of Fiduciary Duties (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2317580
scope_conditions: In re Abbott Laboratories Derivative Shareholders Litigation
a six year history of documented FDA noncompliance

claims.claim: Courts assume that the boards of companies that executed a CIA have more knowledge and can exercise more control, and therefore hold those directors to a heightened fiduciary duty, rejecting directors' claims of ignorance because executing a CIA or a CIA like agreement means directors do know or should know about the noncompliance.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Elizabeth R. Malay, The Role of Corporate Integrity Agreements in the Expansion of Fiduciary Duties (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2317580
scope_conditions: companies that executed a CIA or a comparable agreement such as a voluntary compliance plan

claims.claim: It is unclear whether corporations with CIAs will be uniformly affected, and future courts are likely to expand the basic legal duty of care only where the facts suggest that the CIA actually provided directors with more knowledge about compliance activities.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Elizabeth R. Malay, The Role of Corporate Integrity Agreements in the Expansion of Fiduciary Duties (2013). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2317580

facts showing the CIA increased director knowledge
