scope_conditions: Form PF counterparty credit exposure disclosures

claims.claim: If advisers' allegations that Form PF disclosures cannot be answered other than by guessing are correct, then the SEC's capacity to evaluate the data is compromised, and regulation built on incomplete and misleading data will itself be questionable.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Disclosures Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2447306
scope_conditions: conditional on the accuracy of anecdotal reports from advisers

claims.claim: Prior scholarship, including the author's own earlier work, established that Form PF created core challenges for the private fund industry but did not clarify what impact the disclosure requirements actually have on managers; this study is designed to fill that gap.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Disclosures Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2447306
scope_conditions: literature available before the first mandatory Form PF collection

claims.claim: High quality private fund data is scarce because the industry's entrenched interest in confidentiality combined with decades of regulatory exemption from registration and transparency requirements left no reservoir of comparable disclosure to study.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Disclosures Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2447306
scope_conditions: empirical research on the private fund industry

claims.claim: Enlarging the sample does not cure selection bias in non-statistical sampling: a bigger sample neither compensates for the bias of non-statistical techniques nor guarantees that the sample is representative.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Disclosures Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2447306
scope_conditions: non-statistical or haphazard sampling techniques

claims.claim: Further randomization of the sample was not available as a remedy, because respondents drawn from outside the private fund adviser population would never have been exposed to the new disclosure requirements and so could say nothing about them.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Disclosures Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2447306
scope_conditions: surveys measuring the experience of complying with a new disclosure regime

claims.claim: The near identity between respondents who reported completing Sections 2 through 5 of Form PF and respondents who reported quarterly filing shows the answers are internally consistent, which the author treats as evidence that the survey responses carry above average reliability.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Disclosures Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2447306
scope_conditions: comparison of survey Questions 2 and 3
n=52 respondents

claims.claim: Despite contacting the entire population of 3669 SEC-registered private fund advisers by fax and e-mail over more than five months, the study obtained only 52 respondents, a response rate of 0.014 percent.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Disclosures Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2447306
scope_conditions: survey fielded after the first mandatory Form PF filing deadline

claims.claim: Advisers themselves understand Form PF's purpose the way the statute frames it: most respondents identified assessing systemic risk and closing the historical information gap about private funds as the form's purpose.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Disclosures Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2447306
scope_conditions: responses to survey Question 10

claims.claim: Initial Form PF compliance was inexpensive for most filers: 59.18 percent of respondents put the total cost of completing Form PF for the first time under $10,000.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Disclosures Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2447306
scope_conditions: n=52 survey respondents
first-time Form PF filing

claims.claim: Form PF compliance cost is sharply size dependent: quarterly filing large funds spent on average $155,286 on the initial filing, roughly sixteen times the $9,520 average reported by annually filing smaller funds.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Disclosures Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2447306
scope_conditions: initial Form PF filing
small sample of large quarterly filers

claims.claim: Measured against this study's survey data, the SEC marginally overestimated the cost of the initial Form PF filing for both annually filing smaller advisers and quarterly filing larger advisers.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Disclosures Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2447306
scope_conditions: comparison with SEC estimates in 76 Fed. Reg. 71128-01
data for larger advisers rests on a small sample

claims.claim: Recurring Form PF cost is also size dependent: quarterly filing large fund advisers pay on average $72,143 for subsequent filings while smaller advisers spend on average $5,262.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Disclosures Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2447306
scope_conditions: subsequent, post initial Form PF filings
small sample of large quarterly filers

claims.claim: For quarterly filing larger private fund advisers, the SEC substantially overestimated the cost of subsequent Form PF filings; the survey's estimate is roughly half of what the SEC projected.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Disclosures Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2447306
scope_conditions: subsequent Form PF filings by large advisers
based on a small sample of larger advisers

claims.claim: The SEC's error runs in the opposite direction for small advisers on recurring filings: the agency marginally underestimated the cost of subsequent Form PF filings for annually filing smaller private fund advisers.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Disclosures Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2447306
scope_conditions: subsequent Form PF filings by annually filing smaller advisers

claims.claim: The SEC's time burden estimates for Form PF are miscalibrated in the same direction as its cost estimates for large filers: the study's data suggest the agency overestimates the hours larger private fund advisers need.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Disclosures Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2447306
scope_conditions: relatively small sample of quarterly filing larger private fund advisers

claims.claim: Form PF compliance is not staff intensive for most filers: 67.35 percent of respondents used only one to three individuals and 69.39 percent reported the work took staff less than 50 hours.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Disclosures Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2447306
scope_conditions: n=52 survey respondents
first-time Form PF completion

claims.claim: The Form PF burden is concentrated in a few identifiable items: respondents ranked Question 16 on types of investors as the most time consuming, followed by Question 17 on performance and Question 7 on related persons.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Disclosures Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2447306
scope_conditions: responses to survey Question 14a

claims.claim: The dominant driver of Form PF time consumption is data gathering rather than form completion: 36 percent of respondents named data gathering as the task consuming most of their time, followed by delta options and ambiguous questions or unclear instructions.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Disclosures Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2447306
scope_conditions: open-ended responses to survey Question 14b

claims.claim: Asked what the SEC should fix first, respondents named the burdensome nature and the ambiguity of Form PF as the most pressing issues, not the substance of what is disclosed.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Disclosures Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2447306
scope_conditions: responses to survey Question 9

claims.claim: Complaints about Form PF's ambiguity coexist with acceptance of its substance: the same majority that flagged ambiguity as the most pressing issue also considered their existing reporting systems adequate and agreed with the SEC's definitions and instructions.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Disclosures Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2447306
scope_conditions: n=52 survey respondents

claims.claim: Form PF's definition of leverage is overinclusive: respondents reported that it is inappropriately constructed and sweeps in funds that use neither leverage nor derivative securities.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Disclosures Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2447306
scope_conditions: responses to follow-up survey Question 6b(ii)

claims.claim: Regulatory assets under management is an unstable reporting concept: commenters split evenly on whether Form PF's RAUM questions required them to interpret the term in order to answer.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Disclosures Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2447306
scope_conditions: responses to survey Question 19

claims.claim: Contrary to the industry's public complaints about SEC support, a majority of respondents rated the best level of SEC staff guidance available for completing Form PF as sufficient or good.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Disclosures Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2447306
scope_conditions: responses to survey Question 13

claims.claim: Where SEC guidance failed, the failure was localized: respondents who found guidance inadequate pointed predominantly to Form PF Section 1c, Item B, which concerns information about the reporting fund.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Disclosures Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2447306
scope_conditions: respondents who rated SEC guidance inadequate
responses to survey Question 13b

claims.claim: SEC flexibility in answering Form PF questions is valued by filers: 72.92 percent of respondents said the flexibility the SEC provides is helpful.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Disclosures Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2447306
scope_conditions: responses to survey Question 7a

claims.claim: SEC flexibility helps filers through a specific mechanism: it authorizes advisers to apply their own internal methodologies when interpreting and answering Form PF questions and to state their own assumptions, rather than forcing them onto an unfamiliar measurement basis.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Disclosures Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2447306
scope_conditions: responses to follow-up survey Question 7a(i)

claims.claim: Regulatory flexibility can backfire: a category of respondents reported that the flexibility the SEC provides is not useful precisely because it is unclear and generates confusion.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Disclosures Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2447306
scope_conditions: minority of respondents to survey Question 7a(ii)
low overall response rate to this question

claims.claim: Most private fund advisers did not need new infrastructure to comply: 65.22 percent reported that their existing internal reporting systems adequately capture the information Form PF requires.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Disclosures Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2447306
scope_conditions: responses to survey Question 15

claims.claim: For a substantial minority, existing systems fail Form PF for a specific reason: 34.78 percent of respondents said their internal reporting systems were insufficient because the required answers demand further analysis and calculation beyond what the systems already produce.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Disclosures Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2447306
scope_conditions: responses to survey Question 15 and follow-up 15b

claims.claim: Form PF's counterparty disclosure proved far less burdensome in practice than anticipated: 93.75 percent of respondents encountered no difficulty identifying counterparties for the counterparty credit exposure questions.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Disclosures Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2447306
scope_conditions: responses to survey Question 16b
predominantly smaller, annually filing advisers

claims.claim: Because only 27.08 percent of respondents used a service provider to complete Form PF, the widespread concern that outside service providers would overinterpret required Form PF data on filers' behalf appears unjustified.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Disclosures Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2447306
scope_conditions: responses to survey Question 11

claims.claim: Working with a service provider imposes its own costs: filers reported that the arrangement requires investing time and money to develop interaction processes and bearing the burden of supplying the provider with the underlying information.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Disclosures Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2447306
scope_conditions: respondents who used a service provider
responses to survey Question 11b(ii)

claims.claim: Investor demand for Form PF filings is limited: 74.47 percent of respondents had never been asked by an investor for a copy of their Form PF filing.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Disclosures Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2447306
scope_conditions: responses to survey Question 17
within the first year of Form PF filing

claims.claim: Form PF fund performance metrics are not accurate or comparable across filers, because reporting entities employ different calculation methodologies to produce them.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Disclosures Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2447306
scope_conditions: Form PF Item C, Question 17 on reporting fund performance

claims.claim: Respondents argued that the SEC's systemic risk objective would have been advanced more directly by asking a smaller set of targeted questions, emphasizing open derivatives positions, the entity's total market exposure, and its total underlying capital.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Disclosures Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2447306
scope_conditions: open-ended responses to survey Question 8b

claims.claim: The measured effect of Form PF data reporting on the private fund industry is milder than the pre-adoption debate predicted.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Disclosures Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2447306
scope_conditions: first year of mandatory Form PF filing
n=52 respondents

claims.claim: On the cost evidence collected here for both smaller and larger advisers, the industry's long standing objection that mandatory registration and disclosure would inappropriately burden investment advisers is mostly unfounded.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Disclosures Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2447306
scope_conditions: cost data from this survey
short-run costs only

claims.claim: Most of the identified problems with Form PF are self correcting over time, as the SEC issues additional and improved guidance or revises the core questions and definitions that filers flagged as problematic.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Disclosures Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2447306
scope_conditions: assumes the SEC continues to issue guidance and revise the form

claims.claim: Standardizing private fund adviser reporting obligations is the author's proposed remedy for the shortcomings advisers identified, because standardization attacks the ambiguity and inefficiency in the reporting requirements at their source and simplifies the disclosure regime.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Disclosures Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2447306
scope_conditions: private fund adviser reporting obligations under Form PF

claims.claim: A single standardized reporting model will not suffice: because different types of private fund advisers have competing needs, policy makers should evaluate several different models for standardizing Form PF reporting.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Disclosures Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2447306
scope_conditions: heterogeneous private fund adviser population

claims.claim: The study's cost findings are bounded to the short run: the data cannot establish what it will cost the private fund industry to keep completing and filing Form PF annually or quarterly over time.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Disclosures Under the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2447306
scope_conditions: data collected during a six month period after the initial filing deadline

claims.claim: The increasing use of non prosecution and deferred prosecution agreements has allowed federal prosecutors to expand their traditional role incrementally, marking a shift in prosecutorial culture away from an ex post focus on punishment toward an ex ante emphasis on compliance.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, The Effect of Deferred and Non-Prosecution Agreements on Corporate Governance Evidence from 1993-20 (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2486570

claims.claim: Prior scholarship on the corporate governance effects of non and deferred prosecution agreements rests largely on anecdotal evidence and individual case studies rather than on systematic evidence, which is why its conclusions about those effects are unreliable.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, The Effect of Deferred and Non-Prosecution Agreements on Corporate Governance Evidence from 1993-20 (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2486570

claims.claim: Because the population of executed non and deferred prosecution agreements is now large, their real trends and real governance impact are quantifiable and measurable, so policy makers can be given evidence based guidance rather than conjecture.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, The Effect of Deferred and Non-Prosecution Agreements on Corporate Governance Evidence from 1993-20 (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2486570
scope_conditions: requires access to publicly available executed N/DPAs in sufficient number

claims.claim: Once prosecutors have investigated and identified corporate wrongdoing, non and deferred prosecution agreements let them avoid an expensive trial against a sophisticated and well funded corporate defendant, which is one reason both sides have strong incentives to settle.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, The Effect of Deferred and Non-Prosecution Agreements on Corporate Governance Evidence from 1993-20 (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2486570

claims.claim: Prosecutors favor non and deferred prosecution agreements because those agreements avoid the uncertainty of potentially catastrophic collateral consequences for the company, unlike an indictment.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, The Effect of Deferred and Non-Prosecution Agreements on Corporate Governance Evidence from 1993-20 (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2486570

claims.claim: Existing corporate criminal liability combined with the absence of clear Department of Justice standards for charging businesses can push organizations to adopt unproven compliance programs and generate other inefficiencies.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, The Effect of Deferred and Non-Prosecution Agreements on Corporate Governance Evidence from 1993-20 (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2486570
scope_conditions: holds where DOJ charging standards remain vague

claims.claim: The authors contest the conventional wisdom that a corporate criminal indictment amounts to a corporate death penalty, pointing to recent guilty pleas in which BNP Paribas paid a record fine and Credit Suisse kept its investment banking license.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, The Effect of Deferred and Non-Prosecution Agreements on Corporate Governance Evidence from 1993-20 (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2486570

claims.claim: At the pre charging stage the government typically holds extraordinary bargaining power, which lets it extract fines and sanctions comparable to those following a criminal conviction while avoiding the risk and cost of trial.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, The Effect of Deferred and Non-Prosecution Agreements on Corporate Governance Evidence from 1993-20 (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2486570
scope_conditions: applies at the pre charging stage

claims.claim: The McCallum Memorandum failed as a corrective because it only supplemented rather than replaced the Thompson Memorandum and did little if anything to curb the widespread use of attorney client and work product privilege waivers in deferred prosecution agreements.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, The Effect of Deferred and Non-Prosecution Agreements on Corporate Governance Evidence from 1993-20 (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2486570

claims.claim: The McNulty Memorandum did not resolve the privilege waiver problem because it still left prosecutors ample opportunity to treat a corporate defendant's unwillingness to waive attorney client privilege as bearing on cooperation, and its attorney's fees provision had similar shortcomings.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, The Effect of Deferred and Non-Prosecution Agreements on Corporate Governance Evidence from 1993-20 (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2486570

claims.claim: Coding of all publicly available non and deferred prosecution agreements executed between 1993 and 2013 shows that 97.41 percent of them, or 264 of 271 agreements, contained relevant corporate governance changes.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, The Effect of Deferred and Non-Prosecution Agreements on Corporate Governance Evidence from 1993-20 (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2486570
scope_conditions: publicly available N/DPAs only
sample period 1993 to 2013

claims.claim: The sharp proliferation of non and deferred prosecution agreements after 2002 is explained by a cluster of events: the collapse of Enron, the dismantling of Arthur Andersen, the creation of the Corporate Fraud Task Force, and the Thompson Memorandum.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, The Effect of Deferred and Non-Prosecution Agreements on Corporate Governance Evidence from 1993-20 (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2486570

claims.claim: In 63.47 percent of the coded non and deferred prosecution agreements the agreement itself referenced preemptive remedial measures the corporation had instituted before the agreement was executed.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, The Effect of Deferred and Non-Prosecution Agreements on Corporate Governance Evidence from 1993-20 (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2486570
scope_conditions: counts only measures referenced within the text of an executed N/DPA

claims.claim: Where coded categories such as cooperating, disclosure, and internal review fall well short of 100 percent of the sample, the shortfall may reflect a gap in what the agreements record rather than a real absence of those corporate actions, so the coded frequencies understate actual conduct.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, The Effect of Deferred and Non-Prosecution Agreements on Corporate Governance Evidence from 1993-20 (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2486570
scope_conditions: applies to categories whose coded frequency is not near 100 percent

claims.claim: Waiver of rights provisions are the most prevalent governance term in the sample, appearing in 96 percent of agreements, followed by cooperation with the government at 91 percent and improved compliance programs at 75 percent.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, The Effect of Deferred and Non-Prosecution Agreements on Corporate Governance Evidence from 1993-20 (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2486570
scope_conditions: sample of 271 publicly available N/DPAs, 1993 to 2013

claims.claim: The less prevalent categories of governance change mandated by non and deferred prosecution agreements are increased monitoring at 46 percent of the sample, board changes at 38 percent, business changes at 30 percent, and senior management changes at 30 percent.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, The Effect of Deferred and Non-Prosecution Agreements on Corporate Governance Evidence from 1993-20 (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2486570
scope_conditions: sample of 271 publicly available N/DPAs, 1993 to 2013

claims.claim: Business change provisions in non and deferred prosecution agreements can go as far as requiring the entity to fundamentally change its business model or to shut down entire business units.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, The Effect of Deferred and Non-Prosecution Agreements on Corporate Governance Evidence from 1993-20 (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2486570

claims.claim: Cooperation requirements appear in 91.10 percent of the sampled agreements, and within that category document production requirements, meaning the identification, assembly, organization, and production of relevant documentation for the Department of Justice, appear in 79.70 percent of agreements.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, The Effect of Deferred and Non-Prosecution Agreements on Corporate Governance Evidence from 1993-20 (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2486570

claims.claim: Although 45 percent of sampled agreements required improved communication and training, only 11 percent required the entity to create the position of chief compliance officer, so the most structural compliance remedy is the rarest.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, The Effect of Deferred and Non-Prosecution Agreements on Corporate Governance Evidence from 1993-20 (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2486570

claims.claim: The trend in attorney client privilege waivers reversed after 2008: agreements requiring no privilege waiver increased steadily from 2008, and provisions requiring an attorney client privilege waiver disappeared completely by 2009.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, The Effect of Deferred and Non-Prosecution Agreements on Corporate Governance Evidence from 1993-20 (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2486570

claims.claim: The increasing execution of non and deferred prosecution agreements since 2002 has raised the overall regulatory burden borne by the corporate entities subject to them.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, The Effect of Deferred and Non-Prosecution Agreements on Corporate Governance Evidence from 1993-20 (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2486570
scope_conditions: applies to entities that are subject to an N/DPA

claims.claim: If leading corporations in an industry are bound by substantially similar agreements, the government's privileged access to information and its continuing oversight beyond the agreement term can make business and governance practices in that industry change lastingly.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, The Effect of Deferred and Non-Prosecution Agreements on Corporate Governance Evidence from 1993-20 (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2486570
scope_conditions: requires the DOJ to target one industry with substantially similar or overlapping N/DPA terms

claims.claim: Because the board changes mandated by non and deferred prosecution agreements consist largely of additional reporting obligations and committee reform rather than removal of officers or directors, those reforms alone may not create sufficient incentives for boards and management to improve governance and avoid execution of an agreement.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, The Effect of Deferred and Non-Prosecution Agreements on Corporate Governance Evidence from 1993-20 (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2486570

claims.claim: The threat of bad press, reputational harm, legal costs, stock price declines, and the cost of implementing mandated governance changes can partly substitute for the weak direct incentives, pushing boards and management to optimize governance and keep the entity out of an agreement.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, The Effect of Deferred and Non-Prosecution Agreements on Corporate Governance Evidence from 1993-20 (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2486570

claims.claim: Because 63.47 percent of the sampled agreements were executed even after the corporation had already instituted preemptive remedial measures, the current quantity, quality, comprehensiveness, and effectiveness of those preemptive measures may be insufficient to prevent an agreement.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, The Effect of Deferred and Non-Prosecution Agreements on Corporate Governance Evidence from 1993-20 (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2486570

claims.claim: High quality and effective preemptive remedial measures are themselves part of good corporate governance and can help a corporation avoid investigation, prosecution, and the execution of a non or deferred prosecution agreement.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, The Effect of Deferred and Non-Prosecution Agreements on Corporate Governance Evidence from 1993-20 (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2486570

claims.claim: Generic industry advice on building an effective compliance program cannot work in practice because it is written to apply to many firms at once while no two companies are sufficiently alike for general guidance to be effective.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, The Effect of Deferred and Non-Prosecution Agreements on Corporate Governance Evidence from 1993-20 (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2486570

claims.claim: Regulators can learn from the preemptive remedial measures corporate wrongdoers institute, because those measures reveal where governance concerns lie in a particular industry and where regulatory action is increasingly needed.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, The Effect of Deferred and Non-Prosecution Agreements on Corporate Governance Evidence from 1993-20 (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2486570

claims.claim: Department of Justice investigations of particular corporate wrongdoers generate highly relevant, decentralized, and institution specific information that is usable for rulemaking.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, The Effect of Deferred and Non-Prosecution Agreements on Corporate Governance Evidence from 1993-20 (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2486570

claims.claim: Governance reform delivered through non and deferred prosecution agreements is comparatively cheap for corporations because it adversely affects only a small number of board and management positions.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, The Effect of Deferred and Non-Prosecution Agreements on Corporate Governance Evidence from 1993-20 (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2486570

claims.claim: Corporate wrongdoers are unlikely to prefer regulation by prosecution over regulation by legislation because prosecution and execution of an agreement carry large reputational implications.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, The Effect of Deferred and Non-Prosecution Agreements on Corporate Governance Evidence from 1993-20 (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2486570

claims.claim: Regulation by prosecution denies corporations the channels of influence available under legislative and administrative rulemaking, since it offers no comment process and no opportunity to lobby regulations in their favor.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, The Effect of Deferred and Non-Prosecution Agreements on Corporate Governance Evidence from 1993-20 (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2486570

claims.claim: In the long run, increased regulation by prosecution may be able to offset many of the shortcomings of legislative governance reform, even though it is less predictable than legislation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, The Effect of Deferred and Non-Prosecution Agreements on Corporate Governance Evidence from 1993-20 (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2486570

claims.claim: Because non and deferred prosecution agreements typically run for a limited term, it remains unclear whether the governance reforms they impose survive in the long term.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, The Effect of Deferred and Non-Prosecution Agreements on Corporate Governance Evidence from 1993-20 (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2486570
scope_conditions: applies because N/DPAs have a limited duration

claims.claim: If corporate wrongdoing is not in fact caused by deficient corporate governance, then the governance reform imposed through a non or deferred prosecution agreement is merely a method of settlement rather than a lasting reform effort.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, The Effect of Deferred and Non-Prosecution Agreements on Corporate Governance Evidence from 1993-20 (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2486570
scope_conditions: holds where the wrongdoing has no identifiable governance cause

claims.claim: The underlying corporate governance problems in United States corporations may be more severe than non and deferred prosecution agreements are capable of adequately addressing.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, The Effect of Deferred and Non-Prosecution Agreements on Corporate Governance Evidence from 1993-20 (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2486570

claims.claim: The governance trends reported in this study apply only to corporations that actually executed an agreement, so because a disproportionately large number of corporations self correct or self report instead, the findings may capture only the tip of the iceberg.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, The Effect of Deferred and Non-Prosecution Agreements on Corporate Governance Evidence from 1993-20 (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2486570
scope_conditions: sample restricted to corporations that executed an N/DPA

claims.claim: The cooperation requirements documented in this study are likely to produce an increasing need for corporations and their counsel to anticipate prosecutorial actions in advance.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, The Effect of Deferred and Non-Prosecution Agreements on Corporate Governance Evidence from 1993-20 (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2486570

claims.claim: The evidence assembled in this study supports the conclusion that non and deferred prosecution agreements can play a legitimate role in addressing corporate governance shortcomings, contrary to the broad legitimacy critique in the literature.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, The Effect of Deferred and Non-Prosecution Agreements on Corporate Governance Evidence from 1993-20 (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2486570

claims.claim: Corporate governance provisions in non and deferred prosecution agreements increased significantly over the decade to 2013, raising prosecutors' influence over corporate governance to unprecedented levels.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, The Effect of Deferred and Non-Prosecution Agreements on Corporate Governance Evidence from 1993-20 (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2486570
scope_conditions: based on all publicly available N/DPAs from 1993 to 2013

claims.claim: This study finds no evidence of an inverse relationship between the size of regulated hedge fund advisers and the per-unit cost of compliance, contrary to the common complaint that financial regulation brings increasing returns to scale.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Impact of Dodd-Frank Act Compliance Cost on the Hedge Fund Industry (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2389423
scope_conditions: survey data collected after the March 2012 registration effective date for hedge fund advisers under Title IV
hedge fund advisers, not banks

claims.claim: The cost of Title IV compliance, and the other independent variables used as proxies for compliance cost, are associated with the size of hedge fund advisers as measured by assets under management.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Impact of Dodd-Frank Act Compliance Cost on the Hedge Fund Industry (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2389423
scope_conditions: survey respondents registered before the SEC registration effective date of March 30, 2012

claims.claim: Anecdotal evidence suggests that Title IV of the Dodd-Frank Act more than doubled the market entry threshold requirements for smaller hedge fund advisers.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Impact of Dodd-Frank Act Compliance Cost on the Hedge Fund Industry (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2389423
scope_conditions: market entry for new hedge fund advisers after the Dodd-Frank Act

claims.claim: Before Title IV, launching a hedge fund could be accomplished by raising roughly $25 to $50 million, whereas after the Dodd-Frank Act the required initial amount may have risen to around $100 million.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Impact of Dodd-Frank Act Compliance Cost on the Hedge Fund Industry (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2389423
scope_conditions: hedge fund startups
comparison of pre and post Dodd-Frank Act market entry

claims.claim: Below $100 million in initial assets under management, the administrative cost of running a hedge fund in a post Dodd-Frank environment could be prohibitive.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Impact of Dodd-Frank Act Compliance Cost on the Hedge Fund Industry (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2389423
scope_conditions: hedge fund advisers with initial AUM below $100 million
post Dodd-Frank regulatory environment

claims.claim: If the administrative and compliance costs created by Title IV disproportionally affect smaller hedge fund advisers, then over time smaller fund advisers could be forced out of the market or pushed to merge with other funds.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Impact of Dodd-Frank Act Compliance Cost on the Hedge Fund Industry (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2389423
scope_conditions: conditional on the anecdotal evidence of a disproportionate effect being true

claims.claim: A disproportionate effect of Title IV on startup hedge funds and smaller advisers could create barriers to market entry and precipitate a trend toward consolidation among smaller hedge fund advisers.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Impact of Dodd-Frank Act Compliance Cost on the Hedge Fund Industry (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2389423
scope_conditions: conditional on Title IV compliance cost falling disproportionately on smaller advisers

claims.claim: A surplus of larger private fund advisers holding correspondingly larger amounts of assets under management could increase systemic risk, so a regulation that consolidates the industry may work against its own systemic risk objective.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Impact of Dodd-Frank Act Compliance Cost on the Hedge Fund Industry (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2389423
scope_conditions: if Title IV compliance cost drives consolidation toward larger advisers

claims.claim: The new regulatory framework for private funds in the United States requires hedge fund manager registration in combination with enhanced disclosure of sensitive proprietary information, a combination that marks a shift in how private funds are regulated.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Impact of Dodd-Frank Act Compliance Cost on the Hedge Fund Industry (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2389423
scope_conditions: United States private fund regulation after the Dodd-Frank Act

claims.claim: Because there is no evidence of an inverse relationship between adviser size and per-unit compliance cost, industry concerns over the effect of Title IV compliance cost and possible barriers to entry for smaller funds and startups appear unjustified.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Impact of Dodd-Frank Act Compliance Cost on the Hedge Fund Industry (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2389423
scope_conditions: hedge fund advisers in the 2012 survey sample

claims.claim: Based on these findings, adviser size may not matter as much for policy adjustments and SEC rule making as the hedge fund industry and its representatives have claimed.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Impact of Dodd-Frank Act Compliance Cost on the Hedge Fund Industry (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2389423
scope_conditions: SEC rule making under Title IV
policy adjustments keyed to adviser size

claims.claim: Title IV mandates hedge fund adviser registration in order to increase record keeping and disclosure, requiring advisers above the statutory AUM threshold to register as investment advisers and to disclose information about their trades and portfolios to the SEC.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Impact of Dodd-Frank Act Compliance Cost on the Hedge Fund Industry (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2389423
scope_conditions: hedge fund advisers above the Title IV registration threshold

claims.claim: Registered investment advisers must report systemic risk relevant information to the SEC, including trading practices, trading and investment positions, the amount of assets under management, valuation policies, and side letters.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Impact of Dodd-Frank Act Compliance Cost on the Hedge Fund Industry (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2389423
scope_conditions: investment advisers registered under Title IV

claims.claim: The study's core hypothesis, drawn from the industry view and the anecdotal evidence, is that smaller hedge fund advisers pay more relative to their size than larger hedge fund advisers for Title IV compliance.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Impact of Dodd-Frank Act Compliance Cost on the Hedge Fund Industry (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2389423
scope_conditions: hedge fund advisers across the AUM spectrum

claims.claim: Prior work shows that registration and the increased compliance requirements under the Dodd-Frank Act only marginally increase the cost structure of hedge funds.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Impact of Dodd-Frank Act Compliance Cost on the Hedge Fund Industry (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2389423
scope_conditions: hedge funds subject to Dodd-Frank Act registration requirements

claims.claim: Linear, robust, and non-linear regression models all show positive and statistically significant coefficients, and compliance costs per unit of AUM do not diminish in the sample, so the hypothesis that smaller advisers pay relatively more is not supported.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Impact of Dodd-Frank Act Compliance Cost on the Hedge Fund Industry (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2389423
scope_conditions: the 2012 survey sample of registered private fund advisers

claims.claim: Form PF is structured so that single strategy fund advisers collect and provide only a fraction of the information a multi strategy adviser must make available, which makes reporting burden a function of strategy count rather than of adviser size.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Impact of Dodd-Frank Act Compliance Cost on the Hedge Fund Industry (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2389423
scope_conditions: reporting under Form PF
comparison of single strategy and multi strategy advisers

claims.claim: Because Form PF requires less information from single strategy advisers, hedge fund advisers that apply only a single strategy to their portfolios may incur overall lower compliance cost.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Impact of Dodd-Frank Act Compliance Cost on the Hedge Fund Industry (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2389423
scope_conditions: advisers using a single investment strategy
Title IV and Form PF compliance

claims.claim: Least squares linear regression is non-robust to outliers: in the presence of outliers its predictions can be dragged toward the outliers and the variance of the estimates can be artificially inflated.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Impact of Dodd-Frank Act Compliance Cost on the Hedge Fund Industry (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2389423
scope_conditions: least squares linear regression applied to samples containing outliers

claims.claim: Because the distribution in this sample is heteroscedastic, treating each data point equally would allocate inappropriate weight to data points in the distribution, which is why the author used robust and weighted regression specifications.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Impact of Dodd-Frank Act Compliance Cost on the Hedge Fund Industry (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2389423
scope_conditions: survey samples with heteroscedastic distributions
small datasets with data points of varying importance

claims.claim: Weighted least squares regression depends on estimated weights, and contrary to the theory behind the method the exact weights are almost never determinable in real applications such as this study.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Impact of Dodd-Frank Act Compliance Cost on the Hedge Fund Industry (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2389423
scope_conditions: real world applications of weighted least squares regression

claims.claim: Selection bias is a valid concern in this study because of the lower sample sizes available for Models 1 through 5.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Impact of Dodd-Frank Act Compliance Cost on the Hedge Fund Industry (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2389423
scope_conditions: regression models 1 through 5 in this study
survey based samples

claims.claim: The analysis uses data from a 2012 survey study of a population of 1,264 private fund advisers registered before the SEC's registration effective date for private funds of March 30, 2012.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Impact of Dodd-Frank Act Compliance Cost on the Hedge Fund Industry (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2389423
scope_conditions: private fund advisers registered before March 30, 2012

claims.claim: In the open ended survey question on the effects of Title IV, 43.59 percent of respondents, the largest group, said the industry would be affected predominantly by increased costs.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Impact of Dodd-Frank Act Compliance Cost on the Hedge Fund Industry (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2389423
scope_conditions: responses to open ended survey question five

claims.claim: The majority of survey respondents believed that Title IV compliance costs $100,000.00 annually.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Impact of Dodd-Frank Act Compliance Cost on the Hedge Fund Industry (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2389423
scope_conditions: frequency of survey responses on the annual cost of Title IV compliance

claims.claim: The most common fund adviser response, at 47.67 percent of the 86 respondents to the question, estimates the annual compliance cost of Title IV in the range of $50,000 to $100,000.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Impact of Dodd-Frank Act Compliance Cost on the Hedge Fund Industry (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2389423
scope_conditions: 86 respondents to survey question 6bi
median cost measures for Title IV compliance

claims.claim: On the median annual time measure for Title IV compliance, 46 percent of respondents estimated between 100 and 250 hours per year and 32 percent estimated between 250 and 500 hours per year.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Impact of Dodd-Frank Act Compliance Cost on the Hedge Fund Industry (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2389423
scope_conditions: survey responses on annual time required for Title IV compliance

claims.claim: The clear majority of respondents prefer an asset size above the $150 million AUM registration threshold after the enactment of Title IV, indicating that advisers respond to the threshold by growing past it rather than staying below it.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Impact of Dodd-Frank Act Compliance Cost on the Hedge Fund Industry (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2389423
scope_conditions: survey responses on preferred asset size after Title IV enactment

claims.claim: The compliance and administrative costs created by Title IV of the Dodd-Frank Act are associated with the size of hedge fund advisers' assets under management.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Impact of Dodd-Frank Act Compliance Cost on the Hedge Fund Industry (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2389423
scope_conditions: entire sample and the single and multi strategy subsamples

claims.claim: All regression models show positive and predominantly statistically significant coefficients, with 18 out of 30 coefficients in the entire sample statistically significant.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Impact of Dodd-Frank Act Compliance Cost on the Hedge Fund Industry (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2389423
scope_conditions: five regression specifications applied to the entire sample

claims.claim: Compliance costs per unit of AUM do not diminish in the entire sample or in the multi strategy subsample, so there is no support for the hypothesis that smaller advisers bear relatively higher Title IV compliance cost.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Impact of Dodd-Frank Act Compliance Cost on the Hedge Fund Industry (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2389423
scope_conditions: entire sample and multi strategy subsample

claims.claim: The results contradict other studies finding an inverse relationship between the size of regulated firms and the per-unit cost of compliance, and suggest that financial regulation does not bring increasing returns to scale in the private fund industry.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Impact of Dodd-Frank Act Compliance Cost on the Hedge Fund Industry (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2389423
scope_conditions: private fund industry
Title IV compliance cost measured by survey data

claims.claim: Financial regulation has disparate effects on private fund advisers in comparison with other financial services providers, so evidence of scale economies in compliance drawn from banking does not transfer to private funds.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Impact of Dodd-Frank Act Compliance Cost on the Hedge Fund Industry (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2389423
scope_conditions: comparison of the private fund industry with banking and other financial services providers

claims.claim: The results suggest that the private fund industry may be more robust and less affected by financial regulation than other financial services providers.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Impact of Dodd-Frank Act Compliance Cost on the Hedge Fund Industry (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2389423
scope_conditions: private fund advisers subject to Title IV

claims.claim: The findings of this study are based on limited data and a small sample size, so additional research is required to fully investigate the impact of Title IV on the private fund industry.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Impact of Dodd-Frank Act Compliance Cost on the Hedge Fund Industry (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2389423
scope_conditions: survey sample of 94 respondents from a population of 1,264 advisers

claims.claim: While all coefficients are positive in the entire sample and the multi strategy subsample, the negative coefficients in the single strategy subsample suggest that the strategy employed by a hedge fund adviser could change the assessment of the effect of compliance cost.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Impact of Dodd-Frank Act Compliance Cost on the Hedge Fund Industry (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2389423
scope_conditions: single strategy subsample in Exhibit 12 compared with Exhibits 11 and 13

claims.claim: Even in the single strategy subsample only 9 of 30 coefficients are negative, so the strategy based qualification to the main finding is limited.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Impact of Dodd-Frank Act Compliance Cost on the Hedge Fund Industry (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2389423
scope_conditions: single strategy subsample in Exhibit 12

claims.claim: There is no evidence that private fund adviser regulation in Title IV of the Dodd-Frank Act increases returns to scale, which counters the most damning putative concern raised about regulatory compliance costs.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Impact of Dodd-Frank Act Compliance Cost on the Hedge Fund Industry (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2389423
scope_conditions: private fund advisers subject to Title IV

claims.claim: Based on these findings, there appears to be no immediate need for policy makers to address concerns over a possible effect of Title IV on startup hedge funds and smaller hedge fund advisers.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Impact of Dodd-Frank Act Compliance Cost on the Hedge Fund Industry (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2389423
scope_conditions: current policy making on Title IV
subject to the study's data limitations

claims.claim: A long-term study of the effects of Title IV compliance costs could change the assessment that no policy intervention is needed, so the finding is provisional on the short observation window.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Impact of Dodd-Frank Act Compliance Cost on the Hedge Fund Industry (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2389423
scope_conditions: longer time horizon than the period immediately after the March 2012 registration effective date

claims.claim: The SEC data collected from private fund advisers feeds every stage of the FSOC's systemic risk assessment, and the FSOC leans most heavily on precisely those disclosure items that are the most problematic.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Systemic Risk of Private Funds after the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2470008
scope_conditions: private fund advisers reporting under SEC Form PF
FSOC systemic risk assessment of nonbank financial companies

claims.claim: Accuracy and consistency problems in the SEC's private fund data collection can impair the FSOC's ability to evaluate the systemic risk posed by private fund advisers.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Systemic Risk of Private Funds after the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2470008
scope_conditions: data collected through Form PF
FSOC evaluation of nonbank systemic risk

claims.claim: Prior studies and anecdotal evidence indicate that the data collection mandated by Form PF could itself create problems for the FSOC when it evaluates hedge fund systemic risk.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Systemic Risk of Private Funds after the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2470008
scope_conditions: hedge fund systemic risk evaluation by FSOC

claims.claim: Even though the private fund industry broadly accepted Form PF, the form's core problems for the SEC are the ambiguity of several questions, advisers' disagreement with the definition of funds, and correspondingly insufficient SEC guidance.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Systemic Risk of Private Funds after the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2470008
scope_conditions: Form PF as implemented by the SEC
registered private fund advisers

claims.claim: The systemic risk of hedge funds arises principally from the combination of aggressive investment strategies and high leverage with adverse price movements that can dry up credit and depress the market price of collateral.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Systemic Risk of Private Funds after the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2470008
scope_conditions: hedge funds employing leverage
periods of adverse market price fluctuations

claims.claim: Hedge funds threaten the financial system through two distinct channels: directly, by damaging systemically important financial institutions, and indirectly, by generating liquidity shocks and raising volatility in key markets.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Systemic Risk of Private Funds after the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2470008
scope_conditions: hedge funds active in key markets
counterparty relationships with systemically important institutions

claims.claim: The 2008 to 2009 financial crisis altered market conditions and the factors driving private fund systemic risk, which triggered a second, distinct wave of scholarship on private funds' systemic implications.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Systemic Risk of Private Funds after the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2470008
scope_conditions: post crisis period after 2009

claims.claim: Some estimates place private funds ahead of banks in size and importance during and after the financial crisis.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Systemic Risk of Private Funds after the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2470008
scope_conditions: during and after the 2008 to 2009 financial crisis

claims.claim: The unprecedented growth of the private fund industry combined with the low interest rate environment created by post crisis quantitative easing drove private fund managers to reach for yield.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Systemic Risk of Private Funds after the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2470008
scope_conditions: low interest rate environment following quantitative easing
post 2009 private fund industry

claims.claim: Because private fund advisers supply liquidity and perform liquidity transformation in the manner of banks, the vulnerabilities their bank like activities create can carry large consequences for financial stability.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Systemic Risk of Private Funds after the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2470008
scope_conditions: private fund advisers engaging in bank like activities
use of leverage, liquidity transformation, or funding mismatches

claims.claim: International regulators agree on designation criteria but not on the unit of assessment: the FSB and IOSCO assess systemic importance at the fund level while the OFR would assess it at the asset manager level with all funds combined.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Systemic Risk of Private Funds after the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2470008
scope_conditions: designation of globally active investment funds as systemically important

claims.claim: National regulators reached opposite conclusions on the same question: unlike the OFR, FSB and IOSCO, the United Kingdom's Financial Services Authority concluded from its first comprehensive survey of London's hedge fund industry that the industry poses no systemic risk.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Systemic Risk of Private Funds after the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2470008
scope_conditions: London hedge fund industry as surveyed by the FSA
conditions prevailing at the time of the survey

claims.claim: The absence of financial market repercussions from the Amaranth failure suggests that indirect regulation of private funds, achieved by having regulators press banks to limit leverage extended to their fund clients, worked.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Systemic Risk of Private Funds after the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2470008
scope_conditions: post LTCM supervisory practice of monitoring fund clients through bank leverage limits
the Amaranth failure in 2006

claims.claim: Form PF data was tailored primarily for the FSOC rather than for the SEC's own purposes, a design choice that shaped the level of reporting required.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Systemic Risk of Private Funds after the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2470008
scope_conditions: Form PF as adopted by the SEC Division of Investment Management

claims.claim: The FSOC's powers over nonbank financial institutions are broad and without precedent in United States financial regulation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Systemic Risk of Private Funds after the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2470008
scope_conditions: nonbank financial institutions subject to Dodd-Frank Title I

claims.claim: The quantitative measures used in systemic risk assessment are not codified in statute, so the FSOC can alter its thresholds and its analysis through rulemaking.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Systemic Risk of Private Funds after the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2470008
scope_conditions: SIFI determinations under Dodd-Frank section 113

claims.claim: Commonly managed investment funds holding $50 billion or more in aggregate total consolidated assets can be designated systemically important, and following a similar investment strategy across those funds makes designation more likely.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Systemic Risk of Private Funds after the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2470008
scope_conditions: aggregate total consolidated assets at or above $50 billion
funds under common management pursuing similar strategies

claims.claim: Stage one of the FSOC's designation process is a mechanical screen: six quantitative thresholds filter out nonbank financial institutions unlikely to pose significant systemic risk before any institution specific or qualitative analysis begins.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Systemic Risk of Private Funds after the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2470008
scope_conditions: FSOC three stage SIFI designation process

claims.claim: SIFI designation changes the nature of regulation for a nonbank financial institution, subjecting it to substantial additional regulation and forcing it to change how it does business, which can in turn constrain its growth.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Systemic Risk of Private Funds after the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2470008
scope_conditions: nonbank financial institutions designated as systemically important

claims.claim: The FSOC's three stage SIFI review process depends heavily on information that private fund investment advisers supply through Form PF.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Systemic Risk of Private Funds after the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2470008
scope_conditions: SIFI review of private funds and their advisers

claims.claim: Form PF information addresses most of the FSOC's stage one thresholds either directly or indirectly, so the mechanical screen runs largely on adviser reported data.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Systemic Risk of Private Funds after the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2470008
scope_conditions: FSOC stage one threshold assessment
except the threshold for credit default swaps written on the company

claims.claim: The SEC itself reports that the consistency of investment advisers' responses on Form PF is not ensured and may be questionable.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Systemic Risk of Private Funds after the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2470008
scope_conditions: Form PF filings as analyzed by SEC staff

claims.claim: Advisers take different approaches and make different assumptions when completing Form PF, which the SEC identifies as a further challenge to the usability of the data.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Systemic Risk of Private Funds after the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2470008
scope_conditions: Form PF filings by registered private fund advisers

claims.claim: The SEC's initial analysis of Form PF data turned up anomalies attributed to filer error, which prompted SEC concern about the quality of the information private fund advisers report.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Systemic Risk of Private Funds after the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2470008
scope_conditions: early Form PF filing cycles

claims.claim: Expanding the uses of Form PF data remains difficult so long as there is insufficient confidence in the accuracy of what advisers report, notwithstanding SEC efforts to improve quality through interpretive FAQs and curative amendments.

scope_conditions: current state of Form PF data accuracy
SEC remedial measures limited to FAQs and curative amendments

claims.claim: Form PF data quality and utility are likely to improve over time as filers grow familiar with the form's requirements and calculation methods, because the SEC's experience with the data is still early.

scope_conditions: early stage of SEC experience with Form PF
assumes filers become more familiar with requirements

claims.claim: The FSOC itself conceded that available data was insufficient when it tried to identify the activities of the twenty largest United States fund managers as possible sources of systemic risk.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Systemic Risk of Private Funds after the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2470008
scope_conditions: FSOC 2013 annual report
counterparty risk, leverage, repo, securities lending, and separate accounts

claims.claim: The substantive defects in Form PF data are the ambiguity of several key questions, inaccurate definitions paired with insufficient SEC guidance, and difficulty aggregating the required information.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Systemic Risk of Private Funds after the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2470008
scope_conditions: Form PF as filed by private fund advisers

claims.claim: More than forty percent of respondents in a prior study disagreed with the definitions or instructions in Form PF.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Systemic Risk of Private Funds after the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2470008
scope_conditions: survey respondents in the author's prior private fund disclosure study

claims.claim: The Form PF definition of Regulatory Assets under Management is the leading example of a definition that forced filers to interpret what they were required to report.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Systemic Risk of Private Funds after the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2470008

claims.claim: The interpretation Form PF demands generated particular concern among filers about the definition of counterparties and about counterparty performance measures.

claims.claim: Form PF instructions need clarification and its definitions, including those for RAUM and AUM, need improvement, since there is evidence that questions and definitions had to be optimized.
