scope_conditions: Form PF as currently drafted

claims.claim: Because several core Form PF questions feeding the FSOC's stage one threshold screen are themselves defective, the FSOC's systemic risk assessment process could be compromised.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Systemic Risk of Private Funds after the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2470008
scope_conditions: FSOC stage one threshold assessment
reliance on Form PF questions with identified defects

claims.claim: Because the FSOC uses RAUM related valuations directly and indirectly to set stage one thresholds, and because RAUM requires substantial filer interpretation, it is questionable whether the FSOC can use that Form PF data effectively and sustainably for systemic risk evaluations and SIFI designations.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Systemic Risk of Private Funds after the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2470008
scope_conditions: stage one thresholds computed from RAUM related asset valuations
Form PF Questions 8, 9, 13, 44, 46, and 58

claims.claim: The Form PF counterparty questions most affected by filer interpretation, Questions 22 and 23, are the very ones the FSOC uses in stage two to determine the interconnectedness of private funds.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Systemic Risk of Private Funds after the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2470008
scope_conditions: FSOC stage two analysis of interconnectedness

claims.claim: Widespread filer disagreement with Form PF definitions implies that a large share of filers are uncertain how to answer, which raises the possibility that they complete the form with estimates and varied assumptions.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Systemic Risk of Private Funds after the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2470008
scope_conditions: filers who disagreed with Form PF definitions or instructions

claims.claim: If the FSOC relies on inaccurate Form PF data in its systemic risk assessment, its work on private funds may itself be erroneous.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Systemic Risk of Private Funds after the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2470008
scope_conditions: FSOC reliance on Form PF data subject to inaccuracies

claims.claim: Private fund advisers reporting under Form PF encountered issues that could affect the FSOC's systemic risk assessment, but the author does not claim that the FSOC is unable to fulfill its congressional mandate.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Systemic Risk of Private Funds after the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2470008
scope_conditions: scope limited to the effects of Form PF reporting issues

claims.claim: Matching the identified Form PF defects against the FSOC's specific uses of that data suggests possible inaccuracies in the FSOC's systemic risk assessment process, although the author disclaims scientific or empirical precision for the analysis.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Systemic Risk of Private Funds after the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2470008
scope_conditions: method of matching known data defects to documented FSOC uses
no claim of empirical precision

claims.claim: Fixing the identified problems with Form PF data would help optimize the FSOC's systemic risk assessment of private funds.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Systemic Risk of Private Funds after the Dodd-Frank Act (2014). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2470008
scope_conditions: Form PF data defects identified in this article

claims.claim: Stock prices respond significantly and predictably in a positive direction to the DOJ press release announcing execution of a non- or deferred prosecution agreement and to the start of the N/DPA term.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, Stock Price Response to Non- and Deferred Prosecution Agreements (2015). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2629451
scope_conditions: publicly traded U.S. firms that executed N/DPAs between 1993 and 2015
event windows measured around the DOJ press release date and the start date of the N/DPA term

claims.claim: The market does not price the three defining N/DPA events in isolation; it treats the announcement, the start of the term, and the end of the term as sequential and conditional events.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, Stock Price Response to Non- and Deferred Prosecution Agreements (2015). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2629451
scope_conditions: sample of 94 publicly traded N/DPA firms, 1993 to 2015

claims.claim: Investor response to N/DPAs is not uniform: it varies with the firm's industry, the severity of the financial fine, and the extent of the governance improvements the N/DPA mandates.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, Stock Price Response to Non- and Deferred Prosecution Agreements (2015). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2629451
scope_conditions: ten industry sub-clusters in the sample
partitions relative to median fines and median governance intensity

claims.claim: There is no systematic price momentum beyond the three core N/DPA event dates, which the authors read as evidence that the market is reasonably efficient with respect to N/DPA information.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, Stock Price Response to Non- and Deferred Prosecution Agreements (2015). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2629451
scope_conditions: information about N/DPAs specifically
sample of publicly traded N/DPA firms, 1993 to 2015

claims.claim: Investors react negatively to impending N/DPA driven changes in the period before the agreement is executed, but once the N/DPA is executed they generally treat it as a positive event for the firm.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, Stock Price Response to Non- and Deferred Prosecution Agreements (2015). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2629451
scope_conditions: pre-execution versus post-execution windows around the DOJ announcement

claims.claim: Investors treat the expiration of an N/DPA term as a negative event for the firm.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, Stock Price Response to Non- and Deferred Prosecution Agreements (2015). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2629451
scope_conditions: end of N/DPA term date, ENDPAT
reduced sample of 59 firms where the end date fell on a trading day

claims.claim: The combination of a positive market reaction at the start of the N/DPA term and a negative reaction at its end is evidence that the governance changes N/DPAs mandate actually matter to firm value.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, Stock Price Response to Non- and Deferred Prosecution Agreements (2015). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2629451
scope_conditions: governance changes become mandatory at the start of the term and unenforceable at its end

claims.claim: Because N/DPAs are contractual arrangements between corporations and the Department of Justice that remedy identified governance shortcomings, it is the DOJ, rather than Congress or the courts, that is changing U.S. corporate governance practice.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, Stock Price Response to Non- and Deferred Prosecution Agreements (2015). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2629451
scope_conditions: United States, 1993 to 2015
governance historically a matter of state law

claims.claim: The study's hand-selected dataset covers all institutions that executed N/DPAs from 1993 to 2015, a population of 330 agreements, of which 94 involved publicly traded firms usable for stock price tests.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, Stock Price Response to Non- and Deferred Prosecution Agreements (2015). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2629451
scope_conditions: publicly available N/DPAs recorded in the University of Virginia Law Library database
stock price data availability limits the tested sample to 94 firms

claims.claim: The U.S. financial corporations subject to N/DPAs collectively exceed $690 billion in market capitalization and more than $20 trillion in assets under management, making N/DPA governance intervention economically consequential.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, Stock Price Response to Non- and Deferred Prosecution Agreements (2015). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2629451
scope_conditions: U.S. financial corporations subject to N/DPAs as of the Copland 2012 count

claims.claim: This is the first study to examine stock price reactions to non- and deferred prosecution agreements, using all publicly available N/DPAs across several industries from 1993 to 2015 (N=330).
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, Stock Price Response to Non- and Deferred Prosecution Agreements (2015). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2629451
scope_conditions: publicly available N/DPAs across several industries

claims.claim: The event study design is appropriate for N/DPAs because the wrongdoing event is identifiable through the execution of a reasonably standardized agreement and because information about the firm's wrongdoing can change the distribution of stock returns.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, Stock Price Response to Non- and Deferred Prosecution Agreements (2015). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2629451
scope_conditions: N/DPA executions are reasonably similar in format
events are evenly distributed and cross-sectionally independent

claims.claim: The date of the DOJ press release announcing execution is the only reliable announcement date for an N/DPA, so it is the defensible event date for measuring market reaction.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, Stock Price Response to Non- and Deferred Prosecution Agreements (2015). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2629451
scope_conditions: press release generally issued on the day the agreement is signed for NPAs or filed with the court for DPAs

claims.claim: The DOJ announcement is the only ascertainable point at which the market can assess the impact of the governance changes an N/DPA mandates, because the announcement typically accompanies release of the agreement document itself.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, Stock Price Response to Non- and Deferred Prosecution Agreements (2015). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2629451
scope_conditions: judicial approval may follow later without adding public information

claims.claim: Pre-announcement leaks about a pending N/DPA, including leaks by prosecutors, should not move markets significantly because leaked details carry no certainty or finality as to final terms or fine amount.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, Stock Price Response to Non- and Deferred Prosecution Agreements (2015). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2629451
scope_conditions: leaks of fine amounts or agreement form weeks or months before the announcement

claims.claim: Unlike legislative mandates, N/DPA governance changes are preceded by no public debate or publicity, so their effect on firm value is not gradually incorporated into prices and is therefore testable by event study.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, Stock Price Response to Non- and Deferred Prosecution Agreements (2015). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2629451
scope_conditions: contrast with congressional regulatory changes whose effects are anticipated gradually

claims.claim: Around the DOJ announcement, N/DPA firms show a significant positive cumulative abnormal return trend before day minus five, a significant drop at day minus five, and negative CARs relative to matched competitors from day minus four to day minus one.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, Stock Price Response to Non- and Deferred Prosecution Agreements (2015). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2629451
scope_conditions: 94 N/DPA firms matched to 94 direct competitors by market capitalization
window t=-25 to t=25 around ANDPAE

claims.claim: After the DOJ announcement, competitor firms' cumulative abnormal returns trend negative from day zero to day twenty five while N/DPA firms' CARs continue on a neutral to positive trend.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, Stock Price Response to Non- and Deferred Prosecution Agreements (2015). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2629451
scope_conditions: matched competitor sample of 94 firms
post-announcement window t=0 to t=25

claims.claim: The negative pricing of N/DPA firms immediately before the announcement reflects the market's negative assessment of the agreement and its associated fines, plausibly driven by uncertainty in the days before the announcement resolves it.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, Stock Price Response to Non- and Deferred Prosecution Agreements (2015). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2629451
scope_conditions: days immediately preceding ANDPAE

claims.claim: The positive post-announcement reaction is best read as the market rewarding both the end of a costly DOJ investigation and the governance terms the N/DPA is expected to impose.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, Stock Price Response to Non- and Deferred Prosecution Agreements (2015). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2629451
scope_conditions: window t=0 to t=25 after the DOJ announcement

claims.claim: Immediately before the N/DPA term becomes effective, from day minus three to day minus one, the market prices the onset of the term as a negative event.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, Stock Price Response to Non- and Deferred Prosecution Agreements (2015). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2629451
scope_conditions: window immediately preceding BNDPAT

claims.claim: From the first day of the N/DPA term through day twenty five, the period in which mandated governance improvements are in force, the market prices the N/DPA as a positive event for the firm.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, Stock Price Response to Non- and Deferred Prosecution Agreements (2015). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2629451
scope_conditions: window t=0 to t=25 after BNDPAT
period during which N/DPA governance improvements are in effect

claims.claim: The sign of the market reaction reverses at the end of the N/DPA term: where the announcement and the start of the term produce positive CARs, the end of the term produces negative CARs at day zero and from day one through day fifteen.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, Stock Price Response to Non- and Deferred Prosecution Agreements (2015). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2629451
scope_conditions: 59 firm ENDPAT sample excluding terms ending on non-trading days

claims.claim: Negative returns after the end of the N/DPA term are evidence that investors regard the expiration of the term, and the consequent unenforceability of the associated governance improvements, as bad news for the firm.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, Stock Price Response to Non- and Deferred Prosecution Agreements (2015). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2629451
scope_conditions: days t=1 to t=15 after ENDPAT

claims.claim: The authors reject Hypothesis 1: they find no evidence that the market reacts negatively to the N/DPA announcement and the start of the term and positively to the end of the term, contrary to the cost-imposition view of N/DPAs.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, Stock Price Response to Non- and Deferred Prosecution Agreements (2015). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2629451
scope_conditions: 94 firm sample, three event dates

claims.claim: The data support Hypothesis 2: the market reacts positively at the DOJ announcement and at the start of the N/DPA term and negatively at the end of the term.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, Stock Price Response to Non- and Deferred Prosecution Agreements (2015). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2629451
scope_conditions: evidence drawn from Figures 2 through 4a
94 firm sample, 59 firms at ENDPAT

claims.claim: The positive market reaction at announcement and at the start of the term is the market acknowledging that an N/DPA gives the firm an opportunity to be better managed, more compliant, and less exposed to penalties.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, Stock Price Response to Non- and Deferred Prosecution Agreements (2015). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2629451
scope_conditions: post-announcement and post-start-of-term windows

claims.claim: The negative market reaction at the end of the N/DPA term is the market acknowledging that suboptimal governance practices are likely to resume once the term expires.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, Stock Price Response to Non- and Deferred Prosecution Agreements (2015). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2629451
scope_conditions: post-expiration windows in Figures 4 and 4a

claims.claim: The data support Hypothesis 3: the market reacts positively when N/DPA governance changes become mandatory at the start of the term and negatively when they cease to be mandatory at its end.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, Stock Price Response to Non- and Deferred Prosecution Agreements (2015). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2629451
scope_conditions: evidence drawn from Figures 3, 3a, 4, and 4a

claims.claim: The paired positive reaction at the start and negative reaction at the end of the N/DPA term is direct evidence that N/DPA mandated governance changes matter to investors.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, Stock Price Response to Non- and Deferred Prosecution Agreements (2015). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2629451
scope_conditions: governance changes are effective and mandatory only during the N/DPA term

claims.claim: The market values N/DPA governance changes during the term because those changes effectively address the underlying corporate wrongdoing and its damage to goodwill and reputation while reducing the likelihood of continuing fines and litigation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, Stock Price Response to Non- and Deferred Prosecution Agreements (2015). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2629451
scope_conditions: during the term of the N/DPA

claims.claim: Market reaction to N/DPAs is industry specific, supporting the hypothesis that investors in some industries are more sensitive to N/DPA effects than investors in others.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, Stock Price Response to Non- and Deferred Prosecution Agreements (2015). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2629451
scope_conditions: ten industry sub-clusters identified via Morningstar categories and Russell 1000 industry indices

claims.claim: Because the market reacts positively both to N/DPA announcements and to the governance improvements taking effect, the DOJ's escalation of N/DPA executions beginning in 2002 could be justified on market value grounds.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, Stock Price Response to Non- and Deferred Prosecution Agreements (2015). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2629451
scope_conditions: holds to the extent market reaction is an acceptable measure of policy value

claims.claim: The study's results may be biased toward low impact N/DPAs, because firms that were acquired, merged, or went bankrupt as a result of an N/DPA had to be dropped for lack of public trading data, and those are precisely the highest impact cases.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, Stock Price Response to Non- and Deferred Prosecution Agreements (2015). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2629451
scope_conditions: applies to any stock price study of N/DPAs relying on continuous trading data

claims.claim: The findings rest on a small sample and limited data, so they should be treated as provisional pending replication on a larger set of publicly traded N/DPA firms.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, Stock Price Response to Non- and Deferred Prosecution Agreements (2015). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2629451
scope_conditions: 94 firm sample, 59 firms at the end of term event

claims.claim: Despite wide-ranging criticism of N/DPAs on authority, fairness, and expertise grounds, scholars agree that N/DPAs do influence corporate governance.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, Stock Price Response to Non- and Deferred Prosecution Agreements (2015). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2629451
scope_conditions: scholarly literature on N/DPAs through 2015

claims.claim: The existing literature has barely engaged the financial market implications of N/DPAs, which is the gap this study fills.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, Stock Price Response to Non- and Deferred Prosecution Agreements (2015). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2629451
scope_conditions: legal and governance literature on N/DPAs as of 2015

claims.claim: The observed growth in N/DPA execution, especially since 2002, indicates that N/DPAs will continue to shape major U.S. corporations across a range of industries.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, Stock Price Response to Non- and Deferred Prosecution Agreements (2015). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2629451
scope_conditions: extrapolated from the 1993 to 2015 time series of 330 executed N/DPAs

claims.claim: Prior coding of all publicly available N/DPAs from 1993 to 2013 across more than 230 governance categories shows that N/DPAs have a substantial effect on corporate governance.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy Lacine, Stock Price Response to Non- and Deferred Prosecution Agreements (2015). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2629451
scope_conditions: N=271 agreements, 1993 to 2013

claims.claim: Confluence between mutual and hedge funds runs in two directions at once: mutual funds are converging on hedge funds along the dimension of investment strategy, while hedge funds are converging on mutual funds along the dimension of regulation.
claims.citation: Kaal, Confluence of Mutual and Private Funds (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2715083
scope_conditions: post financial crisis U.S. fund markets
after the Dodd-Frank Act and the JOBS Act

claims.claim: Regulatory convergence is not driven only by tightened post crisis rules: the liberalization of advertising restrictions after the Dodd-Frank Act also pushes hedge funds toward mutual fund form, so deregulation and reregulation work in the same convergent direction.
claims.citation: Kaal, Confluence of Mutual and Private Funds (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2715083
scope_conditions: U.S. private fund regulation after Dodd-Frank and the JOBS Act

claims.claim: Mandatory registration and increased disclosure for certain hedge fund advisers under the Dodd-Frank Act place hedge fund advisers under registration and reporting obligations similar to those long borne by mutual fund advisers.
claims.citation: Kaal, Confluence of Mutual and Private Funds (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2715083
scope_conditions: advisers meeting the Dodd-Frank registration thresholds

claims.claim: Lifting the advertising ban for hedge fund advisers under the JOBS Act, combined with FSOC treating mutual and hedge funds alike for SIFI designation, effectively assimilated the advertising requirements applicable to the two asset classes.
claims.citation: Kaal, Confluence of Mutual and Private Funds (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2715083
scope_conditions: Rule 506(c) offerings after September 2013
FSOC nonbank SIFI designation process

claims.claim: The private fund industry grew 26 percent between 2013 and 2015, rising from just over 2 trillion dollars of assets under management to 2.7 trillion dollars.
claims.citation: Kaal, Confluence of Mutual and Private Funds (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2715083
scope_conditions: BarclayHedge industry data, 2013 to 2015

claims.claim: The author stipulates that retail alternative funds are funds regulated under the Investment Company Act that attempt to replicate private fund strategies, including leverage, derivatives, short selling, and nontraditional asset classes; this definition carries the chapter's confluence analysis.
claims.citation: Kaal, Confluence of Mutual and Private Funds (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2715083
scope_conditions: as used throughout this chapter
covers liquid alternatives, unconstrained funds, alternative mutual funds, and synthetic hedge funds

claims.claim: Net assets of mutual funds using alternative strategies quadrupled between 2007 and 2014, a 27 percent annualized growth rate, while the number of such funds rose from 181 to 402.
claims.citation: Kaal, Confluence of Mutual and Private Funds (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2715083
scope_conditions: Investment Company Institute data, 2007 to 2014
author's own analysis presented in Exhibit 1

claims.claim: Growth in retail alternatives is expected to continue rather than plateau, with projections that 15.8 percent of all mutual fund assets under management will sit in alternative mutual funds by 2022, making it a multi-trillion dollar industry.
claims.citation: Kaal, Confluence of Mutual and Private Funds (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2715083
scope_conditions: JP Morgan and Strategic Insight projections
horizon of 2022

claims.claim: Unconstrained mutual funds differ from traditional fixed income mutual funds not only in trading strategy, using futures, short sales, and derivatives, but also in turnover and fee structure, which more closely resemble those of hedge funds.
claims.citation: Kaal, Confluence of Mutual and Private Funds (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2715083
scope_conditions: fixed income unconstrained mutual funds studied in Kaal and Anderson (2016)

claims.claim: Operating a mutual fund is materially more capital intensive than operating a hedge fund: the mutual fund adviser's required investment in trading and operational technology and in specialized staffing substantially exceeds what a hedge fund manager must spend.
claims.citation: Kaal, Confluence of Mutual and Private Funds (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2715083
scope_conditions: comparison of registered mutual fund advisers with unregistered hedge fund managers

claims.claim: Private party litigation against hedge fund managers stays minimal because well counseled managers make extensive disclosures to investors who are presumed sophisticated, unlike mutual fund advisers who face ongoing high value investor suits.
claims.citation: Kaal, Confluence of Mutual and Private Funds (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2715083
scope_conditions: U.S. hedge funds and offshore vehicles chartered in the Caymans or BVI
assumes industry standard disclosure practice

claims.claim: Hedge fund investors have almost no statutory remedy: the regime establishing a hedge fund investor's rights is severely limited, nearly to the point of nonexistence, in the United States and in the offshore jurisdictions where many hedge funds are chartered.
claims.citation: Kaal, Confluence of Mutual and Private Funds (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2715083
scope_conditions: United States, Cayman Islands, and British Virgin Islands

claims.claim: The author stipulates the term nominal confluence: legal requirements that are formally identical for mutual and hedge fund managers but that operate in materially different ways in practice, so formal legal convergence overstates actual convergence.
claims.citation: Kaal, Confluence of Mutual and Private Funds (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2715083
scope_conditions: applies where the same statute or rule governs both fund types

claims.claim: Identical rules diverge in practice because the two vehicle types are structured, operated, and run as businesses differently; the Investment Advisers Act applies to both, yet its obligations are far more onerous for mutual fund managers.
claims.citation: Kaal, Confluence of Mutual and Private Funds (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2715083
scope_conditions: Investment Advisers Act obligations
registered mutual fund advisers compared with hedge fund advisers

claims.claim: Best execution is a leading instance of nominal confluence: the obligation is nominally the same, but it is far more complicated and burdensome for the mutual fund manager than for the hedge fund adviser.
claims.citation: Kaal, Confluence of Mutual and Private Funds (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2715083
scope_conditions: best execution obligations for trades directed to brokers

claims.claim: Freedom from significant regulatory oversight is what historically enabled hedge funds to run more exotic, more leveraged strategies aimed at absolute returns.
claims.citation: Kaal, Confluence of Mutual and Private Funds (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2715083
scope_conditions: hedge funds operating under securities law safe harbors before the Dodd-Frank Act

claims.claim: Alternative mutual funds generally cannot deliver the same absolute returns as hedge funds, a shortfall some attribute to the lighter touch regulation and better incentives available to hedge funds.
claims.citation: Kaal, Confluence of Mutual and Private Funds (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2715083
scope_conditions: comparison of registered alternative funds with unregistered hedge funds

claims.claim: Alternative funds gave retail investors access to hedge fund strategies and higher returns than traditional mutual funds while charging mutual fund fees, and that combination is what increased retail demand.
claims.citation: Kaal, Confluence of Mutual and Private Funds (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2715083
scope_conditions: retail investor segment in the early 2010s

claims.claim: The traditional mutual fund governance model, in which one board serves multiple discrete funds within a sponsor's group, is subject to significant oversight challenges.
claims.citation: Kaal, Confluence of Mutual and Private Funds (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2715083
scope_conditions: traditional single board mutual fund complexes

claims.claim: In a multimanager series trust the board is largely independent of any adviser in the fund group, because the structure is centered on an unaffiliated administrator rather than on the sponsoring investment adviser.
claims.citation: Kaal, Confluence of Mutual and Private Funds (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2715083
scope_conditions: multimanager series trust arrangements

claims.claim: Despite open issues and possible shortcomings, the multimanager series trust structure appears to offer lasting substantive governance improvements for mutual funds.
claims.citation: Kaal, Confluence of Mutual and Private Funds (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2715083
scope_conditions: multimanager series trust governance model

claims.claim: The cost savings of the multimanager series trust model are a confluence mechanism: they let a growing number of smaller hedge fund advisers reach retail investors by launching a mutual fund.
claims.citation: Kaal, Confluence of Mutual and Private Funds (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2715083
scope_conditions: smaller investment advisers by assets under management
advisers seeking retail distribution

claims.claim: The inherent conflict of interest facing an adviser who simultaneously runs a mutual fund and a hedge fund is an important limiting factor on the continued rise of side-by-side management.
claims.citation: Kaal, Confluence of Mutual and Private Funds (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2715083
scope_conditions: side-by-side management of a mutual fund and a hedge fund by the same adviser

claims.claim: The subadvisory route leaves a regulatory gap: none of the mutual fund manager's obligations, such as daily valuation, public and SEC reporting, or independent boards, reach the private fund adviser serving as subadviser.
claims.citation: Kaal, Confluence of Mutual and Private Funds (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2715083
scope_conditions: private fund managers subadvising a mutual fund, subfund, or account

claims.claim: For the first time in the industry's history, the Dodd-Frank Act required most hedge fund advisers to register with the SEC, mandating disclosure of information previously treated as proprietary and private.
claims.citation: Kaal, Confluence of Mutual and Private Funds (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2715083
scope_conditions: investment advisers with more than 150 million dollars of assets under management

claims.claim: FSOC's SIFI designation framework does not distinguish between mutual and hedge funds, even though evidence indicates designation would have disparate effects on the two asset classes.
claims.citation: Kaal, Confluence of Mutual and Private Funds (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2715083
scope_conditions: FSOC three stage nonbank SIFI designation process

claims.claim: The confluence trends identified are correlational, not causal: the author expressly disclaims any claim of cause and effect and presents the peripheral effects as long term possibilities warranting monitoring.

claims.claim: Confluence factors help move the hedge fund industry from the fringes of finance into recognition as part of mainstream finance, aided by increased oversight under Title IV of the Dodd-Frank Act and the JOBS Act.

denominator close to 1

months surrounding March 30, 2012

evidence described as non-robust

scope_conditions: private fund industry over its history

scope_conditions: comparison to prior studies of Dodd-Frank effects on private funds

claims.claim: The pacing problem arises from a two sided divergence: innovation driven by science and technology is accelerating at the same time that federal and state agencies' regulatory processes have slowed down and continue to slow down.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation for Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2831040

claims.claim: Although the extent and causes of rulemaking ossification remain empirically uncertain, increased legal and evidentiary burdens on regulatory authorities are the consensus explanation for the slowdown in agency rulemaking.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation for Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2831040
scope_conditions: United States federal and state agency rulemaking

claims.claim: Regulators face a two ended timing trap: at the early stage of an innovation they lack information about its possible impact, and at the later stage the innovation is entrenched, so regulatory change becomes far more costly for innovating corporations.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation for Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2831040
scope_conditions: disruptive innovation across a product cycle

claims.claim: Systemic factors widen the divergence between regulation and innovation, including the political and ideological structures of the rulemaking process and the political gridlock of a two party system that impedes the passing of legislation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation for Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2831040
scope_conditions: two party legislative systems

claims.claim: The most widely recognized drawbacks of traditional rulemaking under the Administrative Procedure Act are its lack of speed, its cumbersomeness, and the volume of litigation generated by its notice and comment procedures.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation for Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2831040
scope_conditions: United States APA notice and comment rulemaking

claims.claim: The pacing problem is partly a byproduct of the goal of legal certainty: because regulation is designed to be a durable source of predictability, rulemaking driven by legal certainty cannot keep pace as innovation accelerates.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation for Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2831040
scope_conditions: accelerating innovation

claims.claim: Facts based, ex post, trial and error rulemaking cannot anticipate the regulatory issues created by innovation, so rulemakers may never recognize, or may recognize only much too late, which new regulatory demands apply to a given innovation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation for Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2831040
scope_conditions: ex post trial and error rulemaking in the existing regulatory framework

claims.claim: Rulemakers rely almost exclusively on stable and presumptively optimal rules meant to be permanent solutions, and that reliance ignores the ever changing rule environment driven by exponential growth in technology and innovation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation for Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2831040

claims.claim: Formal rulemaking in the existing regulatory infrastructure is almost always too time consuming, because product innovation moves fast enough that regulations covering an innovative product are obsolete before they are finalized.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation for Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2831040
scope_conditions: formal rulemaking directed at fast moving innovative products

claims.claim: An existing regulatory infrastructure built on stable and presumptively optimal rules is largely incapable of addressing the ever increasing unknown future contingencies associated with disruptive innovation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation for Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2831040
scope_conditions: disruptive innovation

claims.claim: Introducing a regulatory update where genuine regulatory reform is needed can deteriorate the relationship between regulation and innovation, because innovation driven by changing values and societal norms calls for reform rather than incremental updating.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation for Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2831040
scope_conditions: innovation driven by shifting values and societal norms

claims.claim: The existing regulatory framework is sub optimally equipped to remedy both existing and future regulatory challenges associated with exponential innovation, which is the first premise for integrating dynamic elements into the regulation of innovation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation for Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2831040
scope_conditions: exponential innovation

claims.claim: The faster the cycle of disruptive innovation, the shorter the timeline for society to adapt and respond with a familiar pattern of laws, regulation, and frameworks, which gives disruptive exponential innovation a potentially destabilizing effect on society.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation for Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2831040
scope_conditions: accelerating cycles of disruptive innovation

claims.claim: Dynamic elements in the regulation of innovation are a supplement to the existing regulatory framework rather than a replacement for it, and their intent is to optimize that framework.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation for Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2831040

claims.claim: The three core law and technology proposals for the pacing problem, regulation via the judiciary, early stage regulation of innovation, and principles based regulation, all have practical limitations and none of them uses dynamic regulatory elements.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation for Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2831040

claims.claim: Addressing the regulatory issues created by innovation outpacing law through the judiciary is insufficient in the face of exponential innovation, because increasing evidence shows courts cannot sufficiently counterbalance the shortcomings of the legislative system.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation for Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2831040
scope_conditions: exponential innovation

claims.claim: The doctrine of stare decisis and judicial adherence to precedent decided decades or centuries earlier mean the court system is structurally a suspension system for rapid change, built to supply stability and predictability rather than speed.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation for Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2831040
scope_conditions: common law court systems bound by precedent

claims.claim: Litigation in the court system can take years, which increases the likelihood that courts will not react in a timely manner, much less in real time, to exponential innovation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation for Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2831040
scope_conditions: exponential innovation

claims.claim: Dynamic regulatory mechanisms are already replacing litigation and will continue to replace it.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation for Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2831040

claims.claim: Deferred prosecution agreements produce relevant, real time, decentralized, high quality information for regulation in most industries and are used as a preferred alternative to litigation by both prosecutors and corporations.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation for Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2831040
scope_conditions: most industries where DPAs are available

claims.claim: Deferred prosecution agreements produce superior feedback effects for regulation because the prosecutor's investigation and the negotiation and execution of the agreement signal regulatory needs in real time.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation for Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2831040

claims.claim: Despite the consensus favoring it, early regulatory intervention in innovation is rare in practice, and regulation mostly fails to keep pace as the innovation evolves and as understanding and use of the technology spreads.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation for Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2831040

claims.claim: Early regulatory intervention is subject to massive information asymmetries and associated regulatory uncertainty because the early stage of an innovation often provides insufficient information about its possible risks and benefits.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation for Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2831040
scope_conditions: early stage innovation

claims.claim: In the later stages of more matured innovation it is often not possible to alter the regulatory status quo, which closes the window that early intervention proposals depend on.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation for Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2831040
scope_conditions: matured innovation

claims.claim: Early regulatory intervention becomes unnecessary in a dynamic regulatory framework, because the regulatory challenges associated with innovation would become transparent in real time through improved, decentralized information and feedback effects.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation for Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2831040
scope_conditions: a functioning dynamic regulatory framework

claims.claim: In the dynamic regulatory framework, feedback effects and real time information permit regulatory intervention if and only when it is needed, which avoids stunting innovation through negative early signals, the inability to keep pace with later stage innovation, and information asymmetries.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation for Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2831040
scope_conditions: theoretical dynamic regulatory framework

claims.claim: The downsides of principles based regulation are a costly and time consuming transition from rules based regulation, uncertainty, and compliance problems that follow from that uncertainty.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation for Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2831040
scope_conditions: a shift from rules based to principles based regulation

claims.claim: Because dynamic regulation operates as a supplement inside the existing rulemaking framework, it does not require the costly implementation that a shift to principles based regulation would require.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation for Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2831040

claims.claim: Dynamic regulatory mechanisms avoid legal uncertainty better than principles based regulation because in the dynamic framework rulemaking follows feedback processes that are transparent to both the affected industries and the regulators.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation for Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2831040

claims.claim: The pace of innovation is incompatible with existing regulatory approaches that demand comprehensive knowledge as a precondition for regulatory action, because innovation is too decentralized, too fast, and too pervasive.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation for Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2831040
scope_conditions: regulatory approaches conditioned on comprehensive prior knowledge

claims.claim: The United States lacks an anticipatory system at the national level because no mechanism exists for bringing foresight and policymaking into an effective relationship.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation for Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2831040
scope_conditions: United States national government

claims.claim: Anticipatory rulemaking in the dynamic framework is accomplished by combining institution specific, decentralized, and timely information with feedback effects, which can occur between public and private rulemakers, between outcomes and institutions, across jurisdictions, and between rules and rulemaking processes.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation for Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2831040

claims.claim: Deferred prosecution agreements and venture capital investment decisions increase the availability of relevant, decentralized, and timely information for rulemaking and give at least some estimate of where innovative trends exist and what regulatory challenges may accompany them.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation for Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2831040

claims.claim: Dynamic regulatory tools lower unforeseen contingencies in innovation related rulemaking because their feedback effects supply relevant, timely, decentralized, and institution specific information ex ante, which also helps maintain certainty in the rulemaking process.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation for Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2831040

claims.claim: Private rulemakers hold a comparative advantage over public rulemakers because they often can produce and access necessary, comparable, decentralized, and institution specific information for rulemaking and can react more readily to emerging information.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation for Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2831040

claims.claim: Rules operate as a feedback effect on the rulemaking process itself: rules with suboptimal characteristics result from institutional arrangements and then reinforce those suboptimal arrangements, and stable presumptively optimal rules reinforce an institutional structure that perpetuates stability in rules.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation for Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2831040

claims.claim: Consumer choice adds a dynamic element to rulemaking because once consumers opt out of a suboptimal regulatory regime, public rulemakers in that jurisdiction can adjust their rulemaking in response, creating a feedback effect for the public rulemaker.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation for Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2831040
scope_conditions: jurisdictions where consumers can opt out of a regulatory regime

claims.claim: Dynamic regulation optimizes anticipatory governance for innovation by emphasizing adaptation to and anticipation of the unforeseen contingencies associated with innovation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation for Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2831040

claims.claim: Rulemaking in the dynamic framework is an integral part of innovation that both supports innovation and curtails it, for innovation's own sake and for the maximization of societal welfare.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation for Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2831040

claims.claim: Regulation of innovation in a dynamic framework is triggered only as a supplement to the existing rulemaking framework, and only if and when feedback effects anticipate otherwise unforeseen contingencies and regulatory needs associated with innovation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Dynamic Regulation for Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2831040
scope_conditions: existing rulemaking framework remains in place

claims.claim: Government assessments of hedge fund systemic risk conflict directly: the OFR, FSB, and IOSCO treat private fund activities as important threats to the financial system, while the UK Financial Services Authority concluded from its first comprehensive survey of London's private fund industry that hedge funds pose no systemic risk.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy A. Krause, Hedge Funds and Systemic Risk (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2748096
scope_conditions: comparison of post-crisis U.S. and UK regulator reports

claims.claim: Despite conflicting government reports, the weight of post-crisis evidence from leading financial economists supports the conclusion that hedge funds introduce at least some systemic risk into the financial system.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy A. Krause, Hedge Funds and Systemic Risk (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2748096
scope_conditions: post-crisis academic literature
claim is qualified: some, not dominant, systemic risk

claims.claim: Public perception, rather than measured risk, is the principal driver of the hedge fund systemic risk debate and of the policy responses to it, and that perception is shaped chiefly by industry growth and by the collapse of prominent funds.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy A. Krause, Hedge Funds and Systemic Risk (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2748096

claims.claim: Hedge fund assets under management grew from $118 billion at the end of 1997 to more than $2.7 trillion by the end of 2014, a compound annual growth rate of 19 percent.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy A. Krause, Hedge Funds and Systemic Risk (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2748096
scope_conditions: global hedge fund industry, 1997 to 2014
BarclayHedge data

claims.claim: The combination of unprecedented private fund industry growth and the low interest rate environment produced by post-crisis quantitative easing pushed private fund managers into reaching for yield, and the leverage and complex derivative transactions used to boost that yield further increased private funds' systemic risk.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy A. Krause, Hedge Funds and Systemic Risk (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2748096
scope_conditions: post-2008 low interest rate environment
quantitative easing by the Federal Reserve

claims.claim: Because hedge fund losses are absorbed directly by a large and dispersed body of investors and their equity capital, private fund advisers are unlikely to trigger a systemic event, and their activity may even reduce market volatility.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy A. Krause, Hedge Funds and Systemic Risk (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2748096
scope_conditions: applies to funds financed by investor equity rather than short term debt

claims.claim: Post-LTCM counterparty credit risk management, in which regulators pressed banks to monitor and limit the leverage of their hedge fund clients, appears to have worked: the Amaranth failure produced no financial market repercussions.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy A. Krause, Hedge Funds and Systemic Risk (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2748096
scope_conditions: post-1998 regulatory environment
inference drawn from a single episode, the Amaranth failure

claims.claim: Market events like the LTCM failure can escalate into global financial crises when many highly leveraged hedge funds holding illiquid portfolios are obligors of a small number of major financial institutions, because adverse price movements dry up credit and depress collateral values.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy A. Krause, Hedge Funds and Systemic Risk (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2748096
scope_conditions: high leverage
illiquid fund portfolios
concentration of lending among few major financial institutions
adverse fluctuations in market prices

claims.claim: Private fund advisers in the shadow banking system perform bank-like functions, providing liquidity to clients and to financial markets and engaging in various forms of liquidity transformation, and the vulnerabilities this creates may have large implications for financial stability.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy A. Krause, Hedge Funds and Systemic Risk (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2748096
scope_conditions: applies to private fund advisers engaged in liquidity provision and liquidity transformation

claims.claim: Any conclusion that hedge funds contributed to the financial crisis of 2007-2008 is circumstantial or anecdotal, because the data needed to test it, on leverage, counterparty relations, AUM, and portfolio holdings, were not collected for any substantial period before the crisis.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy A. Krause, Hedge Funds and Systemic Risk (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2748096
scope_conditions: applies to retrospective assessment of the 2007-2008 crisis
SEC systemic risk data collection began only after Title IV of the Dodd-Frank Act

claims.claim: The opacity of the hedge fund shadow banking system blocks direct measurement of hedge funds' role in the crisis, leaving researchers with indirect measures extracted from existing data rather than primary pre-crisis sources.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy A. Krause, Hedge Funds and Systemic Risk (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2748096
scope_conditions: absence of access to primary pre-crisis hedge fund data

claims.claim: The contagion story, in which hedge fund losses spread to other financial institutions and undermine systemic stability, is counterbalanced in practice because hedge fund collapses are rarely sudden and almost always unfold in incremental steps over a long period.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy A. Krause, Hedge Funds and Systemic Risk (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2748096
scope_conditions: describes observed hedge fund collapse dynamics rather than theoretical models

claims.claim: Hedge funds' risk management practices are typically evolved enough to constitute a major barrier to systemic shocks, and their trading counterparties and lenders further help prevent losses large enough to disrupt the financial system.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy A. Krause, Hedge Funds and Systemic Risk (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2748096
scope_conditions: assumes counterparties and lenders actively monitor fund exposures

claims.claim: Hedge fund losses large enough to affect the overall economy did not appear until after the crisis and recession had already been triggered by the mortgage market collapse and sustained stock market losses, which places hedge funds downstream of the crisis rather than at its origin.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy A. Krause, Hedge Funds and Systemic Risk (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2748096
scope_conditions: financial crisis of 2007-2008

claims.claim: Pre-crisis regulatory attention was misallocated: although Bernanke identified failure to manage counterparty risk as the primary cause for concern, the SEC and the Senate Banking Committee concentrated on hedge fund transparency instead.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy A. Krause, Hedge Funds and Systemic Risk (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2748096
scope_conditions: U.S. regulatory response between the 1998 LTCM failure and the 2007-2008 crisis

claims.claim: Even if the risks hedge funds pose to financial institutions are often overstated, liquidity risk remains a serious issue because of the critical linkages created by over-the-counter credit risk relations.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy A. Krause, Hedge Funds and Systemic Risk (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2748096
scope_conditions: applies where hedge fund exposures run through over-the-counter credit relationships

claims.claim: The performance pressure on hedge fund managers incentivizes them to take disproportionately high risks in order to deliver sufficient client returns, and those disproportionate risks translate into proportional systemic risks.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy A. Krause, Hedge Funds and Systemic Risk (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2748096
scope_conditions: holds where managers must generate returns sufficient to retain clients

claims.claim: Market-neutral arbitrage strategies implicitly minimize systemic risk, because funds using them construct returns that do not depend on the direction of the market.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy A. Krause, Hedge Funds and Systemic Risk (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2748096
scope_conditions: applies only to funds running some form of market-neutral arbitrage

claims.claim: Redemption driven selling during the financial crisis of 2007-2008 was industry wide in scale: the hedge fund industry liquidated about 30 percent of its stock holdings.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy A. Krause, Hedge Funds and Systemic Risk (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2748096
scope_conditions: financial crisis of 2007-2008
driven by investor and lender redemptions and the need to liquidate positions

claims.claim: The systemic risk of hedge fund leverage comes from its capacity to amplify liquidity losses and to contribute to asset overvaluation during bull markets, not from leverage as such.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy A. Krause, Hedge Funds and Systemic Risk (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2748096

claims.claim: When hedge funds simultaneously liquidate positions and reduce leverage, leverage generates a fire-sale externality that raises systemic risk, arising when a fund must sell assets it regards as drastically undervalued in order to meet margin calls or redemption requests.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy A. Krause, Hedge Funds and Systemic Risk (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2748096
scope_conditions: simultaneous deleveraging across funds
binding margin calls or redemption requests

claims.claim: Concern about hedge fund leverage is empirically overstated: since the collapse of LTCM in 1998 the industry's exposure to leverage has been relatively modest, especially compared with the mean leverage of investment banks and broker/dealers.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy A. Krause, Hedge Funds and Systemic Risk (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2748096
scope_conditions: post-1998 period
comparison benchmark is investment banks and broker/dealers

claims.claim: Strategy diversification does not insulate the hedge fund industry from systemic risk: returns across different hedge fund strategies were more correlated during the financial crisis of 2007-2008 than before it, so the industry can pose systemic risk despite investing across a broad spectrum of assets and strategies.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy A. Krause, Hedge Funds and Systemic Risk (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2748096
scope_conditions: periods of market stress
evidence drawn from the 2007-2008 crisis

claims.claim: Hedge fund contagion is defined as correlation over and above what one would expect from economic fundamentals, and clusters of suboptimal returns across investment styles count as contagion precisely because known risk factors for hedge fund performance cannot explain them.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy A. Krause, Hedge Funds and Systemic Risk (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2748096
scope_conditions: definition adopted from Bekaert, Harvey, and Ng (2005)

claims.claim: The growth of hedge fund replication strategies packaged in exchange traded funds may further increase the systemic risks associated with certain hedge fund strategies.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy A. Krause, Hedge Funds and Systemic Risk (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2748096
scope_conditions: applies to ETF based replication of hedge fund strategies

claims.claim: Title IV of the Dodd-Frank Act addresses alleged hedge fund systemic risk through an information strategy rather than a substantive one: it authorized the SEC to require registration and enhanced disclosure from private fund advisers and to facilitate data collection for assessing systemic risk.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy A. Krause, Hedge Funds and Systemic Risk (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2748096
scope_conditions: U.S. private fund advisers with more than $150 million AUM

claims.claim: The FSOC's powers over hedge funds and other nonbank financial institutions are broad and unprecedented in U.S. financial regulation, including the power to subject hedge funds to extensive Federal Reserve supervision and to designate a fund systemically important on its own initiative by a two-thirds vote.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy A. Krause, Hedge Funds and Systemic Risk (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2748096
scope_conditions: post-Dodd-Frank U.S. regulatory structure

claims.claim: The SIFI designation regime does not reach hedge funds in practice: because the asset threshold is set high, at $50 billion or more in aggregate total consolidated assets, hedge funds are unlikely to be designated as systemically important financial institutions.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy A. Krause, Hedge Funds and Systemic Risk (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2748096
scope_conditions: U.S. SIFI designation under the Dodd-Frank Act
$50 billion aggregate total consolidated asset threshold

claims.claim: About 18 percent of hedge funds ceased operations in 2008, yet little evidence exists that these failures generated losses at prime brokers or other financial institutions, which weakens the direct transmission account of hedge fund systemic risk.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy A. Krause, Hedge Funds and Systemic Risk (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2748096
scope_conditions: hedge fund closures during 2008
RAND Corporation study

claims.claim: The theoretical link between hedge funds and systemic risk rests on limits to arbitrage: speculators' capital is finite, their capacity to supply liquidity depends on funding, and that funding can dry up abruptly in periods of financial distress, producing liquidity spirals amplified by rising return correlations, higher volatility, and flight to quality.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy A. Krause, Hedge Funds and Systemic Risk (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2748096
scope_conditions: periods of financial distress
speculators dependent on external funding

claims.claim: Hedge fund redemptions and margin calls, both liquidity reducing events, were the primary drivers of asset selloffs during the financial crisis of 2007-2008, and hedge fund investors are three times more likely than mutual fund investors to withdraw capital during market downturns.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy A. Krause, Hedge Funds and Systemic Risk (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2748096
scope_conditions: financial crisis of 2007-2008
comparison group is mutual fund investors

claims.claim: Although hedge fund return volatility is less sensitive to financial system risks than that of brokers, banks, and insurance companies, nonlinear Granger causality tests show that between 2001 and 2008 volatility was transmitted across all parts of the system, including from hedge funds to brokers and banks.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy A. Krause, Hedge Funds and Systemic Risk (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2748096
scope_conditions: 2001 to 2008 sample
result depends on nonlinear Granger causality tests rather than principal components analysis

claims.claim: Hedge fund redemption policies are not irrelevant to risk: the rewards to liquidity risk are positive in part because redemption gates allow hedge funds to avoid asset fire sales.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy A. Krause, Hedge Funds and Systemic Risk (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2748096
scope_conditions: funds with redemption restrictions such as gates

claims.claim: Traditional risk-adjusted alphas underestimate hedge fund risk: once correlation risk is controlled for, previously observed significant hedge fund alphas disappear, which makes correlation risk a systematic risk factor for hedge fund returns.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy A. Krause, Hedge Funds and Systemic Risk (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2748096
scope_conditions: cross-sectional analysis of individual hedge fund returns

claims.claim: Once liquidity risk is incorporated into the analysis, the superior performance previously attributed to predictability in managerial skills disappears in hedge fund portfolios.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy A. Krause, Hedge Funds and Systemic Risk (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2748096
scope_conditions: hedge fund portfolios formed on predictability in managerial skill

claims.claim: Risk measures that are not adjusted for serial correlation in hedge fund returns can considerably underestimate the true extent of both individual and systemic hedge fund risk, so empirical work in this area must account for autocorrelation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy A. Krause, Hedge Funds and Systemic Risk (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2748096
scope_conditions: applies to empirical studies of hedge fund returns

claims.claim: Systemic risk rankings that place a loosely defined other financial services sector above banking and insurance are of limited use, because the analysis does not clearly identify the firms included in that category even though a substantial portion of them may be hedge funds.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy A. Krause, Hedge Funds and Systemic Risk (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2748096
scope_conditions: applies to CoVaR based sector rankings of systemic risk contribution

claims.claim: Hedge funds now supply funding to the banking system that may be rapidly withdrawn during a liquidity crisis and supply a substantial share of the sellers' side of the credit default swap market, thereby assuming risks traditionally held by investment banks and insurance companies.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy A. Krause, Hedge Funds and Systemic Risk (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2748096
scope_conditions: applies to hedge funds operating within the shadow banking system

claims.claim: Hedge funds have the potential both to amplify and to mitigate systemic risk, and which effect dominates turns on their particular risk management incentives, leverage, and investment strategies, which is why the academic evidence remains mixed.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy A. Krause, Hedge Funds and Systemic Risk (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2748096
scope_conditions: conclusion drawn from the mixed post-crisis literature

claims.claim: The most useful product of the post-crisis empirical literature for regulators is a set of methodologies for evaluating hedge fund systemic risk and prescribing remedies, especially methodologies addressing the counterparty credit measures of hedge funds and their prime brokers.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Timothy A. Krause, Hedge Funds and Systemic Risk (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2748096
scope_conditions: directed at regulators evaluating hedge fund systemic risk

claims.claim: Regulation is usually reactive because it responds to facts, but the current environment is one of data rather than settled facts; regulation must therefore become proactive and dynamically responsive to data and trends.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, How to Regulate Disruptive Innovation - From Facts to Data (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2808132
scope_conditions: environments of exponential disruptive innovation
where data on emerging trends precedes settled facts

claims.claim: Ex post facts-based, trial-and-error rulemaking combined with stable and presumptively optimal rules often produces suboptimal regulatory outcomes, and those outcomes are no longer sustainable in an environment of exponential disruptive innovation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, How to Regulate Disruptive Innovation - From Facts to Data (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2808132
scope_conditions: existing regulatory framework relying on stable and presumptively optimal rules
environment of exponential disruptive innovation

claims.claim: In an environment of exponential disruptive innovation, the information rulemakers need is less likely to materialize soon enough for traditional rulemaking to be effective, regulatory issues become more complex, and unknown future contingencies increase substantially.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, How to Regulate Disruptive Innovation - From Facts to Data (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2808132
scope_conditions: exponential rather than incremental innovation
traditional information-dependent rulemaking processes

claims.claim: Exponential disruptive innovation has the potential to overwhelm the existing regulatory process entirely, not merely to strain it.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, How to Regulate Disruptive Innovation - From Facts to Data (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2808132
scope_conditions: exponential rates of innovation
existing institutional rulemaking infrastructure

claims.claim: Dynamic regulation is defined as conceptualizing regulatory phenomena in relation to both preceding and succeeding events, using institution-specific and decentralized information to generate feedback effects that support anticipatory rulemaking.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, How to Regulate Disruptive Innovation - From Facts to Data (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2808132

claims.claim: Data derived from venture capital investments can function as a dynamic regulatory supplement for disruptive innovation, because venture capital's financial allocations to innovative projects supply feedback for dynamic regulation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, How to Regulate Disruptive Innovation - From Facts to Data (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2808132
scope_conditions: where venture capital investment allocation data is available to regulators
United States venture capital market, 2005 to 2015

claims.claim: A market leader's failure to invest in disruptive technologies often results in an abrupt loss of market dominance and frequently in total replacement in that market.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, How to Regulate Disruptive Innovation - From Facts to Data (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2808132
scope_conditions: incumbent firms facing disruptive rather than sustaining technologies

claims.claim: Market leaders, successful institutions, and managers fail specifically when they do not distinguish sustaining technologies from disruptive technologies.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, How to Regulate Disruptive Innovation - From Facts to Data (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2808132
scope_conditions: established firms with existing customer bases and mainstream market orientation

claims.claim: Because artificial intelligence is not recognized as a subject of law in national or international law, it has no legal personality and therefore cannot be personally liable for damages it causes.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, How to Regulate Disruptive Innovation - From Facts to Data (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2808132
scope_conditions: current national and international legal frameworks
autonomous AI acting without supervision

claims.claim: When disruptive firms do not comply with existing rules or effectively create their own exemptions because the existing framework does not reach them, public policy goals can be undermined and incumbent firms that remain subject to the rules suffer severe competitive disadvantages.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, How to Regulate Disruptive Innovation - From Facts to Data (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2808132
scope_conditions: disruptive products or services outside existing regulatory categories
no appropriate replacement rules available

claims.claim: Incumbent firms facing a perceived threat from disruptive innovation may respond by using the existing regulatory process itself to create obstacles that prevent disruptive firms from competing.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, How to Regulate Disruptive Innovation - From Facts to Data (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2808132
scope_conditions: incumbents already burdened by existing rules
disruptive entrants operating outside or partly outside those rules

claims.claim: The political system is less likely to be able to resolve the challenges of disruptive innovation because the increasing complexity of innovation-driven regulatory issues causes confusion among political and policy makers about rapidly emerging change.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, How to Regulate Disruptive Innovation - From Facts to Data (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2808132
scope_conditions: rapidly emerging and technically complex disruptive change

claims.claim: The existing regulatory infrastructure cannot sufficiently distinguish beneficial innovation from harmful innovation and therefore cannot harness the beneficial kind.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, How to Regulate Disruptive Innovation - From Facts to Data (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2808132
scope_conditions: existing regulatory infrastructure without dynamic or anticipatory elements

claims.claim: Rulemakers' inability to address disruptive innovation will generate high levels of legal uncertainty and inconsistency that inhibit innovation during technological transition, and technological transition is likely to become a permanent state, so the inhibiting effect becomes permanent too.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, How to Regulate Disruptive Innovation - From Facts to Data (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2808132
scope_conditions: age of continuous disruptive innovation
fragmented multi-agency regulatory structures

claims.claim: The current regulatory framework lacks any mechanism that anticipatorily informs rulemakers of beneficial innovative ideas, and because the rulemaking process prohibits ex parte communications and integrates cross-industry brainstorming poorly, the process may actually undermine innovation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, How to Regulate Disruptive Innovation - From Facts to Data (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2808132
scope_conditions: notice and comment rulemaking under the existing administrative framework

claims.claim: The ex post facts-based approach to rulemaking worked historically because the optimal requirements for rules only become clear once stable and presumptively optimal rules have already emerged as suboptimal; the availability of that information is therefore a prerequisite for rulemaking.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, How to Regulate Disruptive Innovation - From Facts to Data (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2808132
scope_conditions: historically stable economic and market environments
rulemaking dependent on realized facts

claims.claim: Because facts-based rulemaking does not anticipate the regulatory issues created by innovation, rulemakers may realize far too late, or never, what new regulatory demands a given innovation generates.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, How to Regulate Disruptive Innovation - From Facts to Data (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2808132
scope_conditions: age of exponential innovation
purely reactive facts-based rulemaking

claims.claim: Stable and presumptively optimal rules are created to address regulatory issues that lawmakers perceive through centralized information under then-existing economic and market conditions, and are drafted as permanent solutions to those perceived issues.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, How to Regulate Disruptive Innovation - From Facts to Data (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2808132
scope_conditions: Congress, regulatory agencies, self-regulatory bodies, and the regulation literature

claims.claim: Because rulemakers are increasingly unlikely to be able to protect the public through stable and presumptively optimal rules alone, regulatory supplements that enable anticipatory rulemaking become justified.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, How to Regulate Disruptive Innovation - From Facts to Data (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2808132
scope_conditions: exponential growth of technology and associated complexity of regulatory issues
rulemakers unable to adequately protect constituents

claims.claim: The historically evolved rulemaking infrastructure could cope with its own collective action problems, regulatory cycles, and trial-and-error rulemaking without major disruption because the scope of regulatory issues was limited and institutional designs were consensus driven.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, How to Regulate Disruptive Innovation - From Facts to Data (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2808132
scope_conditions: small, stable, less interconnected societies with limited upward mobility
limited and readily identifiable sets of regulatory issues

claims.claim: Regulatory timing under disruptive innovation is a two-sided failure: regulating too early risks inhibiting innovation, while withholding regulation too long risks harm to consumers and markets once regulatory inertia sets in around the disruptive product or service.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, How to Regulate Disruptive Innovation - From Facts to Data (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2808132
scope_conditions: disruptive products or services not yet settled in the market
