claims.claim: Formal rulemaking is simply too time-consuming for an environment of disruptive innovation; the speed of product innovation alone makes formal rulemaking in the existing infrastructure unworkable.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, How to Regulate Disruptive Innovation - From Facts to Data (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2808132
scope_conditions: formal and notice and comment rulemaking in the existing regulatory infrastructure
rapid product innovation cycles

claims.claim: Because formal rulemaking takes months and often years, regulators are still processing the previous product launch while new products reach the market, and new regulations pertaining to an innovative product can be obsolete before they are finalized.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, How to Regulate Disruptive Innovation - From Facts to Data (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2808132
scope_conditions: multi-month or multi-year regulatory procedures
fast product launch cycles

claims.claim: Because it lacks anticipatory capabilities, the existing regulatory system only addresses regulatory issues ex post, and then only if core constituents are burdened enough to generate sufficient political pressure for lawmakers to act.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, How to Regulate Disruptive Innovation - From Facts to Data (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2808132
scope_conditions: existing regulatory infrastructure built on stable and presumptively optimal rules

claims.claim: Evidence exists that the suboptimal ex post timing of rulemaking in the existing regulatory infrastructure regularly forces expedited rulemaking, which in turn produces suboptimal regulatory outcomes.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, How to Regulate Disruptive Innovation - From Facts to Data (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2808132
scope_conditions: crisis-driven and post-crisis legislative episodes
existing regulatory infrastructure

claims.claim: Despite their insufficient anticipatory capabilities and known downsides, stable and presumptively optimal rules remain the uniform response to perceived regulatory issues.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, How to Regulate Disruptive Innovation - From Facts to Data (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2808132
scope_conditions: existing regulatory framework

claims.claim: The current process of rule revisions, amendments, and repeals used to correct the inevitable shortcomings of stable rules is costly and time-consuming, and in the authors' estimation it cannot keep track of future innovations and their corresponding regulatory needs.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, How to Regulate Disruptive Innovation - From Facts to Data (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2808132
scope_conditions: existing regulatory framework relying on ex post rule revision
accelerating pace of innovation

claims.claim: The collective action problem of rulemaking, the problems of trial-and-error rulemaking, and the problems of regulatory cycles derive largely from the nature of stable and presumptively optimal rules themselves, not from unrelated institutional defects.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, How to Regulate Disruptive Innovation - From Facts to Data (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2808132
scope_conditions: regulatory regimes whose outcomes are stable rather than adaptive

claims.claim: Adaptive rulemaking helps overcome the collective action problem of rulemaking because when there are fewer stable rules, latent majority groups and dominant minority groups have fewer opportunities to influence a continuously and timely adapting process.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, How to Regulate Disruptive Innovation - From Facts to Data (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2808132
scope_conditions: rulemaking processes that incorporate dynamic and adaptive elements
presence of organized interest groups competing for influence

claims.claim: Regulatory cycles and trial-and-error rulemaking become less prevalent under adaptive rulemaking because adaptive capabilities supplement stable rules, making rule revisions less frequent.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, How to Regulate Disruptive Innovation - From Facts to Data (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2808132
scope_conditions: rulemaking processes supplemented with adaptive capabilities

claims.claim: Unrestricted exchange of information between public and private rulemakers creates regulatory synergies that increase the availability of relevant, decentralized, and timely information for rulemaking and thereby generate feedback effects.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, How to Regulate Disruptive Innovation - From Facts to Data (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2808132
scope_conditions: settings permitting open information exchange between public and private rulemakers

claims.claim: Through feedback effects, rulemakers in a dynamic regulatory framework can adopt rules that are adaptable to future states of the world rather than fixed to current conditions.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, How to Regulate Disruptive Innovation - From Facts to Data (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2808132
scope_conditions: rulemaking institutions that integrate feedback processes

claims.claim: Dynamic regulatory tools lower unforeseen contingencies in rulemaking because the feedback effect supplies relevant, timely, decentralized, and institution-specific information ex ante, allowing rulemakers to adapt to contingencies as they arise.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, How to Regulate Disruptive Innovation - From Facts to Data (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2808132
scope_conditions: rulemaking supplemented by dynamic regulatory tools generating feedback

claims.claim: A core problem for most regulation is its inaccurate and delayed timing, which follows from the collective action problem of regulation, path dependencies, and political inertia rather than from any single institutional defect.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, How to Regulate Disruptive Innovation - From Facts to Data (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2808132
scope_conditions: most regulation in the existing framework
regulation that follows business cycles rather than preceding crises

claims.claim: By identifying possible contingencies and necessary rule revisions with optimized ex ante information, dynamic regulatory supplements make adaptive rulemaking rather than stable rulemaking the focal point of the regulatory process.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, How to Regulate Disruptive Innovation - From Facts to Data (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2808132
scope_conditions: regulatory processes that incorporate dynamic supplements and feedback effects

claims.claim: Dynamic regulatory supplements would not violate the procedural mandates of the Administrative Procedure Act, because the full lawmaking process still applies; dynamic regulation supplements rather than replaces the existing rulemaking process.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, How to Regulate Disruptive Innovation - From Facts to Data (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2808132
scope_conditions: United States administrative law under the Administrative Procedure Act

claims.claim: Venture capital deal flow, meaning the totality of potential deals and business plans screened by venture capitalists, would provide the optimal assessment of innovation trends, but that data is not available, so realized investment allocations must be used as a second-best proxy.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, How to Regulate Disruptive Innovation - From Facts to Data (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2808132
scope_conditions: current data availability from commercial venture capital databases

claims.claim: The study's evidence base is a PitchBook dataset of 77,508 United States venture capital deals involving 37,298 companies from 2005 through 2015, covering all venture capital deals and all venture capital stages.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, How to Regulate Disruptive Innovation - From Facts to Data (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2808132
scope_conditions: United States venture capital deals, 2005 through 2015

claims.claim: A more granular assessment of venture capital investments in Big Data and software as a service can provide regulators with much needed feedback on the regulatory needs associated with those areas.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, How to Regulate Disruptive Innovation - From Facts to Data (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2808132
scope_conditions: industries disproportionately represented in later venture capital series
regulators willing to conduct granular data analysis

claims.claim: Although aggregate venture capital sector data arguably only confirms what media reporting already showed for 2005 to 2015, the venture capital data, especially examined granularly, may provide earlier signals for regulators to identify areas of prospective regulatory need.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, How to Regulate Disruptive Innovation - From Facts to Data (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2808132
scope_conditions: granular rather than aggregate examination of the venture capital data
areas of increasingly disruptive innovation

claims.claim: The dominance of later stage venture capital investments could be read as risk-averse follow-on behavior, but venture capital funds are unlikely to make later stage investments unless portfolio companies substantially fulfilled their contractual performance obligations, which preserves the signal value of the data.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, How to Regulate Disruptive Innovation - From Facts to Data (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2808132
scope_conditions: later stage venture capital investments following earlier seed investments in the same company

claims.claim: Venture capitalists' finance allocation and their implicit assessment of innovative products, businesses, and initiatives generate highly relevant institution-specific and industry-specific decentralized information on innovation trends.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, How to Regulate Disruptive Innovation - From Facts to Data (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2808132
scope_conditions: United States venture capital investments, 2005 through 2015

claims.claim: Regulation is mostly reactive and follows business cycles rather than being proactive; data on venture capital investments lets regulators see where innovation trends are heading and what risks they entail before the disruptive innovation actually materializes.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, How to Regulate Disruptive Innovation - From Facts to Data (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2808132
scope_conditions: regulators with access to venture capital investment data
innovation still at the investment rather than deployment stage

claims.claim: Feedback effects from venture capitalists' finance allocations toward innovative products give rulemakers timely, decentralized, industry-specific and entity-specific information that allows them to adapt rules in anticipation of regulatory issues.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, How to Regulate Disruptive Innovation - From Facts to Data (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2808132
scope_conditions: industries associated with the highest levels of disruptive innovation
regulators able to access and analyze venture capital investment data

claims.claim: The decline in later stage robotics and drone investment rounds in the United States does not indicate stalled technological development; companies relocate later stage development to other countries because of the regulatory disconnect that exists in the United States.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, How to Regulate Disruptive Innovation - From Facts to Data (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2808132
scope_conditions: robotics and drones industry
United States regulatory environment after 2011

claims.claim: The authors concede that the trend for venture-capital-financed technology companies to stay private and the market undervaluation of formerly venture-capital-financed companies mean the innovation potential identified by venture capital finance allocation may not always be shared by the market at large.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, How to Regulate Disruptive Innovation - From Facts to Data (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2808132
scope_conditions: long-term market valuation of venture-capital-financed innovation
companies remaining private rather than listing

claims.claim: Even if regulators could obtain the depth of information needed for anticipatory rulemaking, acting on venture capital signals risks wasting scarce regulatory resources, because venture capital funds make many investments that do not succeed and companies still incubating may raise no clear regulatory issues.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, How to Regulate Disruptive Innovation - From Facts to Data (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2808132
scope_conditions: anticipatory regulatory action based on venture capital data alone
portfolio companies still in incubation

claims.claim: Regulators should take anticipatory measures only after cross-validation and triangulation, that is, when multiple independent data analyses point unanimously toward a specific demand for regulatory action.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, How to Regulate Disruptive Innovation - From Facts to Data (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2808132
scope_conditions: multiple high-quality decentralized real-time data sources available to regulators
unanimous convergence of those analyses

claims.claim: No regulatory processes or data evaluation capabilities currently exist that could carry out the cross-validated analyses and support the anticipatory regulatory action the authors propose.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, How to Regulate Disruptive Innovation - From Facts to Data (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2808132
scope_conditions: as of 2016 in the United States regulatory system

claims.claim: Companies that received venture capital investments have outrun and continue to outrun regulation and regulatory efforts, and they drive innovation trends in the United States and abroad.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, How to Regulate Disruptive Innovation - From Facts to Data (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2808132
scope_conditions: venture-capital-backed companies in the United States and abroad, 2005 through 2015

claims.claim: Existing regulatory processes are suboptimally equipped to address the challenges of exponential disruptive innovation, and the notice and comment procedures of the Administrative Procedure Act and the SEC illustrate the resulting suboptimal regulatory response rates.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, How to Regulate Disruptive Innovation - From Facts to Data (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2808132
scope_conditions: notice and comment rulemaking under the APA and at the SEC
regulatory challenges presented by venture-capital-backed companies

claims.claim: Venture capital investment allocation data can help facilitate anticipatory regulation of disruptive innovation, but it is only one of several emerging data sources usable for signaling in regulatory process optimization.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, How to Regulate Disruptive Innovation - From Facts to Data (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2808132
scope_conditions: availability of additional and emerging data sources beyond venture capital

claims.claim: The study rests on two datasets: SEC Form ADV Part II filings by private investment fund advisers from 2007 to 2014 (N=100392) and the publicly available litigation record on private fund investor due diligence from 1995 to 2015 (N=572).
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Investor Due Diligence – Evidence from 1995 to 2015 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811718
scope_conditions: United States private investment funds

claims.claim: The private fund industry grew by 26 percent between 2013 and 2015, rising from just above 2 trillion dollars in assets under management to 2.7 trillion dollars.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Investor Due Diligence – Evidence from 1995 to 2015 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811718
scope_conditions: hedge fund industry assets under management as reported by BarclayHedge

claims.claim: Before the financial crisis of 2008 to 2009, the standard AIMA and MFA due diligence questionnaire templates were often deployed defensively: managers used the old versions to steer investors away from questions that would have exposed weaknesses in the managers' controls.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Investor Due Diligence – Evidence from 1995 to 2015 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811718
scope_conditions: pre financial crisis practice
template based questionnaires edited by the manager

claims.claim: After the financial crisis of 2008 to 2009 and the Madoff scandal, relatively sophisticated investors stopped accepting the slanted phrasing of due diligence questionnaires and their answers, and the questionnaires became more rigorous as a result.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Investor Due Diligence – Evidence from 1995 to 2015 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811718
scope_conditions: relatively sophisticated investors
post crisis period

claims.claim: Almost no guidance exists on the standards applicable to private fund investor due diligence, so despite the growing importance of due diligence in capital formation and in litigation the industry is left mostly to its own devices to ensure adequate standards.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Investor Due Diligence – Evidence from 1995 to 2015 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811718
scope_conditions: United States private fund industry
as of 2016

claims.claim: The existing resources fail on both sides: industry materials describe best practices without setting out the legal requirements for private fund due diligence, and the available case law provides only marginal guidance.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Investor Due Diligence – Evidence from 1995 to 2015 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811718
scope_conditions: United States
resources available as of 2016

claims.claim: Because a material omission or misstatement in Form ADV Part 2A can support a serious securities law charge, private fund managers have an incentive to keep the narrative language of that required disclosure as high level, summary, and non committal as possible.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Investor Due Diligence – Evidence from 1995 to 2015 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811718
scope_conditions: Form ADV Part 2A narrative brochure
private fund managers

claims.claim: From 2007 to 2014 an increasing number of Form ADV Part II filers deemed investor due diligence worth mentioning, and an increasing number of filers qualitatively increased their due diligence disclosures in the brochure filings.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Investor Due Diligence – Evidence from 1995 to 2015 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811718
scope_conditions: SEC Form ADV Part II brochure filings

claims.claim: Since 2010 an increasing number of SEC Form ADV Part II brochure filers included investor due diligence disclosures, but the number of filers including such disclosures remained relatively even between 2012 and 2014.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Investor Due Diligence – Evidence from 1995 to 2015 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811718
scope_conditions: SEC Form ADV Part II brochure filings

claims.claim: The intensity of due diligence mentioning relative to total Form ADV Part II brochure filings increased substantially, and the due diligence count exceeded the total number of ADV II filings for the first time in 2014.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Investor Due Diligence – Evidence from 1995 to 2015 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811718
scope_conditions: SEC Form ADV Part II brochure filings

claims.claim: Form ADV Part II filings jumped from 3,024 in 2010 to 21,685 in 2011, and that jump was accompanied by a corresponding increase both in the number of filings mentioning investor due diligence and in the due diligence counts within those filings.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Investor Due Diligence – Evidence from 1995 to 2015 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811718
scope_conditions: SEC Form ADV Part II brochure filings
registration changes after 2010

claims.claim: Although overall Form ADV Part II filings fell between 2012 and 2013, due diligence counts fell only marginally, from 20,828 to 20,031, and filings mentioning due diligence fell from 7,862 to 7,198, less than proportionally to the drop in total filings.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Investor Due Diligence – Evidence from 1995 to 2015 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811718
scope_conditions: SEC Form ADV Part II brochure filings

claims.claim: The Form ADV analysis is limited because the term due diligence carries multiple possible meanings, so counts of the term cannot by themselves distinguish among those meanings.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Investor Due Diligence – Evidence from 1995 to 2015 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811718
scope_conditions: keyword based counting of the phrase due diligence in Form ADV II filings

claims.claim: Litigation research on private fund due diligence requires in depth evaluation of case dockets rather than only published judicial decisions, because opinions are snapshots that do not tell the whole story of a case.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Investor Due Diligence – Evidence from 1995 to 2015 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811718
scope_conditions: empirical legal research on litigation records

claims.claim: Legal decisions involving private fund due diligence increased substantially after 2005 and especially after 2008, and the broad, narrow, and hand selected case categories all increased consistently with a slight lapse in 2014.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Investor Due Diligence – Evidence from 1995 to 2015 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811718
scope_conditions: Westlaw case law searches

claims.claim: In the hand selected sample of cases, the ranking of causes of action differs from the full search results: fiduciary duty leads, followed by negligent misrepresentation and breach of contract.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Investor Due Diligence – Evidence from 1995 to 2015 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811718
scope_conditions: hand selected subsample of 32 cases

claims.claim: While some courts found that a complete lack of investor due diligence can amount to securities fraud or breach of contract, and that lacking due diligence can breach fiduciary duties, the majority of courts evaluate private fund due diligence issues in the context of misrepresentation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Investor Due Diligence – Evidence from 1995 to 2015 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811718
scope_conditions: United States courts
2005 to 2015 litigation record

claims.claim: Successful claims based on lacking investor due diligence typically require a complete failure to perform due diligence despite explicit promises to perform it; promising due diligence and then conducting none except in isolated incidents is actionable misrepresentation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Investor Due Diligence – Evidence from 1995 to 2015 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811718
scope_conditions: private fund due diligence litigation
explicit promise to perform due diligence

claims.claim: Relying solely on a representation by the investment or the fund, without actually performing due diligence, is sufficient to present a fact issue on fraud to a jury.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Investor Due Diligence – Evidence from 1995 to 2015 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811718
scope_conditions: fraud claims against private fund advisers

claims.claim: Deficient due diligence does not create securities fraud liability unless it is intentional or highly reckless; conduct that is merely negligent or professionally incompetent falls short of the scienter requirement.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Investor Due Diligence – Evidence from 1995 to 2015 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811718
scope_conditions: securities fraud claims under section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5
PSLRA pleading standard

claims.claim: Failing to check publicly available documentation on an investment is irresponsible but insufficient to plead fraudulent intent, and failing to perform due diligence commensurate with industry standards is inadequate to plead scienter.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Investor Due Diligence – Evidence from 1995 to 2015 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811718
scope_conditions: securities fraud pleading
Matana v. Merkin and In re Bayou Hedge Fund Litigation

claims.claim: Defendants owe a duty to use reasonable care in conducting financial due diligence consistent with the standards of care in the profession.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Investor Due Diligence – Evidence from 1995 to 2015 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811718
scope_conditions: negligence claims
Baker v. Goldman Sachs

claims.claim: As a contractual matter, due diligence promises made in a brochure, on a website, or in a contract with investors must be in writing to be enforceable.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Investor Due Diligence – Evidence from 1995 to 2015 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811718
scope_conditions: contract claims
Statute of Frauds as applied in South Cherry Street

claims.claim: Failure to supervise and direct investment of assets in accordance with an investment plan's policy, together with offering memoranda or quarterly letters that misrepresent due diligence processes, can show a failure to exercise reasonable care sufficient to plead breach of fiduciary duty.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Investor Due Diligence – Evidence from 1995 to 2015 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811718
scope_conditions: fiduciary duty claims against private fund advisers

claims.claim: Fund managers were incentivized to route capital to Madoff because he charged notoriously low fees for the hedge fund business, taking only transaction fees rather than fees based on assets under management.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Investor Due Diligence – Evidence from 1995 to 2015 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811718
scope_conditions: Madoff feeder funds and funds of funds before December 2008

claims.claim: Funds of funds claimed to select the best managers through skilled due diligence and charged standard 2 and 20 fee structures for that service, while in reality depositing the vast majority of their capital into Madoff's opaque fund.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Investor Due Diligence – Evidence from 1995 to 2015 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811718
scope_conditions: Madoff feeder funds and funds of funds before December 2008

claims.claim: Madoff's reliance on large feeder funds created a massive industry of investor due diligence lawsuits, because those funds collected high advisory fees as due diligence experts yet caused large numbers of investors to lose their investments.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Investor Due Diligence – Evidence from 1995 to 2015 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811718
scope_conditions: post 2008 Madoff related litigation

claims.claim: Because Madoff overtly disallowed scrutiny of his secretive and unconventional practices, it was impossible for feeder funds such as Rye to perform the due diligence they had represented to investors.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Investor Due Diligence – Evidence from 1995 to 2015 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811718
scope_conditions: Madoff feeder funds
In re Tremont

claims.claim: Claims in which investors use hindsight to second guess due diligence practices often fail, even when the manager was clearly incompetent.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Investor Due Diligence – Evidence from 1995 to 2015 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811718
scope_conditions: securities fraud claims
South Cherry Street

claims.claim: Funds that promise due diligence with no intention of actually carrying it out violate federal securities laws rather than merely breaching a contract.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Investor Due Diligence – Evidence from 1995 to 2015 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811718
scope_conditions: In re J.P. Jeanneret Associates
promises made without intent to perform

claims.claim: Advertising an elaborate multi limb due diligence process is no evidence that it was applied: Madoff's asset management advisers FIM Limited and FIM Advisers touted what sounded like above industry standards yet applied none of them to Madoff's firm and admitted as much.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Investor Due Diligence – Evidence from 1995 to 2015 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811718
scope_conditions: In re Bernard L. Madoff Investment Securities LLC
Kingate feeder funds

claims.claim: Expert testimony identifies recurring failures in private fund due diligence, including the absence of any written policy or process to ensure compliance and reliance on individuals with little or no experience, particularly with the particulars of hedge funds.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Investor Due Diligence – Evidence from 1995 to 2015 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811718
scope_conditions: expert reports in the surveyed litigation record

claims.claim: Expert consensus in the examined litigation record converges on a set of standard due diligence practices, beginning with qualitative review of firm marketing materials, offering documents, subscription documents, and manager track records, and onsite manager meetings.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Investor Due Diligence – Evidence from 1995 to 2015 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811718
scope_conditions: expert reports surveyed through Westlaw Expert Materials

claims.claim: The legal standards applicable to private fund investor due diligence are somewhat inconsistent and suboptimal and merit clarification.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Investor Due Diligence – Evidence from 1995 to 2015 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811718
scope_conditions: United States case law from 1995 to 2015

claims.claim: The data suggest that since 2010 private fund advisers increasingly engage in investor due diligence in order to protect themselves from investor criticism and lawsuits.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Investor Due Diligence – Evidence from 1995 to 2015 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811718
scope_conditions: private fund advisers
since 2010

claims.claim: Madoff related cases following the discovery of the Ponzi scheme in 2008 only partially explain the significant increase in the prevalence and importance of private fund investor due diligence after 2009.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Investor Due Diligence – Evidence from 1995 to 2015 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811718
scope_conditions: post 2009 litigation and disclosure record

claims.claim: Lacking standards for private fund investor due diligence can partly be attributed to private funds' unique market position: unlike mutual funds, private funds evolved as unregistered entities free from most regulatory oversight, so their due diligence evolved without regulatory oversight as well.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Investor Due Diligence – Evidence from 1995 to 2015 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811718
scope_conditions: United States private funds compared to registered mutual funds

claims.claim: Private fund investor due diligence may follow the evolutionary path of bank risk evaluation, which fifteen years ago operated without uniformity or applicable standards and is today heavily regulated and has evolved into a science.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Investor Due Diligence – Evidence from 1995 to 2015 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811718
scope_conditions: by analogy to bank risk evaluation
if standardization pressure continues

claims.claim: Investment due diligence may start from the same basic questions as operational due diligence but is almost always idiosyncratic, because it targets the subject manager's investment process, which is typically unique to that manager.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Investor Due Diligence – Evidence from 1995 to 2015 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811718
scope_conditions: investment due diligence as distinguished from operational due diligence

claims.claim: Despite bringing enforcement actions over misrepresentations about due diligence, the SEC has not taken a rigid enforcement position on whether particular due diligence industry practices are effective, and has merely acknowledged that practices became more robust after the financial crisis.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Fund Investor Due Diligence – Evidence from 1995 to 2015 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811718
scope_conditions: SEC enforcement posture as of 2016

claims.claim: The originators of the earliest U.S. hedge funds deliberately structured the funds to maximize trading freedom by minimizing exposure to federal regulation, so the industry's private, unregistered form was a design choice rather than an accident of history.
claims.citation: Kaal and Oesterle, The History of Hedge Fund Regulation in the United States (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2714974
scope_conditions: applies to the founding period of the U.S. hedge fund industry in the early 1950s

claims.claim: Qualifying for one of the Investment Company Act statutory exclusions, fewer than 100 investors or exclusively qualified purchasers, is what permits a hedge fund to use investment techniques such as shorting that are forbidden to registered investment companies.
claims.citation: Kaal and Oesterle, The History of Hedge Fund Regulation in the United States (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2714974
scope_conditions: requires fewer than 100 investors or only qualified purchasers
applies under the Investment Company Act of 1940

claims.claim: The SEC's 1985 safe harbor in Rule 203(b)(3) allowed a limited partnership itself, rather than each of its limited partners, to be counted as a single client of the general partner acting as adviser, which is what kept hedge fund advisers below the registration threshold.
claims.citation: Kaal and Oesterle, The History of Hedge Fund Regulation in the United States (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2714974
scope_conditions: applies to exemption from registration under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940

claims.claim: Expanding the client counting safe harbor in 1997 to cover legal entities generally allowed investment advisers to manage large amounts of securities indirectly for several hundred investors across multiple hedge funds without registering.
claims.citation: Kaal and Oesterle, The History of Hedge Fund Regulation in the United States (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2714974
scope_conditions: requires that advice be based on the objectives of the legal organization rather than of its individual owners

claims.claim: The collapse of Long Term Capital Management in 1998 and its Federal Reserve orchestrated bailout made hedge fund risk to international markets apparent, and concerns over excessive leverage combined with a lack of transparency drove the demand for new regulation.
claims.citation: Kaal and Oesterle, The History of Hedge Fund Regulation in the United States (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2714974
scope_conditions: applies to the post 1998 policy debate

claims.claim: The SEC's 2004 hedge fund adviser registration rule failed in court because the agency lacked authority to define the term client, which the Investment Advisers Act had not otherwise defined, and the D.C. Circuit in Goldstein vacated the rule as arbitrary rulemaking.
claims.citation: Kaal and Oesterle, The History of Hedge Fund Regulation in the United States (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2714974
scope_conditions: applies to rulemaking under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940

claims.claim: Under Title IV of the Dodd-Frank Act, hedge funds with more than $150 million in assets under management must register as investment advisers and disclose information about their trades and portfolios to the SEC.
claims.citation: Kaal and Oesterle, The History of Hedge Fund Regulation in the United States (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2714974
scope_conditions: applies to advisers above the $150 million AUM threshold

claims.claim: Some of the most sensitive Form PF disclosures are not readily obtainable by the funds themselves: counterparty credit exposure often cannot be determined by individual fund managers, which makes the reporting requirement burdensome in practice.
claims.citation: Kaal and Oesterle, The History of Hedge Fund Regulation in the United States (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2714974
scope_conditions: applies to Form PF counterparty credit exposure reporting

claims.claim: Contrary to the hedge fund industry's own predictions, the industry has absorbed Form PF quickly and the impact of the Dodd-Frank registration and disclosure rules has proven much less intense than the industry initially anticipated.
claims.citation: Kaal and Oesterle, The History of Hedge Fund Regulation in the United States (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2714974
scope_conditions: based on the author's survey data from 2012 and 2015

claims.claim: The majority of hedge fund advisers spent less than $10,000 preparing their initial Form PF data reporting to the SEC, and subsequent annual filings cost about half of that initial amount.
claims.citation: Kaal and Oesterle, The History of Hedge Fund Regulation in the United States (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2714974
scope_conditions: applies to advisers filing annually rather than quarterly

claims.claim: Larger hedge fund advisers, which must file Form PF quarterly rather than annually, faced substantially higher compliance costs for both initial and subsequent reporting than smaller advisers did.
claims.citation: Kaal and Oesterle, The History of Hedge Fund Regulation in the United States (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2714974
scope_conditions: applies to advisers subject to quarterly Form PF filing

claims.claim: The most pressing problem with Form PF identified by the majority of SEC registered hedge fund advisers is not the volume of data but the ambiguity of the data reporting requirements themselves.
claims.citation: Kaal and Oesterle, The History of Hedge Fund Regulation in the United States (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2714974
scope_conditions: based on survey responses from SEC registered hedge fund advisers

claims.claim: The cost of hedge fund manager registration under the Dodd-Frank Act brings increasing returns to scale for the industry, meaning compliance burdens fall disproportionately on smaller advisers.
claims.citation: Kaal and Oesterle, The History of Hedge Fund Regulation in the United States (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2714974

claims.claim: Adopting a generic compliance program is not sufficient under Rule 206(4)-7: advisers that fail to specifically tailor their compliance program to their own business have incurred large penalties in SEC enforcement.
claims.citation: Kaal and Oesterle, The History of Hedge Fund Regulation in the United States (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2714974
scope_conditions: applies to funds subject to Rule 206(4)-7

claims.claim: Co-investment arrangements become problematic when a fund grants a co-investment opportunity in exchange for a future or increased fund commitment and the practice is not adequately disclosed, especially where the fund's governing documents would prohibit the allocation.
claims.citation: Kaal and Oesterle, The History of Hedge Fund Regulation in the United States (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2714974
scope_conditions: applies where limited partners are also co-investors
turns on adequacy of disclosure and the fund's governing documents

claims.claim: The long term capital gains treatment of carried interest matters more to private equity, venture capital, and real estate fund advisers than to hedge fund advisers, because those funds hold portfolio company stock longer on average.
claims.citation: Kaal and Oesterle, The History of Hedge Fund Regulation in the United States (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2714974
scope_conditions: applies to profits on securities held more than one year

claims.claim: If Congress changes the tax treatment of carried interest, returns to hedge fund advisers and their investors are likely to fall markedly and the popularity of hedge funds will be severely tested.
claims.citation: Kaal and Oesterle, The History of Hedge Fund Regulation in the United States (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2714974
scope_conditions: conditional on congressional elimination of the carried interest loophole

claims.claim: New Rule 506(c) creates uncertainty for hedge fund advisers considering general solicitation and general advertising, because the SEC required reasonable steps to verify accreditation without supplying a bright line rule for the content of such solicitation.
claims.citation: Kaal and Oesterle, The History of Hedge Fund Regulation in the United States (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2714974
scope_conditions: applies to Regulation D offerings under Rule 506(c) after September 23, 2013

claims.claim: Although the JOBS Act rules freed hedge fund managers to advertise, talk to reporters, and speak at conferences from September 23, 2013, very few managers actually engage in these less restrictive communications with potential investors.
claims.citation: Kaal and Oesterle, The History of Hedge Fund Regulation in the United States (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2714974
scope_conditions: applies to the period after Rule 506(c) took effect

claims.claim: The investor verification requirement defeats the purpose of the Rule 506(c) liberalization: fearing liability for investor misrepresentations of personal wealth, most hedge funds raising money from individuals continue to use old Rule 506 rather than Rule 506(c).
claims.citation: Kaal and Oesterle, The History of Hedge Fund Regulation in the United States (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2714974
scope_conditions: applies to funds raising capital from individual investors

claims.claim: Until the SEC finalizes verification rules and gives a clear, comprehensive definition of the reasonable steps an issuer must take, issuers cannot determine at the time of sale whether their verification attempts made general solicitation permissible.
claims.citation: Kaal and Oesterle, The History of Hedge Fund Regulation in the United States (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2714974
scope_conditions: conditional on the absence of finalized SEC verification guidance

claims.claim: Neither obvious remedy for the increased sales pressure created by the Rule 506 amendment works well: added disclosure obligations such as filing all Rule 506 sales documents with FINRA or the SEC may burden issuers inappropriately, while litigation based enforcement may not reach all offenders equally or appropriately.
claims.citation: Kaal and Oesterle, The History of Hedge Fund Regulation in the United States (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2714974
scope_conditions: applies to private placements where commissions exceed those on other investments

claims.claim: Hedge funds retain a structural short selling advantage because they are unaffected by the restrictions imposed on mutual funds, can use derivatives to avoid margin requirements, and have pioneered procedures that lower the direct costs of shorting.
claims.citation: Kaal and Oesterle, The History of Hedge Fund Regulation in the United States (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2714974

claims.claim: The emergence of hedge funds as short sellers should be viewed as a positive development because it eliminates some of the market overpricing that the high costs of short selling would otherwise sustain.
claims.citation: Kaal and Oesterle, The History of Hedge Fund Regulation in the United States (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2714974

claims.claim: There are no legal limits on hedge fund leverage; the only constraint comes from market discipline supplied by creditors and counterparties through interest rates, credit availability, credit limits, initial margin, and credit spreads.
claims.citation: Kaal and Oesterle, The History of Hedge Fund Regulation in the United States (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2714974
scope_conditions: contrasts with registered investment companies, which face direct statutory limits

claims.claim: Direct regulation of hedge fund leverage collapses on the details because balance sheet leverage is not an adequate measure of risk and would push funds into off-balance sheet avoidance strategies.
claims.citation: Kaal and Oesterle, The History of Hedge Fund Regulation in the United States (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2714974
scope_conditions: applies to proposals for direct leverage regulation

claims.claim: Alternative risk measures such as value at risk have severe measurement problems, so any direct regulation of leverage would be set conservatively and would substantially limit hedge funds' ability to provide market liquidity.
claims.citation: Kaal and Oesterle, The History of Hedge Fund Regulation in the United States (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2714974
scope_conditions: applies to direct regulation of hedge fund leverage

claims.claim: Direct regulation of hedge fund leverage increases moral hazard costs, because lenders and counterparties relax their own vigilance once they rely on government rules to constrain fund risk taking.
claims.citation: Kaal and Oesterle, The History of Hedge Fund Regulation in the United States (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2714974
scope_conditions: applies where government rules substitute for private monitoring

claims.claim: Any prescriptive regulatory regime for hedge funds risks leaving the financial system less stable rather than more stable, because counterparties relax vigilance when they believe authorities are monitoring and constraining fund risk taking.
claims.citation: Kaal and Oesterle, The History of Hedge Fund Regulation in the United States (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2714974
scope_conditions: applies to prescriptive position reporting and monitoring regimes

claims.claim: Proposals for indirect regulation of hedge funds through the regulation of the financial institutions that interact with them are unlikely to become legally binding.
claims.citation: Kaal and Oesterle, The History of Hedge Fund Regulation in the United States (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2714974

claims.claim: Banks are uniquely positioned to discipline hedge fund behavior because their role as lenders, market makers, and product creators lets them use the threat of cutting off future lending as leverage over a fund.
claims.citation: Kaal and Oesterle, The History of Hedge Fund Regulation in the United States (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2714974
scope_conditions: depends on banks' ongoing lending and counterparty relationships with the fund

claims.claim: Indirect regulation through bank capital adequacy standards can reach systemic risk because those standards alter not only banks' credit standards but also counterparty credit risk and therefore hedge funds' level of leverage.
claims.citation: Kaal and Oesterle, The History of Hedge Fund Regulation in the United States (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2714974
scope_conditions: applies to banks and counterparties subject to capital adequacy standards

claims.claim: A system in which hedge funds submit position information to an authority that aggregates and publishes it cannot address liquidity risk, because protecting proprietary information requires so much aggregation that the resulting information loses value to market participants.
claims.citation: Kaal and Oesterle, The History of Hedge Fund Regulation in the United States (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2714974
scope_conditions: applies to position reporting regimes that publish aggregated data

claims.claim: A public database of nonproprietary hedge fund information might demystify the industry, but it would not address the central policy concern that opacity creates liquidity risk.
claims.citation: Kaal and Oesterle, The History of Hedge Fund Regulation in the United States (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2714974
scope_conditions: applies to public databases limited to nonproprietary information

claims.claim: SEC rules should be amended to require public companies, particularly financial institutions, to disclose their material exposure to hedge funds and other highly leveraged institutions in the MD&A or Description of Business sections, which would be consistent with existing SEC disclosure philosophy.
claims.citation: Kaal and Oesterle, The History of Hedge Fund Regulation in the United States (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2714974
scope_conditions: applies to publicly traded lenders and counterparties of hedge funds

claims.claim: The combined restrictions on registered investment company short selling, leverage, and organizational structure create a substantial disincentive for such companies to pursue absolute return strategies that are independent of the aggregate value of the market.
claims.citation: Kaal and Oesterle, The History of Hedge Fund Regulation in the United States (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2714974
scope_conditions: applies to registered investment companies under the Investment Company Act

claims.claim: The prohibition on performance fees for investment companies is the most important structural difference from hedge funds, which rely heavily on performance fees of up to 20 percent of capital gains and appreciation to give advisers incentives to produce absolute returns.
claims.citation: Kaal and Oesterle, The History of Hedge Fund Regulation in the United States (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2714974
scope_conditions: applies to advisers to registered investment companies

claims.claim: Hedge fund and private equity IPOs indicate that the historic contours of the industry as privately held, unregistered, and exempt funds are slowly changing as the industry becomes a more mainstream part of finance.
claims.citation: Kaal and Oesterle, The History of Hedge Fund Regulation in the United States (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2714974
scope_conditions: based on listings since the mid 2000s, which remain rare among hedge funds

claims.claim: The overall effects of enhanced hedge fund regulation are not as immense as industry representatives predicted, but there is evidence that the enhanced Dodd-Frank Act rules do increase compliance costs for the industry.
claims.citation: Kaal and Oesterle, The History of Hedge Fund Regulation in the United States (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2714974

claims.claim: Higher compliance costs from hedge fund regulation can create barriers to entry for new market entrants and can accelerate consolidation of the hedge fund industry.
claims.citation: Kaal and Oesterle, The History of Hedge Fund Regulation in the United States (2016). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2714974
scope_conditions: follows from increased compliance costs under the Dodd-Frank Act

claims.claim: Title IV of the Dodd-Frank Act ended more than fifty years during which the hedge fund industry operated under low-level regulatory oversight, constituting a tectonic shift in the regulatory framework for private funds.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Post Dodd-Frank Act Evolution of the Private Fund Industry Comparative Evidence from 2012 and 2 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2739479
scope_conditions: United States private fund industry
period following the 2010 enactment of Title IV

claims.claim: The SEC's 2004 attempt to require hedge fund adviser registration failed: after the D.C. Circuit vacated the rule in Goldstein v. SEC, the overwhelming majority of private fund advisers that had registered under the 2004 requirements deregistered.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Post Dodd-Frank Act Evolution of the Private Fund Industry Comparative Evidence from 2012 and 2 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2739479
scope_conditions: SEC rulemaking under the Investment Advisers Act before Dodd-Frank
after the 2006 Goldstein decision

claims.claim: The reporting obligations imposed on private fund advisers by Form PF raised regulatory oversight of private funds to unprecedented levels.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Post Dodd-Frank Act Evolution of the Private Fund Industry Comparative Evidence from 2012 and 2 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2739479
scope_conditions: SEC-registered private fund advisers
after Form PF became operative in 2012

claims.claim: Prior survey evidence indicates that the hedge fund industry adjusted well to the Dodd-Frank registration and disclosure requirements, and that the actual impact of those rules was much less significant than the private fund industry had feared.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Post Dodd-Frank Act Evolution of the Private Fund Industry Comparative Evidence from 2012 and 2 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2739479
scope_conditions: short-term period immediately following the 2012 effective date
based on survey responses from registered private fund advisers

claims.claim: Growth in the private fund industry has been concentrated among the largest advisers: assets managed by advisers with more than $5 billion in AUM grew 141 percent, compared with 53 percent for firms below $5 billion.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Post Dodd-Frank Act Evolution of the Private Fund Industry Comparative Evidence from 2012 and 2 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2739479
scope_conditions: private fund advisers
growth measured through 2015

claims.claim: Private fund underperformance may be a product of institutionalization: pension funds have increased their private fund holdings and institutions now make up over two thirds of the private fund investor base, up from 20 percent a decade earlier.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Post Dodd-Frank Act Evolution of the Private Fund Industry Comparative Evidence from 2012 and 2 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2739479
scope_conditions: hedge fund investor base as of 2015
explanation offered as possible, not established

claims.claim: As the private fund investor profile shifts toward institutional investors, fees fall; institutional investors made up 65 percent of hedge fund AUM in 2015 compared with roughly 20 percent a decade earlier.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Post Dodd-Frank Act Evolution of the Private Fund Industry Comparative Evidence from 2012 and 2 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2739479
scope_conditions: hedge fund fee levels

claims.claim: Underperformance combined with the influx of institutional money means that pension funds, endowments and other institutions, which now outnumber wealthy individuals as private fund investors, hold more bargaining power over fees.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Post Dodd-Frank Act Evolution of the Private Fund Industry Comparative Evidence from 2012 and 2 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2739479
scope_conditions: private fund fee negotiation
as of 2015

claims.claim: Smaller private funds spend more on compliance than larger ones, both as a share of AUM and relative to operating costs, which means increasing regulatory scrutiny falls disproportionately on smaller funds.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Post Dodd-Frank Act Evolution of the Private Fund Industry Comparative Evidence from 2012 and 2 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2739479
scope_conditions: private fund advisers subject to Dodd-Frank compliance obligations
compliance measured as share of AUM and of operating costs

claims.claim: The private fund industry generated a disproportionate share of asset management profits: it produced 34 percent of the industry's 2013 profits, $31.2 billion of $93.0 billion, while controlling only 4 percent of total AUM.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Post Dodd-Frank Act Evolution of the Private Fund Industry Comparative Evidence from 2012 and 2 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2739479
scope_conditions: global asset management industry
2013 profit figures

claims.claim: Because the Dodd-Frank Act discouraged banks from growing too large and made bank lending harder, private funds and other alternative lenders filled the resulting void by financing small and medium sized businesses that traditional banks no longer served.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Post Dodd-Frank Act Evolution of the Private Fund Industry Comparative Evidence from 2012 and 2 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2739479
scope_conditions: United States lending markets after Dodd-Frank
small and medium sized business borrowers

claims.claim: The stronger performance of activist strategies lets activist private fund managers keep charging the higher 2 and 20 fee structure that other fund managers can no longer demand.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Post Dodd-Frank Act Evolution of the Private Fund Industry Comparative Evidence from 2012 and 2 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2739479
scope_conditions: activist private funds
as of 2015

claims.claim: Firms that outsource the chief compliance officer role to third parties face heightened SEC scrutiny and examination risk, and the SEC has signaled that CCO liability arises where CCOs mislead regulators, engage in affirmative misconduct, or fail to carry out assigned compliance responsibilities.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Post Dodd-Frank Act Evolution of the Private Fund Industry Comparative Evidence from 2012 and 2 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2739479
scope_conditions: SEC-registered advisers and funds
since 2015

claims.claim: Lifting the ban on general solicitation and general advertising was a significant formal change for private funds, but the new advertising opportunities are being taken up only reluctantly, and uncertainty about investor verification rules together with specific restrictions makes advertising by private fund advisers unlikely for the foreseeable future.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Post Dodd-Frank Act Evolution of the Private Fund Industry Comparative Evidence from 2012 and 2 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2739479
scope_conditions: Rule 506(c) offerings after the September 2013 effective date
private fund and private equity advisers

claims.claim: Registered investment advisers should expect a more demanding regulatory environment ahead, including new or proposed regulations, more SEC enforcement actions against private fund managers, and longer and more intrusive examinations.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Post Dodd-Frank Act Evolution of the Private Fund Industry Comparative Evidence from 2012 and 2 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2739479
scope_conditions: SEC-registered private fund advisers
years following 2015

claims.claim: The traditional distinction between mutual funds and private funds is dissipating: mutual funds are becoming more like hedge funds in investment strategy, while hedge funds are becoming more like mutual funds in regulatory framework.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Post Dodd-Frank Act Evolution of the Private Fund Industry Comparative Evidence from 2012 and 2 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2739479
scope_conditions: United States asset management industry after the 2008 to 2009 credit crisis

claims.claim: Survey research on private fund advisers is structurally constrained because these advisers traditionally oppose publicity and hold a strong preference for confidentiality and privacy, which makes a substantial effective sample size difficult to obtain.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Post Dodd-Frank Act Evolution of the Private Fund Industry Comparative Evidence from 2012 and 2 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2739479
scope_conditions: survey research on registered private fund advisers

claims.claim: Neither the 2012 nor the 2015 sample is biased, and the comparison across the two populations is consistent because respondents in both surveys were equally subject to Title IV compliance obligations.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Post Dodd-Frank Act Evolution of the Private Fund Industry Comparative Evidence from 2012 and 2 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2739479
scope_conditions: comparison of the 2012 and 2015 survey samples
both drawn from the same 1267 adviser population

claims.claim: The decline in survey response rate between 2012 and 2015 is itself evidence of the private fund industry's relatively rapid adaptation to the new statutory and regulatory regime.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Post Dodd-Frank Act Evolution of the Private Fund Industry Comparative Evidence from 2012 and 2 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2739479
scope_conditions: comparison of 2012 and 2015 responses from the same adviser population

claims.claim: A majority of private fund adviser respondents in both surveys, 72 percent in 2012 and 75 percent in 2015, did not plan any strategic response, meaning any action to avoid or limit the impact of Title IV.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Post Dodd-Frank Act Evolution of the Private Fund Industry Comparative Evidence from 2012 and 2 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2739479
scope_conditions: survey respondents in 2012 (N = 94) and 2015 (N = 69)

claims.claim: The share of advisers reporting that they changed their communications with investors nearly doubled from 25 percent in 2012 to 47 percent in 2015, a shift the author attributes to advisers increasing investor communications on advice of counsel.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Post Dodd-Frank Act Evolution of the Private Fund Industry Comparative Evidence from 2012 and 2 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2739479
scope_conditions: survey respondents in 2012 and 2015

claims.claim: Although rare in absolute terms, structural responses grew: at least part of the industry is increasingly changing the legal structure of its funds and closing funds to new investors in response to the post-2012 regulatory changes.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Post Dodd-Frank Act Evolution of the Private Fund Industry Comparative Evidence from 2012 and 2 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2739479
scope_conditions: least common actions reported in the 2012 and 2015 surveys
rates doubled or tripled between the two surveys from a low base

claims.claim: Rather than outsourcing required compliance work, the industry is on some metrics increasingly performing that work in-house, a shift consistent with the SEC's emphasis on compliance officer liability and post-2012 enforcement actions aimed at compliance departments.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Post Dodd-Frank Act Evolution of the Private Fund Industry Comparative Evidence from 2012 and 2 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2739479
scope_conditions: comparison of 2012 and 2015 survey responses
holds under some metrics only

claims.claim: Between 2012 and 2015 the annual cost of Dodd-Frank compliance doubled for many survey respondents, moving from the $50,000 to $100,000 range into the $100,000 to $200,000 range.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Post Dodd-Frank Act Evolution of the Private Fund Industry Comparative Evidence from 2012 and 2 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2739479
scope_conditions: respondents to the 2012 and 2015 surveys
self-reported total compliance costs

claims.claim: The shift of reported compliance hours out of the 251 to 500 hour band and into the 100 to 250 hour band suggests the industry became more effective at satisfying Dodd-Frank reporting obligations between 2012 and 2015.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Post Dodd-Frank Act Evolution of the Private Fund Industry Comparative Evidence from 2012 and 2 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2739479
scope_conditions: hours reported for Dodd-Frank Act compliance specifically, not all federal regulation

claims.claim: If compliance hour requirements are treated as a proxy for compliance cost, the survey data indicate that the cost of complying with all federal regulation, not just Dodd-Frank, increased between 2012 and 2015.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Post Dodd-Frank Act Evolution of the Private Fund Industry Comparative Evidence from 2012 and 2 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2739479
scope_conditions: conditional on hours being a valid proxy for cost
all federal regulation applicable to private fund advisers

claims.claim: Private fund advisers increasingly factor the regulatory structure into decisions about the size of their assets under management, a shift partly explained by the higher post-Dodd-Frank cost structure, since higher AUM and the corresponding fee revenue can offset higher compliance costs.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Post Dodd-Frank Act Evolution of the Private Fund Industry Comparative Evidence from 2012 and 2 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2739479
scope_conditions: comparison of 2012 and 2015 survey respondents
AUM sizing decisions

claims.claim: The finding that advisers size AUM around regulatory cost is in tension with anecdotal evidence, since only a minority of private investment funds pay expenses out of the management fee at all.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Post Dodd-Frank Act Evolution of the Private Fund Industry Comparative Evidence from 2012 and 2 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2739479
scope_conditions: private fund expense allocation practice
survey inference about the AUM decision

claims.claim: Advisers typically try to allocate as many operating expenses as possible to the fund so that as much of the net management fee as possible becomes manager compensation, a practice that private fund investors heavily criticize.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Post Dodd-Frank Act Evolution of the Private Fund Industry Comparative Evidence from 2012 and 2 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2739479
scope_conditions: standard private fund adviser compensation practice

claims.claim: Sensitivity to the Form PF quarterly reporting threshold rose sharply: only 19 percent of 2012 respondents took the $1.5 billion threshold into account, compared with 33 percent in 2015.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Post Dodd-Frank Act Evolution of the Private Fund Industry Comparative Evidence from 2012 and 2 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2739479
scope_conditions: survey respondents in 2012 and 2015
the $1.5 billion Form PF quarterly reporting threshold

claims.claim: Because quarterly Form PF filing costs roughly $10,000 per reporting fund, the $1.5 billion threshold that triggers quarterly filing gives advisers a direct cost reason to factor that threshold into the AUM decision.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Post Dodd-Frank Act Evolution of the Private Fund Industry Comparative Evidence from 2012 and 2 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2739479
scope_conditions: advisers approaching $1.5 billion in AUM
per reporting fund cost basis

claims.claim: A majority of respondents in both surveys, 76.1 percent in 2012 and 65 percent in 2015, believed the Dodd-Frank Act did not affect their reporting funds' earnings.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Post Dodd-Frank Act Evolution of the Private Fund Industry Comparative Evidence from 2012 and 2 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2739479
scope_conditions: survey respondents in 2012 and 2015
perceived effect on fund earnings, not measured returns

claims.claim: Although Dodd-Frank compliance costs fall primarily on the investment adviser rather than the fund, advisers have increasingly built fund structures that pass most of those compliance expenses through to their reporting funds.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Post Dodd-Frank Act Evolution of the Private Fund Industry Comparative Evidence from 2012 and 2 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2739479
scope_conditions: adviser and private fund contractual structures
between 2012 and 2015

claims.claim: Passing compliance costs through to reporting funds applies those costs against the funds' trading revenues, which produces an overall adverse impact on fund earnings and so shifts the burden of regulation onto investors.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Post Dodd-Frank Act Evolution of the Private Fund Industry Comparative Evidence from 2012 and 2 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2739479
scope_conditions: funds subject to adviser expense pass-through terms

claims.claim: Among advisers who saw an earnings effect, the attributed cause shifted from direct expense to opportunity cost between 2012 and 2015, with opportunity cost references rising from 9 percent to 32 percent while increased expense references fell from 53 percent to 36 percent.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Post Dodd-Frank Act Evolution of the Private Fund Industry Comparative Evidence from 2012 and 2 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2739479
scope_conditions: only respondents who reported an effect on fund earnings
2012 and 2015 surveys

claims.claim: By 2015 a clear majority of respondents, 93 percent, attributed effects on their investment management company's profits to additional expenses associated with the Dodd-Frank Act, and no respondent reported no additional expenses, compared with 19 percent in 2012.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Post Dodd-Frank Act Evolution of the Private Fund Industry Comparative Evidence from 2012 and 2 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2739479
scope_conditions: survey respondents reporting on management company profits
2012 and 2015 surveys

claims.claim: Even though the Dodd-Frank Act's overall regulatory impact on the private fund industry was low, the compliance costs generated by the evolving regulatory environment carry many unexpected consequences with the potential to further reshape industry practices.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Post Dodd-Frank Act Evolution of the Private Fund Industry Comparative Evidence from 2012 and 2 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2739479
scope_conditions: private fund advisers
period from 2012 to 2015

claims.claim: Changing AUM preferences driven by compliance costs could eventually produce industry consolidation aimed at cost savings, or drive a shift toward family offices that manage no third-party assets and therefore escape the regime.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Post Dodd-Frank Act Evolution of the Private Fund Industry Comparative Evidence from 2012 and 2 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2739479
scope_conditions: long-run private fund industry structure
author marks it as unclear whether AUM preference changes become permanent

claims.claim: The comparative evidence suggests the long-term effects of the evolving post-Dodd-Frank regulatory environment may be more substantial than either the industry or regulators initially anticipated.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Post Dodd-Frank Act Evolution of the Private Fund Industry Comparative Evidence from 2012 and 2 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2739479
scope_conditions: private fund advisers and their reporting funds
based on 2015 responses citing lower returns and plans to consolidate or close funds

claims.claim: Barriers to entry for small firms are becoming an increasing problem in the private fund industry under the evolving post-Dodd-Frank legal environment, with references to such barriers rising from 24 percent of respondents in 2012 to 33 percent in 2015.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Post Dodd-Frank Act Evolution of the Private Fund Industry Comparative Evidence from 2012 and 2 (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2739479
scope_conditions: small private fund market entrants
2012 and 2015 survey responses about the next five years

claims.claim: Five years after the Dodd-Frank Act, the private fund industry is most affected by the uncertainty and the higher costs the Act generates, yet on multiple metrics the industry is coping well with the evolving post Dodd-Frank regulatory landscape.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Private Fund Industry Five Years after the Dodd-Frank Act – A Survey Study (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2732915
scope_conditions: survey of a population of 1267 registered investment advisers, N=69 respondents
United States, post Title IV registration

claims.claim: The private fund industry is adjusting well to the evolving post Dodd-Frank regulatory landscape, and the long-term impact of that landscape is much less intense than the industry itself initially anticipated.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Private Fund Industry Five Years after the Dodd-Frank Act – A Survey Study (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2732915
scope_conditions: registered U.S. private fund advisers five years after enactment

claims.claim: The long-term cost implications of Title IV registration and reporting obligations are absorbed relatively quickly after registration, so that Dodd-Frank compliance costs are largely manageable depending on the size of the investment adviser.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Private Fund Industry Five Years after the Dodd-Frank Act – A Survey Study (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2732915
scope_conditions: cost absorption measured after the initial registration period
manageability varies with adviser size

claims.claim: Although the industry adapted well to the post Dodd-Frank environment, the Act has already produced some negative effects on the private fund industry and may produce further negative long-term effects.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Private Fund Industry Five Years after the Dodd-Frank Act – A Survey Study (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2732915
scope_conditions: based on survey responses about the next five years

claims.claim: The survey achieved a response rate of 5.44 percent from a population of 1267 registered private fund advisers.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Private Fund Industry Five Years after the Dodd-Frank Act – A Survey Study (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2732915
scope_conditions: e-mail survey of advisers registered before the March 30, 2012 effective date

claims.claim: Because private fund advisers prefer confidentiality and generally oppose publicity, most do not respond to survey questions, which makes obtaining a substantial effective sample size for survey studies of this industry difficult.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Private Fund Industry Five Years after the Dodd-Frank Act – A Survey Study (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2732915
scope_conditions: survey research targeting private fund advisers

claims.claim: Guaranteeing complete anonymity is essential to obtaining a sufficient response rate from private fund advisers, but that guarantee prevents a broader descriptive statistical analysis of the sample.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Private Fund Industry Five Years after the Dodd-Frank Act – A Survey Study (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2732915
scope_conditions: survey studies of private fund advisers who fear identification

claims.claim: After the D.C. Circuit vacated the SEC's 2004 hedge fund adviser registration rule in Goldstein v. SEC, the overwhelming majority of private fund advisers who had registered under that rule deregistered.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Private Fund Industry Five Years after the Dodd-Frank Act – A Survey Study (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2732915
scope_conditions: private fund advisers registered under the SEC 2004 rule
after the 2006 Goldstein decision

claims.claim: Title IV requires private fund advisers with more than $150 million in assets under management to register with the SEC as investment advisers.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Private Fund Industry Five Years after the Dodd-Frank Act – A Survey Study (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2732915
scope_conditions: advisers acting solely as advisers to private funds
assets under management in the United States

claims.claim: Form PF raised regulatory oversight of private funds to unprecedented levels by requiring managers to disclose, for the first time, information about themselves, their funds, their investors, performance, financing, risk metrics, strategies, and credit exposure.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Private Fund Industry Five Years after the Dodd-Frank Act – A Survey Study (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2732915
scope_conditions: registered investment managers subject to periodic Form PF reporting

claims.claim: Prior studies acknowledge that the SEC's mandated collection of private fund data through Form PF created several core challenges for the industry, but they do not sufficiently clarify the long-term impact of the Form PF disclosure requirements.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Private Fund Industry Five Years after the Dodd-Frank Act – A Survey Study (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2732915
scope_conditions: literature on Form PF available as of 2016
