claims.claim: Form PF required disclosures of counterparty credit exposure constitute sensitive information that individual fund managers often cannot readily determine, which makes that reporting requirement hard to satisfy.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Private Fund Industry Five Years after the Dodd-Frank Act – A Survey Study (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2732915
scope_conditions: Form PF counterparty credit exposure items

claims.claim: The SEC estimates that 230 U.S. hedge fund advisers with at least $1.5 billion in RAUM attributable to hedge funds at the end of any month in the prior fiscal quarter will file Form PF.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Private Fund Industry Five Years after the Dodd-Frank Act – A Survey Study (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2732915
scope_conditions: SEC estimate in the Form PF adopting release

claims.claim: Approximately 155 investment advisers managing over $2 billion in private equity fund assets may represent roughly 75 percent of the U.S. private equity fund industry, so a small number of filers covers most industry assets.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Private Fund Industry Five Years after the Dodd-Frank Act – A Survey Study (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2732915
scope_conditions: SEC and Preqin estimates cited in the Form PF release

claims.claim: Form PF data from the SEC Risk and Examinations Office for the fourth quarter of 2014 show net asset value of about $3,399 billion for hedge funds, $2,672 billion for Qualifying Hedge Funds, and $1,744 billion for private equity.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Private Fund Industry Five Years after the Dodd-Frank Act – A Survey Study (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2732915
scope_conditions: fourth calendar quarter 2014 Private Funds Statistics

claims.claim: A 2013 survey found that Form PF compliance costs for first time filers were under $10,000 for 59.18 percent of respondents, while subsequent annual Form PF filings cost no more than $5,000 for 57.14 percent of respondents.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Private Fund Industry Five Years after the Dodd-Frank Act – A Survey Study (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2732915
scope_conditions: 2013 survey of private fund advisers
larger quarterly filers incurred substantially higher costs

claims.claim: Industry concerns about the burdensome nature of Title IV's mandatory private fund adviser registration and disclosure requirements appear mostly unfounded, although data inconsistencies remain a concern.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Private Fund Industry Five Years after the Dodd-Frank Act – A Survey Study (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2732915
scope_conditions: measured through adviser reported cost and time of Form PF compliance

claims.claim: A majority of private fund adviser respondents, 74.5 percent, do not plan any strategic response to Title IV of the Dodd-Frank Act.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Private Fund Industry Five Years after the Dodd-Frank Act – A Survey Study (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2732915
scope_conditions: N=69 survey respondents
strategic response understood as action to avoid or limit the impact of Title IV

claims.claim: The most common adviser responses to Title IV are outsourcing compliance work, hiring additional counsel, instituting new record keeping policies, hiring additional staff, changing marketing materials, and changing communications with investors, all compliance updates rather than fundamental legal or strategic change.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Private Fund Industry Five Years after the Dodd-Frank Act – A Survey Study (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2732915
scope_conditions: N=69 survey respondents

claims.claim: Private fund advisers in the sample did not terminate existing employment relationships, and only few severed advising relationships, changed fund legal structure, liquidated positions, changed investment styles or portfolio structure, or closed funds to new investors.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Private Fund Industry Five Years after the Dodd-Frank Act – A Survey Study (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2732915
scope_conditions: N=69 survey respondents

claims.claim: Among respondents answering the open ended question on other actions taken, 30.8 percent hired a compliance firm, 15.4 percent said they otherwise wasted time and money reacting to Dodd-Frank requirements, and 15.4 percent implemented new policies and programs.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Private Fund Industry Five Years after the Dodd-Frank Act – A Survey Study (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2732915
scope_conditions: open ended survey question 3b, coded into response clusters

claims.claim: Compliance cost is a significant issue for the private fund industry: a majority of respondents put Dodd-Frank compliance costs between $50,000 and $200,000, while a significant minority estimates total compliance cost between $200,000 and over $400,000.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Private Fund Industry Five Years after the Dodd-Frank Act – A Survey Study (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2732915
scope_conditions: N=69 survey respondents
cost defined as actual expenses incurred

claims.claim: Up to $100,000 in additional Dodd-Frank compliance cost is a significant imposition on a smaller private fund adviser, whereas larger and mid sized advisers can absorb it relatively easily or pass it on to clients, so the burden of Title IV is size dependent.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Private Fund Industry Five Years after the Dodd-Frank Act – A Survey Study (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2732915
scope_conditions: anecdotal evidence supplementing the survey results
distinguishes smaller advisers from larger and mid sized advisers

claims.claim: The largest group of respondents, 26.5 percent, estimated annual compliance cost for all federal regulations at between $100,000 and $200,000, while a smaller group of 14.3 percent estimated it at more than $400,000 a year.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Private Fund Industry Five Years after the Dodd-Frank Act – A Survey Study (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2732915
scope_conditions: all federal regulations pertaining to private fund advisers, not only Dodd-Frank

claims.claim: Reported compliance time tracks reported compliance cost: a clear majority of adviser respondents spent fewer than 500 hours complying with Title IV, while a noticeable minority of 11.5 percent estimated more than 1000 hours.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Private Fund Industry Five Years after the Dodd-Frank Act – A Survey Study (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2732915
scope_conditions: N=69 survey respondents
time treated as a proxy for cost

claims.claim: For all federal regulations, 65.1 percent of respondents estimate total compliance time at between 100 and 500 hours, while a noticeable minority of 20.9 percent estimate it above 1000 hours.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Private Fund Industry Five Years after the Dodd-Frank Act – A Survey Study (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2732915
scope_conditions: all federal rules and procedures including Treasury, SEC, and CFTC

claims.claim: Of the advisers who responded, 70.60 percent would not take the current regulatory regime into account in determining the assets under management size of their funds.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Private Fund Industry Five Years after the Dodd-Frank Act – A Survey Study (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2732915
scope_conditions: responses to survey question 7

claims.claim: The majority of private fund advisers in the United States are not considering changing their assets under management in order to lower Dodd-Frank compliance costs, notwithstanding the $150 million registration threshold and the $1.5 billion Form PF quarterly reporting threshold.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Private Fund Industry Five Years after the Dodd-Frank Act – A Survey Study (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2732915
scope_conditions: inference from responses to survey question 7
$150 million registration threshold and $1.5 billion Form PF threshold in force

claims.claim: Among advisers who factor the regulatory regime into fund sizing, the direction of adjustment is split: 18.2 percent would lower assets under management to avoid the regulatory hassle, while 27.3 percent would still increase AUM and another 27.3 percent seek the right size to cover expenses.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Private Fund Industry Five Years after the Dodd-Frank Act – A Survey Study (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2732915
scope_conditions: respondents who answered yes to survey question 7

claims.claim: A majority of respondents already took the regulatory regime into account in sizing assets under management before the Dodd-Frank Act was enacted, which implies that Dodd-Frank did not make much difference in how they run their business.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Private Fund Industry Five Years after the Dodd-Frank Act – A Survey Study (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2732915
scope_conditions: responses to survey question 7.b.ii
a significant minority of 47.1 percent did not consider the regime before enactment

claims.claim: The largest group of respondents prefers an assets under management size between $500 million and $1 billion, and no clear majority preference emerges around the $1.5 billion Form PF quarterly reporting threshold.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Private Fund Industry Five Years after the Dodd-Frank Act – A Survey Study (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2732915
scope_conditions: responses to survey question 8 on desired AUM after Dodd-Frank

claims.claim: A majority of adviser respondents, 66.7 percent, did not take the $1.5 billion Form PF quarterly reporting threshold into account when determining the appropriate assets under management for the funds they manage.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Private Fund Industry Five Years after the Dodd-Frank Act – A Survey Study (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2732915
scope_conditions: responses to survey question 10

claims.claim: Sixty five percent of adviser survey respondents believed that their fund earnings were not affected by the Dodd-Frank Act.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Private Fund Industry Five Years after the Dodd-Frank Act – A Survey Study (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2732915
scope_conditions: responses to survey question 11 on fund earnings and net rate of return to investors

claims.claim: Among the minority of respondents who believed Dodd-Frank affected fund earnings, the majority attributed that effect to additional compliance costs rather than to lower returns.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Private Fund Industry Five Years after the Dodd-Frank Act – A Survey Study (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2732915
scope_conditions: respondents who answered yes to survey question 11

claims.claim: Of those who responded, 75.4 percent indicated that the profits of their investment management company were affected by the new registration and disclosure requirements, consistent with the management company, rather than the fund, bearing most of those costs.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Private Fund Industry Five Years after the Dodd-Frank Act – A Survey Study (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2732915
scope_conditions: responses to survey question 12
supported by anecdotal evidence on cost allocation

claims.claim: Half of the respondents indicated that the Dodd-Frank registration and disclosure rules create higher costs that will affect their funds over the next five years, while 17.4 percent expected no effect and 6.5 percent expected lower returns.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Private Fund Industry Five Years after the Dodd-Frank Act – A Survey Study (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2732915
scope_conditions: respondents forecasting the next five years

claims.claim: Asked how Title IV will affect the private fund industry over the next five years, the largest groups of respondents identified additional expenses, at 34.9 percent, and barriers to entry for private fund market entrants, at 32.6 percent.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Private Fund Industry Five Years after the Dodd-Frank Act – A Survey Study (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2732915
scope_conditions: responses to the survey question on industry effects over five years

claims.claim: The long-term effect of the Dodd-Frank Act on the private investment fund industry is likely to be characterized by increasing additional expenses and associated barriers to entry for new market entrants.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Private Fund Industry Five Years after the Dodd-Frank Act – A Survey Study (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2732915
scope_conditions: inference from respondent forecasts for the next five years

claims.claim: The SEC's clarifying and optimizing of the legal framework after the Dodd-Frank Act effectively supports the private fund industry in its efforts to comply with the revised standards.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Private Fund Industry Five Years after the Dodd-Frank Act – A Survey Study (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2732915
scope_conditions: SEC rule amendments, guidance, and frequently asked questions issued after 2012

claims.claim: The same SEC implementation and clarification of Dodd-Frank registration and reporting requirements that helps the industry comply also creates uncertainty and higher costs for it, so continuing rule development cuts both ways.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Private Fund Industry Five Years after the Dodd-Frank Act – A Survey Study (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2732915
scope_conditions: continuing SEC amendment of rules and reporting forms after Title IV

claims.claim: The proliferation of unconstrained mutual funds calls into question whether the retail investor protections built into the Investment Company Act of 1940 remain effective.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Unconstrained Mutual Funds and Retail Investor Protection (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811729
scope_conditions: U.S. registered open-end investment companies
unconstrained credit strategies sold to retail investors

claims.claim: Unconstrained mutual funds share multiple investment strategy and risk attributes with fixed income hedge funds, a finding the authors ground in trading data and prospectuses of all such funds launched from 2010 through 2015.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Unconstrained Mutual Funds and Retail Investor Protection (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811729
scope_conditions: hand-selected sample of unconstrained mutual funds launched 2010 through 2015

claims.claim: The authors stipulate that an unconstrained mutual fund strategy is generally not tethered to any benchmark and instead gives the manager operational freedom to pursue risk-adjusted returns using any debt instruments or securities, regardless of issuer, sector, jurisdiction, liquidity, or quality.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Unconstrained Mutual Funds and Retail Investor Protection (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811729
scope_conditions: registered open-end investment management companies pursuing credit strategies

claims.claim: Unconstrained mutual funds combine the regulatory structure of a mutual fund with the investment strategy of a private fund implementing a credit strategy and principally trading fixed income instruments, which lets them transcend traditional investment and legal distinctions.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Unconstrained Mutual Funds and Retail Investor Protection (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811729
scope_conditions: credit-focused unconstrained funds registered under the Company Act

claims.claim: The investor eligibility line has become arbitrary in the credit space: private funds implementing substantially the same investment strategy as a fixed income unconstrained mutual fund, and carrying substantially the same risks, may be sold only to high net worth and sophisticated investors through private placements.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Unconstrained Mutual Funds and Retail Investor Protection (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811729
scope_conditions: fixed income focused unconstrained mutual funds compared with credit private funds

claims.claim: The emergence of unconstrained mutual funds is driven by market forces: post-crisis structural and regulatory changes to the capital markets, a low interest rate environment, and the growth of private funds together created and then increased retail demand for alternative mutual funds.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Unconstrained Mutual Funds and Retail Investor Protection (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811729
scope_conditions: United States capital markets after the 2007 to 2008 financial crisis
sustained low interest rate conditions

claims.claim: Post-crisis legislation accelerated the convergence of mutual funds and private funds, because the registration and increased disclosure requirements the Dodd-Frank Act imposed on certain private fund advisers subject them to substantively the same obligations that apply to advisers of mutual funds.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Unconstrained Mutual Funds and Retail Investor Protection (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811729
scope_conditions: private fund advisers required to register under the Dodd-Frank Act

claims.claim: Unconstrained mutual funds have not delivered superior performance: Morningstar data for funds with three years of investing history offer no evidence that they outperform mutual funds in comparable asset classifications.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Unconstrained Mutual Funds and Retail Investor Protection (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811729
scope_conditions: unconstrained mutual funds with at least three years of investing history

claims.claim: Average unconstrained mutual fund performance over the three years preceding the study was lower than the return on the ten-year Treasury, and poor performance was often accompanied by high fees and increased credit risk.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Unconstrained Mutual Funds and Retail Investor Protection (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811729
scope_conditions: three-year period preceding the study

claims.claim: The complexity of unconstrained mutual fund trading has grown to the point that even leading professional analysts struggle to assess these funds' portfolios and their performance.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Unconstrained Mutual Funds and Retail Investor Protection (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811729
scope_conditions: professional fund research analysts evaluating unconstrained funds

claims.claim: The go anywhere features of unconstrained mutual funds impede a retail investor's ability to ascertain and understand what the fund is invested in and what risks those investments carry.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Unconstrained Mutual Funds and Retail Investor Protection (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811729
scope_conditions: retail investors relying on fund disclosures

claims.claim: Three features make it uniquely challenging for retail investors to evaluate the risks of unconstrained mutual funds: the lack of standard benchmarks, the recent emergence of the fund type, and the diversity and complexity of the strategies and risk exposures involved.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Unconstrained Mutual Funds and Retail Investor Protection (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811729
scope_conditions: retail investors evaluating unconstrained mutual fund securities

claims.claim: Because unconstrained mutual funds comply with the Company Act, they may be marketed and sold to all classes of retail investors, including those with limited or even no experience investing in securities.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Unconstrained Mutual Funds and Retail Investor Protection (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811729
scope_conditions: funds registered and compliant under the Investment Company Act

claims.claim: The SEC's interpretation of Section 18 leaves a mutual fund subject to no statutory limitation or cap on its ability to borrow through the use of derivative instruments, provided the fund adheres to its asset segregation obligations.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Unconstrained Mutual Funds and Retail Investor Protection (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811729
scope_conditions: mutual funds using derivatives under SEC Section 18 guidance as of 2016

claims.claim: Proposed Rule 18f-4 would be highly limited in mitigating liquidity and other risks in an unconstrained mutual fund portfolio, because material leverage, counterparty, and liquidity risks in such a fund can arise from investments in a range of non-derivative instruments that the rule does not reach.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Unconstrained Mutual Funds and Retail Investor Protection (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811729
scope_conditions: proposed Company Act Rule 18f-4 as proposed in December 2015
unconstrained mutual funds with broad investment authority

claims.claim: If a private fund's offering process successfully limits its investors to accredited investors or qualified purchasers, the retail investor protection principles of the Company Act do not apply to the fund's trading, operation, and governance.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Unconstrained Mutual Funds and Retail Investor Protection (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811729
scope_conditions: private funds relying on Sections 3(c)(1) or 3(c)(7)

claims.claim: The authors operationalize unconstrained status by binary coding eleven prospectus characteristics and treating a score of nine or better as unconstrained, producing a final study sample of 84 funds out of 114 funds identified in the Morningstar Nontraditional Bond index.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Unconstrained Mutual Funds and Retail Investor Protection (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811729
scope_conditions: Morningstar Nontraditional Bond index constituents
most recent fund-level prospectuses as of the study

claims.claim: Unconstrained mutual funds are predominantly credit-oriented funds intended to be sold on a retail basis that nonetheless authorize the investment manager, similar to a private fund manager, to trade any type of credit security or derivative.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Unconstrained Mutual Funds and Retail Investor Protection (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811729
scope_conditions: the authors' sample of 84 unconstrained mutual funds

claims.claim: Unconstrained mutual funds are proliferating at a significant rate, growing steadily since 2007, with the overall trend between 2010 and 2015 showing a steady increase in launches.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Unconstrained Mutual Funds and Retail Investor Protection (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811729
scope_conditions: fund inception data for the sample of 84 unconstrained mutual funds

claims.claim: In the unprecedented low interest rate environment prevailing since 2005, investment managers responded to retail investors reaching for yield by offering unconstrained mutual funds, a product that authorizes absolute return strategies in the fixed income world.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Unconstrained Mutual Funds and Retail Investor Protection (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811729
scope_conditions: United States fixed income markets since 2005

claims.claim: Among the factors driving unconstrained mutual fund growth, the Dodd-Frank Act decreased the number of eligible private fund investors by raising the minimum net worth requirement for individuals to qualify as accredited investors.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Unconstrained Mutual Funds and Retail Investor Protection (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811729
scope_conditions: individuals near the accredited investor net worth threshold after Dodd-Frank

claims.claim: Unconstrained mutual funds exceed typical mutual fund trading engagements in almost all quantifiable categories, often by double or quadruple the average engagements for mutual funds as a group.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Unconstrained Mutual Funds and Retail Investor Protection (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811729
scope_conditions: N-SAR Question 70 filings, March 2016 for the 84 fund sample, compared with December 2015 SEC report data

claims.claim: Average unconstrained mutual fund portfolio turnover exceeds the turnover of other fixed income mutual funds by over 150 percent.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Unconstrained Mutual Funds and Retail Investor Protection (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811729
scope_conditions: Morningstar turnover data as of March 2016
comparison against all taxable bond funds, N equals 5543

claims.claim: The high turnover rate of unconstrained mutual funds distinguishes them from other mutual funds and makes them directly comparable to private funds, which typically trade at high levels.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Unconstrained Mutual Funds and Retail Investor Protection (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811729
scope_conditions: comparison of unconstrained mutual funds with private funds on trading intensity

claims.claim: Unconstrained mutual funds engaged in almost 50 percent more futures contract transactions than other mutual funds, and the overall scope and nature of their derivative use is consistent with what the authors would expect of a private fund.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Unconstrained Mutual Funds and Retail Investor Protection (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811729
scope_conditions: schedule of investments from the sample funds' latest N-CSR filings, April 2016

claims.claim: Because unconstrained mutual funds share investment strategy and risk attributes with private funds, the average unconstrained fund's risk profile is substantially more complex and generally involves more risk than the average mutual fund, and is closer to that of a private fund.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Unconstrained Mutual Funds and Retail Investor Protection (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811729
scope_conditions: comparison of the sample funds against average mutual funds and private funds

claims.claim: Unconstrained mutual funds take on private fund-like risk without a corresponding return advantage: private funds' incentives and investment flexibility help explain their performance advantage over mutual funds, but the performance record of unconstrained mutual funds is less clearly distinguished from that of other mutual funds.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Unconstrained Mutual Funds and Retail Investor Protection (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811729
scope_conditions: comparison of unconstrained mutual funds with private funds and conventional mutual funds

claims.claim: Existing evidence about risk-shifting by the average derivative-using mutual fund is less relevant to unconstrained mutual funds, because their derivative use is closer to that of a typical private fund.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Unconstrained Mutual Funds and Retail Investor Protection (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811729
scope_conditions: unconstrained mutual funds whose derivative use resembles private fund practice

claims.claim: Reliance on prospectuses and other disclosures by an unconstrained mutual fund that in all material respects complies with the Company Act may be insufficient to protect retail investors.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Unconstrained Mutual Funds and Retail Investor Protection (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811729
scope_conditions: unconstrained mutual funds in full compliance with the Company Act
retail investors relying on prospectus disclosure

claims.claim: It is questionable whether retail investors typically have the experience or training to fully appreciate the risks disclosed in unconstrained mutual fund prospectuses.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Unconstrained Mutual Funds and Retail Investor Protection (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811729
scope_conditions: average retail investors reading unconstrained fund prospectuses

claims.claim: The broad investment authority of unconstrained mutual fund managers exposes retail investors to fluid trading and investing patterns that the average retail investor is unlikely to sufficiently appreciate, regardless of the nature and quantum of disclosure, so additional disclosure cannot close the gap.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Unconstrained Mutual Funds and Retail Investor Protection (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811729
scope_conditions: retail investors in funds whose managers hold broad go anywhere authority

claims.claim: Because an unconstrained mutual fund's performance is typically not assessed against any established benchmark, the retail investor must evaluate the fund without the contextual information routinely available for mutual funds pursuing more traditional credit strategies.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Unconstrained Mutual Funds and Retail Investor Protection (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811729
scope_conditions: unconstrained funds that decline to adopt a benchmark

claims.claim: Retail investors may be led to believe that unconstrained mutual funds are safe relative to other fixed income mutual funds precisely because they are marketed, offered, and regulated as mutual funds, a risk that is unique to retail investors in these funds.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Unconstrained Mutual Funds and Retail Investor Protection (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811729
scope_conditions: retail investors purchasing unconstrained funds through mutual fund channels

claims.claim: A retail investor's experience investing in traditional mutual funds is likely to be a poor indicator of whether that investor will understand the risks of investing in an unconstrained mutual fund.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Unconstrained Mutual Funds and Retail Investor Protection (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811729
scope_conditions: retail investors extrapolating from prior traditional mutual fund experience

claims.claim: The proliferation of unconstrained mutual funds has contributed to the confluence of mutual and private funds and weakened the traditional public/private distinction in federal securities regulation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Unconstrained Mutual Funds and Retail Investor Protection (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811729
scope_conditions: United States federal securities regulation of pooled investment vehicles

claims.claim: The Company Act's retail investor protection policies do not take sufficiently into account the investment strategy and risk attributes that unconstrained mutual funds share with private funds.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Unconstrained Mutual Funds and Retail Investor Protection (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811729
scope_conditions: Investment Company Act protections as applied to unconstrained mutual funds

claims.claim: Given the risks to retail investors of investing in complex unconstrained mutual funds and the SEC's own concern about the retailization of private funds, it is unclear why the SEC has not acted to enhance protections for retail purchasers of unconstrained mutual fund shares.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Unconstrained Mutual Funds and Retail Investor Protection (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811729
scope_conditions: SEC regulatory posture as of 2016

claims.claim: The SEC should re-evaluate its reliance on the Company Act's disclosure regime in its current form as the best means of protecting retail investors from the risks of investing in unconstrained mutual funds.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Unconstrained Mutual Funds and Retail Investor Protection (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811729
scope_conditions: SEC policy toward unconstrained mutual funds

claims.claim: The SEC continues to rely on disclosure as the means of mitigating investor risk from unconstrained and other mutual funds irrespective of the complexity of those funds' portfolios and strategies.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Unconstrained Mutual Funds and Retail Investor Protection (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811729
scope_conditions: SEC disclosure policy for mutual funds as of 2016

claims.claim: The absence of any current requirement to present unconstrained portfolio risks in detail raises the question whether unconstrained mutual fund prospectuses provide the adequate, accurate, and explicit information required by Section 1(b)(1) of the Company Act.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Unconstrained Mutual Funds and Retail Investor Protection (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2811729
scope_conditions: unconstrained mutual fund prospectuses under existing disclosure requirements

claims.claim: Ex post trial and error rulemaking built on stable and presumptively optimal rules produces suboptimal regulatory outcomes that are no longer sustainable once disruptive innovation grows exponentially.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, Venture Capital as Dynamic Regulation of Disruptive Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2740477
scope_conditions: environment of exponential disruptive innovation
existing regulatory framework of stable rules

claims.claim: Under exponential disruptive innovation the information rulemakers need arrives too late for trial and error rulemaking to be effective, regulatory issues grow more complex, and unknown future contingencies in the rulemaking process increase substantially.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, Venture Capital as Dynamic Regulation of Disruptive Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2740477
scope_conditions: exponential rates of disruptive innovation

claims.claim: Exponential disruptive innovation has the potential to overwhelm the existing regulatory process outright, not merely to strain it.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, Venture Capital as Dynamic Regulation of Disruptive Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2740477

claims.claim: Dynamic regulation is defined as the study of regulatory phenomena in relation to both preceding and succeeding events, using institution specific and decentralized information to generate feedback effects that support anticipatory rulemaking.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, Venture Capital as Dynamic Regulation of Disruptive Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2740477

claims.claim: Venture capital can function as a dynamic regulatory supplement for disruptive innovation because venture capitalists' financial allocations to innovative projects generate feedback that regulators can use.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, Venture Capital as Dynamic Regulation of Disruptive Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2740477

claims.claim: The empirical base for the argument is a PitchBook dataset covering 77,508 completed United States venture capital deals involving 37,298 companies across all venture capital stages from 2005 to 2015.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, Venture Capital as Dynamic Regulation of Disruptive Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2740477
scope_conditions: United States headquartered companies
completed deals, all venture capital stages, 2005 to 2015

claims.claim: Artificial intelligence cannot be held personally liable for damage it causes because national and international law do not currently recognize it as a subject of law, so compensation must be forced through existing provisions never designed for it.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, Venture Capital as Dynamic Regulation of Disruptive Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2740477
scope_conditions: current state of national and international law
damage caused by autonomous AI

claims.claim: Disruptive innovative technology frequently does not fit the legal categories created by recalcitrant regulatory structures, so the classification problem itself is a source of regulatory failure.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, Venture Capital as Dynamic Regulation of Disruptive Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2740477

claims.claim: When disruptive firms do not comply with existing rules or write their own exemptions because no appropriate rules exist, consumer protection and public safety goals are undermined and incumbent firms still bound by the rules suffer severe competitive disadvantages.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, Venture Capital as Dynamic Regulation of Disruptive Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2740477
scope_conditions: disruptive products or services that fall outside or evade the existing regulatory framework

claims.claim: Incumbent firms facing the competitive disadvantage created by disruptive entrants respond by using the existing regulatory process itself to build obstacles to competition, which converts rulemaking into an instrument of incumbent protection.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, Venture Capital as Dynamic Regulation of Disruptive Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2740477
scope_conditions: incumbents perceive a threat from disruptive firms
incumbents remain subject to rules the entrants avoid

claims.claim: The rising complexity of innovation driven regulatory issues confuses political and policy makers about rapidly emerging disruptive change, which makes a coherent political and policy solution to those challenges less likely.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, Venture Capital as Dynamic Regulation of Disruptive Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2740477
scope_conditions: rapidly emerging and complex disruptive change

claims.claim: Rulemakers' inability to address the regulatory issues raised by disruptive innovation will generate high levels of legal uncertainty and inconsistency, and that uncertainty inhibits innovation during technological transition periods.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, Venture Capital as Dynamic Regulation of Disruptive Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2740477
scope_conditions: technological transition periods

claims.claim: Technological transition will be a permanent state in the age of disruptive innovation, so the uncertainty and inconsistency caused by rulemakers' inability to react in time is a standing condition rather than a transitional cost.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, Venture Capital as Dynamic Regulation of Disruptive Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2740477

claims.claim: The current regulatory framework contains no mechanism that succinctly and anticipatorily informs rulemakers of beneficial innovative ideas, which is the specific informational gap the article proposes to fill.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, Venture Capital as Dynamic Regulation of Disruptive Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2740477
scope_conditions: notice and comment rulemaking under the existing framework

claims.claim: The existing rulemaking process prohibits ex parte communications and insufficiently integrates brainstorming and ideas across industries, and therefore may actually undermine innovation rather than merely lag behind it.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, Venture Capital as Dynamic Regulation of Disruptive Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2740477
scope_conditions: formal notice and comment rulemaking

claims.claim: Ex post trial and error rulemaking requires as a precondition that information about optimized rule requirements becomes available, and in an age of exponential innovation that information may never materialize or may arrive too late for the method to work.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, Venture Capital as Dynamic Regulation of Disruptive Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2740477
scope_conditions: exponential rates of innovation

claims.claim: The existing regulatory infrastructure, including Congress, agencies, self regulatory bodies, and the regulation literature itself, relies almost exclusively on stable and presumptively optimal rules.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, Venture Capital as Dynamic Regulation of Disruptive Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2740477

claims.claim: If rulemakers cannot adequately protect their constituents through stable and presumptively optimal rules, then regulatory supplements that facilitate anticipatory rulemaking are justified.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, Venture Capital as Dynamic Regulation of Disruptive Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2740477
scope_conditions: exponential growth of technology and innovation
rulemakers unable to protect constituents with stable rules

claims.claim: Regulatory timing under disruptive innovation is a two sided risk: regulate too early and innovation is inhibited, withhold regulation too long and consumers and markets are harmed once regulatory inertia has formed around the disruptive product or service.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, Venture Capital as Dynamic Regulation of Disruptive Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2740477
scope_conditions: regulation of a disruptive product or service

claims.claim: Formal rulemaking is simply too time consuming for disruptive innovation: the speed of product innovation lets a new product reach the market while a rulemaking that takes months or years is still processing the previous product launch.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, Venture Capital as Dynamic Regulation of Disruptive Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2740477
scope_conditions: formal rulemaking in the existing regulatory infrastructure
high speed of product innovation

claims.claim: New regulations aimed at an innovative product can be obsolete before they are finalized.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, Venture Capital as Dynamic Regulation of Disruptive Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2740477
scope_conditions: formal rulemaking timelines of months to years

claims.claim: Because it lacks anticipatory rulemaking capability, the existing regulatory system addresses issues only ex post, and only once they have materialized and burdened core constituents enough to generate political pressure on lawmakers.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, Venture Capital as Dynamic Regulation of Disruptive Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2740477
scope_conditions: issues must materialize and burden core constituents before action

claims.claim: Evidence shows that the suboptimal ex post timing of rulemaking regularly forces expedited rulemaking, and expedited rulemaking itself produces suboptimal regulatory outcomes.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, Venture Capital as Dynamic Regulation of Disruptive Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2740477

claims.claim: Accepting suboptimal rules temporarily buys rule certainty and predictability but guarantees a later cycle of revision, amendment, and repeal, so rulemakers trade short term certainty for a costly correction process.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, Venture Capital as Dynamic Regulation of Disruptive Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2740477
scope_conditions: rulemakers knowingly accept suboptimalities tied to unknown future contingencies

claims.claim: The current process of rule revisions, amendments, and repeals used to fix the inevitable shortcomings of stable rules is costly, time consuming, and in the authors' estimation cannot keep track of future innovations and the regulatory needs they create.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, Venture Capital as Dynamic Regulation of Disruptive Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2740477

claims.claim: Exponential innovation will intensify the frequency of the regulatory sine curve, because rulemakers are still trying to comprehend the regulatory demands of the last wave of innovation while the next wave is already in full force.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, Venture Capital as Dynamic Regulation of Disruptive Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2740477
scope_conditions: exponential rates of innovation

claims.claim: The collective action problem of rulemaking, the problems of trial and error rulemaking, and regulatory cycles all derive largely from the nature of stable and presumptively optimal rules rather than from independent causes.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, Venture Capital as Dynamic Regulation of Disruptive Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2740477

claims.claim: Adaptive rulemaking reduces the collective action problem because with fewer stable rules, latent majority groups and dominant minority groups have fewer opportunities to influence a continuously and timely adapting rulemaking process.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, Venture Capital as Dynamic Regulation of Disruptive Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2740477
scope_conditions: rulemaking uses institution specific, decentralized, and timely information
fewer stable rules

claims.claim: Dynamic regulatory tools let rulemakers adapt to regulatory contingencies as they arise, because feedback effects deliver relevant, timely, decentralized, and institution specific information ex ante.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, Venture Capital as Dynamic Regulation of Disruptive Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2740477
scope_conditions: feedback processes are in place within the regulatory framework

claims.claim: Regulation is mostly reactive and follows business cycles rather than preempting crises, because of the collective action problem of regulation, path dependencies, and political inertia, so rules arrive when governance improvements are least available.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, Venture Capital as Dynamic Regulation of Disruptive Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2740477

claims.claim: Private rulemakers hold a comparative advantage over public rulemakers because, unlike their public counterparts, they can produce the comparable, decentralized, and institution specific information that rulemaking requires.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, Venture Capital as Dynamic Regulation of Disruptive Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2740477

claims.claim: The existing framework for optimal rules is self reinforcing: it perpetuates rulemaking processes that produce more optimal rules requiring costly revision, updating, and revocation, so suboptimal rules and suboptimal processes reproduce each other.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, Venture Capital as Dynamic Regulation of Disruptive Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2740477

claims.claim: Dynamic regulatory supplements do not violate the procedural protections mandated by the Administrative Procedure Act, because the full lawmaking process still applies and dynamic regulation only supplements and optimizes the existing rulemaking process.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, Venture Capital as Dynamic Regulation of Disruptive Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2740477
scope_conditions: United States administrative law under the APA

claims.claim: The data analysis shows that venture capitalists' finance allocation, and the implicit assessment of innovative products and businesses it embodies, generates highly relevant institution specific and industry specific decentralized information on innovation trends.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, Venture Capital as Dynamic Regulation of Disruptive Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2740477
scope_conditions: United States venture capital data 2005 to 2015

claims.claim: Data on venture capital investments lets regulators see where innovation trends are forming and what risks they entail before the disruptive innovation materializes, which is the specific remedy for regulation's reactive timing.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, Venture Capital as Dynamic Regulation of Disruptive Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2740477
scope_conditions: regulators have access to and integrate venture capital investment data

claims.claim: Industry specific venture capital investment data allows regulators to anticipate regulatory needs in the industries carrying the highest levels of disruptive innovation, and the level of disruptive innovation can be quantified by the venture capital dollars flowing into those industries.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, Venture Capital as Dynamic Regulation of Disruptive Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2740477
scope_conditions: industry level venture capital investment data is available

claims.claim: By identifying possible contingencies and necessary rule revisions from venture capital investment data ex ante, before disruptive innovation creates problems, regulators could anticipate regulatory needs instead of reacting to them.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, Venture Capital as Dynamic Regulation of Disruptive Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2740477
scope_conditions: regulators integrate venture capital data into rulemaking processes or legislative proposals

claims.claim: The authors concede a limitation of their own proposal: the innovation potential identified by venture capital finance allocation may not always be shared by the market at large.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, Venture Capital as Dynamic Regulation of Disruptive Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2740477
scope_conditions: technology companies increasingly staying private
market undervaluation of formerly venture capital financed companies

claims.claim: Venture capital has outrun regulation and regulation is now too slow to react, and that lag itself damages the process.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, Venture Capital as Dynamic Regulation of Disruptive Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2740477

claims.claim: The notice and comment procedures of the SEC are too slow, and the SEC's outdated micromanagement of markets is itself slowing down venture capital.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P.M. Vermeulen, Venture Capital as Dynamic Regulation of Disruptive Innovation (2016). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2740477
scope_conditions: United States securities regulation

claims.claim: Private fund advisers' increasing use of blockchain technology, artificial intelligence, and big data is a distinct source of downward pressure on the traditional 2/20 fee structure that commentators have not examined.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Applications and Fee Structure Developments in Private Investment Funds (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2959730
scope_conditions: private investment fund industry
period of roughly 2007 to 2017

claims.claim: The majority of private fund advisers that deploy blockchain technology, artificial intelligence, and big data in their operations or strategy charge their investors lower fees, even though not all blockchain enabled funds charge per transaction fees.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Applications and Fee Structure Developments in Private Investment Funds (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2959730
scope_conditions: advisers using the technologies in operations or strategy

claims.claim: Using a hand coded dataset of 98 private investment fund advisers that use blockchain technology in their strategy or internal operations, the article shows that advisers using the new technology are able to charge overall lower fees.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Applications and Fee Structure Developments in Private Investment Funds (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2959730
scope_conditions: sample of 98 blockchain using private fund advisers
hand coded by the author and two research assistants

claims.claim: As the use of blockchain technology grows in the private investment fund industry, pressure on the traditional fee structure is likely to continue to grow, even though the proportion of fund strategies applying such technologies remains small.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Applications and Fee Structure Developments in Private Investment Funds (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2959730
scope_conditions: current adoption of modern technologies is still a small proportion of fund strategies

claims.claim: The historical private fund management fee of 2% has shifted in recent years to roughly 1.0% for new managers and 1.5 to 1.8% for established managers with an adequate track record.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Applications and Fee Structure Developments in Private Investment Funds (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2959730
scope_conditions: private equity and hedge fund managers
established managers require an adequate track record

claims.claim: First time managers are disproportionately affected by the new fee environment: unlike in the recent past they are now often forced to share the business budget, such as rent and employee salaries, in order to justify a 1.5% management fee.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Applications and Fee Structure Developments in Private Investment Funds (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2959730
scope_conditions: first time or new fund managers
fund formation and seed investment negotiations

claims.claim: New managers increasingly face contested track records, meaning the new firm cannot get a consensus from the manager's old employer about the manager's track record with that employer.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Applications and Fee Structure Developments in Private Investment Funds (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2959730
scope_conditions: first time managers spinning out of a prior employer

claims.claim: Early limited partnership investors increasingly use their leverage to negotiate tough fee terms with first time managers.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Applications and Fee Structure Developments in Private Investment Funds (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2959730
scope_conditions: first time managers raising an initial fund

claims.claim: Market evidence of pressure on the fee structure includes investor withdrawals of $70.1 billion from the private investment fund industry in 2016 and 1,057 fund closures in 2016, exceeding the 1,023 liquidations in 2009 and approaching the record 1,471 closures in 2008.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Applications and Fee Structure Developments in Private Investment Funds (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2959730
scope_conditions: calendar year 2016 compared with 2008 and 2009

claims.claim: Market oversaturation increases pressure on private investment fund managers' performance and produces compromise fee arrangements such as charging fees on invested capital only.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Applications and Fee Structure Developments in Private Investment Funds (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2959730
scope_conditions: oversaturated and highly competitive fundraising market

claims.claim: In the Buffett and Seides wager on net of fee returns, the passive S&P 500 index position produced a 7.1% compounded annual return after nine years against 2.2% for the five hedge funds of funds, evidence that industry performance does not justify the 2/20 fee structure.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Applications and Fee Structure Developments in Private Investment Funds (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2959730
scope_conditions: nine years into the ten year 2008 to 2017 wager
returns measured net of fees

claims.claim: Private investment fund management fees deviate from the market rate of 1.5% to 2% of the fund's capital commitments because affiliates and other employees of the investment manager who invest in the fund are not charged management fees.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Applications and Fee Structure Developments in Private Investment Funds (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2959730
scope_conditions: funds with affiliate or employee investors

claims.claim: The new fee structure also results from fund managers foregoing market rate management fees, larger investors requiring reduced management fees as a condition of investing, and side-by-side co-investment vehicles charging less than 2% management fees.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Applications and Fee Structure Developments in Private Investment Funds (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2959730
scope_conditions: funds using side by side or co investment vehicles
funds seeking large anchor investors

claims.claim: Pressure on the incentive fee side operates through blackened carried interest, under which a manager cannot collect carry until all limited partners have had their capital returned within the lifetime of the private equity model.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Applications and Fee Structure Developments in Private Investment Funds (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2959730
scope_conditions: private equity funds and, similarly, hedge funds
carry measured over the lifetime of the fund model

claims.claim: Shifting inflation indexed hurdle rates from quarterly to monthly calculation lowers manager compensation: for managers with pension plan limited partners this often means receiving 5% plus inflation instead of an 8% hurdle rate.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Applications and Fee Structure Developments in Private Investment Funds (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2959730
scope_conditions: managers with pension plan limited partners
inflation indexed hurdle rates

claims.claim: The author stipulates that a blockchain is a shared digital ledger or database that maintains a continuously growing list of transactions among participating parties regarding digital assets, described as blocks.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Applications and Fee Structure Developments in Private Investment Funds (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2959730
scope_conditions: used as the operative definition for the remainder of the article

claims.claim: Blockchain removes fraudulent transactions primarily through completely decentralized network connectivity via the Internet, rather than through digital signatures alone, which only establish the identity and authenticity of the parties.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Applications and Fee Structure Developments in Private Investment Funds (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2959730
scope_conditions: decentralized peer to peer networks with Internet connectivity

claims.claim: The decentralized, fully distributed nature of the blockchain makes it practically impossible to reverse, alter, or erase information recorded in it.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Applications and Fee Structure Developments in Private Investment Funds (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2959730
scope_conditions: fully distributed networks where multiple copies are held by all participants

claims.claim: Blockchain's distributed consensus model, in which network nodes verify and validate chain transactions before execution, makes it extremely rare for a fraudulent transaction to be recorded in the blockchain.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Applications and Fee Structure Developments in Private Investment Funds (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2959730
scope_conditions: distributed consensus models with node verification prior to execution

claims.claim: Cryptographic hashing makes blockchain manipulation immediately detectable because the hash incorporates all previous transactions, so that even a single digit change produces a different hash value.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Applications and Fee Structure Developments in Private Investment Funds (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2959730
scope_conditions: chained hashing that incorporates all prior transactions

claims.claim: Complex smart contract arrangements involving several parties require a verifiable and unhackable system, which blockchain technology supplies.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Applications and Fee Structure Developments in Private Investment Funds (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2959730
scope_conditions: multi party smart contract arrangements

claims.claim: Smart contracting on the blockchain often makes legal contracting unnecessary because smart contracts emulate the logic of legal contract clauses.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Applications and Fee Structure Developments in Private Investment Funds (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2959730
scope_conditions: contract terms whose logic can be expressed in computer code

claims.claim: The current legal and administrative processes that support private equity are time consuming, expensive, lack transparency, and involve lengthy, duplicative, and fragmented investment and administrative processes.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Applications and Fee Structure Developments in Private Investment Funds (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2959730
scope_conditions: private equity deal administration prior to blockchain adoption

claims.claim: The rise of blockchain applications in private investment funds can exacerbate the industry's already changing fee structure.

claims.claim: Enforcement against the blockchain is unlikely to work because it is maintained and owned by a distributed group of anonymous users worldwide who would not likely recognize or comply with any legal authority.

claims.claim: As of publication, no American or European court had recognized blockchain technology or scrutinized its applications, leaving it unclear how courts will treat the technology.

claims.claim: Smart contracting often makes legal contracting unnecessary, because smart contracts frequently emulate the logic of legal contract clauses.

claims.claim: Private investment funds that are first movers in implementing blockchain infrastructure in finance directly contribute to disintermediation and accelerate the evolution of blockchain infrastructure in finance.

claims.claim: Larger fund managers will adopt blockchain only once the long term benefits exceed implementation cost, and because that cost is much larger for them than for the smaller managers now experimenting, the threshold is higher for larger managers.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Blockchain Innovation in Private Investment Funds - A Comparative Analysis of the United States and (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3002908

claims.claim: The market for private investment funds that invest in and utilize blockchain technology is close to equally divided between the United States and the European Union, with Russia and China playing significant roles.

scope_conditions: based on the article's hand coded dataset of 120 private investment fund advisers using blockchain technology

claims.claim: The size distribution of blockchain using funds differs sharply across regions: in the United States most such funds hold between one and fifty million dollars in AUM, while in Europe funds with more than two hundred million dollars in AUM are the majority.

claims.claim: The authors interpret the AUM difference as suggesting that larger European advisers are more willing to fund blockchain infrastructure, while in the United States legacy systems used by larger advisers create a barrier to entry.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Blockchain Innovation in Private Investment Funds - A Comparative Analysis of the United States and (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3002908
scope_conditions: an interpretation of the AUM distribution, not a tested result

claims.claim: The authors undercut their own legacy systems explanation: legacy systems in the EU should theoretically create the same barriers, and there is no reason to believe US legacy systems are more of an obstacle than European ones.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Blockchain Innovation in Private Investment Funds - A Comparative Analysis of the United States and (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3002908

claims.claim: A competing explanation for the transatlantic size gap is compositional: American blockchain funds are mostly newly created ad hoc vehicles focused exclusively on blockchain, while European ones are more established and older financial institutions.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Blockchain Innovation in Private Investment Funds - A Comparative Analysis of the United States and (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3002908

claims.claim: Larger European private fund advisers implement more conservative investment strategies, using blockchain technology predominantly to invest in and secure crypto assets.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Blockchain Innovation in Private Investment Funds - A Comparative Analysis of the United States and (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3002908

claims.claim: Because American funds lean on smart contracting, they have a better opportunity to launch disruptive blockchain implementations, but they may also experience a higher rate of failure from greater exposure to technological risk.

scope_conditions: conditional on American funds continuing to emphasize smart contracting over conservative crypto asset strategies

claims.claim: Raw country level counts overstate American leadership: normalizing by population shows roughly 7.5 million people per blockchain fund in the United States against roughly 2.8 million in the United Kingdom, so the distribution across countries is more even than the map suggests.

claims.claim: The absence of Luxembourg funds from the dataset is most likely an artifact of unavailable public information rather than evidence that Luxembourg funds do not invest in blockchain.

scope_conditions: applies to the article's own dataset construction from public and contacted sources

claims.claim: Fund type composition diverges across regions: in the United States hedge funds dominate the blockchain using sample, while in Europe venture capital funds clearly predominate.

claims.claim: Whether private investment funds succeed in disintermediating banks through blockchain implementation depends on their ability to find scale opportunities.

claims.claim: The Northern Trust and IBM blockchain program removes the need for parties to reconcile multiple copies of deal documents by letting every party to a private equity deal look at a single compiled version of the transaction.

claims.claim: The Numerai model reduces overhead costs because there is no cost of human capital, and it eliminates barriers to entry because participating users need neither capital nor any special finance or data knowledge.

scope_conditions: applies to the Numerai crowdsourced data science model running on the Ethereum blockchain

claims.claim: Initial coin offerings have overtaken venture capital as a funding channel for blockchain start ups, raising 331 million dollars in twelve months, and may become an alternative funding method for traditional companies as well.

scope_conditions: twelve month window reported as of mid 2017

claims.claim: American fund advisers use the smart contracting features of blockchain more frequently than European advisers, in order to build more advanced and innovative crypto businesses and business structures.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Blockchain Innovation in Private Investment Funds - A Comparative Analysis of the United States and (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3002908
scope_conditions: based on the nine term cluster coding of fund marketing language, n equals 74 strategies

claims.claim: Blockchain technology delivers anonymous and secure transactional guarantees through democratized trust and disintermediation, and its anti-discrimination features allow minorities and disenfranchised communities to benefit from the technology.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Technology and Race in Corporate America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3071378
scope_conditions: public, permissionless blockchain networks

claims.claim: In the Fortune 1000 sample, minorities hold about 15 percent of employee positions but only 6 percent of management positions and 3 percent of executive level management positions, so representation falls as seniority rises.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Technology and Race in Corporate America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3071378
scope_conditions: Fortune 1000 sample dataset cited in the text

claims.claim: Because the public blockchain is public and immutable, the technology increases transparency while significantly reducing transaction costs, and intermediaries including lawyers are replaced by code, connectivity, crowd, and collaboration.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Technology and Race in Corporate America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3071378
scope_conditions: public blockchains rather than private ones

claims.claim: Because network nodes verify and validate chain transactions before execution under a distributed consensus model, recording a fraudulent transaction on the blockchain is extremely rare.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Technology and Race in Corporate America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3071378
scope_conditions: distributed consensus with node verification before execution

claims.claim: Because each new block's hash value is generated from all previous transactions, the smallest change to the blockchain produces a different hash value, which makes any form of manipulation immediately detectable.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Technology and Race in Corporate America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3071378
scope_conditions: chained cryptographic hashing of prior transactions

claims.claim: Smart contracting often makes legal contracting unnecessary because smart contracts emulate the logic of legal contract clauses.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Technology and Race in Corporate America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3071378
scope_conditions: transactions whose logic can be expressed in code

claims.claim: Ledger-keeping legal services such as notary and registry services, legal motions practice in court, and legal title companies are likely to be among the first services to disappear.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Technology and Race in Corporate America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3071378
scope_conditions: services whose core function is keeping a legal ledger

claims.claim: The lack of maturity of blockchain technology has slowed its integration into the corporate world, and the absence of a legal framework leaves the whole industry operating in a grey area of the law, which introduces uncertainty and a new level of volatility.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Technology and Race in Corporate America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3071378
scope_conditions: before Congress adopts a policy on the treatment of blockchain services

claims.claim: Even where a smart contract reflects the underlying bargain between the parties, lawyers may argue that smart contracts are void and unenforceable under the law.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Technology and Race in Corporate America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3071378
scope_conditions: existing contract law doctrine applied to code-based agreements

claims.claim: Although blockchain technology itself offers genuine data and privacy protection, storing blockchain data across a global network of nodes often will not comply with specific consumer protection rules, directives, and guidelines.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Technology and Race in Corporate America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3071378
scope_conditions: global node distribution under jurisdiction-specific consumer protection regimes

claims.claim: Judging by the legal issues that arose around sharing platforms, blockchain-enabled sharing services will likely not be accepted quickly or without resistance from incumbents challenged by new ways of delivering a service or product.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Technology and Race in Corporate America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3071378
scope_conditions: services that displace incumbent delivery models

claims.claim: The DAO failed because its code had not yet been perfected: hackers took a third of the DAO tokens and transferred them to another account, and that hack together with other technological limitations led to the demise of the DAO.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Technology and Race in Corporate America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3071378
scope_conditions: The DAO, launched May 2016 on Ethereum

claims.claim: Because of societal perceptions of minorities, minority groups face an uphill battle navigating the political environment of corporate America, which in turn significantly affects their positioning and success there.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Technology and Race in Corporate America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3071378
scope_conditions: corporate environments where promotion depends on political navigation

claims.claim: Minorities can overcome the promotion gap in corporate America if their superiors see them as value enhancers, and promoted minorities tend to share characteristics such as risk-taking, overconfidence, team play, and a perceived capacity to manage other non-whites.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Technology and Race in Corporate America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3071378
scope_conditions: where superiors perceive the minority employee as value enhancing

claims.claim: Promotion to high level executive positions turns on subjectively assessed skillsets such as leadership, personality, judgment, attitude and initiative, and these facially objective criteria can be distorted with relative ease.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Technology and Race in Corporate America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3071378
scope_conditions: high level executive promotions assessed on subjective criteria

claims.claim: Promoted minorities do not necessarily use their new position to promote other minorities; in the existing American corporate structure they often have incentives to race to the top while lifting the ladder behind them.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Technology and Race in Corporate America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3071378
scope_conditions: existing individualistic and aggressive American corporate culture

claims.claim: Top management retains support only so long as others in the corporate structure keep them in power, which gives incumbents an incentive to keep upper management composition unchanged.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Technology and Race in Corporate America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3071378
scope_conditions: hierarchical corporate structures where incumbency depends on internal support

claims.claim: Diversity training, diversity performance evaluations, and grievance procedures did not change workforce composition.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Technology and Race in Corporate America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3071378
scope_conditions: corporate diversity programs studied in the cited research

claims.claim: Diversity programs fail when managers are defined as the source of the problem and succeed when they engage managers in finding solutions, as with task forces and targeted recruiting.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Technology and Race in Corporate America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3071378
scope_conditions: corporate diversity programs studied in the cited research

claims.claim: Companies should focus more on mentoring programs and less on formal evaluations, because mentorship with a superior manager helped minorities succeed.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Technology and Race in Corporate America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3071378
scope_conditions: corporate diversity and advancement programs

claims.claim: As minority attainment of bachelors and graduate degrees rises and labor markets tighten, a business imperative for hiring minorities will emerge because firms that expand their labor pool gain an advantage over firms with limited access to diverse workers.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Technology and Race in Corporate America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3071378
scope_conditions: continued growth in minority degree attainment
overall tightening of labor markets

claims.claim: The clone syndrome, meaning companies' desire to hire people similar to the existing workforce, causes minority underrepresentation and makes it difficult for minorities and women to break into jobs predominantly held by white men.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Technology and Race in Corporate America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3071378
scope_conditions: hiring into roles predominantly held by white men

claims.claim: A corporation that lacks diversity and allows group thinking will struggle to identify issues because it needs a fresh perspective, which harms the corporation long term by reducing its ability to identify its own strengths and weaknesses.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Technology and Race in Corporate America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3071378
scope_conditions: boards and corporations without diverse membership

claims.claim: The discriminatory effect of existing corporate hierarchies may originate in the education system, because children in struggling school systems lack access to the resources available in better functioning districts.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Technology and Race in Corporate America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3071378
scope_conditions: unequal resourcing across school districts

claims.claim: By some estimates the lack of inclusion of minorities in corporate America costs the U.S. economy one trillion dollars per year once the pay gap between whites and minorities is taken into account.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Technology and Race in Corporate America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3071378
scope_conditions: estimates accounting for the white-minority pay gap

claims.claim: Allowing minorities onto the board increases creativity through the different perspectives they represent, which acts as a defense against groupthink.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Technology and Race in Corporate America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3071378
scope_conditions: corporate boards
