claims.claim: Because directors must act in good faith and in the best interests of the corporation, and a diverse board helps protect against group thinking, fiduciary obligations supply a business reason for board diversity.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Technology and Race in Corporate America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3071378
scope_conditions: boards subject to fiduciary duties of care and good faith

claims.claim: Minority board members are expected to bring in minority clientele, so where the corporation's product is not used by minorities the minority director is perceived as a failure, which stigmatizes minority board members and damages their careers.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Technology and Race in Corporate America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3071378
scope_conditions: corporations whose products are not used by minority consumers

claims.claim: Because a small group of minorities serves on a large number of boards, corporations in fact lose the diversity of viewpoints they were seeking when appointing a minority board member.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Technology and Race in Corporate America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3071378
scope_conditions: overextended minority directors sitting on many boards

claims.claim: By establishing a network of transacting parties that trust each other despite anonymity, blockchain technology enables unbiased transactions and eliminates prejudices against minorities.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Technology and Race in Corporate America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3071378
scope_conditions: anonymous or pseudonymous transacting parties on a blockchain network

claims.claim: Because transacting parties judge transaction parameters and products on quality perceptions rather than on less rational and biased factors, quality becomes the true deciding factor in the marketplace, which eliminates prejudices.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Technology and Race in Corporate America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3071378
scope_conditions: blockchain-enabled marketplaces where counterparty identity is not salient

claims.claim: Eliminating bias-driven inefficiencies removes the associated diseconomies of scale and waste, estimated at around one trillion dollars annually in the existing centralized business infrastructure.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Technology and Race in Corporate America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3071378
scope_conditions: existing centralized business infrastructure

claims.claim: People who work for a DAO are free from existing corporate hierarchies and their possible discriminatory effects because they are not subject to a supervisor, boss, or CEO.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Technology and Race in Corporate America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3071378
scope_conditions: DAO structures with no directors, managers, or employees

claims.claim: Disenfranchised communities will increasingly be able to afford the buy-in to a DAO, and increasing access to DAOs eradicates a possible income based or wealth based bias, since participation requires purchasing a coin or token.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Technology and Race in Corporate America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3071378
scope_conditions: DAO membership conditioned on acquiring a token

claims.claim: Because the total supply of DAO tokens is pre-determined in code, dilution by central administrators such as government officials or self-interested or biased executives is impossible.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Technology and Race in Corporate America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3071378
scope_conditions: DAOs with a fixed token supply fixed in open source code

claims.claim: In a DAO, disenfranchised community members cannot be judged by race or cultural biases because performance in an anonymized proposal voting scheme is the only basis for assessment and payment.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Technology and Race in Corporate America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3071378
scope_conditions: anonymized proposal voting and token-based remuneration

claims.claim: Reputational penalties for non-performance in a DAO are entirely free from racial implications because token holders are unlikely to even know each other.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Technology and Race in Corporate America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3071378
scope_conditions: pseudonymous token holder communities

claims.claim: Unlike traditional hierarchical organizations where face-time and unproductive meetings are the norm, the self-governing DAO token optimizer avoids corporate hierarchy inefficiencies and the bad outcomes that come from top-down direction.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Technology and Race in Corporate America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3071378
scope_conditions: self-governing DAO structures without supervisors

claims.claim: The value to effort focus of DAO work flows makes racial and cultural biases much less pronounced and protects disenfranchised communities.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Technology and Race in Corporate America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3071378
scope_conditions: DAO work flows organized around value contribution

claims.claim: Equality is a natural byproduct of the blockchain-driven evolution of the crypto economy, because the trust enhancing consensus model, smart contracting in anonymous networks, and DAOs together allow a more equal society to evolve.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Blockchain Technology and Race in Corporate America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3071378
scope_conditions: continued evolution of the crypto economy

claims.claim: The existing legal infrastructure cannot address the legal challenges presented by crypto transaction disputes, because it is impossible to consistently identify the parties to a dispute arising from crypto transactions on the blockchain.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Craig Calcaterra, Crypto Transaction Dispute Resolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2992962
scope_conditions: public blockchains where parties transact anonymously

claims.claim: The authors stipulate distributed jurisdiction as a regulatory alternative in which conflict resolution for blockchain transactions is supplied by governance solutions inherent in the blockchain technology itself rather than by external legal authorities.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Craig Calcaterra, Crypto Transaction Dispute Resolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2992962

claims.claim: If the jurisdictional means necessary for conflict resolution mechanisms covering Ethereum blockchain based smart contracting are absent, consumers will mistrust the new technology, and that mistrust can undermine the evolution of the blockchain based crypto economy.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Craig Calcaterra, Crypto Transaction Dispute Resolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2992962
scope_conditions: Ethereum blockchain based smart contracting

claims.claim: Personal jurisdiction technically still applies to parties transacting in encrypted distributed smart contracts, but the practicability of enforcement is impossible because physical identifiers are separated from the encrypted distributed contracts.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Craig Calcaterra, Crypto Transaction Dispute Resolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2992962
scope_conditions: parties anonymized through public-key encryption and virtual private networks

claims.claim: Even if every user and supporter of the blockchain and their locations were known, it would still not be possible to exercise jurisdiction in the traditional meaning of the word, because the system operates largely autonomously.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Craig Calcaterra, Crypto Transaction Dispute Resolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2992962
scope_conditions: autonomously run public blockchains

claims.claim: Because the challenges crypto transactions pose to the existing legal and jurisdictional infrastructure are severe, including good governance in crypto transactions requires instituting governance solutions inherent in the blockchain technology itself.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Craig Calcaterra, Crypto Transaction Dispute Resolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2992962

claims.claim: Proof of work mining carries significant externalities: the authors estimate that the total energy cost of running the global network of computers solving proof of work puzzles was around 700 million US dollars per year before publication.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Craig Calcaterra, Crypto Transaction Dispute Resolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2992962
scope_conditions: proof of work consensus, before publication of the article in 2017

claims.claim: Anonymity survives the blockchain's permanent public record because a new private key can be created for each transaction, so although public key addresses are stored eternally, each transaction allows an entirely new cryptographically secured private identity.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Craig Calcaterra, Crypto Transaction Dispute Resolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2992962
scope_conditions: public-key cryptography as implemented in bitcoin and Ethereum

claims.claim: A government cannot control a blockchain by pressuring individuals within its territory; it would need complete control of 51 percent of the anonymous global users before it could change any part of the code.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Craig Calcaterra, Crypto Transaction Dispute Resolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2992962
scope_conditions: decentralized public blockchains

claims.claim: The authors treat the near absence of decided case law on crypto smart contracting disputes as evidence that the existing legal infrastructure is too far removed from crypto dispute resolution, or incapable of adequately addressing the disputes crypto transactions generate.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Craig Calcaterra, Crypto Transaction Dispute Resolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2992962
scope_conditions: US federal and state case law searched before publication in 2017

claims.claim: Uniform Law Commission style registration of virtual currency businesses may give courts more information about registered businesses, but jurisdiction over the parties to a smart contract remains largely elusive because smart contracting is distributed and global.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Craig Calcaterra, Crypto Transaction Dispute Resolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2992962
scope_conditions: the draft Uniform Regulation of Virtual Currency Business Act as released in July 2017

claims.claim: Regulating blockchain through the non anonymous application of the technology creates large inefficiencies that will be bypassed by the more efficient anonymous applications, and it is for those more advanced applications that a system of distributed jurisdiction will be needed.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Craig Calcaterra, Crypto Transaction Dispute Resolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2992962
scope_conditions: uniform application of Bank Secrecy Act and anti money laundering compliance to virtual currency businesses

claims.claim: Proving personal jurisdiction over smart contracting parties by physical presence, domicile or place of business, consent, or minimum contacts becomes impossible, because none of these elements are known of the parties to a smart contract.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Craig Calcaterra, Crypto Transaction Dispute Resolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2992962
scope_conditions: smart contracts where parties are anonymized by public-key encryption and VPNs

claims.claim: Even if a state or the federal government passed a law granting a court authority over blockchain smart contract disputes, it is hard to see how the court could in fact exercise that authority short of limiting access to the internet itself.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Craig Calcaterra, Crypto Transaction Dispute Resolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2992962
scope_conditions: anonymous parties transacting on public blockchains

claims.claim: Not all smart contracts are fully anonymous and untouchable by traditional jurisdictional means, because contracts with a physical performance element, such as peer to peer transportation, do not automatically anonymize the parties.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Craig Calcaterra, Crypto Transaction Dispute Resolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2992962
scope_conditions: consumer smart contracts with a physical performance element

claims.claim: Breach of a smart contract is arguably not even possible, because the contract simply will not execute if a parameter is not fulfilled.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Craig Calcaterra, Crypto Transaction Dispute Resolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2992962
scope_conditions: fully self executing smart contracts on Ethereum

claims.claim: Because smart contracts are coded for computer programming rather than for a human observer, courts may not be able to hypothesize a reasonable human's interpretation of a given smart contract.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Craig Calcaterra, Crypto Transaction Dispute Resolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2992962
scope_conditions: contract interpretation disputes over coded smart contracts

claims.claim: To institute traditional remedies where a smart contract transaction disadvantages one of the parties, courts would have to change the blockchain, and that is computationally and practically impossible.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Craig Calcaterra, Crypto Transaction Dispute Resolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2992962
scope_conditions: transactions already executed and added to an immutable blockchain

claims.claim: Real world court decisions on smart contract disputes, even where attainable, may not carry the same legitimacy and authority for the parties as intra-blockchain dispute resolution mechanisms.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Craig Calcaterra, Crypto Transaction Dispute Resolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2992962

claims.claim: Even if courts were given authority to order changes to smart contract code, a programmer coerced by a court could not override the will of the majority of anonymous international blockchain users to make an effective change.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Craig Calcaterra, Crypto Transaction Dispute Resolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2992962
scope_conditions: decentralized blockchains maintained by an anonymous global user majority

claims.claim: Because courts cannot effectuate resolutions to disputes arising from blockchain based smart contracts, blockchain based resolution mechanisms are the only possible recourse for smart contract disputes.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Craig Calcaterra, Crypto Transaction Dispute Resolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2992962
scope_conditions: fully decentralized and autonomous blockchains

claims.claim: Hybrid approaches and meta structures that connect the existing legal and regulatory infrastructure with blockchain based smart contracting will accelerate rather than slow the bifurcation of the jurisdictional infrastructure into traditional and crypto prongs.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Craig Calcaterra, Crypto Transaction Dispute Resolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2992962
scope_conditions: transition phase of the crypto economy

claims.claim: The legacy infrastructure bridge between fiat and crypto currencies accelerates the growth of the blockchain based economy and infrastructure, but it cannot curtail the anonymous nature of that economy.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Craig Calcaterra, Crypto Transaction Dispute Resolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2992962
scope_conditions: fiat to crypto currency conversion channels

claims.claim: Governing the creation and use of a blockchain may be the only practical way of exercising any form of traditional jurisdiction over blockchain technology.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Craig Calcaterra, Crypto Transaction Dispute Resolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2992962
scope_conditions: blockchains whose creators live in identifiable geographic locations

claims.claim: Coding regulatory conditions into smart contracts lowers regulators' cost of supervision and enforcement while substantially increasing their oversight, because a smart contract cannot execute unless all regulatory conditions and parameters are fully complied with.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Craig Calcaterra, Crypto Transaction Dispute Resolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2992962
scope_conditions: hybrid approach where existing legal rules are coded as smart contract parameters

claims.claim: The benefits of coding existing law into smart contracts are only temporary, because as smart contracting evolves over time fewer smart contracting solutions will have a real world equivalent.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Craig Calcaterra, Crypto Transaction Dispute Resolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2992962
scope_conditions: over the course of smart contracting's evolution

claims.claim: Without strong external pressure from existing regulatory structures and a distributed jurisdiction responsive to that pressure, the anonymity of smart contracting will ultimately undermine the coding of existing legal rules into smart contracts.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Craig Calcaterra, Crypto Transaction Dispute Resolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2992962
scope_conditions: anonymous parties transacting through Ethereum and virtual private networks

claims.claim: The first of the two core requirements the authors set for distributed jurisdiction is that the anonymity of blockchain based smart contracting be maintained as the technology evolves.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Craig Calcaterra, Crypto Transaction Dispute Resolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2992962

claims.claim: The second core requirement of distributed jurisdiction is governance from within the blockchain technology itself, which is what allows the problems inherent in blockchain based smart contracts to be effectively addressed.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Craig Calcaterra, Crypto Transaction Dispute Resolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2992962

claims.claim: Problems with smart contracts are inevitable because of subjectivity in human relationships, bounded rationality of coders and contracting parties, incomplete foresight, incomplete information, and opportunistic behavior.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Craig Calcaterra, Crypto Transaction Dispute Resolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2992962
scope_conditions: commercial smart contracting between human parties

claims.claim: As blockchain use grows, node operation will eventually require special equipment affordable only by large corporations in the existing legal infrastructure, creating the possibility of dangerous centralization and a threat to anonymity.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Craig Calcaterra, Crypto Transaction Dispute Resolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2992962
scope_conditions: blockchains with eternal storage and rapidly growing size

claims.claim: Giving disputants the power to select between notary pools, as OpenBazaar does, is a clear improvement over Aragon's method of completely random selection of judges from the entire group of users posting bonds.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Craig Calcaterra, Crypto Transaction Dispute Resolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2992962
scope_conditions: distributed anonymous trading platforms with arbiter pools

claims.claim: Aragon appears not to post even a summary of its arbiters' reasoning, which may cause the losing party to second guess the legitimacy of the entire Aragon dispute resolution mechanism.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Craig Calcaterra, Crypto Transaction Dispute Resolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2992962
scope_conditions: the Aragon Network dispute resolution design as described in its whitepaper

claims.claim: Without judge expertise in the subject matter of a smart contract dispute, user confidence in effective and fair conflict resolution is undermined, which reduces confidence in crypto transactions as a whole and can undermine the evolution of the crypto economy.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Craig Calcaterra, Crypto Transaction Dispute Resolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2992962
scope_conditions: dispute resolution systems that select judges at random from all users, such as Aragon

claims.claim: The economic incentive for Aragon judges to follow the more popular vote, since judges keep their bond only if they voted with the majority, calls into question whether the mechanism delivers effective, non arbitrary, and fair dispute resolution.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Craig Calcaterra, Crypto Transaction Dispute Resolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2992962
scope_conditions: the Aragon bond and majority reward mechanism, despite anonymous voting

claims.claim: Because of the fees attached to its extra verification layer, the OpenBazaar dispute resolution mechanism creates substantial transaction costs that pure Ethereum based self executing smart contracts avoid.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Craig Calcaterra, Crypto Transaction Dispute Resolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2992962
scope_conditions: Ricardian contracts that attach a notary to every contract

claims.claim: In contrast with OpenBazaar, the authors' proposed open source ecosystem allows dispute resolution only if and when a smart contract has actually resulted in a dispute, which keeps smart contracting transaction costs near zero.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Craig Calcaterra, Crypto Transaction Dispute Resolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2992962

claims.claim: Dual integration, as the authors define it, is the use of legacy legal infrastructure in smart contracting dispute resolution, such as Ricardian contracts, in combination with intra-blockchain systems for resolving smart contract disputes.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Craig Calcaterra, Crypto Transaction Dispute Resolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2992962
scope_conditions: the implementation and transition phase of the crypto economy

claims.claim: Because no conceivable way exists to permanently hide an arbiter's reputation from the arbiter in an open system, the corruption risk created by high reputation arbiters becoming valued counselors for disputants is an insoluble problem with the authors' own proposal.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Craig Calcaterra, Crypto Transaction Dispute Resolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2992962
scope_conditions: open reputation systems for anonymous arbiters

claims.claim: For crypto economy participants who wish to minimize the transaction costs of dual integration and retain anonymity, the authors' proposed open source platform ecosystem is more likely than all other available solutions to provide legal equivalence of dispute resolution mechanisms.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Craig Calcaterra, Crypto Transaction Dispute Resolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2992962
scope_conditions: participants who want both low transaction costs and continuing anonymity

claims.claim: Contingent capital securities are a largely overlooked dynamic regulatory mechanism, and their regulatory value lies in their capacity to generate feedback effects, optimized timing, and improved information for regulation.
claims.citation: Kaal, Dynamic Regulation via Contingent Capital (2017). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2957645

claims.claim: Facts-based, ex-post, trial-and-error rulemaking cannot anticipate the regulatory issues created by innovation, so rulemakers may not realize, or may realize far too late, what new regulatory demands a given innovation generates.
claims.citation: Kaal, Dynamic Regulation via Contingent Capital (2017). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2957645
scope_conditions: regulation of innovative products and markets
existing regulatory framework built on stable rules

claims.claim: Formal rulemaking in the existing regulatory infrastructure is too time consuming, and the speed of product innovation frequently renders regulations pertaining to an innovative product obsolete before those regulations are even finalized.
claims.citation: Kaal, Dynamic Regulation via Contingent Capital (2017). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2957645
scope_conditions: environments of exponential or rapid product innovation
formal notice and comment style rulemaking

claims.claim: The existing regulatory infrastructure, resting on stable and presumptively optimal rules, is largely incapable of addressing the unknown future contingencies associated with disruptive innovation.
claims.citation: Kaal, Dynamic Regulation via Contingent Capital (2017). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2957645
scope_conditions: regulation confronting disruptive innovation
reliance on stable and presumptively optimal rules

claims.claim: Because the pace of innovation continues to accelerate, future contingencies in rulemaking are likely to grow substantially, which makes the dynamic anticipation of those contingencies increasingly important for rulemaking.
claims.citation: Kaal, Dynamic Regulation via Contingent Capital (2017). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2957645
scope_conditions: continued exponential growth of technology and innovation

claims.claim: The issuance of contingent capital securities is a promising dynamic regulatory mechanism that can help address the suboptimal regulatory outcomes associated with disruptive innovation.
claims.citation: Kaal, Dynamic Regulation via Contingent Capital (2017). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2957645
scope_conditions: financial institutions capable of issuing contingent capital securities

claims.claim: By internalizing the costs of bank failure, contingent capital may be able to minimize moral hazard, avoid financial contagion, and limit systemic risk.
claims.citation: Kaal, Dynamic Regulation via Contingent Capital (2017). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2957645
scope_conditions: bank failure costs are actually borne by the institution's own capital structure

claims.claim: Supplementing the existing regulatory infrastructure with dynamic elements can reduce suboptimal regulatory outcomes, because dynamic regulation as a supplement addresses the shortcomings of the existing rulemaking framework and curtails increased demands on the institutional infrastructure.
claims.citation: Kaal, Dynamic Regulation via Contingent Capital (2017). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2957645
scope_conditions: dynamic elements are used as a supplement rather than a replacement for existing rulemaking

claims.claim: Increased availability of relevant, decentralized, and timely information for rulemaking is what makes anticipatory action possible, because such information facilitates rulemakers' predictions and anticipation of otherwise unforeseeable contingencies.
claims.citation: Kaal, Dynamic Regulation via Contingent Capital (2017). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2957645
scope_conditions: a dynamic regulatory framework in which such information flows exist

claims.claim: Feedback effects, defined as informational exchange processes between public and private rulemakers, between outcomes and institutions, between rules and rulemaking processes, and across jurisdictions, are a central tenet of the theory of dynamic regulation.
claims.citation: Kaal, Dynamic Regulation via Contingent Capital (2017). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2957645

claims.claim: Feedback effects change the timing of regulatory information: instead of acquiring necessary information only after rules have already proven suboptimal, they increase the availability of relevant information ex ante and support anticipation of necessary revisions.
claims.citation: Kaal, Dynamic Regulation via Contingent Capital (2017). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2957645
scope_conditions: an informational exchange process between regulated entities and rulemakers is in place

claims.claim: Anticipatory regulation, which uses institution-specific and timely information together with feedback effects to create new rules, can minimize costly and suboptimal ex-post trial-and-error experimentation with stable and presumptively optimal rules.
claims.citation: Kaal, Dynamic Regulation via Contingent Capital (2017). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2957645
scope_conditions: institution-specific and timely information is actually available to rulemakers

claims.claim: Deferred prosecution agreements and venture capital investment decisions function as dynamic regulatory tools because they increase the availability of relevant, decentralized, and timely information for rulemaking and facilitate feedback effects.
claims.citation: Kaal, Dynamic Regulation via Contingent Capital (2017). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2957645
scope_conditions: regulators can observe the content of DPAs and venture capital investment trends

claims.claim: Section 165(b) of the Dodd-Frank Act already authorizes the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve to utilize contingent capital, so the mechanism has a statutory foundation in United States law.
claims.citation: Kaal, Dynamic Regulation via Contingent Capital (2017). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2957645
scope_conditions: United States law after the Dodd-Frank Act

claims.claim: Contingent capital is an automatic mechanism for increasing capital while reducing debt, and its long term benefit is lowering leverage.
claims.citation: Kaal, Dynamic Regulation via Contingent Capital (2017). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2957645

claims.claim: For purposes of this article, contingent capital is stipulated to mean the predefined conversion of a certain percentage of a financial institution's debt securities into equity securities.
claims.citation: Kaal, Dynamic Regulation via Contingent Capital (2017). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2957645
scope_conditions: the definition is stipulated for this article and other labels exist for the same concept

claims.claim: Strained financial institutions may find the automatic conversion of debt into equity through contingent capital securities an attractive alternative to being forced into restructuring or liquidation.
claims.citation: Kaal, Dynamic Regulation via Contingent Capital (2017). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2957645
scope_conditions: the institution is already financially strained
restructuring or liquidation is the realistic alternative

claims.claim: The conversion feature of contingent capital securities has the potential to change the control dynamic, the distribution of power, and the dependencies within systemically important financial institutions.
claims.citation: Kaal, Dynamic Regulation via Contingent Capital (2017). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2957645
scope_conditions: systemically important financial institutions with outstanding contingent capital securities
conversion is actually triggered

claims.claim: Regulators are often unable to supervise financial institutions effectively because of insufficient public funding, and contingent capital securities could help fill the void that this supervisory incapacity leaves.
claims.citation: Kaal, Dynamic Regulation via Contingent Capital (2017). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2957645
scope_conditions: supervisory agencies operating under funding constraints

claims.claim: Contingent capital may be more efficient than simply raising capital requirements, because the capital injection is available only when it is needed and, when triggered, only as much of the contingent capital converts as is necessary to recapitalize the firm.
claims.citation: Kaal, Dynamic Regulation via Contingent Capital (2017). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2957645
scope_conditions: the trigger design causes conversion only in the amount necessary for recapitalization

claims.claim: Appropriate use of contingent capital triggers can further lower the default risk of the contingent capital securities themselves, on top of the moral hazard reduction that comes from internalizing bank failure costs.
claims.citation: Kaal, Dynamic Regulation via Contingent Capital (2017). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2957645
scope_conditions: triggers are designed and evaluated appropriately

claims.claim: The threat of dilution of stock holdings, combined with the threat of loss upon conversion, could help reduce the pressure shareholders place on management of systemically important financial institutions to take increasing risks.
claims.citation: Kaal, Dynamic Regulation via Contingent Capital (2017). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2957645
scope_conditions: conversion dilutes existing common shareholders
shareholders anticipate the dilution ex ante

claims.claim: Where conversion has a negative effect on stock price, management is further incentivized to maintain and manage risk in order to avoid reputational loss and the income reduction caused by losses in stock options.
claims.citation: Kaal, Dynamic Regulation via Contingent Capital (2017). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2957645
scope_conditions: conversion depresses the issuer's stock price
management compensation includes stock options

claims.claim: Contingent capital could create a regime for providing countercyclical regulatory capital that further enhances the regulatory capital requirements of the Federal Reserve and those under Basel III.
claims.citation: Kaal, Dynamic Regulation via Contingent Capital (2017). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2957645
scope_conditions: contingent capital is used alongside, not instead of, existing minimum capital requirements

claims.claim: Contingent capital qualifies as a dynamic regulatory mechanism because capital injection is available only if and when needed and because the conversion of contingent capital securities into near worthless equity signals impending regulatory issues to regulators, which creates feedback effects.
claims.citation: Kaal, Dynamic Regulation via Contingent Capital (2017). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2957645
scope_conditions: contingent capital securities are outstanding and their conversion is observable by regulators

claims.claim: Contingent capital securities optimize information for rulemaking because, when issued and triggered, they produce highly valuable, real time, decentralized information on the financial wellbeing of a given regulated entity.
claims.citation: Kaal, Dynamic Regulation via Contingent Capital (2017). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2957645
scope_conditions: the securities have been issued and the trigger has occurred

claims.claim: Contingent capital creates feedback effects because the conversion of debt to equity signals to regulators that the entity's management was unable to avoid the trigger, which is itself a call for increased regulatory scrutiny.
claims.citation: Kaal, Dynamic Regulation via Contingent Capital (2017). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2957645
scope_conditions: regulators observe conversion events

claims.claim: The occurrence of the debt to equity trigger creates real time regulatory information that a centralized system would require months or years to generate, and it enables regulators to open a regulatory investigation if and when one is needed.
claims.citation: Kaal, Dynamic Regulation via Contingent Capital (2017). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2957645
scope_conditions: comparison is to centralized information gathering by regulators

claims.claim: Contingent capital enables anticipatory regulation because regulators may observe and react in real time to triggering events, before the regulated entities encounter financial calamity.
claims.citation: Kaal, Dynamic Regulation via Contingent Capital (2017). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2957645
scope_conditions: triggering events occur before, not after, financial distress becomes terminal

claims.claim: Information generated by contingent capital securities may allow regulators to adjust their regulatory requirements and the intensity of regulatory investigations anticipatorily rather than after the fact.
claims.citation: Kaal, Dynamic Regulation via Contingent Capital (2017). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2957645
scope_conditions: depends on the disclosure regime applicable to the respective contingent capital securities

claims.claim: Most of the design features of contingent capital securities and their triggering events remain underdeveloped, yet despite these shortcomings such securities could still help regulators anticipate regulatory needs in real time through feedback effects and improved information.
claims.citation: Kaal, Dynamic Regulation via Contingent Capital (2017). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2957645
scope_conditions: state of contingent capital design as of the time of writing

claims.claim: Initial Coin Offerings are the most efficient means of financing entrepreneurial initiatives in the history of capital formation, because they minimize transaction cost and democratize finance while dis-intermediating banks.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: ICO market as of November 2017

claims.claim: Tokens sold in an ICO are structurally different from equity: they do not generally confer ownership rights, no right to dividends, and no claim on company assets in bankruptcy, so the risk and reward profile of a token is not that of a share.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: comparison of ICOs to initial public offerings

claims.claim: ICOs cannot be qualified as donations and are therefore distinguishable from crowdfunding, because ICO participants acquire a financial stake in the company and, as the case may be, a right to vote on future decisions.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: comparison of ICOs to crowdfunding platforms such as Kickstarter

claims.claim: Because Ethereum's decentralized platform incorporating smart contracts lets developers build applications directly on its blockchain, the majority of developers chose to write smart contracts on the Ethereum Virtual Machine rather than create their own blockchain technology, giving ICOs a uniform protocol.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: ICO market through 2017

claims.claim: Because whitepapers are not audited by any authority, the preliminary steps of the ICO roadmap, project announcement, executive summary, and investor comments, carry the burden of building market credibility and investor trust in the soundness of the project.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: standard ICO roadmap practice as of 2017

claims.claim: The pre-ICO price of a cryptocurrency is set arbitrarily by the start-up team that structured the offering, while post-ICO price dynamics are left to supply and demand determined by the network of participants rather than any central authority.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: standard ICO pricing practice as of 2017

claims.claim: The rapid evolution of ICOs was enabled in part by the negative factors that had depressed start-up fundraising, namely post crisis banking regulation and a shadow banking sector that only marginally supports new ventures and highly innovative start-ups.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: start-up fundraising conditions before and during the emergence of the ICO market

claims.claim: ICOs filled the void left by constrained bank and non-bank start-up financing and enabled a democratization and inclusion process that facilitated banking disintermediation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: start-up fundraising environment at the inception of the ICO market

claims.claim: An issuer can pre-define monetary policy in crypto economics by fixing the number of tokens created and issued, and a maximum token issuance combined with controlled token supply releases can make small increases in demand drive token prices higher.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: token issuances with a predetermined maximum supply

claims.claim: To avoid a token price crash, token escrow accounts should provide usage and access controls that assure investors escrowed tokens will not be issued at a discount, and lockups or phased releases of escrowed tokens further minimize crash risk.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: issuers holding unissued tokens in escrow for future funding

claims.claim: Adjusting the commercial benefits attached to a token operates as a quasi fiscal policy tool: increasing those benefits raises aggregate demand for a given token supply and can offset the depreciating effect of a large supply in circulation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: tokens carrying discounts or other usage-linked commercial benefits

claims.claim: Adjusting commercial benefits associated with a token issuance is preferable to blunt monetary intervention, because it avoids more drastic measures such as emergency sales, building token reserves, or changing the token supply in circulation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: issuer management of an outstanding token issuance

claims.claim: The disruption of venture capital by ICOs is in part self-inflicted: venture capital funds continuously invested in innovation while insufficiently innovating their own business model, leaving them exposed to a more efficient financing tool.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: venture capital industry financing highly innovative start-ups

claims.claim: In the second quarter of 2017 ICO issuances exceeded venture capital financing of start-ups for the first time, with $210 million invested in ICOs versus $180 million invested into start-ups via traditional venture capital funds.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: second quarter of 2017
crypto and blockchain start-up financing

claims.claim: The trend of ICO issuance exceeding venture capital financing can be expected to continue, because ICOs allocate capital more efficiently and at lower cost.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: crypto start-up financing after the second quarter of 2017

claims.claim: ICOs are preferable to venture capital funding for many start-ups first and foremost because ICO promoters and their developers are not forced to sacrifice equity in the project in exchange for the funds they raise.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: start-ups choosing between ICO and venture capital financing

claims.claim: Given the advantages of ICOs, traditional regulated IPOs and venture capital funds increasingly fail to adequately capitalize crypto and legacy ventures driven by new economic paradigms.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: ventures driven by new economic paradigms, including crypto ventures

claims.claim: The 2012 to 2017 ICO model allowed cryptocurrencies to be raised through a token sale without any conditions, landmark requirements, or security measures to protect investors, so that in essence promoters could use ICO proceeds as they pleased.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: ICO models prevailing between 2012 and 2017

claims.claim: Token holders, unlike shareholders in the traditional corporate infrastructure, cannot vote for or against directors or nominate directors, so ordinary ICO investors have no governance channel and simply must trust the promoters and their business intent.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: typical ICO token structures
ordinary investors as distinct from institutional pre-sale investors

claims.claim: The only real control power available to token holders is the decision to hold or sell their tokens, and even that exit right may be unavailable until the token is fully listed on an exchange.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: typical ICO token structures
period before full exchange listing

claims.claim: Crypto platforms typically launch an ICO when they have only an intangible product based on a basic crypto idea, so token holders invest in the future promise of an idea, and while that works for core infrastructure products such as Ethereum, most other platforms struggle to fulfill that promise.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: crypto platforms other than core infrastructure products

claims.claim: Associated with the lack of an existing product is the inability of most crypto platforms to generate revenue to offset costs the way traditional businesses do, since they typically have neither employees who create and advertise a product nor customers who generate revenue.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: crypto platforms organized as foundations

claims.claim: Because the token supply is controlled by ICO promoters who must reserve tokens for future funding needs, token holders can be diluted by later issuance of reserve tokens and their token value can be diminished without any ability to protect themselves against such events.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: platforms that reserve tokens for future funding needs

claims.claim: Hardcoded lockup periods can protect token holders against supply side induced devaluation, but they also decrease the token economic flexibility the promoter team needs to raise additional funds, so the remedy trades investor protection against issuer financing capacity.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: tokens subject to hardcoded lockup periods

claims.claim: ICOs provide the highest possible liquidity for investors at the very beginning of a platform's lifecycle, before the reporting, accounting, and legal infrastructure that gives the investing public assurance of underlying business success, so investors trade on very limited information and volatility of the tokens and the whole cryptocurrency market increases.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: ICOs occurring at the beginning of a crypto business lifecycle

claims.claim: Because token offerings are built on open source code, the utility of an issued token can at any time be recreated in another token with essentially identical features at marginal cost, so investors cannot rely on the implicit promise that promoters and developers will increase the value of the acquired token rather than launch a duplicate.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: token offerings based on open source software

claims.claim: Legacy businesses own their code and can sue competitors who copy it, whereas open source crypto start-ups rely only on licenses, and this weaker incentive structure makes ICO investments riskier.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: open source crypto start-ups compared to legacy code-owning businesses

claims.claim: On bankruptcy or termination of the platform, token holders typically have no liquidity preference and no recourse at all once debt holders and outside creditors are satisfied, so unlike a venture capital seed investor with at least a simple liquidity preference, they typically lose everything they invested.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: bankruptcy or termination of the promoter's business or platform

claims.claim: The lack of a regulatory framework creates significant legal uncertainty in the ICO market, and because cryptocurrencies are censorship-resistant and arguably regulation-resistant by design, that uncertainty may sooner or later lead the Securities and Exchange Commission to declare ICOs illegal.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: ICO market as of November 2017
United States securities regulation

claims.claim: ICOs are not subject to predefined regulatory procedures: whitepapers do not follow prospectus disclosure guidelines, are not reviewed or audited by any authority, and are not subject to any form of rating of the new entrepreneurial initiative.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: ICO market as of November 2017

claims.claim: Private initiatives are emerging to fill the ICO disclosure and rating gap, including a joint venture between Ambisafe and the rating agency ICOrating created to ensure high quality standards and support investor due diligence.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: ICO market as of November 2017

claims.claim: Identifying legitimate projects and distinguishing them from scams is a necessary condition both for investor protection and for creating the conditions in which ICOs can proliferate.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: ICO market as of November 2017

claims.claim: Zombie ICOs, which have little chance of creating a successful market for their tokens, became increasingly common in 2017 and are identifiable by their inability to answer core questions about the problem solved, the allocation of proceeds, the viability of the product, and the team's business experience.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: ICO market in 2017

claims.claim: An ICO that proposes an uncapped raise without an underlying product is a very serious red flag, because uncapped raises are perceived by the crypto community as greedy and raise investor uncertainty about the valuation of the platform or product being bought.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: ICOs without an underlying product

claims.claim: Capped token issuances became the dominant structure between 2016 and 2017 because a cap increases the likelihood that the ICO will be oversubscribed, which creates a significant incentive for investors to attempt to get in first.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: ICO structures between 2016 and 2017

claims.claim: The Gnosis ICO shows how a reverse dutch auction can mitigate the inefficiencies and risks of a capped sale: the offering was capped at $12.5 million and the time needed to complete the sale determined the quantity of tokens distributed to investors, with the rest held by the start-up team.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: capped token sales exposed to first mover rush dynamics

claims.claim: ICO promoters should not allow tokens to be traded before the underlying protocol network or application is live, and should not use a landing page that focuses almost exclusively on the ICO while providing less content on the product, project, technology, and team.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: emerging bad ICO practices identified in 2017

claims.claim: ICO promoters should make significant and ongoing disclosures on vesting and lockup periods and should never manipulate the smart contract to change ICO sales rules mid-course during the offering.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: ongoing ICO sales governed by smart contracts

claims.claim: ICO disclosures should be as clear as possible: promoters should avoid an unclear or uncertain use of proceeds pie chart and should be very clear on plans for converting cryptocurrency into actual company reserves.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: ICO issuers seeking to meet emerging good practice standards

claims.claim: Through continuous evolution and improvement of ICO practices, the ICO industry and the underlying crypto businesses can become the foundation of the emerging crypto economy.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Marco Dell'Erba, Initial Coin Offerings Emerging Practices, Risk Factors, and Red Flags (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3067615
scope_conditions: continued voluntary or mandated improvement of ICO industry practice

claims.claim: The core lawyer characteristics and skillsets produced by the existing legal education and regulatory framework are incompatible with what the practice of law in the 21st century demands.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: existing law school curricula and bar regulatory frameworks
21st century practice conditions shaped by disruptive technology

claims.claim: Disruptive innovation in law renders obsolete many and probably most of the traditional legal skills and characteristics that law schools currently cultivate.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: areas of practice exposed to disruptive innovation in law

claims.claim: Even the law firms that are best at finding innovative solutions for clients remain reluctant to fully adopt Legal Tech innovations, so quality of client service does not predict willingness to adopt.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: law firms and in-house legal departments as of 2017

claims.claim: Law schools that invest early in artificial intelligence, machine learning, and blockchain will gain a comparative advantage over peer schools irrespective of ranking, because demand for lawyers trained in those technologies is likely to spike once law firm adoption crosses a threshold.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: first mover law schools that make the financial investment
a threshold point of law firm adoption is reached

claims.claim: The curriculum of American law schools has changed only marginally over the past thirty plus years, even as the practice environment has been transformed.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: American law schools
period of roughly 1985 to 2017

claims.claim: The challenges created by Legal Tech, the new economy, and platform technologies justify a fundamentally more creative and innovative approach to legal education in the 21st century.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127

claims.claim: The first generations of Legal Tech did not reduce demand for lawyers; by making far greater volumes of legal material available faster, they created a need for additional lawyers to evaluate that material.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: Legal Tech from the 1970s legal databases through early practice management software

claims.claim: The decentralization of law pursued by Legal Tech startups has broad repercussions for the legal profession, the first of which is that existing legal services are rendered increasingly irrelevant or are replaced outright by Legal Tech.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: legal services amenable to online delivery, matching, AI review, or blockchain settlement

claims.claim: Legal Tech applications will soon perform most of the work junior lawyers do, and will do so without the human elements that produce imprecision, flaws, inaccuracies, potential lawsuits, and delay; junior legal professionals and support staff are therefore the first casualties.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: high volume, standardizable junior lawyer tasks
near future relative to 2017

claims.claim: Legal Tech startups will force the legal profession to innovate perpetually, a demand that overextended and cumbersome legal organizations which have lost the capacity for agile reinvention cannot easily meet.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: incumbent legal organizations with traditional hierarchical structures

claims.claim: Legal Tech's disruptive innovation combined with the principles of the sharing economy requires lawyers and lawmakers to reevaluate their understanding of many areas of law.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: areas of law touched by sharing and decentralized peer to peer platforms

claims.claim: Redesigning legal doctrine around sharing and decentralized peer to peer platforms demands out of the box thinking from a profession whose members were trained, both in law school and across their careers, to think inside the box.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: lawyers trained in conventional law school and practice environments

claims.claim: The counseling, deal making, matchmaking, gatekeeping, and enforcement roles historically performed by lawyers are increasingly performed by technology, and blockchain technology and smart contracting will accelerate that substitution.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: transactional legal roles that can be encoded
near future relative to 2017

claims.claim: Because a public blockchain is genuinely public and immutable, it increases transparency while simultaneously and significantly reducing transaction costs.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: public blockchains rather than consortium or fully private blockchains

claims.claim: Intermediaries, lawyers among them, are replaced by code, connectivity, crowd, and collaboration.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: transactions capable of being executed on blockchain infrastructure

claims.claim: It is the completely decentralized network connectivity of the blockchain via the Internet, more than the use of digital signatures to establish party identity and authenticity, that provides the strongest protection against fraud.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: fully decentralized, internet connected blockchain networks

claims.claim: Blockchain's distributed consensus model permits node verification of transactions without compromising the privacy of the parties, which makes it arguably safer than a traditional model requiring third party intermediary validation.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: blockchains using node based distributed consensus

claims.claim: Smart contract arrangements involving several parties and greater complexity require the verifiable and unhackable system that blockchain technology supplies.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: multiparty and complex smart contract arrangements

claims.claim: Smart contracting on a blockchain often makes conventional legal contracting unnecessary, because smart contracts emulate the logic of legal contract clauses.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: transactions whose terms can be expressed in code

claims.claim: Increased connectivity enabled by blockchain technology, combined with increased decentralization, allows the removal of intermediaries including lawyers, financial intermediaries, and platform companies.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: environments where blockchain enabled connectivity and decentralization advance together

claims.claim: Venture capital investment in blockchain startups has grown exponentially since 2012, which the authors read as an indicator of the technology's commercial maturity.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: VC investment in blockchain startups, 2007 to 2016

claims.claim: Once blockchain technology gains wider acceptance and its applications reach consumers, existing legal processes and structures will likely be among the first processes to become redundant.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: wider acceptance of blockchain technology
spread of blockchain applications into consumer markets

claims.claim: Leveraging the big data collected through Legal Tech solutions and blockchain applications in combination with machine learning produces more creative and faster tools, which in turn generates a surge of innovative platforms that disrupt the legal industry.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: settings where Legal Tech and blockchain generate usable data at scale

claims.claim: The world of blockchain and smart contracting has clearly not reached maturity, which is the first of several technological and legal limitations facing blockchain and smart contracts.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: state of the technology as of 2017

claims.claim: Contrary to the widespread belief among legal professionals that code can only handle very simple transactions, blockchain enabled smart contracts generally do not require legal involvement across the spectrum of transactions.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: transactions capable of being coded
contested against the prevailing view in the legal community

claims.claim: Because the legal origin of smart contracting is unsettled, lawyers may argue that smart contracts are void and unenforceable under the law even where the smart contract accurately reflects the parties' underlying agreement.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: smart contracts assessed under existing contract law doctrine

claims.claim: Contract law rules on formation, interpretation, conditions, and remedies require substantive adjustment before smart contracts can be accommodated.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: existing contract law doctrine applied to blockchain smart contracts

claims.claim: Although blockchain technology itself offers unprecedented data and privacy protection, storing blockchain data across a global network of nodes often will not comply with the consumer protection rules, directives, and guidelines of particular jurisdictions.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: global node distribution of blockchain data
jurisdiction specific consumer protection and data rules

claims.claim: The legal disputes already generated by sharing platforms indicate that future blockchain enabled sharing services will not be accepted quickly or without resistance from incumbents whose service or product delivery is challenged.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: blockchain enabled sharing services entering markets with entrenched incumbents

claims.claim: Fundamental flaws in the DAO's code let hackers move one third of its total funds to a subsidiary account, and that hack together with further technological limitations destroyed the DAO initiative.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: the DAO as launched in May 2016 on Ethereum

claims.claim: Because a series of smart contracts granted DAO token holders voting rights, the blockchain based smart contracts performed the function of articles of association or corporate bylaws, in an organization that had no directors, managers, or employees.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: decentralized autonomous organizations structured like the DAO

claims.claim: Open legal questions about the DAO, including which regime governs token issuance, minority token holder protection, taxation, the binding force of DAO smart contracts, ownership of intellectual property, and conflict resolution, must be answered before future DAO structures can operate seamlessly.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: future decentralized autonomous organization setups

claims.claim: Exponentially increasing disruptive innovation will lead clients to routinely bring legal professionals problems that those lawyers cannot fully understand, inside a legal framework that does not always supply clear or helpful answers.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: worldwide acceleration of disruptive innovation

claims.claim: Law schools should educate lawyers who add value by helping clients and society adjust to the technological environment rather than lawyers who impose unnecessary or unwise restrictions on it, since such restrictions will not stop technological development anyway.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127

claims.claim: The traditional legal tool kit worked adequately when innovation cycles were long, but where innovation is exponential it is regularly out of touch with the radically different needs of a decentralized world and often produces disastrous outcomes.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: exponential rather than long innovation cycles
decentralized technological environments

claims.claim: Most lawyers and law industry representatives underestimate the implications of emerging Legal Tech.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: law firm and corporate lawyers in Asia, Europe, and the United States

claims.claim: Advising on blockchain contracts requires that law students and lawyers become familiar with the technology and learn at least basic coding as it pertains to Ethereum smart contracts.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: lawyers who intend to advise on blockchain based contracts

claims.claim: Law schools must enable students to work in interdisciplinary teams with software engineers, and a greater appreciation of how code can be used and integrated in legal contexts is essential to that capability.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: law school curricular design for 21st century practice

claims.claim: Future lawyers will have to distinguish blockchain based contracting from traditional legal contracting and advise clients on the optimal allocation between the two.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: dealmaking that mixes blockchainable and non blockchainable elements

claims.claim: For the parts of dealmaking and other legal tasks that cannot be placed on a blockchain, the role of non blockchainable agents of trust may expand, and blockchain driven disintermediation of law may itself create additional legal tasks requiring human lawyers.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Legal Education in the Blockchain Revolution (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2939127
scope_conditions: legal tasks that require the ambiguity and flexibility of law

claims.claim: The Investment Advisers Act safe harbor let an adviser count an entire legal organization as one client, provided the advice followed the organization's objectives rather than those of its individual owners, which is what allowed advisers to manage money for hundreds of underlying investors while staying exempt.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Investment Fund Regulation - Theory and Empirical Evidence from 1998 to 2016 (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2998097
scope_conditions: United States
before the Dodd-Frank Act of 2010

claims.claim: The 2004 registration rule failed in court because the term client was not defined in the Investment Advisers Act, leaving the SEC without authority to fix its meaning, and the D.C. Circuit vacated the rule in Goldstein as arbitrary rulemaking.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Investment Fund Regulation - Theory and Empirical Evidence from 1998 to 2016 (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2998097
scope_conditions: United States
Goldstein v. SEC, July 2006

claims.claim: Because banks and brokers had let LTCM borrow the full value of its collateral, LTCM's 4.8 billion dollars in capital dissipated quickly once banks began making margin calls.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Investment Fund Regulation - Theory and Empirical Evidence from 1998 to 2016 (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2998097
scope_conditions: LTCM, 1998
100 percent collateral lending by banks and brokers

claims.claim: Banks overexposed themselves to private investment fund lending, which allowed LTCM and similar funds to grow significantly and led banks as counterparties to put their own existence at risk.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Investment Fund Regulation - Theory and Empirical Evidence from 1998 to 2016 (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2998097
scope_conditions: banks lending to private investment funds
pre 1998 lending practices

claims.claim: Post LTCM proposals for clearer credit risk strategies and credit risk management policies at financial intermediaries were inappropriately applied across the whole range of business models and lacked concrete implementation elements.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Investment Fund Regulation - Theory and Empirical Evidence from 1998 to 2016 (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2998097
scope_conditions: post LTCM regulatory proposals
author's critique beginning in 2005

claims.claim: Stress tests, Value at Risk, and Monte Carlo scenarios imposed on financial intermediaries that lend to private investment funds necessarily rely on historical data, so they are of limited value as indicators of high risk sensitivity to future events.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Investment Fund Regulation - Theory and Empirical Evidence from 1998 to 2016 (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2998097
scope_conditions: risk models used by intermediaries exposed to private funds
