claims.claim: Proposals to improve close-out netting agreements and to harmonize standard documentation across jurisdictions are likely to run into jurisdictional arbitrage and national protectionism.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Investment Fund Regulation - Theory and Empirical Evidence from 1998 to 2016 (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2998097
scope_conditions: cross border regulatory harmonization proposals after LTCM

claims.claim: Fund managers are unlikely to escape bank based indirect supervision by terminating a lending relationship, because their dynamic trading strategies depend on the immediate availability of capital and lending relationships now face increased scrutiny.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Investment Fund Regulation - Theory and Empirical Evidence from 1998 to 2016 (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2998097
scope_conditions: contemporary banking environment with heightened lending scrutiny
funds running dynamic trading strategies

claims.claim: Data on the credit derivatives market show that since 2000 private investment funds steadily increased their share of that market while banks' role declined, which supports shifting regulatory emphasis onto banks' lending exposure to those funds.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Investment Fund Regulation - Theory and Empirical Evidence from 1998 to 2016 (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2998097
scope_conditions: credit derivatives market since 2000

claims.claim: Investor suitability standards requiring independent verification of an investor's ability to evaluate complex financial products and investment risk would make wealth redundant as a proxy for sophistication in determining investor eligibility.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Investment Fund Regulation - Theory and Empirical Evidence from 1998 to 2016 (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2998097
scope_conditions: private investment fund investor eligibility
proposed in 2009, before Title IV

claims.claim: Under PFIARA, private investment fund advisers with more than 150 million dollars of assets under management must register as investment advisers and disclose information about their trades and portfolios to the SEC.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Investment Fund Regulation - Theory and Empirical Evidence from 1998 to 2016 (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2998097
scope_conditions: United States
Title IV of the Dodd-Frank Act

claims.claim: The private fund industry's central fear about Form PF was not the filing itself but eventual publicity: if the disclosures ever became public, competitors could reverse engineer fund strategies and largely eliminate managers' ability to generate absolute returns.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Investment Fund Regulation - Theory and Empirical Evidence from 1998 to 2016 (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2998097
scope_conditions: Form PF disclosures held confidentially by the SEC

claims.claim: Some Form PF disclosure requirements are not answerable as designed, because counterparty credit exposure is sensitive information that individual private fund managers often cannot readily determine.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Investment Fund Regulation - Theory and Empirical Evidence from 1998 to 2016 (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2998097
scope_conditions: Form PF counterparty credit exposure items

claims.claim: Because advisers and third party service providers can flatten out and sanitize the information disclosed in Forms ADV and PF, the resulting disclosures may be less useful to the FSOC and the SEC in determining the systemic risk posed by private funds.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Investment Fund Regulation - Theory and Empirical Evidence from 1998 to 2016 (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2998097
scope_conditions: Forms ADV and PF disclosures
level of sanitizing could not be verified in the study

claims.claim: The second survey found long-term negative effects of Title IV: 34.9 percent of respondents expected it to affect the industry over the next five years through additional expenses, and 32.6 percent expected it to create barriers to entry for new private fund market entrants.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Investment Fund Regulation - Theory and Empirical Evidence from 1998 to 2016 (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2998097
scope_conditions: 2015 survey of registered investment advisers

claims.claim: The SEC's efforts to clarify and optimize the post Dodd-Frank framework cut both ways: they supported industry compliance with the revised standards while simultaneously creating uncertainty and higher costs for the industry.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Investment Fund Regulation - Theory and Empirical Evidence from 1998 to 2016 (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2998097
scope_conditions: SEC implementation and clarification of Title IV registration and reporting rules

claims.claim: The industry largely absorbed the increased expenses of the Dodd-Frank Act by increasing the use of pass-through expense terms in adviser and fund arrangements, which is why advisers increasingly attributed earnings effects to opportunity costs rather than to expenses between 2012 and 2015.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Investment Fund Regulation - Theory and Empirical Evidence from 1998 to 2016 (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2998097
scope_conditions: investment adviser and private fund contractual relationships

claims.claim: Because Title IV compliance costs bring increasing returns to scale and therefore favor larger firms, Title IV may create barriers to entry for smaller private fund advisers, forcing them out of the market or into consolidation with other advisers.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Investment Fund Regulation - Theory and Empirical Evidence from 1998 to 2016 (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2998097
scope_conditions: smaller private fund advisers
if Title IV compliance costs bring increasing returns to scale

claims.claim: Rules become adaptable when institutions and rulemaking processes integrate feedback effects, including feedback between industry and regulators, that generate timely, relevant, and decentralized information before rules are finalized.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Investment Fund Regulation - Theory and Empirical Evidence from 1998 to 2016 (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2998097
scope_conditions: dynamic regulation of the private investment fund industry

claims.claim: Using a regression discontinuity design around the 150 million dollar registration threshold with five years of performance data on more than 3500 reporting private funds, the study finds no significant effect of Dodd-Frank requirements on private fund performance, with all p-values above the 5 percent level.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Investment Fund Regulation - Theory and Empirical Evidence from 1998 to 2016 (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2998097
scope_conditions: private funds reporting performance data, 2010 to 2015
regression discontinuity around the $150 million AUM registration threshold

claims.claim: The SEC's private fund data collection encountered accuracy and consistency problems that hampered the FSOC's ability to evaluate the systemic risk of private funds.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Investment Fund Regulation - Theory and Empirical Evidence from 1998 to 2016 (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2998097
scope_conditions: SEC data collection under Title IV
FSOC systemic risk assessment

claims.claim: The FSOC relied most heavily on some of the most problematic disclosure items the SEC collects, even though SEC data played a crucial role at every stage of its systemic risk assessment of private funds.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Investment Fund Regulation - Theory and Empirical Evidence from 1998 to 2016 (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2998097
scope_conditions: FSOC systemic risk assessment of private funds
post Dodd-Frank Form PF data

claims.claim: Form PF data suffer from core shortcomings: ambiguity in several key questions, inaccurate definitions with correspondingly insufficient SEC guidance, and difficulty aggregating the required information.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Investment Fund Regulation - Theory and Empirical Evidence from 1998 to 2016 (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2998097
scope_conditions: Form PF as implemented after the Dodd-Frank Act

claims.claim: Several core Form PF questions that feed the FSOC's stage one threshold assessment are defective, most importantly because the definition of RAUM required substantive interpretation by the filers themselves.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Investment Fund Regulation - Theory and Empirical Evidence from 1998 to 2016 (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2998097
scope_conditions: FSOC stage one threshold assessment
Form PF valuation questions tied to RAUM

claims.claim: If the FSOC relies on Form PF data that is subject to inaccuracies, because uncertain filers complete the form using estimates and assumptions, then the FSOC's own work on private funds may in turn be subject to errors.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Investment Fund Regulation - Theory and Empirical Evidence from 1998 to 2016 (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2998097
scope_conditions: over 40 percent of surveyed filers disagreed with Form PF definitions or instructions

claims.claim: The mere threat that hedge funds' Form PF systemic risk filings could become public, or be shared between the SEC and the federal bankruptcy bench, could impose some discipline on distressed debt investors' conduct in the bankruptcy process.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Investment Fund Regulation - Theory and Empirical Evidence from 1998 to 2016 (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2998097
scope_conditions: distressed debt investing by hedge funds
overlap between Title IV disclosures and Revised Bankruptcy Rule 2019

claims.claim: The threat of public disclosure of systemic risk filings through the bankruptcy process only marginally affected hedge funds' tactics and their role in distressed investing, because disclosure obligations under the Dodd-Frank Act remained generic and unstandardized.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Investment Fund Regulation - Theory and Empirical Evidence from 1998 to 2016 (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2998097
scope_conditions: at the time of the study
before the SEC standardized systemic risk disclosure requirements

claims.claim: Despite the rising relevance of investment due diligence and increasing due diligence litigation, the private fund industry is largely left to its own devices to ensure adequate due diligence standards.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Investment Fund Regulation - Theory and Empirical Evidence from 1998 to 2016 (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2998097
scope_conditions: private fund investor due diligence
United States, since the 2008 to 2009 financial crisis

claims.claim: Since 2010 private fund advisers increasingly engaged in investor due diligence partly to protect themselves from investor criticism and lawsuits, rather than in response to regulatory mandate.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Investment Fund Regulation - Theory and Empirical Evidence from 1998 to 2016 (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2998097
scope_conditions: SEC Form ADV Part II filings 2007 to 2014, N=100392
due diligence litigation record 1995 to 2015, N=572

claims.claim: The legal standards applicable to private fund investor due diligence are somewhat inconsistent and suboptimal and merit clarification.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Investment Fund Regulation - Theory and Empirical Evidence from 1998 to 2016 (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2998097
scope_conditions: private fund investor due diligence litigation record, 1995 to 2015

claims.claim: The absence of due diligence standards traces to private funds' unique market position: unlike mutual funds, private funds evolved as unregistered entities free from most regulatory oversight, so their investor due diligence also evolved without oversight.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Investment Fund Regulation - Theory and Empirical Evidence from 1998 to 2016 (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2998097
scope_conditions: private funds compared with mutual funds
United States

claims.claim: Private investment fund due diligence may follow the same trajectory as banks' risk evaluation, which moved from unstandardized general strategies in the early 2000s to a heavily regulated and scientific practice today.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Investment Fund Regulation - Theory and Empirical Evidence from 1998 to 2016 (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2998097
scope_conditions: analogy to the evolution of bank risk evaluation

claims.claim: Confluence runs in both directions: mutual funds are becoming more like hedge funds as a matter of investment strategy, while hedge funds are becoming more like mutual funds as a matter of regulatory framework.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Investment Fund Regulation - Theory and Empirical Evidence from 1998 to 2016 (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2998097
scope_conditions: United States asset management industry after the 2008 to 2009 crisis

claims.claim: Unconstrained mutual funds carry private fund style investment strategies inside the regulatory framework of a traditional mutual fund, and they are widely offered to retail investors who would otherwise be excluded from private fund investments.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Investment Fund Regulation - Theory and Empirical Evidence from 1998 to 2016 (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2998097
scope_conditions: unconstrained mutual funds launched from 2010 through 2015

claims.claim: Merging the regulatory requirements applicable to mutual funds with the formerly distinct rules applicable to private investment funds creates incentives for private investment managers to set up retail alternative funds.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Investment Fund Regulation - Theory and Empirical Evidence from 1998 to 2016 (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2998097
scope_conditions: provisions of the Dodd-Frank Act that assimilated mutual and hedge fund legal requirements

claims.claim: Hedge fund advisers already required to register with the SEC have an incentive to also manage mutual funds or set up retail alternative funds, because the incremental regulatory burden of doing so is only minimally higher than their post registration requirements.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Investment Fund Regulation - Theory and Empirical Evidence from 1998 to 2016 (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2998097
scope_conditions: advisers with more than $150 million AUM required to register under the Dodd-Frank Act

claims.claim: The confluence of mutual and private investment funds contributes to the gradual erosion of the public/private distinction in federal securities regulation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Investment Fund Regulation - Theory and Empirical Evidence from 1998 to 2016 (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2998097
scope_conditions: United States federal securities regulation

claims.claim: The proliferation of unconstrained mutual funds calls into question the effectiveness of retail investor protections under the Investment Companies Act of 1940, because shares in funds that carry private fund strategies and risks may be bought by retail investors with limited or no investment experience.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Investment Fund Regulation - Theory and Empirical Evidence from 1998 to 2016 (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2998097
scope_conditions: unconstrained mutual funds sold to retail investors
United States

claims.claim: Blockchain's structural characteristic as a decentralized model for financial transactions disintermediates and disrupts the existing financial infrastructure, so private funds that adopt it first directly accelerate that disintermediation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Investment Fund Regulation - Theory and Empirical Evidence from 1998 to 2016 (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2998097
scope_conditions: private investment funds adopting blockchain infrastructure

claims.claim: Blockchain technology enables managers to charge per-transaction fees, which undermines the existing 2 and 20 fee model, because it allows fully automated allocation of the correct fee to each executed trade without manual reconciliation or settlement.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Private Investment Fund Regulation - Theory and Empirical Evidence from 1998 to 2016 (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2998097
scope_conditions: blockchain enabled private investment funds

claims.claim: The obstacles preventing consumers and entrepreneurs from accessing a workable new technology are frequently not technological limits but human choices embodied in law: legal and regulatory rules prohibit or limit commercial exploitation of, and public access to, new technology.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: once the main technical problems of a technology have been solved

claims.claim: Because neither national nor international law recognizes artificial intelligence as a subject of law, AI has no legal personality and therefore cannot itself be held liable for the damages it causes.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: under the legal frameworks in force as of 2017

claims.claim: Increasing the quantity of data does not dissolve the foundational methodological problems of data: construct validity, measurement, reliability, and data dependencies remain the same regardless of how much data is collected.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: where big data is used as a basis for analysis or inference

claims.claim: Regulation is never grounded in the full set of facts about a technology; it is always premised on a prior selection of the facts that regulators themselves treat as relevant when deciding what, when, and how to intervene.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531

claims.claim: The time frame for rulemaking in the existing regulatory infrastructure is largely inadequate to address the regulatory challenges created by disruptive innovation.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: notice and comment rulemaking in the existing regulatory infrastructure
technologies developing at exponential rates

claims.claim: The speed of product innovation allows a new product to reach the market while formal rulemaking, which takes months and often years of procedure, is still occupied with the previous product launch.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: formal rulemaking in the existing regulatory infrastructure

claims.claim: New regulations addressed to an innovative product can be obsolete before they are even finalized.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: rules aimed at products subject to rapid innovation cycles

claims.claim: The existing regulatory infrastructure cannot sufficiently distinguish beneficial innovation from other innovation, and therefore cannot harness it.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531

claims.claim: Because technological transition is becoming a permanent state rather than an episode, rulemakers' inability to address the regulatory issues created by disruptive innovation will generate high levels of legal uncertainty and inconsistency.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: age of continuous disruptive innovation
existing rulemaking framework

claims.claim: The current regulatory framework contains no mechanism that informs rulemakers of beneficial innovative ideas succinctly and in advance, so regulators learn about innovation only after the fact.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531

claims.claim: Establishing the facts about a new technology is often impossible in practice because there is no adequate sample or other reliable data on the effects of that technology yet.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: early stage or emerging technologies

claims.claim: The identification of which facts count as relevant or irrelevant can be distorted by the concerns of entrenched interests that find the new technology commercially threatening.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: where incumbents face competitive displacement by the technology

claims.claim: The relevant facts on which regulation rests are never going to be obvious or settled, so the regulation of any disruptive new technology will always be reactive and built on an uncertain and politicized factual basis.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: disruptive new technologies

claims.claim: Regulators too often define success negatively, as the avoidance of catastrophe, which makes regulatory experimentation unattractive to them.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: where regulators are exposed to criticism for adverse outcomes

claims.claim: Because regulators seek to avoid grounds for criticism, they inevitably adopt an overly cautious posture, which is what the precautionary principle amounts to in practice.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531

claims.claim: Regulatory caution produces a systematic disconnect between the regulation of an innovation and the commercial and consumer ability to access it.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: from the perspective of entrepreneurs and consumers

claims.claim: Faced with disruptive innovation, regulators believe their only options are reckless action, meaning regulation without sufficient facts, or paralysis, meaning doing nothing; in that bind caution beats risk and the precautionary principle becomes the default.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: constant, complex and disruptive technological innovation

claims.claim: Regulatory caution is not neutral: it functions to reinforce the status quo, with the result that new technologies struggle to reach the market in a timely or efficient manner.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531

claims.claim: A fact based approach to regulation worked relatively well only under a specific historical condition: innovation cycles were long and disruption unfolded over decades, giving regulators time to get their facts in order before intervening.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: past eras of slow technological disruption

claims.claim: The automobile illustrates how long the old disruption lag was: Benz's engine did not displace the horse and carriage industry, and mainstream adoption came only in 1908 when Ford began mass producing the Model T, decades after the 1879 patent.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: the origins of the modern automobile industry

claims.claim: The delegation of technology policy to politicians advised by experts rested on public trust that has since eroded: consistent empirical evidence shows that trust in both government and experts has declined in recent years.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: recent decades, drawing on Pew survey evidence

claims.claim: Time pressure produces two distinct fact failures: the facts about a new technology may simply not exist yet, or regulators may select the wrong, contested, or irrelevant facts as the basis of regulation.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: conditions of incessant and accelerating technological change

claims.claim: In the Airbnb case, the selection of the relevant facts and the residency rule that followed from it benefit vested interests, most obviously the hotel industry that stands to lose from Airbnb's competition.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: short term rental rules requiring hosts to reside in the property

claims.claim: The premises on which regulation of a new technology is built may not be facts at all, or at least not the most relevant facts about that innovation, as the assumption that Airbnb hosts are simply chasing easy money illustrates.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: regulation of platform based innovations such as Airbnb

claims.claim: Contesting the safety rationale offered for restricting Uber, the authors argue that the two way rating system and the algorithmic matching of drivers and customers already provide an effective means of policing drivers and ensuring a safe ride.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: ride hailing platforms with reciprocal ratings and algorithmic matching

claims.claim: There is a systematic disconnect between the facts regulators identify as important and the actual experience and wishes of most consumers.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: regulatory debates over platform services such as Uber

claims.claim: The problem is not regulator bad faith: the acceleration of innovation cycles means that selecting the relevant facts is difficult even under the best conditions and with the best intentions, while simply waiting is likely to bring further complications and criticism.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: accelerating innovation cycles
independent of agency capture

claims.claim: The post truth diagnosis is self defeating as a basis for regulation: if there is no objective basis on which to act, the conclusion is inertia or reproduction of the status quo, which is precisely the regulatory paralysis the diagnosis purports to describe.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: if the skeptical post fact account of regulation is accepted

claims.claim: The response to contested facts should not be to abandon facts, but to identify alternative grounds for regulation that would make the regulation of innovative products and services more effective and more legitimate.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531

claims.claim: In a world where regulatory competition is the new normal, regulators can pay a heavy economic price for being overly cautious or for abandoning the attempt to establish a meaningful basis for regulation, because first mover markets capture the benefits.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: global markets with mobile investment and jurisdictional competition

claims.claim: Lawmaking and regulatory design need to become more proactive, dynamic, and responsive.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531

claims.claim: Data on investment in new technology can be used as an index or proxy for the necessity of regulation, supplying the signal that fact based regulation cannot generate in time.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: where venture and investment data on the technology are available

claims.claim: Using investment data would let regulators act proactively, avoid wasting resources on technologies unlikely to reach the market, and define the scope of a technology more accurately by focusing on the type of firm attracting investor attention.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531

claims.claim: Data on the timing of investment is a reliable indicator of a technology's commercial maturity, because high levels of investor activity signal that the technology is about to be ready for commercial exploitation, which tells regulators when to intervene.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: when early stage investments peak and later stage investments take off

claims.claim: Regulation should be demand driven, meaning its substantive direction should follow the interests of consumers, and where there is genuine demand for a product or technology it should in principle be permitted.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: where genuine consumer demand for the technology can be shown

claims.claim: A demand driven approach does not require ignoring the risks and negative side effects of new technology; what it requires is that entrenched interests with a clear stake in obstructing a disruptive product or service not be allowed to dominate the debate.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531

claims.claim: Regulatory experimentation matters within a single jurisdiction and not only across jurisdictions, because it gives regulators data on the real world effects of a particular regulatory scheme in a comparable setting.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: comparable settings within one jurisdiction

claims.claim: Regulators must abandon their fixation on finality and legal certainty and instead treat regulatory decisions as contingent and open ended stages in a longer process.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: regulation of fast moving technologies

claims.claim: A principle based approach gives regulators greater openness and flexibility and prevents innovative technologies and the companies developing them from becoming bogged down in the regulatory thicket produced by a rule focused approach.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: regulation of disruptive technologies

claims.claim: The principle based approach has a shortcoming the authors concede: it is usually impossible to comply with principles that could change after the fact, and the approach may let regulators promulgate fact based laws and rules through the backdoor.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: from the perspective of regulated companies operating under principles

claims.claim: The regulatory sandbox provides a safe space in which innovative products and services can be tested without being forced to comply with the otherwise applicable set of rules and regulations.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: the FCA sandbox announced in April 2016 for Fintech firms

claims.claim: The most interesting feature of the sandbox is that ideas, products, and services are tested in a live environment, made possible by a set of default parameters the FCA defined that can be altered case by case.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: default duration of three to six months
customer numbers sufficient for statistically relevant data
pre agreed safeguards and disclosure to customers

claims.claim: The sandbox generates legitimacy as well as information: because the tested technology remains open to discussion and democratic supervision, public entitlement to participate in regulatory debates creates a renewed sense of legitimacy that justifies the regulation.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: where the technology has consequences that flow into everyday lives

claims.claim: A data based regulatory environment requires measures built on flexible and inclusive processes that involve startups and established companies, regulators, experts, and the public.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: data based regulatory environments

claims.claim: The flexible, data based, sandbox style regulatory approach already adopted in the financial industry is expected to expand into other areas of innovation and technology.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, Regulation Tomorrow What Happens When Technology Is Faster Than the Law (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2834531
scope_conditions: starting from financial regulation

claims.claim: The 1991 passage of Section 7.32 of the Model Business Corporation Act triggered a wave of state authorization of shareholder control agreements, adopted specifically to secure the validity of such agreements rather than leaving validity to uncertain judicial development.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: United States state corporate law
post 1991

claims.claim: US corporate codes function as enabling statutes that give enterprises wide flexibility, but that flexibility stops at mandatory provisions, which the parties cannot contract around.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: United States corporate codes

claims.claim: Although shareholder agreements are authorized and shaped by corporation code provisions, their construction is governed by ordinary contract interpretation rules, so statutory authorization does not displace contract doctrine.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: United States, Delaware law illustrated by Salamone v. Gorman

claims.claim: Shareholder agreement terms that limit board authority are vulnerable to invalidation, and the dominant judicial rationale is that such agreements tie the hands of directors and make it impossible for them to exercise discretion over the matters the agreement settles.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: provisions that encroach on the directors' statutory authority to manage the business and affairs of the corporation

claims.claim: Under MBCA Section 7.32 the ten year duration limit is only a default rule, unlike the corresponding limit for voting trusts, so parties who specify a longer term are permitted to have it.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: agreements formed under MBCA Section 7.32

claims.claim: Duration ceilings contained in voting trust statutes do not carry over to other types of shareholder agreements, and courts have repeatedly sustained shareholder agreements intended to run indefinitely.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: agreements other than voting trusts

claims.claim: Because public and close corporation shareholders differ materially in bargaining power, close corporation shareholders should be granted greater flexibility to order their affairs by agreement.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: closely held corporations

claims.claim: A shareholder agreement authorized under MBCA Section 7.32 ceases to be effective once the corporation's stock is listed on a national securities exchange or regularly traded in a dealer maintained market, so the going public event terminates the arrangement.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: MBCA jurisdictions
corporation becomes publicly traded

claims.claim: MBCA Section 7.32 requires unanimity, so agreements that bind only a block of shareholders rather than all of them cannot rely on that section and must find authorization elsewhere.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: agreements seeking MBCA Section 7.32 protection

claims.claim: MBCA Section 7.32 requires a writing but, departing from earlier statutes, does not require the agreement to sit in the articles or bylaws, so stand alone written shareholder agreements are expressly valid.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: MBCA Section 7.32 agreements

claims.claim: The Model Act conditions the arrangement on notice to the market for shares by requiring a legend on the stock certificates that flags the agreement to purchasers of covered shares.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: MBCA Section 7.32 agreements

claims.claim: Shareholder agreements matter more in closely held corporations because minority holders have sunk substantial time or capital into the enterprise yet cannot exit through sale, since their shares lack a ready market.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: closely held corporations
dissatisfied minority shareholders

claims.claim: Voting arrangements are not self executing: their existence does not relieve the corporation of observing the legal formalities of director and shareholder action.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: voting trusts, pooling agreements, and irrevocable proxies

claims.claim: Courts are split on whether a corporation is bound by a shareholder agreement it did not sign: some hold the corporation bound where all shareholders are parties to a valid agreement, while others refuse to bind it.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: all shareholders are parties to the agreement
corporation is not formally a party

claims.claim: Corporate claims frequently go unpursued because the decision to sue rests with directors who are often the wrongdoers themselves, which is why shareholders resort to derivative actions.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: injury is to the corporation rather than to shareholders individually

claims.claim: A shareholder suing derivatively sues on the corporation's behalf and cannot convert the action into a personal one, even where the corporate injury has impaired the value of that shareholder's own stock.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: injury runs to the corporation

claims.claim: To escape the procedural hurdles of derivative litigation and recover directly, a shareholder must persuade the court that those abusing control of the corporation harmed the shareholder directly rather than the entity.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: direct as opposed to derivative suits
Delaware courts ask who suffered the harm and who would receive the recovery

claims.claim: Under the MBCA a purchaser of shares who bought without knowledge of an existing shareholder control agreement may obtain rescission of the purchase.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: purchaser lacked knowledge of the agreement at the time of purchase

claims.claim: Veto rights are the price minority shareholders extract for capital: minority holders may withhold capital contributions unless they receive veto powers over major corporate decisions.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: closely held corporations seeking minority capital

claims.claim: Courts have recognized an enhanced fiduciary duty among participants in closely held corporations, holding that majority shareholders owe fiduciary duties not only to the corporation but to minority shareholders as a class.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: closely held corporations
majority or controlling shareholders

claims.claim: Fiduciary responsibility follows actual control rather than formal office: a shareholder exercising absolute de facto control over a corporation owes fiduciary duties regardless of whether that shareholder holds de jure title.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: shareholder exercises absolute de facto control or dominance

claims.claim: Contractual consent to a cash out does not extinguish fiduciary claims: a minority shareholder who agreed to receive cash for shares may still challenge the merger as a breach of fiduciary duty.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: close corporations
merger structured to eliminate a minority shareholder
Third Circuit in Coleman v. Taub

claims.claim: US law gives corporate participants wide latitude to restrict share transfers, and such restrictions are usually upheld unless their terms are unreasonable in the circumstances.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: restrictions imposed by articles, bylaws, or shareholder agreement

claims.claim: Transfer restrictions cannot be imposed on shareholders who did not consent: Delaware refuses to allow them unless the holders are parties to the agreement or voted for the restriction, and courts have refused to apply restrictions retroactively to nonconsenting shares.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: Delaware and states following the same rule
previously issued shares

claims.claim: Drag-along rights raise the price the majority can obtain because a buyer facing the prospect of continuing with remaining minority shareholders would otherwise discount its offer for the majority stake.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: sale of a majority stake in a closely held corporation

claims.claim: Drag-along rights are likely enforceable in Delaware absent fraud or duress, because Delaware rejects the de facto merger doctrine and therefore does not trigger statutory formalities such as appraisal rights.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: Delaware corporations
no fraud or duress

claims.claim: A buy-sell agreement survives bankruptcy more reliably when it is not merely executory: because bankruptcy trustees may void executory agreements, an agreement that obliges both the shareholders and the entity to buy and sell is more likely to be enforced.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: shareholder becomes insolvent or enters bankruptcy

claims.claim: Standstill agreements defraud shareholders who are not parties to them in two distinct ways: by violating the shareholder's right to the best available merger or transaction and by discouraging unsolicited tender offers in which a significant control premium could be realized.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: standstill agreements binding only some shareholders
applying the Schreiber v. Carney definition of fraud

claims.claim: Standstill agreements entrench management and can lead a company into stagnation, so they may operate prejudicially on shareholders' property rights.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: standstill agreements restricting voting

claims.claim: The articles function as the corporation's constitution and are deliberately hard to change, requiring action by both directors and shareholders unlike most corporate decisions.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: United States corporations

claims.claim: Where a shareholder agreement is folded into the charter or bylaws, it thereby becomes subject to whatever amendment procedure those documents or the statute provide, so charter integration exposes the arrangement to later modification.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: agreement incorporated into charter or bylaws rather than free standing

claims.claim: Because shareholder agreements are designed to displace corporate formalities such as majority rule, it is reasonable to require that the intended degree of deviation be set out explicitly in the agreement.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: agreements that deviate from default corporate norms

claims.claim: Shareholders frequently fail to place their agreements in the charter or bylaws, sometimes through ignorance or inadvertence and sometimes deliberately, because charters are public records and the parties prefer not to expose their arrangement to outsiders.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: closely held corporations

claims.claim: Absent explicit statutory authorization, many courts have refused to enforce veto provisions contained in shareholder agreements, which is why such provisions should be implemented through charter or bylaw amendment.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: states without statutes specifically authorizing shareholder control agreements
veto or supermajority provisions

claims.claim: States lacking specific authorization for shareholder control agreements generally still permit departure from the default rule of director control if the departure is set forth in the corporation's charter or bylaws.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: states without shareholder control agreement statutes

claims.claim: Even though New York decisions such as Adler v. Svingos suggest veto arrangements outside the charter will be specifically enforced, the better practice remains to amend the charter to insert them.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: New York close corporations
high voting or unanimity requirements

claims.claim: Damages are usually an inadequate remedy for breach of a shareholder agreement because they are too speculative, even where the aggrieved shareholder holds a direct cause of action.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: breach of a valid shareholder agreement

claims.claim: Because damages rarely provide an adequate remedy for breach of a shareholder agreement, refusing specific enforcement amounts in substance to declaring the agreement invalid.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Shareholder Agreements - National Report of the United States of America (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3017612
scope_conditions: suits to enforce shareholder voting agreements

claims.claim: The extent to which a company uses data and algorithms will separate the winning companies of the future from the rest, because algorithmically driven firms gather consumer behavior data and instantaneously feed it back into an improved consumer experience.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, The ‘Unmediated’ and ‘Tech-Driven’ Corporate Governance of Today's Winning Companies (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2922176
scope_conditions: applies to companies competing on consumer relevance in digitized, networked markets

claims.claim: Algorithms substitute for human middlemen inside firms, and this substitution is what produces flatter, unmediated organizations in which the best idea, rather than hierarchical position, prevails.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, The ‘Unmediated’ and ‘Tech-Driven’ Corporate Governance of Today's Winning Companies (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2922176

claims.claim: Platform disruptors such as Uber and Airbnb did not decentralize their industries by eliminating intermediaries; they decentralized by replacing incumbent intermediaries with algorithmic ones.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, The ‘Unmediated’ and ‘Tech-Driven’ Corporate Governance of Today's Winning Companies (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2922176
scope_conditions: transportation and hospitality industries as the worked examples

claims.claim: A focus on quarterly earnings and short-term stock price performance distracts an organization from identifying the strategies that would keep the firm relevant, which is why financially successful companies can still lose their market.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, The ‘Unmediated’ and ‘Tech-Driven’ Corporate Governance of Today's Winning Companies (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2922176
scope_conditions: listed companies are particularly prone to overweighting financial metrics

claims.claim: In companies that concentrate on established products, the executives who understand innovation and consumer experience, the very people responsible for the firm's initial success, are pushed to the margins of core decision making.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, The ‘Unmediated’ and ‘Tech-Driven’ Corporate Governance of Today's Winning Companies (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2922176
scope_conditions: companies built around existing and successful products or services

claims.claim: Microsoft lost relevance under Steve Ballmer because it optimized for short-term financial metrics instead of designing products for the next generation of consumers, even while sales tripled and profits doubled.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, The ‘Unmediated’ and ‘Tech-Driven’ Corporate Governance of Today's Winning Companies (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2922176
scope_conditions: Ballmer era, 2000 to 2015

claims.claim: Reforms that increase executive accountability to shareholders and increase shareholder control over executives do not solve the problem of corporate short-term focus.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, The ‘Unmediated’ and ‘Tech-Driven’ Corporate Governance of Today's Winning Companies (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2922176
scope_conditions: post-2000 shareholder-empowerment reforms

claims.claim: Increasing shareholder control over executives can be actively counterproductive: it further incentivizes the damaging emphasis on quarterly financial reporting that reform was meant to cure.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, The ‘Unmediated’ and ‘Tech-Driven’ Corporate Governance of Today's Winning Companies (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2922176

claims.claim: Top-down corporate governance reform measures rarely, if ever, produce genuine change in the governance or culture of firms, and are commonly met with indifference, skepticism, or hostility from management.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, The ‘Unmediated’ and ‘Tech-Driven’ Corporate Governance of Today's Winning Companies (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2922176
scope_conditions: listed companies and their governance experts

claims.claim: Much corporate governance reform consists of repackaging old content under new or revised labels rather than introducing new governance.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, The ‘Unmediated’ and ‘Tech-Driven’ Corporate Governance of Today's Winning Companies (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2922176
scope_conditions: illustrated by the 2016 Commonsense Principles of Corporate Governance

claims.claim: Corporate governance intermediaries such as lawyers, accountants, auditors and consultants respond to governance requirements with minimum compliance, applying minimal effort for maximum compliance.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, The ‘Unmediated’ and ‘Tech-Driven’ Corporate Governance of Today's Winning Companies (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2922176
scope_conditions: intermediaries advising listed companies

claims.claim: Corporate governance initiatives designed to encourage long-term thinking rarely work as policymakers expect them to.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, The ‘Unmediated’ and ‘Tech-Driven’ Corporate Governance of Today's Winning Companies (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2922176
scope_conditions: stewardship codes and comparable long-termism initiatives

claims.claim: Mobilizing investors as stewards leads managers to ask the wrong questions about sustainable success: rather than pushing firms toward innovation and relevancy, such measures simply reinforce the centralized shareholder primacy view they were meant to soften.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, The ‘Unmediated’ and ‘Tech-Driven’ Corporate Governance of Today's Winning Companies (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2922176
scope_conditions: jurisdictions that have adopted stewardship codes

claims.claim: Stewardship pressures push companies toward an unhealthy focus on short-term dividends and share buybacks designed to please the stock market, the opposite of the long-term orientation the codes intend.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, The ‘Unmediated’ and ‘Tech-Driven’ Corporate Governance of Today's Winning Companies (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2922176
scope_conditions: companies subject to institutional investor stewardship pressure

claims.claim: A focus on dividends and share buybacks makes it extremely difficult for a company to fund the innovation investment on which long-term relevancy depends.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, The ‘Unmediated’ and ‘Tech-Driven’ Corporate Governance of Today's Winning Companies (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2922176
scope_conditions: S&P 500 companies, 2012 to 2016 revenue growth data

claims.claim: Ten of the thirteen S&P 500 companies with above-average revenue growth over the 2012 to 2016 period had never paid a dividend and had never engaged in share buybacks.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, The ‘Unmediated’ and ‘Tech-Driven’ Corporate Governance of Today's Winning Companies (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2922176
scope_conditions: thirteen S&P 500 companies with above-average revenue growth, 2012 to 2016

claims.claim: Code guidance assigning the board responsibility for long-term value creation, as in the 2016 Dutch Corporate Governance Code, is difficult to implement because neither long-term value nor the intended beneficiary of that value is defined.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, The ‘Unmediated’ and ‘Tech-Driven’ Corporate Governance of Today's Winning Companies (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2922176
scope_conditions: Dutch Corporate Governance Code, December 2016

claims.claim: Society is moving from a centralized infrastructure to a decentralized, unmediated, and interconnected one, and from vertical hierarchies to horizontal, open, and autonomous networks; this transition, not the short-term versus long-term debate, is the relevant frame for corporate governance.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, The ‘Unmediated’ and ‘Tech-Driven’ Corporate Governance of Today's Winning Companies (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2922176
scope_conditions: driven and accelerated by rapid technological change

claims.claim: Platform companies embrace an unmediated, flat, and inclusive culture in which trust and value are generated through the platform itself rather than through the management of workers and physical assets.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, The ‘Unmediated’ and ‘Tech-Driven’ Corporate Governance of Today's Winning Companies (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2922176
scope_conditions: platform companies built on peer-to-peer transactions, such as Airbnb and Uber

claims.claim: Blockchain-based smart contracts in digital marketplaces are the technology most likely to extend and lead the decentralization of the relationship between businesses and their counterparties.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, The ‘Unmediated’ and ‘Tech-Driven’ Corporate Governance of Today's Winning Companies (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2922176
scope_conditions: further accelerated by the sharing economy, the Internet of Things, and artificial intelligence

claims.claim: Despite the obvious benefits of technology applications in corporate governance, the technological revolution has not yet produced wide acceptance of unmediated or decentralized corporate governance structures and practices.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, The ‘Unmediated’ and ‘Tech-Driven’ Corporate Governance of Today's Winning Companies (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2922176
scope_conditions: as of 2017

claims.claim: Only seven percent of the 250 leading companies on the Forbes Global 2000 list have a CEO who is personally active and connected on Twitter.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, The ‘Unmediated’ and ‘Tech-Driven’ Corporate Governance of Today's Winning Companies (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2922176
scope_conditions: 250 leading companies on the Forbes Global 2000 list, data as of 2017

claims.claim: Traditional coordination through hierarchy, command, and control is suboptimal for generating the innovation a firm needs to survive.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, The ‘Unmediated’ and ‘Tech-Driven’ Corporate Governance of Today's Winning Companies (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2922176
scope_conditions: firms competing in fast-moving, technology-driven markets

claims.claim: Inclusive and unmediated stakeholder relationships demand a much higher degree of cooperation, loyalty, and mutual trust than control-oriented, centralized, and vertical organizational forms do.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, The ‘Unmediated’ and ‘Tech-Driven’ Corporate Governance of Today's Winning Companies (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2922176

claims.claim: Even after recent reforms, the corporate governance framework remains framed in terms of hierarchy, which is why it fits poorly with looser and unmediated stakeholder relationships.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, The ‘Unmediated’ and ‘Tech-Driven’ Corporate Governance of Today's Winning Companies (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2922176
scope_conditions: applies to the reform wave through 2017

claims.claim: The use of legalese and substantial involvement of the legal department in corporate communications substantially damages the originality and authenticity of those communications, making them mediated and less effective.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, The ‘Unmediated’ and ‘Tech-Driven’ Corporate Governance of Today's Winning Companies (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2922176
scope_conditions: corporate communications intended to build trust and dialogue with stakeholders

claims.claim: Centralized, hierarchical environments do not value honesty and reward good news only, so nobody wants to carry bad news upward, and problems are therefore detected late.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, The ‘Unmediated’ and ‘Tech-Driven’ Corporate Governance of Today's Winning Companies (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2922176
scope_conditions: heavily mediated and redacted corporate environments; illustrated by Nokia, Volkswagen and Samsung

claims.claim: Unmediated corporate communications generate real-time feedback for executives, because social media platforms return instant crowd reactions in the form of comments, likes, and shares that can be measured and acted on.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, The ‘Unmediated’ and ‘Tech-Driven’ Corporate Governance of Today's Winning Companies (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2922176

claims.claim: Corporate lawyers and governance experts still discourage executives from communicating in a personalized, speech-like way, particularly on social media, out of fear of market misunderstanding and subsequent liability.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, The ‘Unmediated’ and ‘Tech-Driven’ Corporate Governance of Today's Winning Companies (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2922176
scope_conditions: current advisory practice as of 2017

claims.claim: The monitoring and advising roles of the board are no longer sufficient, and a board confined to those roles is a missed opportunity to obtain unmediated and relevant market feedback on company initiatives.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, The ‘Unmediated’ and ‘Tech-Driven’ Corporate Governance of Today's Winning Companies (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2922176
scope_conditions: successful companies already operating beyond the academic monitoring debate

claims.claim: The authors stipulate a category of director, the feedback provider, defined as a director appointed to supply management with unmediated and relevant input from the market, which is what a firm needs in order to plan for continued relevancy.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, The ‘Unmediated’ and ‘Tech-Driven’ Corporate Governance of Today's Winning Companies (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2922176
scope_conditions: directors with technologist, entrepreneurial, or academic backgrounds

claims.claim: Forty-five percent of directors at the thirteen S&P 500 companies with above-average revenue growth over the last five years are feedback providers who make board decisions more data-driven.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, The ‘Unmediated’ and ‘Tech-Driven’ Corporate Governance of Today's Winning Companies (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2922176
scope_conditions: thirteen S&P 500 companies with above-average five-year revenue growth

claims.claim: It is feasible that in the not too distant future an artificial intelligence will hold an independent board seat with voting authority and be trusted to make smarter, data-driven choices than human directors.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, The ‘Unmediated’ and ‘Tech-Driven’ Corporate Governance of Today's Winning Companies (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2922176
scope_conditions: extrapolated from the appointment of the algorithm Vital at Deep Knowledge Ventures and Alicia T at Tieto

claims.claim: Critics who dismiss artificial intelligence on boards as science fiction not worth engaging are wrong: AI on boards is a real prospect, and technologies such as blockchain-based smart contracts will both disrupt corporate governance and supply solutions to it.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, The ‘Unmediated’ and ‘Tech-Driven’ Corporate Governance of Today's Winning Companies (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2922176

claims.claim: Fundamental flaws in the DAO's code allowed hackers to move one third of contributed funds to a subsidiary account, ending that initiative, but the flaws were in the implementation and do not defeat the DAO vision, which developers continue to rebuild.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, The ‘Unmediated’ and ‘Tech-Driven’ Corporate Governance of Today's Winning Companies (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2922176
scope_conditions: the original DAO, launched May 2016 on Ethereum

claims.claim: In a decentralized autonomous organization a series of smart contracts grants token holders voting rights, so the blockchain-based smart contract performs the function that articles of incorporation or bylaws perform in a conventional company.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, The ‘Unmediated’ and ‘Tech-Driven’ Corporate Governance of Today's Winning Companies (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2922176
scope_conditions: the original DAO structure, running on the Ethereum public blockchain

claims.claim: Contemporary corporate governance reforms are unlikely to work as policymakers and regulators intend, because experts agree improvement is needed but disagree widely on what good corporate governance is or how to achieve it.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, The ‘Unmediated’ and ‘Tech-Driven’ Corporate Governance of Today's Winning Companies (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2922176

claims.claim: The corporate governance frameworks developed in the 2000s had little or no impact on the performance of listed companies during the financial crisis, and the number, scale, and effects of corporate scandals are not diminishing.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, The ‘Unmediated’ and ‘Tech-Driven’ Corporate Governance of Today's Winning Companies (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2922176
scope_conditions: listed companies during the 2008 financial crisis

claims.claim: Regulators should nudge companies and their stakeholders toward recognizing the strategic and financial benefits of an unmediated and technology-based approach to corporate governance, rather than mandating further top-down reform.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, The ‘Unmediated’ and ‘Tech-Driven’ Corporate Governance of Today's Winning Companies (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2922176

claims.claim: Companies that adopt unmediated and technology-driven governance gain a competitive advantage in attracting talent, raising capital, finding partners, and above all in remaining relevant in hyper-competitive global markets.
claims.citation: Mark Fenwick, Wulf A. Kaal, Erik P. M. Vermeulen, The ‘Unmediated’ and ‘Tech-Driven’ Corporate Governance of Today's Winning Companies (2017). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=2922176
scope_conditions: hyper-competitive global markets shaped by social media, blockchain, DAOs and artificial intelligence

claims.claim: The crypto economy can continue to develop without falling back on centralized regulating authorities only if two things exist: a system for evaluating reputation and trust, and a fair dispute resolution system that guarantees certainty of outcomes.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vlad Andrei, Blockchain Infrastructure for Measuring Domain Specific Reputation in Autonomous Decentralized and A (2018). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3125822
scope_conditions: applies to transaction systems between anonymous parties
assumes centralized regulators are to be avoided

claims.claim: Reputation value in any decentralized reputational system can be corrupted through three channels: direct purchase of reputation, automated worthless work, and degeneration of the system into a majority of inexpert opinions.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vlad Andrei, Blockchain Infrastructure for Measuring Domain Specific Reputation in Autonomous Decentralized and A (2018). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3125822
scope_conditions: decentralized reputation systems
anonymous participants

claims.claim: The problems of corruption, Sybil attacks, and tyranny of the majority have plagued every previous autonomous decentralized reputation platform, so they are the design constraints any new architecture must meet.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vlad Andrei, Blockchain Infrastructure for Measuring Domain Specific Reputation in Autonomous Decentralized and A (2018). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3125822
scope_conditions: prior autonomous decentralized reputation platforms

claims.claim: The novel element of the architecture is a dynamical evolutionary feedback system that ties an expert's reputation to their proof of ability and productive contributions, verified by validation pools that are generated by public fees sent to the system.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vlad Andrei, Blockchain Infrastructure for Measuring Domain Specific Reputation in Autonomous Decentralized and A (2018). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3125822
scope_conditions: reputation is only created by fee bearing validation requests

claims.claim: When a fee bearing evidence of work post enters the platform, half the newly minted sem tokens are staked in the poster's name as an upvote bet and the other half are staked against the post and left unassigned, so the poster's only direct reward for off-platform work is a contested stake.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vlad Andrei, Blockchain Infrastructure for Measuring Domain Specific Reputation in Autonomous Decentralized and A (2018). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3125822
scope_conditions: post must be linked to a previous post in the forum
minting is proportional to the fee at a preset conversion ratio

claims.claim: Every validation request opens a betting pool in which experts stake expertise specific sem tokens for or against the post, the winning side splits the losing side's stakes, and upvotes win ties.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vlad Andrei, Blockchain Infrastructure for Measuring Domain Specific Reputation in Autonomous Decentralized and A (2018). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3125822
scope_conditions: staking is limited to the expertise specific token

claims.claim: The hidden voting scheme depends on the choice of symmetric encryption protocol: a poorly chosen protocol exposes the platform to a birthday problem attack in which malicious voters submit an encrypted key that can be decrypted in two different ways, letting them retroactively choose their vote.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vlad Andrei, Blockchain Infrastructure for Measuring Domain Specific Reputation in Autonomous Decentralized and A (2018). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3125822
scope_conditions: applies to the hidden vote reveal step of a validation pool

claims.claim: A newcomer cannot buy reputation with money because the 50/50 staking of newly minted tokens leaves incumbent experts with complete power to decide whether the newcomer's contribution was positive; a losing applicant forfeits all reputation in the expertise.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vlad Andrei, Blockchain Infrastructure for Measuring Domain Specific Reputation in Autonomous Decentralized and A (2018). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3125822
scope_conditions: applies at entry into an existing expertise tag
assumes incumbent experts vote in their own interest

claims.claim: The platform's ability to function among anonymous and potentially hostile users is conditional: it holds only if smart contracts that engage experts for off-platform work voluntarily include the recommended protocol choices, which the minimal core itself does not require.
