claims.claim: What the authors call a breach on a particular insurance contract does not necessarily imply any losses for the consumer, so underwriter breach and consumer harm are decoupled in this design.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Decentralized Underwriting (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396542

claims.claim: Hedge fund managers adopt emerging technology because it converts into a fee premium: technology driven outperformance makes them more competitive than other funds and financial institutions, which in turn lets them charge higher fees.
claims.citation: Kaal, Financial Technology and Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3409548
scope_conditions: private investment fund managers competing on performance

claims.claim: The traditional 2 and 20 fee model has become increasingly difficult to justify, and embracing modern financial products is what allows managers to produce returns that still support that model.
claims.citation: Kaal, Financial Technology and Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3409548
scope_conditions: recent years of compressed hedge fund returns

claims.claim: Current hedge fund trading technology is hard coded by humans, whereas deep learning systems can be given a simple command and derive a result from data on their own; this is the operative difference between legacy quantitative tools and machine learning.
claims.citation: Kaal, Financial Technology and Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3409548

claims.claim: Easier access to trading data and to information about the hedge fund industry has been a significant factor in the growth of hedge fund assets, because analytic platforms let managers manipulate peer and style data and build targeted marketing materials.
claims.citation: Kaal, Financial Technology and Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3409548
scope_conditions: commercial hedge fund databases and analytic platforms available

claims.claim: Systematic, computer model driven funds do not reliably outperform human managed funds: research finds the typical systematic fund does not always perform as well as funds run by human managers.
claims.citation: Kaal, Financial Technology and Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3409548
scope_conditions: typical systematic fund
Preqin research as of 2016

claims.claim: Hedge funds that base their strategies on artificial intelligence have delivered better results than the industry average over the preceding five years.
claims.citation: Kaal, Financial Technology and Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3409548
scope_conditions: five year window preceding 2019

claims.claim: Machine learning improves portfolio diversification by searching for instruments that are uncorrelated with each other and that still match the requirements of the target risk profile.
claims.citation: Kaal, Financial Technology and Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3409548
scope_conditions: portfolio construction against a defined risk profile

claims.claim: In the Numerai model, using artificial intelligence to synthesize competing data scientist models into a meta model raises efficiency and improves capital allocation by reducing overhead costs.
claims.citation: Kaal, Financial Technology and Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3409548
scope_conditions: crowdsourced data science model with a synthesized meta model

claims.claim: Repeated use of the same data set by data scientists creates an overfitting risk: the training model overfits the test set, which limits the performance of the applied model on a different dataset.
claims.citation: Kaal, Financial Technology and Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3409548
scope_conditions: data scientists reusing a single data set repetitively

claims.claim: Requiring data scientists to stake a cryptocurrency on their own predictions is a workable remedy for overfitting, because the stake expresses confidence in live performance and lets the fund select the optimal model.
claims.citation: Kaal, Financial Technology and Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3409548
scope_conditions: crowdsourced modeling competition with a stakeable token

claims.claim: Blockchain adoption by private investment funds followed a staged path: minimal use from 2000 to 2012, then experimentation through separate new fund entities beginning in 2012, and from 2015 the creation of blockchain substructures inside existing funds.
claims.citation: Kaal, Financial Technology and Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3409548
scope_conditions: private investment fund industry, 2000 to 2015

claims.claim: High levels of investor activity in the blockchain sector are a reliable indicator of the commercial maturity of blockchain technology.
claims.citation: Kaal, Financial Technology and Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3409548

claims.claim: Business, administrative, and legal processes that depend on legal intermediaries may become redundant as blockchain technology advances and is accepted, with ledger keeping services such as notary and registry services, motions practice, and title companies among the first to disappear.
claims.citation: Kaal, Financial Technology and Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3409548
scope_conditions: as blockchain acceptance and implementation advance

claims.claim: The 2018 ICO boom exposed a core limitation of blockchain technology: ICOs sold investors decentralized infrastructure products on the assumption that a baseline infrastructure already existed, and that assumption proved false.
claims.citation: Kaal, Financial Technology and Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3409548
scope_conditions: ICO market of 2018
projects presupposing mature base layer infrastructure

claims.claim: Smart contracts face a legal origin problem: lawyers may argue that they are void and unenforceable, and contract law rules on formation, interpretation, conditions and remedies require substantive adjustment before smart contracts fit within it.
claims.citation: Kaal, Financial Technology and Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3409548
scope_conditions: absent statutory recognition of smart contracts

claims.claim: The legal limitations on smart contracts are slowly disappearing through state legislation, as shown by Arizona's 2017 law making smart contracts fully enforceable and Delaware's parallel Blockchain Initiative proposals.
claims.citation: Kaal, Financial Technology and Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3409548
scope_conditions: United States state law, as of 2017 to 2019

claims.claim: Blockchain-enabled sharing services are unlikely to be accepted quickly or without resistance, because incumbents challenged by new ways of delivering a service or product will resist, as the existing legal disputes over sharing platforms demonstrate.
claims.citation: Kaal, Financial Technology and Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3409548
scope_conditions: services that displace incumbent delivery models

claims.claim: The absence of regulatory recognition of blockchain technology is not merely an inconvenience: it hinders implementation of the technology across industries and undermines the conversion of infrastructure to blockchain.
claims.citation: Kaal, Financial Technology and Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3409548
scope_conditions: jurisdictions lacking regulatory recognition of blockchain

claims.claim: The Northern Trust and IBM blockchain removes a specific inefficiency in private equity deal practice by letting all involved parties in a deal look at a single compiled version of the transaction and all data relating to it, rather than reconciling multiple copies of the deal documents.
claims.citation: Kaal, Financial Technology and Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3409548
scope_conditions: private equity deal administration
Northern Trust and IBM partnership from February 2017

claims.claim: Blockchain-based funds can invert the traditional secrecy of hedge funds: the LendingRobot ledger discloses detailed holdings and supplies a hash code signature evidencing that the data is tamper proof.
claims.citation: Kaal, Financial Technology and Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3409548
scope_conditions: funds recording trades to a public blockchain ledger

claims.claim: A fund constituted purely through smart contracts on the Ethereum blockchain may have no domicile, foreign or domestic, which makes jurisdiction over blockchain transactions a genuine problem for the funds that use the technology.
claims.citation: Kaal, Financial Technology and Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3409548
scope_conditions: funds set up entirely through Ethereum smart contracting

claims.claim: Managers of funds that exist entirely in cyberspace cannot assume they are judgment proof; the practical consequence of operating across a global node network is exposure to more regulation, not less.
claims.citation: Kaal, Financial Technology and Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3409548
scope_conditions: funds operating through digital currencies and smart contracts without a domicile

claims.claim: Legacy systems at private investment funds and banks are more expensive, more error prone, and slower than emerging blockchain technologies, a gap illustrated by the $1.7 trillion in processing fees banks charged in 2014.
claims.citation: Kaal, Financial Technology and Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3409548
scope_conditions: comparison of bank and fund legacy processing systems with blockchain

claims.claim: Because blockchain is transparent, verifiable, self-authenticating and self-enforcing, transactions can settle instantaneously at near zero cost, and it is this combination plus technology-driven democratized trust that drove the financial industry's large blockchain investments out of fear of obsolescence.
claims.citation: Kaal, Financial Technology and Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3409548

claims.claim: Machine learning applied to execution algorithms lets large orders be split into thousands of smaller transactions without moving the market, with the algorithm adjusting its aggressiveness to market conditions.
claims.citation: Kaal, Financial Technology and Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3409548
scope_conditions: large order execution

claims.claim: Artificial intelligence and machine learning are used far more heavily for idea generation and portfolio optimization than for execution: two thirds of surveyed funds use them to generate trading ideas and optimize portfolios, while only just over a quarter use automation to execute trades.
claims.citation: Kaal, Financial Technology and Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3409548
scope_conditions: 2018 BarclayHedge survey respondents

claims.claim: Adoption of artificial intelligence in hedge funds remains partial rather than total: more than four out of ten survey respondents still rely on conventional human thinking to guide their investment processes.
claims.citation: Kaal, Financial Technology and Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3409548
scope_conditions: 2018 BarclayHedge survey respondents

claims.claim: Whether deep learning can identify particular features of a stock that would be profitable remains contested rather than settled.
claims.citation: Kaal, Financial Technology and Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3409548

claims.claim: Digital currencies can serve as a hedge against traditional investments even though crypto investments can be as volatile as or more volatile than traditional ones, because they are not tied to the vicissitudes of the equity markets.
claims.citation: Kaal, Financial Technology and Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3409548
scope_conditions: portfolios seeking diversification away from traditional equity markets

claims.claim: Crypto hedge funds deliver diversification by giving investors exposure to a wide range of digital currencies without the risk of investing in either the underlying organization behind a protocol or the digital currency itself.
claims.citation: Kaal, Financial Technology and Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3409548
scope_conditions: crypto funds holding broad baskets of digital assets

claims.claim: The shift of the digital asset market back from the ICO model to the venture model since late 2017 has reduced, not increased, diversification for investors.
claims.citation: Kaal, Financial Technology and Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3409548
scope_conditions: digital asset market after late 2017

claims.claim: ICO funding collapsed as a share of blockchain startup fundraising, falling from 80% to around 35% by August 2018, recovering only marginally to 40% to 50% between September 2018 and February 2019, and dropping to 20% in March 2019.
claims.citation: Kaal, Financial Technology and Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3409548
scope_conditions: blockchain startup fundraising, 2018 to March 2019

claims.claim: The legacy private investment fund model delays liquidity: the investment process is long, complex and time intensive and leads up to a very late liquidity event in the form of an IPO or acquisition, which is why funds seek the early liquidity cryptocurrencies provide.
claims.citation: Kaal, Financial Technology and Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3409548
scope_conditions: private investment funds investing in blockchain start-ups

claims.claim: Cryptocurrencies created by blockchain start-ups generate investment returns that legacy investments cannot match.
claims.citation: Kaal, Financial Technology and Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3409548
scope_conditions: 2017 to 2018 cryptocurrency price appreciation

claims.claim: Recording every fund transaction together with its associated documentation on a blockchain cuts the significant costs of human oversight in recording, organizing and maintaining investment fund data and records.
claims.citation: Kaal, Financial Technology and Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3409548
scope_conditions: fund back office and recordkeeping functions

claims.claim: Recording all transactions in the public blockchain is what lets LendingRobot comply with its best execution obligations, making the public ledger a compliance instrument and not only an investment record.
claims.citation: Kaal, Financial Technology and Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3409548
scope_conditions: funds writing executed trades to a public ledger

claims.claim: Most large private equity and hedge fund advisers have not yet even considered combining blockchain with big data and artificial intelligence, leaving first mover efficiency gains to smaller competitors.
claims.citation: Kaal, Financial Technology and Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3409548
scope_conditions: large fund advisers as of 2019

claims.claim: Large managers will begin innovating only once the long-term benefits of the technologies exceed their implementation cost, and because that cost is much larger for large managers than for the smaller managers currently experimenting, the threshold for change is higher for them.
claims.citation: Kaal, Financial Technology and Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3409548
scope_conditions: larger fund managers facing higher implementation costs than smaller rivals

claims.claim: The structural characteristic of blockchain as a decentralized model for financial transactions disintermediates and disrupts the existing financial infrastructure, so funds implementing it are spearheading radical change in financial markets rather than merely adopting a tool.
claims.citation: Kaal, Financial Technology and Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3409548
scope_conditions: funds implementing decentralized financial infrastructure

claims.claim: Continued evolution and blockchain integration in the private investment fund industry depends on regulatory guidance, which the author identifies as essential rather than optional.
claims.citation: Kaal, Financial Technology and Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3409548
scope_conditions: private investment fund industry adopting blockchain

claims.claim: Direct hedge fund regulation faces a two sided trap: strong direct rules push hedge funds offshore where they escape regulation altogether, while weak rules leave investors without adequate protection.
claims.citation: Kaal, Indirect Regulation of Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3405660
scope_conditions: regulators rely on national direct regulatory tools
hedge funds retain the option to relocate offshore

claims.claim: Moral hazard in hedge fund lending persists even when the lender is fully informed, because high enforcement costs can make prevention too costly for the lender.
claims.citation: Kaal, Indirect Regulation of Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3405660
scope_conditions: lender to hedge fund relationship
enforcement costs are high relative to expected loss

claims.claim: Hedge fund secrecy is not incidental but competitively necessary: the less the market knows about a fund's activities, the easier it is for the fund to compete and generate the returns clients demand.
claims.citation: Kaal, Indirect Regulation of Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3405660

claims.claim: Neither national nor international regulators have the resources to fully investigate or regulate hedge fund activity, and the industry actively lobbies to preserve the resulting information asymmetries.
claims.citation: Kaal, Indirect Regulation of Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3405660

claims.claim: Indirect regulation of hedge funds attains most regulatory objectives while still leaving the industry the operating freedom it needs, which makes it preferable to the direct alternatives.
claims.citation: Kaal, Indirect Regulation of Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3405660

claims.claim: LTCM was diversified across markets but not across strategy, so its positions failed together; market level diversification does not imply strategy level diversification.
claims.citation: Kaal, Indirect Regulation of Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3405660
scope_conditions: stress conditions in which risk spreads widen across markets simultaneously

claims.claim: Conventional risk models understated LTCM's losses because the models were estimated during more stable periods and therefore did not describe behavior under stress.
claims.citation: Kaal, Indirect Regulation of Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3405660
scope_conditions: models calibrated on data from stable market periods
subsequent stress conditions

claims.claim: The same leverage that produced LTCM's high returns magnified its losses, so leverage is a symmetric amplifier rather than a one directional source of performance.
claims.citation: Kaal, Indirect Regulation of Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3405660

claims.claim: Before its collapse LTCM held roughly $4.8 billion in capital while controlling $160 billion in stocks and bonds, with derivatives of a notional value of $1 trillion.
claims.citation: Kaal, Indirect Regulation of Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3405660
scope_conditions: position as of the period immediately before the 1998 crash

claims.claim: Hedge fund disclosure to counterparties and investors relies on balance sheet concepts that are uninformative about the actual nature of market risk and credit risk exposures.
claims.citation: Kaal, Indirect Regulation of Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3405660

claims.claim: LTCM reached systemically dangerous size because banks lent to it without regard to repayment capacity, and in doing so the banks endangered their own existence.
claims.citation: Kaal, Indirect Regulation of Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3405660

claims.claim: Banks continue to find hedge fund business desirable because hedge funds take risks other participants will not, borrow heavily and pay a premium for borrowing, which sustains the lending relationship despite its dangers.
claims.citation: Kaal, Indirect Regulation of Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3405660

claims.claim: A single global financial regulator is not a serious policy option because national political interests are incoherent and cannot readily be united to establish such a body.
claims.citation: Kaal, Indirect Regulation of Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3405660

claims.claim: Additional direct limitations on hedge funds spill over onto other private investment pools such as venture capital funds and structured financings, which do not present the same systemic risk concerns.
claims.citation: Kaal, Indirect Regulation of Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3405660
scope_conditions: rules drafted broadly enough to capture private investment pools generally

claims.claim: Coordinated international cooperation in hedge fund regulation will ultimately be hindered by administrative costs, immense transaction costs, setup costs and, above all, the divergent interests of offshore havens and the resulting jurisdictional arbitrage, so it may never become a realistic regulatory option.
claims.citation: Kaal, Indirect Regulation of Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3405660

claims.claim: If coordinated international regulation forces hedge funds out, the funds can absorb the costs of relocating offshore while the market segments and jurisdictions they leave will inevitably suffer.
claims.citation: Kaal, Indirect Regulation of Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3405660
scope_conditions: coordinated international cooperation is actually implemented

claims.claim: There is currently no precise formula for devising effective integrated prudential hedge fund regulation, so the prudential model remains underspecified.
claims.citation: Kaal, Indirect Regulation of Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3405660

claims.claim: The complex trading, investing and corporate structures of active international hedge funds are a major constraint on effective prudential supervision.
claims.citation: Kaal, Indirect Regulation of Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3405660
scope_conditions: internationally active hedge funds with complex group structures

claims.claim: Indirect regulation is defined as a regulatory approach that regulates the counterparties and intermediaries of hedge funds rather than the hedge funds themselves, addressing the critical regulatory issues without acting on the funds directly.
claims.citation: Kaal, Indirect Regulation of Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3405660

claims.claim: Indirect regulation is often the only feasible tool available, because in many jurisdictions regulators lack full direct regulatory authority over hedge funds and can act only through the regulated entities they do control.
claims.citation: Kaal, Indirect Regulation of Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3405660
scope_conditions: jurisdictions where regulators lack full direct authority over hedge funds
regulators have authority over broker dealers, prime brokers and affiliates

claims.claim: Indirect regulation minimizes regulatory expense by relying on the private sector risk practices of counterparties and creditors, producing an equilibrium between regulatory cost and regulatory attainment.
claims.citation: Kaal, Indirect Regulation of Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3405660
scope_conditions: counterparties and creditors actually maintain disciplined private sector practices

claims.claim: Indirect regulation lets hedge funds preserve the opacity their strategies require, on the condition that their counterparties rather than the funds become the primary regulatory targets.
claims.citation: Kaal, Indirect Regulation of Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3405660
scope_conditions: hedge fund counterparties are made the primary regulatory targets

claims.claim: Indirect regulation asks banks to fully assess the risk they incur from hedge fund counterparties, but that assessment is often dubious at best because of the opacity of hedge fund activity.
claims.citation: Kaal, Indirect Regulation of Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3405660
scope_conditions: banks face opaque hedge fund counterparties

claims.claim: Any risk assessment of hedge funds as counterparties is necessarily incomplete, because there is no common measure for calculating leverage and exposure and because fund trading strategies are dynamic.
claims.citation: Kaal, Indirect Regulation of Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3405660

claims.claim: Competition among creditor banks undermines indirect regulation, because competing banks compromise on important elements of the risk management process and agree to overly generous credit conditions.
claims.citation: Kaal, Indirect Regulation of Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3405660
scope_conditions: multiple banks competing to lend to the same hedge funds

claims.claim: Banks can restrain borrower risk taking because they can credibly threaten to cut off future lending, a disciplinary tool other intermediaries lack.
claims.citation: Kaal, Indirect Regulation of Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3405660
scope_conditions: ongoing lending relationship in which future credit matters to the borrower

claims.claim: The Basel framework serves indirect hedge fund regulation by aligning regulatory capital requirements more closely with underlying risks and by giving banks and supervisors several options for assessing capital adequacy.
claims.citation: Kaal, Indirect Regulation of Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3405660

claims.claim: Basel II was at least partly motivated by the LTCM rescue and the 1998 market turbulence, so it responds to the same concerns that animate hedge fund regulation.
claims.citation: Kaal, Indirect Regulation of Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3405660

claims.claim: The three pillars of Basel II and its successors are rules addressed to banks that thereby indirectly regulate hedge funds.
claims.citation: Kaal, Indirect Regulation of Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3405660

claims.claim: Applying the Basel Framework to hedge fund regulation conforms to the requirements of incomplete contract theory, which supplies the theoretical justification for the indirect approach.
claims.citation: Kaal, Indirect Regulation of Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3405660

claims.claim: Indirect regulation removes the problem of missing jurisdictional authority and therefore of jurisdictional arbitrage, because the Basel Framework applies to banks worldwide rather than to funds in any one jurisdiction.
claims.citation: Kaal, Indirect Regulation of Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3405660
scope_conditions: Basel Framework is broadly adopted across banking jurisdictions

claims.claim: By letting funds implement their own risk monitoring systems, indirect regulation avoids compliance costs that would otherwise threaten the profitability needed to justify the 2 and 20 fee structure to clients.
claims.citation: Kaal, Indirect Regulation of Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3405660

claims.claim: The Basel Framework reduces systemic risk by regulating bank credit standards, which indirectly constrains hedge fund leverage and makes credit markets safer.
claims.citation: Kaal, Indirect Regulation of Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3405660

claims.claim: Market discipline, internal ratings and supervisory review under the Basel Framework change bank lending practice and disclosure, which in turn lowers hedge fund leverage and mitigates moral hazard of the kind seen at LTCM.
claims.citation: Kaal, Indirect Regulation of Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3405660

claims.claim: Indirect regulation makes ex post opportunism by hedge funds less likely because the financial intermediaries, not just the funds, stand to lose reputation and market position if their counterparty risk evaluation proves insufficient.
claims.citation: Kaal, Indirect Regulation of Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3405660
scope_conditions: intermediaries face reputational exposure in the market

claims.claim: The internal ratings based approach reduces information asymmetry because internal ratings capture supplementary borrower information that external credit assessors cannot reach and cover a broader range of borrowers.
claims.citation: Kaal, Indirect Regulation of Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3405660
scope_conditions: banks use the internal ratings based approach

claims.claim: The author concedes a standing tension: hedge funds must remain secretive because less market information about their activities is what keeps them profitable, which limits how far any transparency oriented reform can go.
claims.citation: Kaal, Indirect Regulation of Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3405660

claims.claim: Under an indirect approach hedge funds can remain exempt from disclosure and transparency requirements because only the financial intermediaries are required to reveal the relevant information, which is why the approach reconciles secrecy with reduced information asymmetry.
claims.citation: Kaal, Indirect Regulation of Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3405660

claims.claim: Because the Basel Framework applies on a consolidated basis to the holding companies of banking groups, it captures risks across the whole group and so addresses the complex structures that defeat prudential supervision.
claims.citation: Kaal, Indirect Regulation of Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3405660

claims.claim: Indirect regulation through Basel banking supervision removes the need for joint regulatory action and avoids each national regulator's transaction and implementation costs, because an international framework requires only one implementation and compliance then falls to participating banks.
claims.citation: Kaal, Indirect Regulation of Hedge Funds (2019). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3405660

claims.claim: The unfettered discretion of fiat monetary policy makers can lead to arbitrary outcomes, because the overall value and stability of any fiat currency is contingent on the fluctuations and successes of a country's economy rather than on any fixed valuation basis.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396522

claims.claim: Monetary policy making for fiat currencies largely lacks transparency, and that opacity prevents markets from taking anticipatory action on policy indicators.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396522

claims.claim: Significant failure of decentralization projects is not merely tolerable but necessary and useful, because failures are how appropriate use cases get explored during the immature phase of the technology.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396522
scope_conditions: during the early, pre maturity phase of decentralization technology

claims.claim: Tether's growth in market capitalization, its stability around one dollar, and investors' use of it as a temporary safe haven provide some empirical support for the proposition that stable cryptocurrencies can create market stability.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396522
scope_conditions: support is partial and, on the authors' own framing, possibly only temporary

claims.claim: Every stable cryptocurrency project, Tether included, remains afflicted with significant design challenges; no existing design has solved the stability problem.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396522
scope_conditions: as of the 2019 state of the market

claims.claim: Central bank operated wholesale payment systems are at the end of their technological life cycle, running on largely obsolete database designs and computing languages that are very expensive to maintain, which is one reason central banks are experimenting with token designs.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396522

claims.claim: JPM Coin's closed structure, restricting the token to existing J.P. Morgan clients, is an anachronism, because closed ecosystems are unsustainable in emerging decentralized commerce.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396522
scope_conditions: applies to permissioned stable cryptocurrencies limited to a single institution's clients

claims.claim: Both collateralization strategies carry significant downsides: fiat collateralized pegs bear the brunt of expensive capital requirements, while cryptocurrency pegs face heavy volatility pressures and swings.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396522

claims.claim: A fiat backed stable cryptocurrency that is not fully collateralized is exposed to arbitrage trade attacks of the kind George Soros used against the pound sterling; full collateralization is therefore a necessary defense.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396522
scope_conditions: applies to stable cryptocurrencies claiming a fiat peg

claims.claim: Fiat currency collateralization is expensive and inefficient because the entire backing value must be held liquid; anything less opens arbitrage opportunities of the Soros type.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396522
scope_conditions: assumes the backing must remain fully liquid to prevent arbitrage

claims.claim: The minimum price of a fiat backed stable cryptocurrency is the interest rate of the fiat currency it is pegged to, because the collateral must sit liquid rather than earn a return.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396522
scope_conditions: applies to fully collateralized fiat backed tokens

claims.claim: Cryptocurrency backed tokens are more expensive than fiat backed tokens because stability is sourced from far more volatile assets, so such tokens must be backed by substantially more than 100 percent of the collateral's current value to survive a drop in the collateral basket.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396522
scope_conditions: holds while the backing cryptocurrencies remain more volatile than fiat

claims.claim: No uncollateralized algorithmic stable cryptocurrency, such as Basis or NuBits, had produced a provably stable mechanism for its tokens as of the time of writing.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396522
scope_conditions: as of 2019

claims.claim: Trading a token directly against a well established stable cryptocurrency removes several layers of conversion fees and eliminates the risk that the bridge currency depreciates during the sequence of trades.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396522
scope_conditions: requires the stable cryptocurrency to be traded in pairs with the token in question

claims.claim: A well established stable cryptocurrency and a universal exchange form a positive feedback loop: the exchange's liquidity is enhanced by the stable cryptocurrency, and the stable currency's stability and adoption are enhanced by the exchange.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396522
scope_conditions: requires a universal exchange bridging traditional and crypto assets

claims.claim: Because cryptocurrency transactions are possible without a banking relationship, stable cryptocurrencies can remedy the disproportionate burden that cash economies impose on the poor and the unbanked by equalizing access to the payment system.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396522
scope_conditions: assumes the poor and unbanked can access the technology itself

claims.claim: Conducting commerce on public blockchains counteracts corruption because every transaction becomes publicly visible and traceable to both consumers and the government, removing the untraceability that corrupt dealing requires.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396522
scope_conditions: requires use of public rather than permissioned blockchains

claims.claim: Stability drives a causal chain in commerce: the more stable a cryptocurrency, the more it proliferates, and the more stable cryptocurrencies proliferate in commerce, the less able corruption is to destroy economic growth, making the degree of currency stability negatively correlated with corruption.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396522

claims.claim: The cryptocurrency market structure is fundamentally convoluted because each project requires its own volatile token, which is equivalent to forcing grocery shoppers to buy a different currency for every store and every product.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396522
scope_conditions: describes the market from inception through 2019

claims.claim: Leverage offered by cryptocurrency exchanges worsens rather than cures the market's illiquidity, because borrowed money rather than genuine demand is driving the price.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396522
scope_conditions: applies to exchanges offering five to ten times leverage on crypto trades

claims.claim: Extreme illiquidity combined with the herd mentality of crypto investors systematically benefits speculators, because it lets apparent scarcity materialize out of nowhere precisely when investors are about to decide, prompting misinformed buy and sell decisions.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396522
scope_conditions: holds in deeply illiquid markets where speculators control supply

claims.claim: Capping token supply, the dominant design choice in early cryptocurrency projects, is self defeating: fixing supply removes the core policy tool, minting additional tokens, that would otherwise address overvaluation, excessive speculation, market frenzy, and irrational exuberance.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396522
scope_conditions: applies to hardcoded fixed supply token designs

claims.claim: Central bank price stability is elusive for two structural reasons: central banks are constantly lobbied to move money supply away from equilibrium, and even absent lobbying they face information asymmetries that prevent them from determining the optimal supply at any given moment.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396522

claims.claim: Stable cryptocurrencies escape part of the lobbying problem by hardcoding their policy rationales and outcomes into the protocol, which limits the amount of lobbying that can influence policy decisions.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396522
scope_conditions: holds to the extent policy is genuinely hardcoded rather than discretionary

claims.claim: Because hardcoded cryptocurrency policy is transparent and therefore predictable, market participants can anticipate policy and adjust behavior in advance, and such anticipatory reactions could over time make actual policy making the exception rather than the rule.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396522
scope_conditions: assumes policy rules remain largely hardcoded and transparent

claims.claim: Full hardcoding is impossible: no stable cryptocurrency can encode all required policies and policy actions with full transparency, because future policy needs cannot be anticipated ex ante.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396522

claims.claim: Monetary policy for stable cryptocurrencies should combine hardcoded transparent rules with protocols enabling decentralized autonomous organizations, with decentralized but fully transparent policy DAOs functioning as the policy makers for what cannot be hardcoded.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396522
scope_conditions: depends on DAO governance designs that address expertise and incentive problems

claims.claim: The authors qualify their own case: stable cryptocurrencies can experiment with monetary policy on an unprecedented scale only because they are insulated from real world complexities and political positioning, and that advantage shrinks once real world market factors actually apply to them.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396522
scope_conditions: applies as stable cryptocurrencies scale into real world use

claims.claim: The interoperability deficit in cryptocurrency markets is partly intrinsic to blockchain technology itself, because the consensus mechanism that allows block propagation on one chain in some ways negates interoperability with other chains and their consensus.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396522

claims.claim: The lack of interoperability is a very serious threat to the survivability of cryptocurrency projects, as the crypto winter of 2018 and 2019 demonstrated when thousands of competing, non interoperable projects failed.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396522

claims.claim: Currency stability should be used as the consumer facing proxy for interoperability, because teaching the public to value stability is easier than educating it about the blockchain technology that produces technical interoperability.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396522

claims.claim: The low transaction throughput of public blockchains is a core limitation holding back more advanced distributed applications and, with them, decentralized commerce.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396522
scope_conditions: as of 2019 throughput levels

claims.claim: Decentralization technology is unlikely to proliferate without a core use case beyond store of value; banking, money transmission, and triple entry accounting are natural use cases but fall short of being universal use cases for public blockchains.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396522

claims.claim: A decentralized crypto economy requires a stable coin because no rational party will risk wealth on a long term contract denominated in a volatile currency: neither renter nor landlord will sign a lease whose rent may halve or double in any given week.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396522
scope_conditions: applies to long term business contracts denominated in the currency

claims.claim: Because stable cryptocurrencies are free of the real world pressures that constrain emerging market currencies, they may be able to experiment with solutions that overcome the currency trilemma, attaining a fixed exchange rate, free capital movement, and an independent monetary policy at once.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396522
scope_conditions: hinges on DAO governance protocols that deliver full decentralization and independence

claims.claim: Mass adoption fails at the user level: the average user will not identify, research, and purchase diverse sets of tokens even where those tokens would create value, because the existing cryptocurrency market structure is simply too cumbersome.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396522

claims.claim: Non speculator lay people will not use cryptocurrencies for daily consumption, groceries, or banking transactions unless the value of the currency is stable; stability is a precondition of ordinary consumer use, not merely a convenience.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396522

claims.claim: Merchant adoption of stable cryptocurrencies turns on a concrete threshold: merchants pay 2.9 percent to credit card companies on non cash transactions, so any medium of exchange costing less than 2.9 percent benefits merchants, who can pass the saving to consumers as a discount.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396522
scope_conditions: assumes exchange rate risk for the consumer stays below the 2.9 percent threshold

claims.claim: Near instant settlement with stable cryptocurrencies removes counterparty risk, and the resulting reduction in counterparty risk boosts consumer confidence and increases transactional certainty relative to systems like Visa that take five to seven business days to pay merchants.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396522

claims.claim: The authors adopt Schilling and Uhlig's result that official money and cryptocurrencies can co-exist in a manner consistent with stability, rejecting the framing that private currency and central bank money are necessarily mutually exclusive.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3396522
scope_conditions: drawn from a model with decentralized Bitcoin production and a Dollar supply controlled to an inflation target

claims.claim: A currency that does not hold a stable store of value forces continual recalculation and renegotiation of contracts, so any future decentralized economy will require stable cryptocurrencies.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies - First Order Principles (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3402701
scope_conditions: decentralized economies that rely on contracts denominated in the currency

claims.claim: Fiat currency collateralization is expensive and inefficient because the entire backing value must be held liquid; anything less opens arbitrage attacks of the kind Soros used against the Bank of England.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies - First Order Principles (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3402701
scope_conditions: fiat-backed pegs claiming full collateralization

claims.claim: The minimum cost of a fiat-backed token equals the interest rate of the pegged fiat currency, because the backing capital must sit idle and liquid.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies - First Order Principles (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3402701

claims.claim: Cryptocurrency-backed tokens must be overcollateralized well beyond 100 percent of current value because the backing basket can fall, which makes them even more expensive than fiat-backed tokens.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies - First Order Principles (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3402701
scope_conditions: backing assets are volatile cryptocurrencies

claims.claim: As of the time of writing, no uncollateralized algorithmic stable cryptocurrency project had produced a provably stable mechanism for its tokens.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies - First Order Principles (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3402701
scope_conditions: as of 2019

claims.claim: Transacting in cash imposes large measurable costs: roughly 200 billion dollars annually in the United States, about 637 dollars per person, driven by counting, managing, storing, transporting, guarding and accounting for bank notes.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies - First Order Principles (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3402701
scope_conditions: United States, 2018 estimates

claims.claim: Good governance principles are crucial to every aspect of a long-term stable currency because markets inevitably change and because the Folk Theorems of game theory pose a fundamental obstacle to any fixed protocol.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies - First Order Principles (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3402701
scope_conditions: long-term stable currency designs

claims.claim: Under the quantity theory of money, minting twice as much currency halves its price and burning half of the existing currency doubles it, which is the mechanism by which a supply rule can theoretically stabilize price.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies - First Order Principles (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3402701
scope_conditions: quantity theory of money holds
price measured as an average across exchanges

claims.claim: The quantity theory calculations behind minting and burning hold only in the ideal case; in practice the success of a stabilization scheme depends on how the money is actually printed, distributed or burned.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies - First Order Principles (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3402701

claims.claim: Distributing newly minted coins to shareholders, as Basis planned, is exploitable: shareholders can collude to hold their new money and drive the price up, which triggers further minting that benefits the colluders.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies - First Order Principles (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3402701
scope_conditions: new supply distributed to an identifiable shareholder group

claims.claim: The Folk Theorems of game theory imply that no matter how complicated a stable coin protocol becomes, a powerful and patient player has strategies to subvert the system and profit at the expense of the group.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies - First Order Principles (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3402701
scope_conditions: any fixed protocol, however complex

claims.claim: Because no fixed rule set can resist a patient adversary, any stable coin scheme requires a nimble and responsive governance process whose rules can always be adjusted to changing market conditions.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies - First Order Principles (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3402701
scope_conditions: stable coin schemes operating over time in changing markets

claims.claim: Bonds are the appropriate burning mechanism for a temporary drop in currency price caused by larger economic instability such as an act of God or war, since bonds can be redeemed above their sale price once the economy rebounds.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies - First Order Principles (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3402701
scope_conditions: price decline caused by temporary economy-wide shock, not hot money

claims.claim: A Basis-style bond scheme succeeds only while demand for the currency grows at a sufficient rate; the authors' simulations show it fails when demand is stagnant at equilibrium.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies - First Order Principles (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3402701
scope_conditions: demand stagnant at equilibrium

claims.claim: Because bonds sell below their redemption value, an open-ended bond queue grows without bound, depressing bond prices and creating a positive feedback loop that ends in a death spiral and failure of the peg.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies - First Order Principles (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3402701
scope_conditions: bond redemption contingent on future price recovery
no expiration on bonds

claims.claim: Stable cryptocurrency bonds should be minted with a fixed expiration, following the practice of historical central banks, because fixed expiration makes price discovery more efficient.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies - First Order Principles (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3402701

claims.claim: Reserves, not bonds, are the necessary mechanism for currency instability caused by hot money, that is money frequently moved between institutions or currencies to maximize gain.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies - First Order Principles (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3402701
scope_conditions: instability driven by hot money flows

claims.claim: Because most of the value of contemporary cryptocurrencies comes from speculation on future uses that do not yet exist, the vast majority of cryptocurrency is technically hot money, and reserves are the best defense against the resulting price fluctuations.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies - First Order Principles (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3402701
scope_conditions: contemporary cryptocurrency markets dominated by speculation

claims.claim: Selling currency into a reserve when price is above the peg and buying it back with the reserve when price is below the peg yields an arbitrage profit, so a reserve can fund its own defense of the peg.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies - First Order Principles (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3402701
scope_conditions: the reserve currency is more stable than the base currency
the cost to implement and maintain the reserve is ignored

claims.claim: The reserve argument depends on two requirements, and failing either one grounds a criticism of an existing protocol: the stable-value requirement criticizes MakerDAO and the maintenance-cost requirement criticizes the Reserve protocol.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies - First Order Principles (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3402701
scope_conditions: reserve held in a volatile asset
reserve maintenance cost exceeds arbitrage profit

claims.claim: Contesting the common assumption that a 100 percent reserve is required to guarantee a peg, the authors argue full reserves are not always necessary for any currency that has intrinsic worth.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies - First Order Principles (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3402701
scope_conditions: currency possesses intrinsic worth, for example genuine transactional use

claims.claim: Contesting the standard reading, the authors argue Soros broke the Bank of England not because the pound lacked full foreign reserve backing but because the pound was pegged at an inauthentic value.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies - First Order Principles (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3402701

claims.claim: Determining what fraction of a currency is hot money is necessary for efficient defense of its stability, because the reserve requirement follows from that ratio rather than from a blanket full-backing rule.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies - First Order Principles (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3402701

claims.claim: Misestimating the hot money ratio fails in both directions: overestimation makes the currency more costly to use, and underestimation leaves it insecure, so efficiency and security are in direct tension.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies - First Order Principles (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3402701

claims.claim: Defining the energy of money as the product of economic momentum and velocity gives a basis for discussing economic frictions and for distinguishing genuine from artificial network energy, which is what guards against hot money instability.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies - First Order Principles (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3402701
scope_conditions: proposed research framework, analogy to kinetic theory of gases

claims.claim: In a blockchain cryptocurrency, transaction taxes should be set to match the cost of running the network, meaning the cost of incentivizing enough nodes for the desired level of decentralization plus the cost of maintaining the coin's stability.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies - First Order Principles (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3402701
scope_conditions: blockchain cryptocurrencies with node incentive costs

claims.claim: Holding taxes are the implicit result of inflation borne by coin holders, and they should be set to account for the inefficiencies of the economy rather than the inefficiencies of maintaining the currency.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies - First Order Principles (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3402701

claims.claim: In the contemporary climate these taxes and fees are unlikely to be implemented appropriately, because internet culture has trained users to expect free service from nodes and to hide the costs of running them.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies - First Order Principles (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3402701
scope_conditions: prevailing internet culture of free node service

claims.claim: Blockchain users are likely to demand zero transaction fees while failing to notice holding fees below about 3 percent annually, which a USD peg institutes implicitly through a comparable inflation target.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies - First Order Principles (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3402701
scope_conditions: decentralized economy inheriting internet fee culture
peg to USD

claims.claim: For any long-lived currency, a major shift in perceived value is eventually inevitable, and such a shift is not covered by reserves defending against hot money or by bonds defending against temporary economic instability.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies - First Order Principles (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3402701
scope_conditions: long-lived currencies
black swan events

claims.claim: When a fundamental shift in value occurs, repegging the currency at its more accurate value is more efficient than soldiering on with tax mechanisms to restabilize at the old peg.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies - First Order Principles (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3402701
scope_conditions: fundamental change in the economy, black swan event

claims.claim: The day-to-day stability mechanism can be fully automated by algorithm, but monetary and fiscal policy choices cannot be: the algorithm's parameters must be chosen by hand and adjusted regularly to balance security against efficiency.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies - First Order Principles (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3402701
scope_conditions: stability mechanisms operating in changing markets

claims.claim: Parameter and policy choices for a stable cryptocurrency should be made by a decentralized autonomous organization, the Stability DAO or SDAO, which functions as a transparent, decentralized, open analog of the US Federal Reserve.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies - First Order Principles (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3402701

claims.claim: Centralized hierarchies and decentralized flat organizations fail in opposite ways: hierarchies filter out information signals at the edge, while flat organizations amplify edge noise so important information never finds a champion to drive action.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies - First Order Principles (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3402701

claims.claim: Transparency is not an unqualified good for monetary policy: a currency only partially backed by reserves can be arbitraged by a Soros-style shorting strategy much more easily when the quantity of reserves is public.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies - First Order Principles (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3402701
scope_conditions: partial reserve backing
reserve quantities publicly known

claims.claim: The Folk Theorems of game theory prove that no protocol, however complex or well engineered, can eliminate corruption, understood as behavior that profits a minority at the greater expense of the majority.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies - First Order Principles (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3402701

claims.claim: No static set of rules can prevent the corruption that will eventually cause any stability design to fail, but a changing rule set administered by nimble governance can prevent that failure if enough resources reward anti-corruption effort.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Vadhindran K. Rao, Stable Cryptocurrencies - First Order Principles (2019). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3402701
scope_conditions: governance that devotes resources to detecting and rewarding anti-corruption effort

claims.claim: Because the Folk Theorems make governance protocols permanently provisional, long-term stability requires that the group be organized around a transcendental value, a goal meaningful and commonly held that cannot be captured by any logical rule set.
