claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralized Autonomous Organizations – Internal Governance and External Legal Design (2020). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3652481
scope_conditions: no off chain legal entity has been formed

claims.claim: Equity funding and token funding are substitutes: because equity investment in a blockchain startup makes issuing a digital currency both less likely and less necessary as a funding source, a market shift back toward equity funding should shrink the total volume of digital currencies issued.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: digital asset and blockchain startups
token issuance treated primarily as a funding mechanism

claims.claim: The funding sources for digital asset and blockchain startups cycled through four stages since 2016 and 2017: equity funding, then initial coin offerings, then equity offerings, then initial exchange offerings, and back to equity funding by the early 2020s.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: digital asset and blockchain startups
2016 to early 2020s

claims.claim: The expected growth rate of DeFi, across diverse estimates, is large enough to call into question the long term viability of the existing decentralized technology infrastructure unless core infrastructure improvements are made.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: decentralized finance built on existing public blockchains
growth continues at estimated rates

claims.claim: The article stipulates a broad definition of digital assets covering all virtual and electronic assets regardless of how regulators name or categorize them, including cryptocurrencies, security tokens, utility tokens, virtual collectibles, stablecoins, and altcoins.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: definition adopted for the purposes of this article

claims.claim: The assumption by ICO issuers that token sales let them circumvent securities registration and disclosure requirements proved to be a fallacy for many U.S. issuers, who faced increased SEC enforcement actions in late 2019.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: U.S. issuers of tokens in ICOs
post 2017 enforcement environment

claims.claim: By 2019 the ICO market had lost its defining advantage over venture capital: because most ICOs between 2018 and 2019 imposed one to three year lockups, neither market offered early liquidity to investors or issuers, making the two substantively similar.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: ICOs conducted between 2018 and 2019
lockup periods of one to three years

claims.claim: Once the staggered private sale discounts of up to fifty percent are counted as a cost of capital, the cost structure of an ICO is arguably significantly higher than that of an IPO, notwithstanding the ICO's lower legal and offering expenses.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: ICOs conducted in 2017 and 2018 with staggered discount structures
comparison against average IPO underwriting fees of four to seven percent

claims.claim: ICO issuance exceeded venture capital financing of startups for the first time in the second quarter of 2017, with $210 million invested through ICOs against $180 million invested through traditional venture capital funds.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: second quarter of 2017
blockchain and crypto startups

claims.claim: Initial exchange offerings emerged as a market response to the near disappearance of the ICO market in January 2019, driven by the cryptocurrency exchanges that were most affected by the collapse.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: cryptocurrency exchanges
aftermath of the ICO market collapse in January 2019

claims.claim: The IEO reinserts an intermediary into token offerings: the exchange screens the offering and the issuer no longer interacts with investors directly, reversing the direct issuer to investor structure of the ICO.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: initial exchange offerings
token offerings listed on a cryptocurrency exchange

claims.claim: Capped ICO raises, adopted by the crypto community to reduce investor uncertainty about platform valuation in uncapped raises, backfire because the cap creates strong incentives for investors to get in first, raising the likelihood of retail investor frenzy.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: capped ICO raises
retail investor participation

claims.claim: The absence of mandatory disclosure obligations for ICOs leads promoters to make irregular disclosures or none at all as time passes, producing a significant lack of transparency in the ICO market.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: ICO markets without mandatory disclosure rules
post issuance period

claims.claim: ICO sale terms are not fixed at launch: promoters can alter the smart contract to change the sales rules mid course during an offering, a risk factor for retail investors that has no analogue in a registered offering.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: ICOs administered through promoter controlled smart contracts

claims.claim: Regulatory uncertainty is curtailing the growth of the digital asset industry because investor classes across the spectrum, from retail investors to the largest institutions, are hesitant to participate while the legal treatment of digital assets remains unclear.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: early 2020s digital asset market
absence of sufficient regulatory guidance

claims.claim: Institutional investors face a distinct barrier beyond volatility: fiduciary responsibility to their clients limits the type of risk they may take on, and the lack of custody solutions recognized by regulators compounds the problem.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: institutional investors subject to fiduciary duties
early 2020s absence of regulator recognized custody solutions

claims.claim: Immature markets such as the market for digital assets in 2020 often cannot attract the institutional investors and venture capitalists who have sufficient operating experience in that market, which is a self reinforcing constraint on market development.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: immature or nascent asset markets
digital asset market as of 2020

claims.claim: Early stage investing in digital assets is a relationships business, and without access to a network of core industry expertise early stage investments in the digital asset industry are rarely successful.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: early stage investors in digital asset startups

claims.claim: Anonymity in decentralized networks imposes a specific design constraint: system architects need a special skillset to navigate the limits that anonymity places on system design, and that skillset remains very rare in the early 2020s.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: decentralized networks with anonymous and autonomous participants
incentive compatible token design

claims.claim: Because the digital asset market has been so hype driven, technical experience has not added significantly to overall market development and maturity, leaving many top projects in 2020 still afflicted by unresolved technical issues.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: cryptocurrency market through the early 2020s
hype driven market conditions

claims.claim: Bitcoin functions as a medium of exchange for a number of businesses but arguably fails as a store of value and as a unit of account, because of its volatility and its lack of intrinsic value.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: Bitcoin as evaluated against the three classical money functions

claims.claim: Cyber security incidents contribute to the volatility of the digital asset market through a specific channel: consumers instantaneously withdraw their assets from an exchange affected by an incident.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: digital asset exchanges affected by cyber security incidents
author flags other contributing reasons

claims.claim: Token design must be treated as an iterative process in which data collection and flexibility in core design parameters are essential, because prior crypto economic assumptions routinely turn out to be suboptimal once the network grows and user preferences change.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: token and crypto economic design for growing decentralized networks

claims.claim: The evolution of the DeFi market and its new monetary system depends on the stability of DeFi products and digital assets, and both stability and adoption of DeFi are undermined by the instability of most cryptocurrencies.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: DeFi platforms denominated in volatile cryptocurrencies

claims.claim: DeFi platforms grant the unbanked access to the loan market by disintermediating existing banks, connecting borrowers and lenders directly in peer to peer networks and accepting digital assets as collateral with far less documentation than banks require.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: borrowers excluded from centralized banking for lack of documentation
DeFi lending protocols

claims.claim: The DeFi lending market is highly concentrated: MakerDAO alone accounts for almost ninety percent of the total USD value locked in DeFi projects.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: DeFi projects measured by total USD value locked
period covered by DeFi Pulse data

claims.claim: Centralized financial technology does not complete the disintermediation it promises, because users still deal with a technology company as intermediary instead of a financial institution, which leaves room for the decentralized solutions DeFi attempts to provide.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: centralized FinTech platforms
peer to peer transaction settings

claims.claim: DeFi is more efficient than existing financial intermediation including FinTech, and that superior efficiency traces to its extensive reliance on code and automation, which removes large parts of the human element and the errors and inefficiencies that come with it.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: comparison of DeFi with legacy financial intermediation and FinTech

claims.claim: DeFi's decentralization remains theoretical in one important respect: as of the early 2020s DeFi is still largely relegated to one dominant platform, with 87 percent of all publicly funded DeFi projects built on Ethereum.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: publicly funded DeFi projects
beginning of the 2020s

claims.claim: At the beginning of the 2020s DeFi was not sufficiently user friendly, because core interfaces such as metamask, myetherwallet, and scatter require levels of technical know how in handling public and private keys that most lay users do not possess.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: lay retail users of DeFi interfaces
beginning of the 2020s

claims.claim: The digital asset market resulted from a technology push rather than a market pull: developers were driven by technical advancement rather than by usefulness and user friendliness, and market pull may only evolve once the DeFi technology infrastructure is more developed.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: digital asset and DeFi platform development
immature technology infrastructure

claims.claim: DeFi platform technologies often have limited product market fit because the reliance on code over human judgment produces products built around automation that ignore the human element in financial transactions.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: DeFi products built primarily on automated code execution
transactions involving subjective or non codifiable inputs

claims.claim: Because human interactions in business are often too complex to be fully codified objectively, DeFi systems that exclude all non objective information from their analysis do not fully utilize available information, which limits their efficiency and usefulness.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: DeFi products analyzing only objectively recordable and verifiable inputs
complex commercial interactions

claims.claim: Accountability is a structural concern in DeFi: without a central entity it can become unclear who is responsible for wrongdoing, and when problems arise no central party can freeze transactions, fix problems, or restore normal operations.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: fully decentralized finance systems without a central operator

claims.claim: In the early 2020s the DeFi technology infrastructure was insufficiently developed to support DeFi growth estimates and growth potential, and fulfilling that potential requires significant tradeoffs between scaling, security, and levels of decentralization.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: DeFi infrastructure as of the early 2020s
projected DeFi growth rates

claims.claim: The tradeoff between transaction approval speed and immutability has the potential to undermine the DeFi infrastructure in the long run.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: consensus based decentralized ledgers supporting DeFi

claims.claim: Consensus in decentralized systems presents a two sided cost problem: creating consensus raises the costs of prepping, processing, and storing information, while reducing the number of computational checks increases the risk of collusion attacks that could change the record.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: public distributed consensus systems
information distributed to and validated by all parties

claims.claim: Read together with the network capacity failure that CryptoKitties caused on Ethereum in December 2017, the expected DeFi growth rates imply that the Ethereum network will continue to experience network shortages and throughput problems unless its infrastructure is upgraded to handle the expected transaction volume.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: Ethereum network without infrastructure upgrades
DeFi growth continuing at estimated rates
author cautions that correlation is not causation

claims.claim: Conducting monetary policy through a central bank digital currency imposes a requirement on the technology layer: the underlying network protocol must enable the central bank to adjust the money supply at will and to act as lender of last resort with access to unlimited supply.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: CBDC built on a blockchain style protocol
central bank intends to conduct monetary policy through the CBDC

claims.claim: The Bank of Canada's year long Jasper trial revealed a tradeoff rather than a solution: Ethereum would make the wholesale payment system more resilient but was costly and raised privacy issues, while Corda addressed cost and privacy but made the system less resilient, and the Bank concluded in May 2017 that blockchain was not mature enough to run a national interbank payment system.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: Bank of Canada Jasper trial
national interbank payment system use case
as of May 2017

claims.claim: Although the public realm of coins could not exist without prior private experimentation, it is possible that the public realm will impact or even pre empt private coin development, for example if central banks attempt to censor the use of digital currencies they did not issue.
claims.citation: Kaal, Digital Asset Market Evolution (2020). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3606663
scope_conditions: coexistence of central bank digital currencies and privately issued coins

claims.claim: The concept of a DAO fails if it becomes centralized, and centralization in governance is the largest single threat to a DAO.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320

claims.claim: Decentralized governance must be dynamic and evolutionary, otherwise the system becomes centralized and brittle over time; most DAOs fail to accomplish this.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: governance that must persist over time
systems relying on information from the edges

claims.claim: Tying a DAO's legal existence to existing legal and jurisdictional frameworks typically requires a representative in the chosen jurisdiction, which centralizes the DAO and results in the failure of the DAO concept.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: DAO anchored in an existing jurisdiction
frameworks that require local representation

claims.claim: Only a jurisdiction that grants a DAO limited liability as an entity and accepts its independent status without requiring representation can be truly favorable to DAO concepts.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: jurisdictions competing to host DAOs

claims.claim: The focus on value enhancement of fungible tokens can drive short termism in DAOs and cause ethical and governance issues to be ignored.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: DAOs whose incentive design centers on fungible token value

claims.claim: Working with suboptimal layer 1 blockchain solutions that carry high gas fees and low throughput delays the evolution of DAO infrastructure design, because innovation is inhibited by those layer 1 features.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: development anchored to first generation layer 1 networks

claims.claim: Regulatory uncertainty is holding back both the development of DAOs and the potential of DAOs to optimize digital assets.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: regulatory environment of the early 2020s

claims.claim: If DAO members do not formalize a legal structure for their entity, courts are very likely to impose one on them, which is a serious risk of DAO membership.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: DAOs with no off-chain legal entity
litigation reaching a court

claims.claim: Default general partnership treatment would hold every stakeholder of a DAO liable for any debts or legal actions the DAO faces, exposing known participants to regulatory enforcement and civil actions.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: no legal entity formed
U.S. partnership default rules apply

claims.claim: Private agreements that limit remedies to DAO assets are unlikely to be upheld if the DAO faces a tort suit.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: tort claims rather than contract claims
off-chain dispute settlement

claims.claim: Cybernetic systems change constantly and are less amenable to jurisdictional reach, which makes it nearly impossible to apply a common legal anchor and traditional jurisdictional principles to them.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: constantly changing cybernetic systems
counterparties that do not concurrently exist

claims.claim: Under current securities laws, DAOs governed solely by smart contracts are restricted in pooling assets and generating profit, because those laws limit their ability to fund ecosystem development and deploy capital efficiently.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: DAOs governed solely by smart contracts
current U.S. securities law

claims.claim: Effective institutional governance requires a duality of incentives, namely incentives for actors to improve their own utility while their actions simultaneously benefit the whole institution over the long run, in order to defeat rational and opportunistic attempts to game the design.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: institutions with rational, opportunistic internal and external constituents

claims.claim: When fungible assets are the dominant incentive design in the governance of a DAO with identifiable actors, rational and opportunistic internal and external participants will typically attempt to corrupt that governance design for their own gain.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: fungible assets used as the dominant governance incentive
actors who are identifiable

claims.claim: The identity of actors in a DAO governance design is itself a source of corruption, so merit identifiers other than individual identity remove the most corruptive influences.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: governance designs that expose actor identity

claims.claim: DAOs cannot exist and persist without ever increasing degrees of decentralization, so DAO legal designs must first and foremost supplement the internal decentralization the DAO has achieved.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: long lived DAOs

claims.claim: Existing legal solutions for DAOs typically require some form of legal representation in the relevant jurisdiction, and such representation is always a point of centralization.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: current legal wrappers available to DAOs

claims.claim: A DAO needs a legal wrapper to represent it, because a DAO cannot by itself rent an office or sign a contract that can only happen on paper.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: DAO operations that touch the real world

claims.claim: Under the legal wrapper concept individual DAO members are not liable and the third party knows exactly with whom she is interacting and where liabilities arise.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: DAO represented by a legal wrapper entity

claims.claim: Because a series of smart contracts grants DAO token holders voting rights, those smart contracts take the place of articles of association or bylaws and of the entire precedent system that a jurisdiction based legal structure would otherwise supply by default.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: DAOs running on public decentralized blockchain platforms

claims.claim: Governance is the common denominator of the shortcomings in existing DAO infrastructure; it is not a bug or an afterthought in system design but the key feature.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320

claims.claim: Without continual effort to maintain decentralized order, the values that initially unite DAO members tend to produce ever tighter and more complex hierarchical structures inside the DAO.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: absence of continual decentralization maintenance

claims.claim: If a DAO's internal voting mechanism is more centralized and carries legacy voting problems, a higher degree of decentralization in its external legal design will typically be canceled out in the long run.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: DAOs pairing centralized internal voting with a decentralized legal design

claims.claim: The DAO of DAOs uses a duality of internal and external governance: internal governance runs on reputation token staking, while external legal relationships are handled by a legal wrapper that represents the DAO of DAOs in real world legal contexts.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: DAO of DAOs architecture

claims.claim: In any open and democratic system, naturally opportunistic rational parties will attempt to circumvent and game the applicable complex static rules to increase their share of power and profit.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: open and democratic systems with complex static rule sets

claims.claim: Because static complex DAO rule sets bring inevitable corruptive gaming and arbitrage behavior, effective DAO governance designs should focus on dynamic elements such as members' ability to re-evaluate existing precedent.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: DAO governance that must both protect members and permit enhancement

claims.claim: Suboptimal voting outcomes in existing decentralized protocols trace to one token one vote mechanisms, which allocate more power to holders of a significant share of total token supply.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: one token one vote governance designs

claims.claim: Reputation based staking removes the corruptive elements of fungible tokens because third parties are less likely able to take over a non fungible asset such as reputation that is organically grown and maintained through actual expertise in the relevant subject matter.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: reputation staked as a non fungible asset
reputation earned through subject matter expertise

claims.claim: Reputation voting has two advantages over one token one vote: it is non fungible, which avoids corruptive elements, and it aligns incentives for members individually and for the institution as a whole at the same time.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: DAO of DAOs internal governance

claims.claim: In the bifurcated DAO of DAOs token design, non fungible reputation tokens give members voting rights while fungible reputation salary tokens let members earn a salary in proportion to their non fungible reputation holdings.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: DAO of DAOs two token architecture

claims.claim: Paying members indirectly, through a fungible stable salary proportional to non fungible reputation, removes corruptive elements and makes the governance design more attack resistant and more stable over the long run.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: salary paid in proportion to non fungible reputation scores

claims.claim: Reputation based governance creates a positive sum game because members have incentives to build lasting non fungible value through a long term record of productive cooperation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: non fungible reputation as the reward

claims.claim: Member reputation is inflationary by design, so non staking of reputation tokens or non voting leads to value depreciation, which incentivizes action and makes liveness faults less likely.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: reputation that depreciates with non-use

claims.claim: Precedent in the DAO of DAOs is replaced dynamically: if a newer template is referenced more often it becomes the prevailing precedent, while the old precedent dissipates over time through non use.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: decentralized on chain precedent system

claims.claim: Charging an admission fee disincentivizes betrayal and defection, because the sunk cost of joining makes cheating expensive when rejoining would also be expensive even under anonymity.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, A Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) of DAOs (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3799320
scope_conditions: members who can be blacklisted

claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Contemporary Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782198
scope_conditions: figures given for June 2020

claims.claim: Proof of stake carries an unresolved failure mode: if anyone devises a clever algorithm for hijacking the block producer selection process, the network would fail.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Contemporary Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782198
scope_conditions: applies to proof of stake designs that select block producers pseudorandomly

claims.claim: Blockchain transactions will always be expensive whether or not proof of stake is solved, because full participation requires downloading the entire transaction history to verify validity, an extreme redundancy that cannot be removed.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Contemporary Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782198
scope_conditions: applies to blockchains that require full history verification

claims.claim: A decentralized banking DAO built on top of the Bitcoin ledger could charge a smaller fee to hold minor transactions temporarily and bundle them into a single larger Bitcoin transaction on the eternal blockchain.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Contemporary Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782198
scope_conditions: proposed as a response to the permanent expense of on chain transactions

claims.claim: Anonymity can exacerbate second and third order discrimination because it makes such discrimination more difficult to detect, so other governance mechanisms in a decentralized organization must be used to combat it.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Contemporary Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782198
scope_conditions: applies where members infer protected characteristics from behavior, and to systemic discrimination

claims.claim: The Tragedy of the Commons is a natural consequence of allowing anonymous participation, which is why the unfiltered layers of platforms such as Twitter, YouTube comments, and Reddit display toxic results.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Contemporary Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782198
scope_conditions: applies to open networks with anonymous broadcasting and no reputation cost

claims.claim: Anonymity should be balanced rather than absolute: a member's power to broadcast should be tied to a pseudonymous account carrying meaningful and valuable reputation that is lost when the broadcasting power is abused.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Contemporary Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782198
scope_conditions: applies to decentralized networks that permit anonymous participation

claims.claim: The r/place experiment showed that anonymous groups can self correct: each time a hate symbol such as a swastika appeared on the shared canvas, it was replaced with something more positive.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Contemporary Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782198
scope_conditions: based on the r/place experiment run from April 2017

claims.claim: Ethereum is Turing complete in theory but cannot practically match even a cheap smartphone, because everything stored on the blockchain must be stored redundantly on thousands of nodes forever, so decentralized smart contract computation is necessarily primitive compared with centralized Web 2.0 services.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Contemporary Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782198
scope_conditions: applies to on chain computation and storage on general purpose blockchains

claims.claim: Truly successful DAOs do not yet exist, but once the architecture of a single DAO succeeds it will be quickly cloned and adapted to every imaginable economic and social organization.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Contemporary Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782198
scope_conditions: stated as of the book's writing

claims.claim: Fully compliant legal custody solutions for digital assets increase legal certainty and mainstream investor confidence, and that increased confidence in turn builds markets in digital assets.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hayley Howe, Custody of Digital Assets (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3936876
scope_conditions: applies to digital asset markets in their formative stage

claims.claim: The more digital assets are held by their owners in self-custody, the less likely intermediation by custody service providers becomes, so self-custody is the key driver of decentralization in emerging blockchain networks.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hayley Howe, Custody of Digital Assets (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3936876
scope_conditions: holds for emerging blockchain networks
assumes users are capable of securing their own keys

claims.claim: Without the ability to rely on proven custody providers, mainstream and legacy institutional investors are restrained from making digital asset investments for legal or business reasons.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hayley Howe, Custody of Digital Assets (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3936876
scope_conditions: applies to mainstream and legacy institutional investors

claims.claim: The majority of digital asset custody providers and digital asset exchanges require customers to surrender ownership of their digital assets as a precondition for access and trading.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hayley Howe, Custody of Digital Assets (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3936876

claims.claim: Custody of a digital asset is not physical possession but ownership and control over a digital asset wallet, which in practice means holding the private keys and bearing responsibility for keeping the funds safe.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hayley Howe, Custody of Digital Assets (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3936876
scope_conditions: applies to intangible digital assets rather than tangible chattel or real estate

claims.claim: Self-custody of securities declined in prevalence after the Stock Market Crash of 1929 because investors recognized how inherently risky the bearer certificate system was.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hayley Howe, Custody of Digital Assets (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3936876
scope_conditions: United States securities markets before and after 1929

claims.claim: The paper certificate system failed at scale: trust companies and intermediaries were overwhelmed by changing ownership records, and from 1967 to 1970 a reported $400 million in securities was lost or stolen.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hayley Howe, Custody of Digital Assets (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3936876
scope_conditions: United States securities markets, 1967 to 1970

claims.claim: The inefficiencies of paperwork based custodial requirements are what produced the first central securities depository, which substituted electronic book entry records for the physical exchange of certificates.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hayley Howe, Custody of Digital Assets (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3936876
scope_conditions: United States securities markets after the 1960s paperwork crisis

claims.claim: Traditional custody has become highly concentrated, with four large banks holding roughly $114 trillion in assets under custody at the end of the first quarter of 2018, and barriers to entry make it likely that this concentration continues.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hayley Howe, Custody of Digital Assets (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3936876
scope_conditions: United States custody market as of 2018

claims.claim: A private key differs from a password in that it is immutable and cannot be reset, so if the key is lost or stolen access to the digital asset may be permanently lost.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hayley Howe, Custody of Digital Assets (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3936876
scope_conditions: applies to key based digital asset ownership on public blockchains

claims.claim: Hot storage buys easy access and quick transferability of digital assets at the cost of exposure to cyber attacks and to the difficulty of keeping private keys safe.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hayley Howe, Custody of Digital Assets (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3936876
scope_conditions: wallets stored and accessible online

claims.claim: Cryptocurrency exchanges store digital assets or private keys in internet connected hot storage because their main function is to provide liquidity rather than custody, unlike registered legacy stock exchanges which facilitate trading without taking custody.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hayley Howe, Custody of Digital Assets (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3936876
scope_conditions: centralized cryptocurrency exchanges

claims.claim: Centralized cryptocurrency exchanges require users to hand over their assets and then act as custodian, issuing what are essentially IOUs for users to trade with on the platform.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hayley Howe, Custody of Digital Assets (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3936876
scope_conditions: centralized exchanges, as distinct from decentralized exchanges

claims.claim: Because a wallet provider or exchange that has custody of a digital asset gains full control over transactions, hacking a digital asset exchange is equivalent to robbing a bank: the attacker obtains valuable cryptocurrency that can be cashed out.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hayley Howe, Custody of Digital Assets (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3936876
scope_conditions: exchanges holding pooled customer assets in hot storage

claims.claim: Between 2011 and 2018 there were 56 cyberattacks on cryptocurrency exchanges, initial coin offerings and other digital currency platforms worldwide, totaling $1.63 billion in hacking related losses.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hayley Howe, Custody of Digital Assets (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3936876
scope_conditions: global, 2011 to 2018

claims.claim: As of 2017, 73 percent of digital asset exchanges took custody of their users' private keys while only 23 percent let users maintain control over their own keys.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hayley Howe, Custody of Digital Assets (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3936876
scope_conditions: global exchange survey data as of 2017

claims.claim: Custodial exchanges are largely unprepared for breach: only 53 percent of small custodial exchanges and 78 percent of large custodial exchanges have a written policy setting out what happens to customer funds if a security breach causes loss.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hayley Howe, Custody of Digital Assets (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3936876
scope_conditions: custodial cryptocurrency exchanges surveyed in the 2017 benchmarking study

claims.claim: The unprecedented growth rate of decentralized exchanges may be an early indicator of increasing reliance on decentralized self-custody by retail users, but mainstream institutional adoption of digital assets is unlikely to materialize through self-custody and DEXs.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hayley Howe, Custody of Digital Assets (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3936876
scope_conditions: as of late 2020 and 2021 DEX growth
distinguishes retail from institutional adoption

claims.claim: Cold storage custody solutions are much more secure and resistant to cyber attacks than hot storage because the digital assets and associated private keys are held in wallets that are not connected to the Internet.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hayley Howe, Custody of Digital Assets (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3936876
scope_conditions: wallets kept offline

claims.claim: Cold storage trades security for accessibility: retrieving digital assets from cold storage can take many hours or even days, which makes cold storage especially ill suited to dynamic trading strategies.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hayley Howe, Custody of Digital Assets (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3936876
scope_conditions: assets held in cold storage devices
matters most for actively traded positions

claims.claim: Cold wallets typically lack the multisig feature that is common in hot storage, so the single employee acting as agent for a corporation may be the only access point to the corporate digital assets.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hayley Howe, Custody of Digital Assets (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3936876
scope_conditions: corporate or treasury holdings in cold storage without multisig

claims.claim: Institutional investors are less likely to engage in digital asset investments where custody solutions for digital assets are underdeveloped, and they find it difficult to commit fully until a reliable and respected custody solution exists.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hayley Howe, Custody of Digital Assets (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3936876
scope_conditions: institutional investors with client safety obligations

claims.claim: Self management of private keys or passphrases for individual digital assets is too cumbersome for institutional investors, so institutional custody solutions must be as robust as those provided for traditional assets.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hayley Howe, Custody of Digital Assets (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3936876
scope_conditions: institutional scale holdings

claims.claim: Applying the trust label to digital asset firms without an accompanying fiduciary duty is problematic, because the typical legal obligation of a trust company is to place customers' interests above its own.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hayley Howe, Custody of Digital Assets (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3936876
scope_conditions: state trust charters used by digital asset firms

claims.claim: Wyoming special purpose depository institutions may obtain FDIC insurance but are not required to, because they are prohibited from making loans with customer deposits of fiat currency.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hayley Howe, Custody of Digital Assets (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3936876
scope_conditions: Wyoming SPDIs under HB 74

claims.claim: State chartered special purpose depository institutions remove some of the legal hurdles that burden technological advances, notably the reluctance of the existing banking sector to tailor AML and BSA compliance processes to the global and censorship resistant nature of cryptocurrencies.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hayley Howe, Custody of Digital Assets (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3936876
scope_conditions: state chartered SPDIs such as those in Wyoming

claims.claim: Operational risk is inherently high in custody services because of the high volume of transactions processed daily, and those risks are magnified in a global custody operation running around the clock across different markets.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hayley Howe, Custody of Digital Assets (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3936876
scope_conditions: custody services generally, and global custody in particular

claims.claim: Information security infrastructure and controls to mitigate hacking, theft, and fraud must be enhanced when maintaining custody of digital assets, because digital assets have unique technical characteristics.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hayley Howe, Custody of Digital Assets (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3936876
scope_conditions: banks and custodians holding digital assets

claims.claim: Custodial service providers spend proportionally less on IT security than non custodial ones: custodians spend between 6 and 10 percent of resources on IT security while non custodial service providers spend between 11 and 20 percent.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hayley Howe, Custody of Digital Assets (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3936876
scope_conditions: surveyed cryptoasset service providers in the 2020 benchmarking study

claims.claim: Every risk in a digital custody operation should carry both a preventative and a detective control, layered so that if some controls fail others remain to reduce the risk.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hayley Howe, Custody of Digital Assets (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3936876
scope_conditions: digital asset custody risk management programs

claims.claim: Specialized digital custody audit procedures for verifying that a bank maintains access controls over a cryptographic key differ from the audit procedures used for physical assets, so some risk management processes must be tailored for digital custody.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hayley Howe, Custody of Digital Assets (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3936876
scope_conditions: national banks providing cryptocurrency custody

claims.claim: Externally led auditing of digital asset reserves among custodial service providers is declining, falling 24 percentage points relative to the 2018 sample.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hayley Howe, Custody of Digital Assets (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3936876
scope_conditions: surveyed custodial service providers, 2020 benchmarking study

claims.claim: Insurance coverage among digital asset service providers is far from universal: 46 percent of surveyed service providers reported not being insured against any risks.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hayley Howe, Custody of Digital Assets (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3936876
scope_conditions: surveyed cryptoasset service providers, 2020 benchmarking study

claims.claim: Credit risk is low in digital asset transactions because the transactions are made instantaneously, which removes the counterparty performance window that generates credit risk in traditional custody.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hayley Howe, Custody of Digital Assets (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3936876
scope_conditions: on chain digital asset transactions

claims.claim: Becoming an OCC regulated trust is one route by which crypto exchanges can operate nationwide without securing state level licenses in each of the 49 states that require one.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hayley Howe, Custody of Digital Assets (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3936876
scope_conditions: United States, national trust charter route

claims.claim: Multi-signature wallets and a combination of hot and cold storage solutions are the advisable custody design for digital assets.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hayley Howe, Custody of Digital Assets (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3936876

claims.claim: While the majority of cryptocurrency spot exchanges require ownership to be surrendered in order to transact, decentralized exchanges introduce the ability for users to transact without exposing their private keys to vulnerability.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hayley Howe, Custody of Digital Assets (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3936876
scope_conditions: comparison of centralized spot exchanges with DEXs

claims.claim: Applying current legacy custody rules developed for traditional assets to digital assets is inconsistent with the foundations of decentralization, because the very nature of a decentralized system mandates the avoidance and eradication of intermediaries for business transactions.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hayley Howe, Custody of Digital Assets (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3936876
scope_conditions: viewed from the perspective of decentralization

claims.claim: Where owners do not rely on the cryptography of the wallet and of each transaction to avoid trusted third parties, single points of failure, rent seeking behaviors and other suboptimal outcomes of legacy systems inevitably seep back into decentralized solutions.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hayley Howe, Custody of Digital Assets (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3936876
scope_conditions: decentralized systems that reintroduce trusted third parties

claims.claim: Delegation of rights to custody providers is only an incremental step toward centralization via delegation to third party investment managers, and it opens a floodgate because each additional level of investment discretion over digital assets exacerbates centralization concerns and compounds rent seeking suboptimalities.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hayley Howe, Custody of Digital Assets (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3936876
scope_conditions: delegation chains that begin with custody and extend to discretionary management

claims.claim: Taking the realities of decentralization and decentralized self-custody seriously would require investment advisers to provide digital asset investment advice for a fee without ever taking custody of the assets.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hayley Howe, Custody of Digital Assets (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3936876
scope_conditions: investment advisers serving digital asset clients

claims.claim: Legacy customer expectations of custodial solutions are what force continuous experimentation with digital asset custody within the existing and evolving legal framework, rather than a clean move to non custodial models.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hayley Howe, Custody of Digital Assets (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3936876
scope_conditions: markets serving legacy customers with traditional expectations

claims.claim: Centralized custody solutions and decentralized non custodial deal platforms will run in parallel until both are more established, and existing DeFi trends suggest the decentralized non custodial deal platforms will produce more innovation and better deals.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hayley Howe, Custody of Digital Assets (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3936876
scope_conditions: based on trends in DeFi as of 2021
author explicitly marks the outcome as uncertain

claims.claim: The six types of decentralization are not independent: each is subject to its own iterative process and affects the others through feedback effects, so proliferation in one type progressively changes the others.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization and Feedback Effects (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808852
scope_conditions: applies across decentralization of science, technology, organization, markets, government, and society

claims.claim: Because the instruments of scientific development and research are themselves centralized, the scientific consensus they produce is naturally centralized as well.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization and Feedback Effects (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808852

claims.claim: Journal publication incentives systematically bias the scientific record: journals prefer papers that reject the null hypothesis, use big datasets, and show big effect sizes, so significant findings failing those criteria may simply be ignored.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization and Feedback Effects (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808852
scope_conditions: applies to ranked scientific journals as the dominant publication channel

claims.claim: Peer review exacerbates publication bias and can produce a cartelization of knowledge, because non-conforming innovative ideas may not receive full recognition and new findings that threaten existing hierarchies are delayed or denied recognition.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization and Feedback Effects (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808852

claims.claim: The centralization of scientific methods and output has produced suboptimal outcomes for society, as evidenced by widespread irreproducibility, by non-expert forecasters often outperforming experts, and by random stock selection outperforming expert selection.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization and Feedback Effects (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808852

claims.claim: Increased networkability drives decentralization of science because it lowers the cost of ascertaining the accuracy of scientific results while raising the price a scientist pays for being inaccurate or wrong.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization and Feedback Effects (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808852
scope_conditions: requires interested parties to be networked through technology

claims.claim: The transition from client-server computing to peer-to-peer networking was the most significant step in the evolution of decentralized technology, because removing centralized hosts lets nodes make disk storage, bandwidth, and processing power directly available to each other.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization and Feedback Effects (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808852

claims.claim: Network effects proliferate in peer-to-peer networks because, unlike client-server architecture with linearly increasing per-unit costs, peer-to-peer network costs decrease with each added node.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization and Feedback Effects (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808852

claims.claim: Because of human shortcomings, bounded rationality, incomplete foresight, and information asymmetries, it is impossible for principals to contract for every possible action or inaction of the agent so as to induce the agent to act in the principal's best interest.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization and Feedback Effects (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808852
scope_conditions: applies to principal agent relationships in limited liability entities

claims.claim: Agency theory and the existing legal framework have failed to resolve the core agency conflict arising from the separation of ownership and control, so peaceable and productive coordination of human behavior remains wanting.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization and Feedback Effects (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808852
scope_conditions: applies to limited liability entities and their constituents

claims.claim: Societal path dependencies toward hierarchy and top-down command and control impose significant obstacles on organizational decentralization, hindering the transition of power from governments and large hierarchical organizations to the edges.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization and Feedback Effects (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808852

claims.claim: Organizational decentralization can raise economic performance without new technology: Jack Welch's separation of GE business units, each with its own profit-and-loss statement and full accountability, allowed efficient and profitable operation and GE's market value skyrocketed as a result.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization and Feedback Effects (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808852
scope_conditions: pre and post internet era corporate structures

claims.claim: Hybrid organizations combining centralized structure and profit optimization with bottom-up decentralization in the form of customer reviews generate significant success but also create tensions, because users who trust each other through ratings still demand consumer safeguards that require command-and-control structures.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization and Feedback Effects (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808852
scope_conditions: applies to internet platform companies such as eBay and Amazon

claims.claim: eBay's user rating system is visibly flawed and illustrates the need for a decentralized reputation verification system, yet no entity or individual has produced a better technology, and those decentralized ratings remained eBay's biggest competitive advantage.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization and Feedback Effects (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808852

claims.claim: Decentralized autonomous organizations epitomize organizational decentralization because the first DAO, built purely on code and smart contracts with no incorporation, physical address, or headquarters, entirely removed all traditional control mechanisms employed by principals in agency relationships.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization and Feedback Effects (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808852
scope_conditions: describes the first DAO launched in May 2016

claims.claim: The DAO focus on enhancing the value of fungible tokens can produce short termism and can cause ethical and governance issues to be ignored, even as it frees non-performance reputational penalties from racial and cultural bias.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization and Feedback Effects (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808852
scope_conditions: applies where DAO membership is organized around fungible token value

claims.claim: DAO developers are subject to path dependencies that undermine the evolution of decentralized DAO designs, because the communication structures of the organizations that design systems invariably shape future designs.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization and Feedback Effects (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808852

claims.claim: Because human brains simplify complex systems for coherence while complex adaptive systems evolve through self-organizing group behavior, decentralizing the interaction of DAO developers would support random developer interaction and make developer perspectives on software development more diverse.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization and Feedback Effects (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808852
scope_conditions: proposed as a remedy for developer path dependencies

claims.claim: At the beginning of the 2020s no forum existed that could support truly decentralized software development with a sufficient incentive design.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization and Feedback Effects (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808852
scope_conditions: as of the beginning of the 2020s

claims.claim: Markets whose trades do not depend on physical location evolved without centralized coordination, as shown by the foreign exchange market, which developed decentralized because currency trading required no physical location.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization and Feedback Effects (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808852
scope_conditions: holds where physical location is not determinative for the trade

claims.claim: The digitization of content is the most lasting contribution to market decentralization, because the physical location of assets matters less as content is digitized and virtual products emerge, so markets are becoming increasingly decentralized.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization and Feedback Effects (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808852

claims.claim: The ICO share of blockchain startup fundraising collapsed from 80 percent to around 35 percent by August 2018, recovered only marginally to 40 to 50 percent between September 2018 and February 2019, and then fell to 20 percent in March 2019.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization and Feedback Effects (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808852
scope_conditions: measured as percentage of total fundraising of blockchain startups

claims.claim: Decentralized cryptocurrency exchanges epitomize market decentralization because they let users interact and trade anonymously in a secure environment without third party intermediation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization and Feedback Effects (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808852

claims.claim: Conflicts of interest and counterparty risks are absent on a decentralized exchange because proprietary trading intermediaries such as market makers and centralized third-party operators cannot inject themselves into a transaction.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization and Feedback Effects (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808852
scope_conditions: applies to DEX where settlement is delivery versus payment directly between trading parties

claims.claim: Most decentralized exchanges have struggled with liquidity and price discovery.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization and Feedback Effects (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808852

claims.claim: A decentralized exchange can be seen as architecturally centralized, because the DEX code and its operational rules in effect create the exchange and provide a central order exchange and price discovery function rather than a peer-to-peer exchange.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization and Feedback Effects (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808852
scope_conditions: applies to DEX whose operational rules are set by code

claims.claim: Even though the creator of a DEX plays a limited role in its evolution, the code that provides the exchange's operational rules may still be subject to the centralized control of certain developers, and a completely open source DEX with no ongoing developer involvement remains untested.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization and Feedback Effects (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808852

claims.claim: Decentralized exchanges may fail to ensure market integrity, because the code that creates a DEX can allow asymmetric distribution of trading information based on user status.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization and Feedback Effects (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808852

claims.claim: Automation and the absence of a human backstop in compliance, back office, and settlement create new risks to market integrity on decentralized exchanges, including wash trading, frontrunning, and insider trading.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization and Feedback Effects (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808852

claims.claim: Governmental decentralization is the transference of responsibility and authority for public functions from centralized governmental agencies to centrally subordinated but quasi-independent public or private entities, and it is incommensurable because of its different kinds, degrees, and dimensions.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization and Feedback Effects (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808852

claims.claim: Local governments and private organizations can rarely fulfill government functions effectively without control over an adequate level of revenues, and that revenue control must be tied to authority over local expenditure decisions to be effective.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization and Feedback Effects (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808852
scope_conditions: applies to fiscal arrangements accompanying governmental decentralization

claims.claim: The degree of success in governmental decentralization is tied to the level of accountability instituted in the process, and accountability in turn depends on the availability of transparent public information that lets the community monitor local government performance.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization and Feedback Effects (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808852

claims.claim: Decentralization is not always efficient, because centralized economies of scale can create the near-optimal efficiencies for economic growth and decentralization may therefore result in the loss of economies of scale.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization and Feedback Effects (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808852

claims.claim: Standardized network-based services are very difficult to improve with decentralized approaches when local technical and administrative know-how is suboptimal, and this suboptimality is worsened when the local government lacks adequate financial resources.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization and Feedback Effects (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808852
scope_conditions: applies to standardized network-based public services

claims.claim: Government decentralization at the local level can favor local elites and may overcomplicate the coordination of national policies.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization and Feedback Effects (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808852

claims.claim: Silent governmental decentralization occurs without explicit policy: unlike affirmative reform, it results from inevitable changes in policy emphasis, networks, and resource availability, and can lead inevitably to a more decentralized system.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization and Feedback Effects (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808852

claims.claim: Governmental decentralization tends to occur during political or economic crises, because the fall of a regime and the resulting power vacuum causes power struggles, and it is during those struggles that forms of political decentralization emerge.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization and Feedback Effects (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808852
scope_conditions: conditioned on regime collapse or crisis of legitimacy

claims.claim: Regulatory sandboxes are an instance of regulatory decentralization: by lowering regulatory barriers and costs for testing disruptive technologies while protecting consumers, the regulator fosters innovation in increasingly decentralized products and services.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization and Feedback Effects (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808852
scope_conditions: based on the UK FCA sandbox introduced April 2016 and later ASIC, MAS, and FSRA sandboxes

claims.claim: The role of central government is increasingly under attack because Bitcoin could not be controlled or regulated by centralized governments, which spawned a community effort to build decentralized applications free from government control.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization and Feedback Effects (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808852
scope_conditions: as observed in the early 2020s

claims.claim: Because social media can move knowledge and views from the edges of society into the mainstream very quickly, this transfer can remove existing societal consensus, social cohesion among established groups, and order in the process.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization and Feedback Effects (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808852

claims.claim: As each form of decentralization empowers heightened proliferation of the other forms, individuals perceive more opportunities for changes in consumer behavior, silent withdrawal, disengagement, and defiance of the established centralized order.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization and Feedback Effects (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808852

claims.claim: The crypto movement illustrates the feedback effects between types of decentralization: its political philosophy could not be instantiated without technological decentralization in the form of cryptocurrencies, the combination created new markets, and the movement then created new organizational forms in DAOs.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization and Feedback Effects (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808852
scope_conditions: describes the crypto movement of the late 2010s

claims.claim: The founders' initial vision of a truly decentralized internet without central points of failure could not be fulfilled, which is why internet idealists continue to seek technological ways to re-decentralize the internet.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization and Feedback Effects (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808852

claims.claim: Improved incentive design is necessary but not sufficient for decentralization: better decentralized incentive designs can accelerate adoption, yet design alone will not produce the decentralization of business and society, because adoption depends on society's acceptance and use of the technology.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization Neutralizers (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808873
scope_conditions: decentralized technology adoption at the level of business and society

claims.claim: Habits formed by analog era socialization are a decentralization neutralizer: people raised in the analog age hold work and social habits that are very hard to change, and they attribute superiority to outdated technology formats even when the content is identical.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization Neutralizers (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808873
scope_conditions: populations socialized before digital and decentralized technologies

claims.claim: Legacy businesses actively neutralize decentralized competition by acquiring little known companies that hold highly competitive decentralized technologies, as Microsoft's acquisition of Skype illustrates.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization Neutralizers (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808873
scope_conditions: incumbent firms facing decentralized technology competitors

claims.claim: The libertarian and reformist orientation of the crypto community itself neutralizes decentralization, because the strong idea of reforming society with decentralized technology makes cooperation with existing centralized structures often suboptimal.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization Neutralizers (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808873
scope_conditions: crypto community formed after the Bitcoin whitepaper
early 2020s

claims.claim: Decentralized issuers treated central bank issued digital currencies as a threat rather than as a pathway to mainstream acceptance of more decentralized cryptocurrencies, and that misreading forfeited a route to broader adoption.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization Neutralizers (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808873
scope_conditions: central bank digital currency debate of the early 2020s

claims.claim: The profit driven influx into the digital asset space brought rampant fraud that created a chasm between the decentralized asset space and mainstream investors, and lacking regulatory certainty and recognition of cryptocurrencies exacerbated that divide.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization Neutralizers (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808873
scope_conditions: digital asset markets between roughly 2010 and 2020

claims.claim: Decentralized technology systems require interoperability for survivability, yet most platforms attempt to go it alone in an effort to become the next Bitcoin, so decentralized community silos proliferate and the required infrastructure, which no single protocol can build, does not get built.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization Neutralizers (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808873
scope_conditions: decentralized protocol ecosystems in the early 2020s

claims.claim: Proof of Work block rewards structurally reintroduce centralization: the economic nature of mining rewards incentivizes degrees of centralization through collective action of nodes that share rewards as a group, that is, mining pools.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization Neutralizers (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808873
scope_conditions: Proof of Work consensus with block rewards
Bitcoin in the early 2020s

claims.claim: Early stage consensus designs such as PoW, PoS and DPoS create a community belief system in certain foundational technology features that in effect inhibits higher degrees of decentralization, so suboptimal early decentralization becomes self perpetuating.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization Neutralizers (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808873
scope_conditions: early stage decentralized technologies such as PoW, PoS and DPoS

claims.claim: The decentralization of network technology is capped by its host environment: decentralized systems are built on and confined by the internet, which is decentralized in its foundation but has a centralized order structure.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization Neutralizers (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808873
scope_conditions: decentralized systems built on existing internet infrastructure

claims.claim: Centralization follows an S curve: in the expansion phase the benefits of centralizing power, capital and control rise faster than its costs, but in the decline phase the rising costs of centralization, including corruption, diseconomies of scale and cronyism, can no longer be offset, so centralized systems function less optimally and less efficiently.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization Neutralizers (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808873
scope_conditions: centralized systems in business and society over their life cycle

claims.claim: Even where superior decentralized technological solutions exist, the centralized elements deeply engrained in business and society can be perpetuated by the efficiency gains of the S curve of centralization, so superiority alone does not displace them.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization Neutralizers (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808873
scope_conditions: societies with deeply engrained centralized infrastructure such as legal systems and financial services

claims.claim: Applying decentralized technology to optimize a legacy system, for example using blockchain to improve the malfunctioning shareholder proxy voting process, perpetuates the outdated and malfunctioning centralized system rather than replacing it with a better performing decentralized one.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Decentralization Neutralizers (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808873
scope_conditions: decentralized technology deployed as an optimization layer on centralized legacy processes

claims.claim: Decentralized system design is itself path dependent on the centralized past: designers' prior experience in centralized structures infiltrates and undermines attempts to create more decentralized systems, through subconscious processes the designer cannot change or influence.
