claims.claim: Modern code review imposes substantial hidden costs because developers spend an average of six hours per week reviewing others' changes and are forced to switch away from their own work, creating an opportunity cost on project development.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How DAOs Optimize Open-Source Code Reviews and Create Open-Source Standards (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3995709
scope_conditions: modern code review in industry and open source settings

claims.claim: The benefit of a code review is negatively correlated with the size of the code under review: the larger the number of files in a single review, the lower the rate of beneficial feedback from reviewers.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How DAOs Optimize Open-Source Code Reviews and Create Open-Source Standards (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3995709
scope_conditions: single review submissions of increasing size

claims.claim: Patch size degrades multiple dimensions of code review performance at once: comment density per reviewer falls as patches grow, the quality and amount of contribution is affected, and the time required to provide significant contributions increases.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How DAOs Optimize Open-Source Code Reviews and Create Open-Source Standards (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3995709
scope_conditions: studies measuring comment density against lines of code

claims.claim: Code review effectiveness is undermined by heavier review loads, because reviewers with longer review queues become overwhelmed and are more likely to submit poor quality code evaluations.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How DAOs Optimize Open-Source Code Reviews and Create Open-Source Standards (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3995709
scope_conditions: reviewers carrying long review queues

claims.claim: Proposed remedies for patch size, namely distributing the workload across a broader set of reviewers and providing better transparency on developer review queues, have not solved the problem; patch size remains an issue affecting the quality, speed, and effectiveness of modern code review.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How DAOs Optimize Open-Source Code Reviews and Create Open-Source Standards (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3995709
scope_conditions: existing remedies deployed within legacy review processes

claims.claim: Confusion during code review lengthens reviews through a message escalation mechanism: more confusion produces more messages exchanged during discussion, so the review takes longer than it should.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How DAOs Optimize Open-Source Code Reviews and Create Open-Source Standards (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3995709
scope_conditions: reviewers encountering unfamiliar code

claims.claim: Code confusion produces blind approval, where a reviewer hopes a co-worker knows what they are doing and approves a change without understanding it, which can result in further bugs and delayed production.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How DAOs Optimize Open-Source Code Reviews and Create Open-Source Standards (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3995709
scope_conditions: reviewers confused by unfamiliar code
peer trust within a team

claims.claim: Failing to maximize developer participation and communication negatively affects the code review process and creates unnecessary costs on software development, and this is difficult to remedy because code review is subject to sensitivities arising from the egos of the individuals involved.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How DAOs Optimize Open-Source Code Reviews and Create Open-Source Standards (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3995709
scope_conditions: code review conducted among human peers

claims.claim: Feedback in modern code review is deficient in both timeliness and substance: receiving feedback in a timely manner is developers' number one reported challenge, and the feedback that arrives is often not insightful because reviewers focus on insignificant details rather than larger issues.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How DAOs Optimize Open-Source Code Reviews and Create Open-Source Standards (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3995709
scope_conditions: surveyed developer populations in industry code review

claims.claim: Organizational metrics, such as the number of developers working on a component, organizational distance between developers, and organizational code ownership, are better predictors of defect proneness than traditional metrics like churn, complexity, coverage, dependencies, and pre release bug measures.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How DAOs Optimize Open-Source Code Reviews and Create Open-Source Standards (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3995709
scope_conditions: large organization software development

claims.claim: Organizational identity and structure affect the time and effectiveness of the code review process, as shown by a statistically significant difference in how quickly Apple accepts its own patches versus Google patches.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How DAOs Optimize Open-Source Code Reviews and Create Open-Source Standards (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3995709
scope_conditions: cross organization patch submission

claims.claim: The more hierarchical the code review process and the more barriers to entry it imposes, the lower the quality of the resulting code.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How DAOs Optimize Open-Source Code Reviews and Create Open-Source Standards (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3995709
scope_conditions: legacy code review firms with hierarchical reviewer selection

claims.claim: In hierarchical legacy review processes the first reviewer's output gets the highest priority and follow on reviewers add only minor upgrades, so the collective of reviewers is not incentivized to find flaws and optimize the code as a collective work product.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How DAOs Optimize Open-Source Code Reviews and Create Open-Source Standards (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3995709
scope_conditions: legacy code review firms
hierarchical ordering of reviewers

claims.claim: Increasing the number of reviewers who ask clarifying questions makes code simpler and clearer and thereby typically increases code quality, but hierarchical review processes make this impossible.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How DAOs Optimize Open-Source Code Reviews and Create Open-Source Standards (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3995709
scope_conditions: hierarchical review structures

claims.claim: The hierarchical approach to code reviews undermines long term participation and opinion from the edges of the reviewer spectrum, because those reviewers either have no access or are in no position to help review the code.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How DAOs Optimize Open-Source Code Reviews and Create Open-Source Standards (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3995709
scope_conditions: hierarchical legacy review processes

claims.claim: Without crowd controls, the reviewer's views and the author's intent are at odds and the reviewer can impose their own logic, forcing the author to rewrite functionally sound code repeatedly, which is highly time consuming and inefficient.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How DAOs Optimize Open-Source Code Reviews and Create Open-Source Standards (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3995709
scope_conditions: legacy code review processes lacking crowd control

claims.claim: A code review should focus on the functionality of the code and on keeping mistaken, badly constructed, and dangerous code out, rather than on the reviewer imposing their own stylistic logic.

claims.claim: Delays in legacy code reviews, which can be exacerbated by digital asset market conditions, can impact development and may require complete rewriting of contracts because the underlying protocol may have upgraded core libraries during the review.

fast moving protocol environments in digital asset markets

claims.claim: Cartel power undermines attempts by other industry players to create internal or external controls on the quality of code reviews, leaving the public with no or very weak control over the quality of the code review services it receives.

claims.claim: Because customers cannot afford to search for better priced code reviews and are forced into cartel pricing to obtain market acceptance of their products, cartelization undermines any form of downward price pressure.

scope_conditions: clients requiring market acceptance signals from audit firms

claims.claim: There is little or no recourse for clients when reviewed code proves to be flawed even after functionality and quality review.

claims.claim: Despite the significant flaws in code reviews and their often flawed results, the existing code review market does not allow for any form of insurance product of the kind associated with products in other markets.

claims.claim: Even if code review and audit firms did engage in thorough insurance underwriting and guarantees for their clients, the remedy would still fail because those firms would remain subject to the flawed and centralized legacy insurance market, which is itself dominated by a cartel of a few core players.

claims.claim: The conveniences and benefits of centralized algorithmic automation carry risks to humanity that cannot be fully quantified, and decentralized systems can counteract those downsides and threats.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How Decentralized Systems Can Upgrade AI (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808867

claims.claim: A single powerful application such as Google already exercises substantial control over human knowledge and thought, and could control societal outcomes by making disparate recommendations to similarly situated users.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How Decentralized Systems Can Upgrade AI (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808867
scope_conditions: dominant internet based applications accumulating societal functions since the early 2010s

claims.claim: The quantification and algorithmic optimization of human thought, feeling, and action can produce an optimization of humans that is too complex for humans to understand without the data driven algorithmic aids themselves.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How Decentralized Systems Can Upgrade AI (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808867
scope_conditions: sensor and wearable derived data on human interaction

claims.claim: Big data and algorithmic data analytics enable centralized algorithmically automated systems such as Google, Facebook, and Amazon to know individuals' political preferences better than the individuals themselves.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How Decentralized Systems Can Upgrade AI (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808867
scope_conditions: centralized algorithmically automated platforms in the early 2020s

claims.claim: As algorithmic analytics and predictions of human preferences become increasingly accepted, exercising human political will by proxy through algorithmic interpretations may become the new normal in the foreseeable future.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How Decentralized Systems Can Upgrade AI (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808867
scope_conditions: increasing acceptance of algorithmic prediction of human choice

claims.claim: In its ultimate state, algorithmic automation negates human input in data systems altogether, because human bounded rationality creates inefficiencies and the human condition yields suboptimal outputs even when algorithmically optimized.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How Decentralized Systems Can Upgrade AI (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808867
scope_conditions: fully realized centralized algorithmic automation

claims.claim: A feedback loop exists between decentralized protection of the human factor in algorithmic systems and the proliferation of both algorithmic automation and decentralized solutions.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How Decentralized Systems Can Upgrade AI (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808867

claims.claim: Because a decentralized system has a blockchain based quasi precedent nature with a human backstop, it enables built in checks and balances capable of supporting resistance even to apocalyptic takeovers of algorithmic systems that would remove human presence to optimize efficiency.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How Decentralized Systems Can Upgrade AI (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808867
scope_conditions: blockchain based systems with accumulated human voting records

claims.claim: Those few entities and individuals who control the data flow and the associated algorithms can use centralized algorithmic human predictors to build autocratic algorithmic systems and structures, and the implied loss of democratic principles in society is perhaps an inevitable side effect.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How Decentralized Systems Can Upgrade AI (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808867
scope_conditions: concentrated control over data flows and algorithms

claims.claim: Because of its autocratic and efficiency focused tendencies, centralized algorithmic automation is prone to create structures for the evolution of dataism, which ultimately denies the value of human inputs and individualism.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How Decentralized Systems Can Upgrade AI (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808867
scope_conditions: centralized algorithmic automation oriented to harmonization and efficiency

claims.claim: Code based trust lowers transaction costs and simultaneously raises consumer and market confidence and certainty, which facilitates economies of scale that are rarely possible in centralized structures, despite the cybersecurity problems associated with cryptocurrencies.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How Decentralized Systems Can Upgrade AI (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808867
scope_conditions: code based decentralized applications
presence of cybersecurity issues in cryptocurrency markets

claims.claim: Because decentralized platforms can remove the consumer fees that are integral to their centralized competitors, they also remove downward pressure on platform worker compensation, since costs are less likely to increase and be passed on to workers and consumers.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How Decentralized Systems Can Upgrade AI (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808867
scope_conditions: decentralized platforms with lower cost structures than centralized competitors

claims.claim: Blockchain based guarantees remove agency costs because principals are less required to institute oversight and monitoring of agents, which addresses inherent agency problems in modern finance and corporate governance.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How Decentralized Systems Can Upgrade AI (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808867
scope_conditions: contracts whose parameters are verified by a majority of miners or nodes

claims.claim: Decentralized payment systems hold a comparative advantage over centralized legacy fiat systems because holding and storing cryptocurrencies requires no banking relationship, whereas centralized fiat payment platforms typically require an existing banking relationship.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How Decentralized Systems Can Upgrade AI (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808867
scope_conditions: consumers without existing banking relationships

claims.claim: High intermediary fees in legacy payment systems make transacting economically viable only at higher transaction volumes, thereby creating barriers to entry that decentralized payment systems do not impose.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How Decentralized Systems Can Upgrade AI (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808867
scope_conditions: centralized legacy fiat payment systems relying on banks and payment processors

claims.claim: Cash usage in the United States, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, Sweden, Finland, Canada, and France and other industrialized nations has fallen well below 50 percent of total transaction volume.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How Decentralized Systems Can Upgrade AI (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808867
scope_conditions: industrialized nations at the beginning of the 2020s

claims.claim: Transacting in cash costs United States consumers roughly 200 billion dollars annually, about 637 dollars per person, driven by the costs of production, storage, and transportation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How Decentralized Systems Can Upgrade AI (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808867
scope_conditions: United States, early 2020s

claims.claim: The end of the technological life cycles of legacy payment systems in the early 2020s, together with emerging payment trends, requires central banks to intensify their examination of alternative payment systems.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How Decentralized Systems Can Upgrade AI (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3808867
scope_conditions: central banks and governments experimenting with digital and cryptocurrencies since 2015

claims.claim: In conventional Proof of Stake, selection probability for block rewards rises with stake and block rewards are constant regardless of node reputation, whereas in Secure Proof of Stake nodes with higher reputation have a higher probability of being selected for rewards.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hybrid Secure Proof of Stake (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3931933
scope_conditions: comparison of conventional PoS and SPoS reward selection

claims.claim: The core proposal of Hybrid Secure Proof of Stake is to separate block consensus from block rewards, making the reward a function of the node's reputation rather than of stake alone.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hybrid Secure Proof of Stake (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3931933

claims.claim: Under HSPoS a node's probability of being selected remains driven by its fungible stake, while the size of the block reward it receives is scaled by a non-fungible reputation multiplier derived from the node's reputation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hybrid Secure Proof of Stake (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3931933
scope_conditions: HSPoS reward layer applied on top of an existing PoS consensus layer

claims.claim: Because HSPoS supplements rather than replaces the consensus layer, an existing PoS consensus algorithm can be kept in operation while reputation is introduced through the reward function, permitting a gradual rather than abrupt transition to SPoS.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hybrid Secure Proof of Stake (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3931933
scope_conditions: networks already running a traditional PoS consensus algorithm

claims.claim: Moving a network from PoS to SPoS should proceed by evolving the rewards mechanism in two steps through HSPoS, rather than by switching the consensus mechanism directly.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hybrid Secure Proof of Stake (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3931933
scope_conditions: networks seeking to adopt Secure Proof of Stake

claims.claim: Platform centralization is especially damaging in developer communities because developers are the channel through which information from the edges of the system and society enters, and through which consensus on emerging technologies is formed.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hybrid Secure Proof of Stake (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3931933
scope_conditions: technology platforms whose direction is controlled centrally

claims.claim: The lack of developer liberalization carries negative societal consequences: when developers are restrained from building what they see as cutting edge and socially beneficial, society's own capacity to experiment with new technology is severely hampered.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hybrid Secure Proof of Stake (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3931933
scope_conditions: developer communities constrained by centralized platform control

claims.claim: The final 2021 Casper testnet used perceived validator node uptime as its single rewarding requirement.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hybrid Secure Proof of Stake (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3931933
scope_conditions: Casper testnet incentivization phase ending September 2021

claims.claim: Early Casper testnet participation was sustained by norms of unpaid mutual support, with participants actively sharing knowledge and supporting other validators without expectation of profit or return favors.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hybrid Secure Proof of Stake (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3931933
scope_conditions: early Casper testnet period before incentivized phases

claims.claim: Detailed and easy to follow operator documentation produced by the early testnet community drove participation up to roughly 950 nodes running on the network, with around 200 nodes rewarded each week.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hybrid Secure Proof of Stake (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3931933
scope_conditions: early Casper testnet days

claims.claim: Publishing each validator's uptime and rewarding status to the community on a weekly basis coincided with active Casper testnet nodes falling below 800, in a period of already volatile validator participation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hybrid Secure Proof of Stake (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3931933
scope_conditions: 2021 Casper testnet incentivized phases

claims.claim: Validators who learned they would receive no reward shut down their nodes rather than waiting for the incentivization phase to end, so a reward scheme that visibly excludes participants loses their contribution immediately.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hybrid Secure Proof of Stake (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3931933
scope_conditions: 2021 Casper testnet incentivization phase

claims.claim: The initial Casper testnet was subject to inevitable centralization, illustrated by a small group of core developers setting validator performance numbers and other rules without broader community input.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hybrid Secure Proof of Stake (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3931933
scope_conditions: initial Casper testnet governance

claims.claim: Opacity about reward eligibility is itself a source of dysfunction: during the first phase of the 2021 Casper testnet it was unclear which validators would be rewarded in each week, which caused friction and non-productive discussions among the validators.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hybrid Secure Proof of Stake (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3931933
scope_conditions: first phase of the 2021 Casper testnet
weekly publication of uptime scores improved the situation only marginally

claims.claim: The initial Casper testnet group was hampered by communication shortcomings, with only around 680 validators present in the telegram group that served as the main channel for news and updates.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hybrid Secure Proof of Stake (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3931933
scope_conditions: 2021 Casper testnet validator community

claims.claim: Uptime based reward policies invite Sybil style abuse: on the original Casper testnet single persons ran fifteen or more validator nodes to exploit cloud provider promotions and the DEVxDAO rewards policy, extracting rewards without contributing to the validator group.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hybrid Secure Proof of Stake (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3931933
scope_conditions: original Casper testnet under a uptime only rewards policy

claims.claim: Lack of validator expertise degraded the initial Casper testnet, with only around 85 percent of testnet nodes up to date and roughly 140 active machines contributing nothing to the network.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hybrid Secure Proof of Stake (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3931933
scope_conditions: initial Casper testnet

claims.claim: Reward focused participation crowds out technical engagement: many Casper testnet participants lacked the expertise to run nodes, and their questions concentrated on reward payments with little to no focus on technical topics.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hybrid Secure Proof of Stake (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3931933
scope_conditions: initial Casper testnet telegram channel discussions

claims.claim: Despite its shortcomings the 2021 Casper testnet fulfilled its purpose, providing a test bed for dApp developers and testing node software upgrades before deployment on the Casper mainnet.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hybrid Secure Proof of Stake (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3931933
scope_conditions: 2021 Casper testnet

claims.claim: Any testnet environment depends on proper governance to allocate power fairly and equitably at equilibrium in a sustainable fashion.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hybrid Secure Proof of Stake (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3931933
scope_conditions: testnet environments generally

claims.claim: The Shasper canary network is designed as an experimental environment for developer teams that want to move fast and innovate, or to prepare deployments destined for the Casper Network.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hybrid Secure Proof of Stake (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3931933
scope_conditions: canary network running parallel to the Casper testnet and mainnet

claims.claim: Shasper governance is funded in a hardcoded way: each validator that succeeds in propagating a block allocates a fixed percentage of its block reward, denominated in SHAS, into a separate SDAO wallet, in addition to the ordinary Casper PoS allocation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hybrid Secure Proof of Stake (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3931933
scope_conditions: Shasper Network validators producing blocks under the Casper PoS consensus algorithm

claims.claim: The same percentage of the block reward that funds the SDAO wallet also mints reputation in the SDAO for the propagating validator, with both the minting and the sharing of the pooled tokens following the DEVxDAO MVPR protocol.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hybrid Secure Proof of Stake (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3931933
scope_conditions: Shasper Network block production

claims.claim: Tokens accumulated in the SDAO wallet are distributed to voting associates in proportion to their SDAO reputation score, so payout tracks reputation rather than stake.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hybrid Secure Proof of Stake (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3931933
scope_conditions: SDAO members holding voting associate status

claims.claim: A voting associate's SDAO reputation score is determined by that associate's merit, level of activity, and engagement in the SDAO.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hybrid Secure Proof of Stake (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3931933
scope_conditions: SDAO reputation accounting

claims.claim: SDAO membership is gated by a vote combined with evidence of NFT ownership and a posted performance record as a Shasper Network validator.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hybrid Secure Proof of Stake (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3931933
scope_conditions: SDAO onboarding of Shasper testnet validators

claims.claim: Although the Shasper Network itself is permissionless, the SDAO deliberately imposes a prior registration requirement in order to push validator candidates to educate themselves about network requirements and to attend to the documentation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hybrid Secure Proof of Stake (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3931933
scope_conditions: SDAO reward program on a permissionless network

claims.claim: The SDAO performance based onboarding metric deliberately goes well beyond validator node uptime, adding criteria such as node performance, running a dApp on the network, response time to upgrades, technical background, adherence to instructions and hardware specifications, and community behavior.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hybrid Secure Proof of Stake (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3931933
scope_conditions: SDAO preregistration workflow for validator candidates

claims.claim: Using the SDAO, the Shasper Network lets its developer community determine by community consensus which technology upgrades to the testnet should be created.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hybrid Secure Proof of Stake (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3931933
scope_conditions: Shasper Network technology upgrade process

claims.claim: Peer governance substitutes for platform gatekeeping: rather than convincing legacy technology leaders and their platforms, developer teams engage their own peers in the Shasper DAO to discuss and vote on proposed upgrades and testnet projects.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hybrid Secure Proof of Stake (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3931933
scope_conditions: Shasper DAO technology upgrade voting

claims.claim: Changes to the Shasper Network codebase require Shasper Network governance votes.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hybrid Secure Proof of Stake (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3931933
scope_conditions: Shasper Network codebase changes

claims.claim: Under HSPoS two nodes holding the same stake retain the same probability of being selected for rewards, but the node with the higher reputation receives the larger reward.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hybrid Secure Proof of Stake (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3931933
scope_conditions: HSPoS reward computation with equal stakes

claims.claim: Nodes accumulate reputation in two ways: by being onboarded into the SDAO and performing well as node validators, and by participating regularly in SDAO governance votes.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hybrid Secure Proof of Stake (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3931933
scope_conditions: HSPoS reputation accrual on the Shasper Network

claims.claim: Because reputation scales the reward, a node with less stake but high reputation may end up with more rewards than a node with more stake but less reputation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hybrid Secure Proof of Stake (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3931933
scope_conditions: HSPoS reward computation

claims.claim: By balancing validator stakes against reputation, HSPoS reaches an equilibrium of incentives in which validators are motivated both to succeed economically as validators and to participate actively in decentralized governance.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hybrid Secure Proof of Stake (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3931933
scope_conditions: validators holding both SHAS stake and SDAO reputation

claims.claim: HSPoS earns validator node reputation through a mechanism that is decoupled from the ordinary monetary system of incentive rewards.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hybrid Secure Proof of Stake (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3931933
scope_conditions: HSPoS reputation layer

claims.claim: Reputation in HSPoS is a form of social capital earned by participating in the network's ecosystem, independent of the participant's financial capacity.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hybrid Secure Proof of Stake (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3931933
scope_conditions: HSPoS and SDAO reputation

claims.claim: Governance decisions such as network upgrades follow a simple vote that mints no reputation, yet reputation in the SDAO can still be lost through a governance vote because each vote follows the DEVxDAO MVPR logic moving from loosely coupled to tightly coupled voting.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hybrid Secure Proof of Stake (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3931933
scope_conditions: SDAO governance votes on network upgrades

claims.claim: The Shasper network extends the Casper testnet in a way that benefits community experimentation and creates significant developer incentives that help retain talent for the Casper network.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Hybrid Secure Proof of Stake (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3931933
scope_conditions: Shasper deployed as a canary network alongside Casper

claims.claim: Human group coordination progresses through three stages: chaos, then decentralized organization, then centralized hierarchy. Decentralized organization is not a deviation but the natural intermediate stage between no organization and a completed hierarchy.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Introduction to Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782192
scope_conditions: human group coordination and institutional development generally

claims.claim: At the decentralized stage the individual nodes remain autonomous and the network assigns no fixed roles; coordination comes from alignment on a shared transcendental goal rather than from formal position, so that, as the authors put it, the values are the organization.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Introduction to Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782192
scope_conditions: decentralized stage of organization, before a hierarchy has formed

claims.claim: Centralization is an optimal and natural evolutionary solution to most specific organizational problems, but only under static conditions, and competition is the most common driving force that produces a centralized structure.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Introduction to Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782192
scope_conditions: static environmental conditions
a specific, well defined organizational problem

claims.claim: Centralization is not the optimal organizational structure under highly dynamic conditions; the very features that make centralized hierarchies efficient become their greatest weaknesses when conditions change.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Introduction to Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782192
scope_conditions: highly dynamic or rapidly changing environments

claims.claim: If a hierarchy becomes too rigid the organization inevitably fails and the result is a return to chaos, which is why revolutions recur as a cyclic pattern in governmental structures throughout history.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Introduction to Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782192
scope_conditions: hierarchies that cannot bend or rearrange their order

claims.claim: Concentrating too much power in any single office of a hierarchy creates a decision making bottleneck that can cripple the organization, so the tree structure that is optimal for transmitting orders downward is also its point of paralysis.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Introduction to Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782192
scope_conditions: centralized tree structures with concentrated decision rights

claims.claim: Because information at the edge does not travel up a centralized hierarchy, the central authority makes decisions without full information, and a centralized organization is therefore not well designed to respond to any crisis it has not anticipated.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Introduction to Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782192
scope_conditions: strongly centralized organizations that leave no decision power at the edges
novel or unanticipated external challenges

claims.claim: Friction is the inefficient allocation of power, meaning that a different distribution of power would let the organization reach its goals more easily, and it is an ever present feature of any hierarchy.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Introduction to Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782192
scope_conditions: any real hierarchy

claims.claim: The most common source of friction is the natural tendency of hierarchies to concentrate power at the top through a rich get richer mechanism: a more powerful member can use their greater power to gain still more power than a weaker member can.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Introduction to Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782192
scope_conditions: hierarchies in which power differences among members already exist

claims.claim: Unchecked concentration of power drives the distribution toward one member holding nearly all resources, which is clearly inefficient for the goals of the group, and the resulting discontent is the main historical reason for revolt.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Introduction to Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782192
scope_conditions: hierarchies where the concentration of power is left unchecked

claims.claim: Corruption is defined as a minority subgroup collecting the power or wealth of an organization for its own benefit at the expense of the larger group.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Introduction to Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782192

claims.claim: The more rigid an organization's structure, the more susceptible it is to corruption; at the chaos stage there is no protocol rigidity and therefore no opportunity for corruption, because with no group goal there is nothing to subvert.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Introduction to Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782192
scope_conditions: comparison across the chaos, decentralized, and centralized stages

claims.claim: Corruption is technically inevitable in any hierarchy, because it is impossible to create a perfectly efficient organization in practice and there is friction in every real system.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Introduction to Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782192
scope_conditions: any real hierarchy

claims.claim: When the letter of the law becomes more important than the spirit of the law, internal competition for power makes the winning strategy to push behavior to the limit of what is acceptable.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Introduction to Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782192
scope_conditions: formal rule based governance inside a centralized hierarchy
internal competition for power

claims.claim: As members constantly probe the edge of acceptable behavior, policing the rules becomes more expensive, the rules become divorced from the shared goals, and relationships become brittle and formal instead of warm and loose.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Introduction to Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782192
scope_conditions: organizations relying on formal rule enforcement

claims.claim: No static set of logical rules can ever succeed in preventing corruption, which is the ultimate problem with relying on letter of the law governance instead of spirit of the law governance.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Introduction to Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782192
scope_conditions: any static, formally specified rule set

claims.claim: The Folk Theorems of game theory prove that any rules that can be formally set down can be subverted: strategies always exist that follow the rules and still allow a minority player to profit at the expense of the majority.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Introduction to Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782192
scope_conditions: any formally specified rule set analyzed as a repeated game

claims.claim: Long-term organizational stability requires a dynamic governance system that can adapt the rules to changing circumstances, a requirement that holds for any organization but especially for decentralized ones.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Introduction to Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782192
scope_conditions: organizations seeking long-term stability
especially decentralized organizations

claims.claim: The second necessity for long-term stability is that the organization hold to its ideals and transcendental values, so that the spirit of the law overrides the letter of the law.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Introduction to Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782192
scope_conditions: organizations seeking long-term stability

claims.claim: Governing by transcendental values, ideals that everyone understands but no one can concretely attain, reduces members' motivation to probe the limits of acceptable behavior and therefore reduces the policing the organization must pay for.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Introduction to Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782192
scope_conditions: organizations whose governing ideals cannot be fully instantiated in concrete rules

claims.claim: Rigidity generates corruption: because a rigid organization ignores new information incompatible with its structure, the unexploited value creates an opportunity for an individual to capture it for personal advantage rather than for the group.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Introduction to Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782192
scope_conditions: rigid organizations facing a changing environment

claims.claim: Even where corruption is avoided, rigidity still leads centralized organizations to catastrophic ends, because failures push members to cling more faithfully to the rules that saved them in the past, making the system still more rigid and brittle.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Introduction to Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782192
scope_conditions: centralized organizations under repeated external shocks

claims.claim: Decentralized organizations thrive under exactly the changing circumstances that break centralized organizations, because information at the edge is naturally incorporated and communicated so the system can adapt to external threats.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Introduction to Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782192
scope_conditions: changing or turbulent external environments

claims.claim: Decentralization, though it may look wastefully redundant, gives every member greater autonomous power, whereas centralization limits members' powers and reduces them to cogs in the machine.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Introduction to Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782192

claims.claim: Advances in technology have given decentralized systems the efficiency they lacked in previous eras, the very deficiency that allowed them to be outcompeted by centralized systems; this is the book's central thesis.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Introduction to Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782192
scope_conditions: the current era of information technology

claims.claim: Nothing external can destroy a decentralized organization: such organizations are invincible unless every single member loses adherence to the values that organized it in the first place.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, Introduction to Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782192
scope_conditions: decentralized organizations whose members retain shared values

claims.claim: Centralization is a natural state that evolves out of decentralization under competition unless it is consciously prevented by guarding members' power, while a centralized organization can always be conquered through its single point of failure at the top.

claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Reputation as Capital – How DAOs Upgrade Finance (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3949098
scope_conditions: after the DAOIC has solidified its market position

claims.claim: Without standards for digital assets it will be very difficult to increase regulatory certainty or coordinate market activity, and without regulatory certainty the digital asset market is less likely to evolve.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Reputation as Capital – How DAOs Upgrade Finance (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3949098
scope_conditions: digital asset markets seeking mass adoption

claims.claim: The decentralized reputation staking governance mechanisms provide a higher form of decentralized governance than most legal standards in any given jurisdiction.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Reputation as Capital – How DAOs Upgrade Finance (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3949098

claims.claim: Conflicts of interest from DAOIC members participating on the public side of a deal are minimized because the loosely coupled reputation staking vote and its transition to a tightly coupled vote are transparent to the public.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Reputation as Capital – How DAOs Upgrade Finance (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3949098
scope_conditions: loosely coupled votes on particular deals are publicly visible

claims.claim: If the DAOIC is perceived as having a market impact, it could significantly increase corruptive influences from other market players, which in turn increases the likelihood of regulatory intervention, so market neutrality is in the DAOIC's long term interest.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Reputation as Capital – How DAOs Upgrade Finance (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3949098
scope_conditions: DAOIC has proliferated and is visible to the market and regulators

claims.claim: The DAOIC pools no assets: the smart contract releases each member's deposit directly to the project after validation pool approval, and returns on purchases are likewise not pooled but paid pro rata to members in proportion to their reputation token holdings.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Reputation as Capital – How DAOs Upgrade Finance (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3949098
scope_conditions: non custodial DAOIC model coordinated by smart contracts

claims.claim: Kaal characterizes the 20 percent of public return on purchases as an access to information fee, paid to the DAOIC in exchange for the ability to learn which deals DAOIC members upvoted through reputation staking.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Reputation as Capital – How DAOs Upgrade Finance (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3949098
scope_conditions: the pooled portion of public returns minted into fungible reputation tokens

claims.claim: The key difference from the traditional venture capital model is that the DAOIC only makes its investment choices public and never provides investment analysis, so public co purchases are entirely voluntary.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Reputation as Capital – How DAOs Upgrade Finance (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3949098
scope_conditions: public co purchases alongside DAOIC deals

claims.claim: Ratio adjustments are the DAOIC's key tool for strategic increases in profitability and overall policy, and they should be subject to a member vote conducted through the decentralized reputation staking governance mechanisms.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Reputation as Capital – How DAOs Upgrade Finance (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3949098
scope_conditions: governance metrics subject to dynamic upgrade over the DAOIC life cycle

claims.claim: Replacing capital with reputation increases liquidity because reputation takes over part of the role of capital and frees otherwise locked capital, letting decentralized investment vehicles deploy capital more effectively since reputation staking on deals requires no capital deployment.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Reputation as Capital – How DAOs Upgrade Finance (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3949098
scope_conditions: decentralized investment vehicles using reputation staking

claims.claim: The rapid growth of digital asset startups into billion dollar businesses with little or no venture capital funding demonstrates that the traditional venture capital model alone was not enough to meet the funding needs of technology startups.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: technology startups, especially digital asset startups

claims.claim: Decentralized reputation governance models in venture capital have the potential to upgrade the venture capital market.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614

claims.claim: Lack of liquidity is one of the biggest problems in the traditional venture capital ecosystem, and the traditional VC model disincentivizes generating early profits because capital is locked in for an extended period of time.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: traditional fiat venture capital funds

claims.claim: Early stage funding fell from thirty five to twenty seven percent of total VC funding as venture capitalists increasingly focused on funding later stage companies.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614

claims.claim: Because traditional fiat VC funds must maintain liquidity to support capital calls from their investors, they are limited in their ability to deploy capital, which affects their return on investment and overall fund performance.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: fiat denominated venture capital funds subject to capital calls

claims.claim: Because time spent raising capital from limited partners is time taken away from portfolio company due diligence, the current VC model tends to reflect the networking and public relations ability of the general partner instead of their capital allocation ability.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: traditional fiat VC funds that must continuously raise capital from limited partners

claims.claim: Deal evaluation and risk assessment in traditional venture capital is fraught with inaccuracies and suboptimal incentives.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: traditional VC screening of early stage ventures

claims.claim: A drawback of the traditional VC evaluation process is that perceptual, emotional, and cognitive processes affect the investment decision alongside financial considerations, because the evaluation criteria are applied through subjective human decision making.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: human applied VC screening criteria

claims.claim: None of the standard VC deal evaluation criteria reflect how a prospective deal may correlate with a deal already held in the capitalist's investment portfolio.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614

claims.claim: Significant information asymmetries in venture capital can lead portfolio company managers to engage in opportunistic behavior after an investment is made.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: post investment stage of a VC financing

claims.claim: Because venture capitalists typically want to cash out their gains five to ten years after the initial investment, they play an active role in directing portfolio companies toward a merger, acquisition, or public offering, which can carry significant downsides for those companies and their products.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: VC backed portfolio companies approaching the exit window

claims.claim: Traditional VCs struggle in the digital asset market because of that market's significant volatility and because they lack expertise in a market still dominated by several key specialized players.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: traditional VCs entering digital asset markets

claims.claim: Traditional VCs often cannot effectively compete with the ever increasing array of decentralized token offering avenues.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: digital asset fundraising markets

claims.claim: Because traditional VCs need to defend their investment choices to their own investors, they are often reluctant to invest in digital asset startups that have little history or sales records.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: traditional VCs accountable to limited partners

claims.claim: As a rule of thumb in early investment rounds, the lower the information asymmetry the lower the payout, and below a certain threshold of established value venture capitalists will rarely invest at all.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: early investment rounds

claims.claim: Alternative early round funding methods matter because they get entrepreneurs over the VC investment threshold or help them bypass the VC model completely.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: technology entrepreneurs below the VC investment threshold

claims.claim: At its peak in the 2019 cycle the volume of initial coin offerings surpassed venture capital firms and business angels as a fundraising method for startups.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: the 2019 market cycle peak

claims.claim: Information asymmetries increase in traditional VC investment rounds because startups are incentivized to self censor when engaging with VCs, having little data to work with and being reluctant to overexpose themselves to prospective investors.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: early round engagement between startups and VCs

claims.claim: The typical VC fee based compensation structure can lead to serious shortcomings, including excessive fundraising, suboptimal investments, misevaluation, and overfunding of portfolio companies during a fund's holding period.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: fee based VC compensation arrangements

claims.claim: Alternative early round funding mechanisms are not necessarily more successful than VCs in early round technology investing, because they tend to act out of intuition and personal experience whereas VCs use a primarily data driven approach to investment decisions and portfolio company evaluation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: early round technology investing

claims.claim: Alternative early round funding methods frequently fail to provide adequate funding to fully launch a new company, and a significant number of tech startups that rely exclusively on these methods fail.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: startups relying exclusively on alternative early round funding

claims.claim: The novelty of reputation as capital lies in the decentralized and democratized capital allocation functionality enabled by the DAO design.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: a VC DAO built on reputation tokens

claims.claim: A VC's proportional holdings of reputation tokens are likely to increase over time if the VC follows sound and successful practices by staking reputation tokens on investment proposals and succeeding in the selection of portfolio companies.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: a VC DAO where members stake reputation for or against proposals

claims.claim: Reputation tokens are separate and distinct from the fiat currency or other fungible tokens used to pay for investments in portfolio companies.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: the reputation as capital DAO design

claims.claim: Only reputation token holders are allowed to participate in the portfolio selection process, which materializes through reputation staking on investment proposals.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: the reputation as capital DAO design

claims.claim: Reputation tokens serve as claims on the future cash flows generated by the DAO, with cash flows in fungible cryptocurrencies paid in proportion to each member's non fungible reputation token holding.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: a DAO that distributes returns as reputation salaries

claims.claim: The value of the reputation tokens is a function of the return on investment of the DAO.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: a DAO that treats ROI as DAO revenue shared as reputation salary

claims.claim: If reputation whales stake reputation on a project and the market commits the capital for that stake, the whales should still receive part of the ROI because it is their reputation that is at stake, and they are not required to commit capital or to support capital calls with liquidity.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: whale reputation that has become meaningful through a track record

claims.claim: Reputation as venture capital must be distinguished from the capital replacement enabled in decentralized underwriting, because in venture capital reputation needs to fill the role of capital for each funded venture deal rather than only when a claim is filed.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: comparison of decentralized underwriting and venture capital DAOs

claims.claim: The basic VC DAO model mixes fungible cryptocurrency investment with minted non fungible reputation, and this duality prevents the full benefits that are generated when non fungible reputation is staked alone on deals.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: early phase VC DAO models that combine capital and reputation staking

claims.claim: Because of significant path dependencies in the capital formation and capital allocation processes of existing venture capital models, the ideal typical reputation based capital allocation model is less likely to be created in the short term.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: short term adoption horizon

claims.claim: In the hybrid VC DAO model eighty percent of returns are allocated to investors pro rata as ROI and twenty percent of returns are allocated to the reputation salary pool.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: the hybrid VC DAO model with a traditional legal structure

claims.claim: Through the decentralized governance precedent system, projects upvoted by the whale validation pool that have the highest comparative ROI get more citations in the reputation system and continually enhance the reputation of the whale who sourced and proposed them.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: a DAO operating a decentralized governance precedent system

claims.claim: A VC DAO needs a legal wrapper in order to interact with the real world, because otherwise everyone involved in the DAO may be jointly and severally liable in any jurisdiction.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: DAOs transacting with counterparties in the offchain world

claims.claim: The hybrid smart contracting model is defective because VCs are partially incentivized to fund and stake only the best deals while staking on less optimal deals that the market mostly funds, which undermines their long term reputation accumulation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: models where VCs can stake reputation without proportionate capital commitment

claims.claim: The incentives that undermine long term success of the hybrid model can be mitigated by mandating that staking on deals requires capital commitments, while allowing VCs to lower their capital commitments and increase their staking over time.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: hybrid VC DAO models transitioning away from capital

claims.claim: A better system emphasizes reputation by prohibiting capital investment into portfolio companies after an initial minting of reputation in proportion to incoming capital.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: the incentive optimized reputation model with smart contracts

claims.claim: In the non custodial DAO investment club model all of the return on purchase is minted into fungible reputation tokens that get paid as reputation salaries following decentralized governance, which provides the best incentive alignment for members and the highest potential return for all involved.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: the non custodial DAO investment club model with smart contracts

claims.claim: Because the public co purchases alongside DAO investment club members and expects to pay for the right to benefit from the collective wisdom of those members and the deal pipeline they generate, the public should expect to pay the usual two and twenty fees.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: public co purchase alongside a DAO investment club

claims.claim: Over time the members of a DAO investment club do not need capital any longer, because the public market funds the deals and members get paid through the twenty percent public return on purchase that is minted into fungible reputation tokens.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: mature phases of a DAO investment club with public co purchase

claims.claim: Removing capital as a necessity for deal participation creates a very high level of flexibility for DAO investment club members, allowing them to invest without ever being forced to invest, and making capital calls entirely unnecessary.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: DAO investment club phases where the public market funds deals

claims.claim: The collective wisdom of DAO investment club members helps hedge against purchase risk, and because decentralized governance with loosely and tightly coupled votes will very likely make all tightly coupled votes unanimous, no member loses reputation NFTs.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: decentralized governance combining loosely and tightly coupled votes

claims.claim: Reputation as capital has the potential to lower capital requirements for VC businesses significantly and to increase liquidity at unprecedented levels, because VCs can sell their fungible reputation tokens to the market as needed.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: a functioning market for fungible reputation tokens

claims.claim: The industry is still experimenting with different forms of DeFi capital replacement schemes, and it will take time to filter out those designs that have unanticipated side effects.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, REPUTATION AS CAPITAL – How Decentralized Autonomous Organizations Address Shortcomings in the Ventu (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3962614
scope_conditions: DeFi experimentation that started in 2020

claims.claim: Market liquidity depends on trustworthiness, and trustworthiness depends on observed momentum: isolated instances of motion are insufficient, because the observations must be collected into a history before they carry weight and meaning.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: marketplaces seeking liquidity

claims.claim: Governance in a decentralized organization depends on meaningful reputation, and the meaning of any reputation is determined by its history and by how that history is analyzed and presented, which makes historiography a governance variable rather than a neutral record.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: decentralized organizations

claims.claim: The choice of historiography is a design choice about the architecture of higher order information storage, and because deciding what is true is the judicial function, historiography is effectively the architecture of judicial governance.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217

claims.claim: Any reliance by a DAO on a centralized feature creates a centralized point of failure that threatens the survival of the organization and renders the system technically centralized despite its decentralized appearance.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: DAOs with any centralized dependency, including oracles

claims.claim: Where a DAO is automated around a single centralized point of failure, the work of decentralizing and giving members redundant power is wasted, because the point of failure functions as a supreme leader and full centralization would be more efficient.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: DAO automated around one centralized component

claims.claim: A DAO that relies on a centralized oracle will eventually be exploited, because the people controlling the oracle will become aware of their power over automated contract triggers and, given the competitive nature of capitalism, are right to take advantage of it.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: DAO automated by smart contracts on oracle data
sufficient value at stake

claims.claim: Legislation is the wrong remedy for oracle exploitation, because the existence of an arbitrage opportunity means systems will evolve around whatever rules exist in order to exploit the advantage; the proper response is to engineer a better system.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: insider information and arbitrage opportunities

claims.claim: A robust decentralized oracle finds better information because averaging across a crowd is typically better for complex situations, being less subject to the prejudices of individuals who hold more limited information, so overestimates and underestimates offset each other.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: all things being equal
complex situations

claims.claim: Condorcet's Jury Theorem cuts both ways: larger groups of slightly stupid people, defined as being wrong slightly more than half the time, are worse than smaller groups of stupid people, so the idiocy of the mob is the counterbalance to the wisdom of the crowd.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: average member correct less than half the time

claims.claim: An oracle DAO must filter its network so that the average member is correct at least slightly more often than incorrect; once that filter holds, larger and more decentralized networks converge on the truth more quickly and more certainly.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: average member better than chance
no systemic bias

claims.claim: In the SchellingCoin approach to oracle design, members stake reputation tokens on their answer to the question a DApp is asking and are rewarded according to how close they came to the resulting median value, which functions as the game theoretic Schelling point.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: questions with a verifiable focal answer

claims.claim: The protocols governing how a particular oracle question is answered should be set by the subject matter experts themselves rather than by a static centralized hierarchy, because the experts know best how their own system can be gamed and how to prevent that gaming to protect their hard earned reputation.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: domain specific oracle questions

claims.claim: Robust decentralized oracles do not yet exist despite well funded proposals, because decentralized oracles are themselves DAOs and therefore inherit the same missing incentive structure, governance processes, and history that all DAOs suffer from.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: state of the technology at the time of writing

claims.claim: A decentralized oracle is not secure until it has significant momentum and history, and it is not even truly decentralized until it has a large network of active members.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: oracle networks

claims.claim: Until decentralized oracle protocols are secure and robustly enacted, projects should rely on centralized oracles while keeping the network's monetary value below the level at which the centralized newsfeed would gain an incentive to manipulate the data.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: pre maturity phase of decentralized oracle technology

claims.claim: Oracle DAOs and decentralized finance DAOs face a bootstrapping deadlock because each relies on the other for its very existence, a chicken and egg problem the authors address by having participants prove their worth in a development period before they can charge other DAOs fees.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: early stage decentralized finance ecosystems

claims.claim: Centralized civic institutions always become corrupt over time, and that corruption becomes obvious only once a new technology disrupts their operation and reveals their weaknesses.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: centralized civic institutions over long time horizons

claims.claim: Institutional corruption follows a repeating cycle: people surrender their power of information transmission to institutions that are initially more effective and efficient, those institutions centralize and ossify into corruption, and new technology then allows people to bypass them.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: information transmission institutions

claims.claim: If transparent democratic institutions are not built to replace the corrupt ones, new opaque centralized institutions will take their place, as Facebook, YouTube, and Twitter already do with secret algorithms that control what stories spread with no democratic oversight.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: current platform era

claims.claim: Truth discovery in the marketplace of ideas is more effective and efficient when news aggregators are more decentralized: ten newspapers reporting on a story produce a more accurate historical picture than one newspaper reporting on the story ten times.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: marketplace of ideas
competing independent aggregators

claims.claim: By 2012, ninety percent of the United States media and entertainment industry was controlled by the top six media conglomerations.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: United States media and entertainment industry, 2012

claims.claim: American faith in media has fallen in direct correlation with the consolidation of broadcasting power for as long as active statistics have been studied.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: United States
period for which statistics exist

claims.claim: The most obvious harm from news consolidation is that national and international centralized corporations do not devote the same degree of focus to the interests of the local communities they serve, because love does not scale.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: consolidated national or international news corporations

claims.claim: Contrary to the common fear, wide scale decentralization of media power will not collapse centralized corporations, just as Napster and BitTorrent did not collapse the centralized music companies; decentralization does not take power from centralized actors, it increases everyone's power.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: incumbents willing to participate in the new collaborative networks
