claims.claim: Popularity based ranking cannot substitute for editorial control, because people end up relying on unconscious algorithms to determine what is authoritative and the Folk Theorems establish that such algorithms can always be gamed.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: user generated content platforms without editorial control

claims.claim: A central authority is perfectly well incentivized to ignore minor problems that only partially eat into its profits, so long as it maintains ultimate control of those profits, which is why platform level abuses persist under centralized ownership.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: platforms with centralized profit control

claims.claim: Existing decentralized news efforts including WikiNews, the Decentralized News Network, and Steemit failed to gain wide adoption because they lacked ambition; the goal should instead be to empower individuals with greater ability to communicate and cooperate.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: decentralized news projects to date

claims.claim: Reputation in a news DAO must be anchored in fungible currency: new reputation should be minted only when articles connect to profitable endeavors such as advertising, paid analyses, or protocols relied upon for decentralized business contracts.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: news DAOs building meaningful reputation

claims.claim: Reviewers in a news review DAO will give honest reviews despite being paid fees, because the reputational system rewards members mostly on the basis of future fees rather than present ones.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: reputation systems weighted toward future fee streams

claims.claim: Tracking and aggregating reputations across DAOs can build a more accurate picture of a person's expertise and experiential gaps than traditional educational institutions provide, which would quickly reveal meaningless certification and licensure programs as worthless.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: reputation systems anchored in profitable endeavor

claims.claim: Transparency in a decentralized network is not optional: every function needs to be publicly auditable for people to trust it, because without a central authority to approve code, unexpected malicious behavior can be built into any opaque code.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: decentralized networks without a central approving authority

claims.claim: From a game theory perspective the open source culture advocated in the Web3 movement is not sustainable in the long term unless it is married with a culture of respect for history.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: long term horizon
absence of a culture acknowledging past contributions

claims.claim: The solution to the game theory problem of getting a player to freely give up intellectual property at one stage of a repeated game is to guarantee a reward at a future stage by fostering a culture that acknowledges past contributions, so players seek future fame by distributing their work in the present.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: repeated game with future stages
culture that reliably acknowledges past contributions

claims.claim: A culture of respect for history is unnatural and must be consciously policed, which makes it another of the essential catalyst institutions that has to be deliberately built into the decentralized economy.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: decentralized economies

claims.claim: Weighting references so that more value is shared with older posts promotes long term contributions and innovation and increases stability, while less value sharing encourages new contributions and immediate work, so the weighting parameters encode whether the DAO values long term or short term contribution.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: citation graph based reputation systems

claims.claim: Reviewing through references enables punishment and reward in DAOs, which shifts members' motivation away from immediate rewards toward the future and encourages delayed gratification and sacrifice for the good of the group.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: DAOs with a functioning citation and review system

claims.claim: Review changes the game theoretical perspective from a single stage game to a repeated game, which produces more efficient cooperation instead of internal competition and is what makes the open source environment sustainable in the long run.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: DAOs where past contributions remain reviewable

claims.claim: Review creates a decentralized history for a DAO, and that history gives the organization momentum, gives meaning and focus to perception, and is the basis for making governance, understood as steering, more effective.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: DAOs with reviewable histories

claims.claim: Long run stability of a decentralized organization requires the momentum gained from a clear history, but momentum is not sufficient: if the system is not moving toward a healthy and productive goal it will not last long.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: long run survival of decentralized organizations

claims.claim: The most important aspect of a decentralized organization, and the feature that ultimately determines its long term success, is the group's set of transcendental values.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of History In Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782217
scope_conditions: long term success of decentralized organizations

claims.claim: Reputation, not money, is the proper incentive for motivating the most efficient cooperation and long-term stability in business.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: business and commercial organizations
settings where long-term cooperation is the goal

claims.claim: Markets collapse when opportunistic behavior saps the efficiency of cooperation: once the environment becomes too adversarial and trust is diminished, collaboration is no longer profitable.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: markets with significant information asymmetries
environments permitting a wide variety of strategies

claims.claim: Strict legal enforcement is an inefficient remedy for opportunism because every unit of energy devoted to policing is energy that could instead have been used to cooperate productively.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210

claims.claim: Strict legal enforcement becomes impossible once a market is sufficiently complex and dynamic, because law cannot keep pace with the creative contracts that leading experts continually invent.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: complex and rapidly evolving markets
markets where experts continually improve business arrangements

claims.claim: Reputation converts a transaction from a single-stage zero-sum game into a repeated positive-sum game by holding out the promise of future business opportunities, so the value created is the improved reputation of both parties.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: parties expect continued participation in the network

claims.claim: The failure of many DAOs to date is traceable to their reliance on the good will of network members rather than on engineered incentives.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: decentralized autonomous organizations observed to date

claims.claim: As a network grows its members become more anonymous and individually less important, which makes cheating more locally enticing and less globally noticeable, so the system eventually collapses once cheating is obviously the best individual strategy.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: networks that grow large
networks lacking a secure reputation mechanism

claims.claim: A Web of Trust style reputation ledger, in which each party rates each transaction and reputation is summed with weightings by rater reputation, will have all of its value drained by the sockpuppet attack, because an attacker can build reputation through transactions between their own fake accounts and then use it to cheat.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: open networks that permit account creation
self-reported transaction ratings

claims.claim: Charging transaction fees or imposing KYC identity protocols does not solve the sockpuppet problem: such defenses push the cost of defending the network onto users, and the defense cost equals what it is worth to break the defense while being multiplied across every transaction with every member.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: defenses that tax ordinary transactions
attacker gain from faked reputation exceeds the cost of faking it

claims.claim: Reducing member anonymity weakens rather than strengthens a decentralized network, because personal privacy protects members and lets them be more transparent in their dealings without fear of victimization.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: open decentralized networks

claims.claim: The Web of Trust works acceptably for low-value information transmission but should not be used for transactions involving larger wealth in the general economy, which is part of why the scheme it originated in is called pretty good privacy rather than good privacy.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: high value economic transactions

claims.claim: The proper solution to reputation security is to give members themselves the power to police their own reputation, because the leading experts in a field are best equipped to invent the regulations for policing their own industry and are best incentivized to defend their own reputation and future profits.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: decentralized networks of domain experts

claims.claim: Because members of a decentralized network are assumed relatively equal, evidence of all bureaucratic work must be posted in a universally accessible location for eternal review, and every reputation token needs an openly verifiable history just as digital currency creation does without a central verifying authority.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: decentralized organizations without a central verifying authority

claims.claim: Reputation must be staked and risked on votes over work evidence, because otherwise the system suffers the Tragedy of the Commons nothing-at-stake problem; staking ensures every expert is motivated to police every reputation-staked action in order to protect the value of their own investment.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: validation pool voting on work evidence

claims.claim: Reputation tokens are meaningful only if grounded in something real, so in a profit-seeking DAO all new reputation tokens must be minted in proportion to the fees the DAO earns.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: DAOs devoted to profit

claims.claim: Newly minted reputation tokens should enter the system neutral, staked half in favor and half against the post that generated the fee, so that existing token holders can judge the action fairly and are not swayed by an unbalanced validation pool created by a large new fee.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: validation pools triggered by fee-generating work

claims.claim: All fees should be shared with the entire network of reputation holders in proportion to their holdings, because this reputational salary is what makes reputation tokens valuable and future-oriented.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: profit-generating DAOs with reputation tokens

claims.claim: Distributing salary equitably, for example equally to all members, is self-defeating: the obvious gaming strategy becomes creating multiple accounts and distributing one's work between them, which is why the salary must be reputation-weighted.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: open membership systems where accounts are cheap to create

claims.claim: Each new post should be able to reference older posts, so that when a new post is validated it can raise or lower the reputational value of past posts depending on how users come to perceive the precedent.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: forums with permanent post histories

claims.claim: Reputation tokens must have their power limited to their proper domain: for each different expertise there must be a separate type of non-interchangeable reputation token, so that a token carries power only within the DAO whose members hold that specific skill.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: organizations spanning multiple domains of expertise

claims.claim: DAOs are free to organize as they choose, and those that fail to find the right incentives for productive behavior will certainly go extinct, because the feedback loop that includes customers outside the DAO punishes unproductive DAOs by loss of fees.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: DAOs that depend on outside customer fees
competitive markets for DAO services

claims.claim: Because eternally perfect protocols are impossible, as illustrated by Arrow's Impossibility Theorem and the Folk Theorems of Game Theory, the remedy is not a better static ruleset but a system that continually improves its protocols and smart contracts in reaction to market change.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: governance systems that must adapt over time

claims.claim: Reputation dilates time: it slows immediate transfers of wealth so that past and future enter present decisions, with future-oriented incentives supplied by reputation-based salaries and past-oriented incentives supplied by the editability of reputation.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: systems where reputation can be retroactively slashed or augmented

claims.claim: In hierarchical structures where members are siloed and have few formal connections across tiers, letting service providers create the regulations produces moral hazard, because the provider has an incentive to weaken standards and regulations.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: hierarchical, siloed organizations
self-regulation by service providers

claims.claim: Sockpuppet attacks are inevitable in any organization that wants open membership and anonymous members, and since those properties are essential to the autonomy that makes a global decentralized organization efficient, reputation must be weighted every time it is used.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: open membership
anonymous or pseudonymous members

claims.claim: Every single reputational implementation the authors have audited in the blockchain DAO space carries the flaw of vulnerability to the sockpuppet attack on the Web of Trust model.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: blockchain DAO reputation systems audited by the authors as of writing

claims.claim: SingularityNet's reputation system, which tracks self-reported transaction quality, transaction value, duration of satisfaction, and prior reputation weights, will have its value eroded by the sockpuppet attack once the system becomes valuable enough to merit attack, because it does not implement the other necessities.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: systems implementing only a subset of the seven necessities
once the reputation becomes valuable enough to merit attack

claims.claim: With the balanced staking and fee-sharing necessities implemented, the cost of faking reputation is at an absolute minimum double the value of that reputation, which is how reputation is made more valuable than money.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: both the balanced staking necessity and the shared salary necessity are implemented

claims.claim: Concentration of power is the greatest threat to any decentralized organization, because a single member or sub-coalition that gains a majority of power in an inherently democratic organization will eventually control it no matter what safeguards are in place, at which point the organization is no longer decentralized.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: democratic decentralized organizations
especially profit-devoted and therefore competitive ones

claims.claim: Fair accounting and transparency in reputation promote decentralization, because customers who can reliably compare reputation harness the available talent rather than waiting for the most talented provider to become free, which keeps reputation differences from accumulating.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: customers can observe and compare member reputations

claims.claim: A reputation token is inherently worth more to the person who earned it than to someone who merely bought it, because of its secondary use in making future earnings, so reputation is harder to accumulate than cash and economies of scale are weakened.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: non-fungible reputation tokens with individual slashable histories

claims.claim: Because reputation tokens are constantly created, the reputation economy is inflationary, and a member with very high reputation must do proportionally more work merely to maintain the disparity, which makes reputation less likely to concentrate and acts as a natural counterbalance to accumulation of individual power.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: steady state growth, not exponential growth of customers
members of comparable talent

claims.claim: One-person-one-vote governance fails on technical questions because half the members have less than average expertise yet equal power, which incentivizes experts to gain power by catering to less expert prejudices instead of pursuing the most effective decisions.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: organizations voting on matters requiring expertise

claims.claim: Contemporary blockchains cannot support the proposed architecture because the technology is too slow and expensive to poll members on every transaction, and the messages required for all nodes to register all votes on every action multiply into an unmanageable number.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: blockchains as of writing, including Ethereum
polling on every member action

claims.claim: Reputation-based governance faces a chicken and egg problem: voting becomes more efficient once reputation is valuable, but reputation cannot become valuable without meaningful voting.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: bootstrapping a reputation system on existing infrastructure

claims.claim: A meaningful reputational system with the potential for retrospective review would let a network rely on fewer nodes, since randomly selected nodes staking their reputation can do the polling work and be reviewed and punished later, which is one reason proof of stake is more efficient than proof of work.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: consensus is near unanimous nearly all the time
Byzantine behavior is detectable on later review

claims.claim: Members should not stake reputation tokens to register an opinion on a contentious topic; strict validation pools should be used only after debate has settled, to verify consensus.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: protocol development debates where votes will not be near unanimous

claims.claim: Reputation has lost much of its meaning during the current institutional disruption: people in dying fields cash in on reputations built over previous generations in a fire sale mentality, and reputation itself is becoming a suspect concept.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: the current period of institutional decline and global society emergence

claims.claim: Reputation is not merely an option for a DAO that holds power or value; it is absolutely essential, and for DAOs built to make money ideology alone is not enough to maintain long-term stability.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: DAOs devoted to profit or holding power
distinct from purely altruistic ideological organizations

claims.claim: The Maghribi traders show that reputation alone can sustain a decentralized network under extreme information asymmetry: using only handwritten letters, Jewish merchants built a reputational system spanning the Silk Road in which nothing but the promise of better reputation deterred agents from cheating.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: historical trading networks with communication latency on the order of months
agents with complete control of assets

claims.claim: Without the promise of improving reputation, a zero-sum mentality dominates a contractual arrangement and each party's best strategy becomes exerting the absolute minimum effort while still technically fulfilling the contract, which destroys the business atmosphere.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: contracts between parties with no expectation of reputational gain

claims.claim: Self-executing, self-regulating smart contracts between anonymous parties in an open system create a near perfect zero-sum situation unless the DAO also includes reputation.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: open systems
anonymous counterparties
code-is-law smart contract execution

claims.claim: Giving all people more power produces a liquid meritocracy in which leaders are continually rediscovered immediately where and when they are needed, and secure meaningful reputation gives that meritocracy momentum and history.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: secure and meaningful decentralized reputation is in place

claims.claim: A revolutionary new system of decentralized governance is a precondition for the Web3 vision succeeding, and because efficiency requires stability, the steering mechanisms must be subtle.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Reputation for the Evolution of Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782210
scope_conditions: decentralized organizations pursuing the Web3 vision

claims.claim: Strong unifying values are the institution most essential to the long-term stability of a decentralized organization, and they demand continual reevaluation rather than one-time specification.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Transcendental Unifying Values for Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782220
scope_conditions: decentralized organizations
long time horizons

claims.claim: Because a single global society is emerging in which everyone is densely interconnected, the more efficient and stable arrangement is power decentralization giving individuals and subgroup DAOs autonomous power, not a single power-centralized hierarchy controlling the whole.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Transcendental Unifying Values for Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782220
scope_conditions: globally interconnected society

claims.claim: Efficiency is only meaningful relative to goals, and understanding goals is the same as understanding values, so maintaining a system's efficiency requires adherence to its values.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Transcendental Unifying Values for Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782220

claims.claim: Transcendental values are necessary for long-term stability because every formal, explicitly specified protocol is permanently exposed to strategies that subvert it, a result the authors draw from the Folk Theorems of game theory.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Transcendental Unifying Values for Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782220
scope_conditions: long-term stability
formally specified protocols

claims.claim: A maximally effective set of unifying values integrates opposing values rather than choosing between them, because the purpose of unification is to bring together individuals holding different perspectives.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Transcendental Unifying Values for Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782220

claims.claim: Building secure walls with well-designed doors is the proper way to embody conservative and liberal values together in an economic system: walls protect the group from the Tragedy of the Commons and malicious threats, while doors admit fresh input from anyone willing and able to help.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Transcendental Unifying Values for Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782220
scope_conditions: economic systems needing both protection and renewal

claims.claim: History reveals three polar opposite sets of fundamental values that any society must integrate in order to stay stable and healthy.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Transcendental Unifying Values for Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782220
scope_conditions: any society seeking long-term stability

claims.claim: The intuition that strengthening one pole of a value pair necessarily diminishes its opposite is plainly false in any complex situation.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Transcendental Unifying Values for Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782220
scope_conditions: complex social systems

claims.claim: A society that levels material outcomes completely undermines its own equity: eliminating all individual reward crushes the meritocratic instinct, power is allocated inefficiently to those who cannot use it well, and the next generation cannot produce as much to share.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Transcendental Unifying Values for Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782220
scope_conditions: complete material leveling
multigenerational time horizon

claims.claim: A society that relies only on meritocratic rewards destroys its own meritocracy: Price's Law differentiates rewards exponentially, the bottom tier cannot afford the training to compete, and the separation widens until the society destabilizes and collapses.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Transcendental Unifying Values for Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782220
scope_conditions: pure meritocratic distribution
multigenerational time horizon

claims.claim: Where a person draws the line between necessities and nonessentials is itself a declaration of values: treating nothing as essential strongly favors meritocracy and treating everything as essential strongly favors equity.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Transcendental Unifying Values for Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782220

claims.claim: Automating insurance away with smart contracts risks a race to the bottom, because foregoing insurance is more efficient in the short term for an individual, yet the resulting rare unprotected tragedies can chill the entire system.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Transcendental Unifying Values for Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782220
scope_conditions: automated smart contract insurance
individually optimizing agents

claims.claim: The efficient arrangement is that all of society shares the essentials while individuals remain free to pursue nonessentials, which puts government business in charge of essentials and leaves private business free to pursue nonessentials.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Transcendental Unifying Values for Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782220

claims.claim: Overhead institutions such as insurance and policing act as catalysts supplying the activation energy that guarantees liquidity in both government and private business.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Transcendental Unifying Values for Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782220

claims.claim: Overhead institutions that protect or promote essentials should be governed and borne by the group, while those protecting nonessentials should be governed and borne privately, with each DAO deciding for itself what is essential to its function.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Transcendental Unifying Values for Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782220
scope_conditions: per DAO determination
democratic decision within the DAO's own system

claims.claim: Because what counts as essential shifts with the market, a network must not only identify its values but also maintain a dynamic governance process for constantly reinterpreting those values as circumstances change.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Transcendental Unifying Values for Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782220
scope_conditions: changing market conditions

claims.claim: Demand for insurance and reputation policing runs counter to prosperity: when the system runs well and everyone profits there is less need for insurance, and when profits fall and competition intensifies cheating becomes more attractive and more policing is needed.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Transcendental Unifying Values for Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782220
scope_conditions: competitive market conditions

claims.claim: A perfectly democratic society would require complete transparency even though most societies draw the line well short of it, so a DAO should specify explicitly where it places the boundary between bureaucratic transparency and secrecy.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Transcendental Unifying Values for Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782220
scope_conditions: perfectly democratic ideal treated as the limiting case

claims.claim: Where the line between public and private information falls is a function of a society's values, as the divergence between American, German, and Chinese practice shows.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Transcendental Unifying Values for Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782220
scope_conditions: cross-national comparison

claims.claim: Failing to maintain a healthy balance among the polar value pairs, one that faithfully reflects the people's own values, is what topples empires and leads to social catastrophe.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Transcendental Unifying Values for Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782220
scope_conditions: societies over long time horizons

claims.claim: Transcendental values must remain transcendental, because once formalized too rigorously they become more manipulable: a clearly specified definition becomes a focal point for competition instead of a unifying principle.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Transcendental Unifying Values for Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782220
scope_conditions: values that have been formalized explicitly

claims.claim: Drawing a clear formal line between where individual rights stop and social responsibilities start makes the system brittle and unstable by turning that line into a focal point for competition, so the line between the two values must remain vague.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Transcendental Unifying Values for Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782220
scope_conditions: values in genuine tension such as freedom and equality

claims.claim: Beyond any Folk Theorem justification for stability, the ultimate reason not to impose a clear distinction between the individual and the social is that no such clear distinction exists in nature, and a network's values must reflect that vagueness.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Transcendental Unifying Values for Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782220

claims.claim: Individual autonomy and group cohesion reinforce rather than substitute for each other: the network effect is achieved only when individuals subsume their freedom to act in concert with the group, and diminishing one quality diminishes the other.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Transcendental Unifying Values for Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782220
scope_conditions: network organizations

claims.claim: Identifying a network's values is not an academic exercise: values determine goals, goals determine how rewards and punishments are set up, and that reward structure determines the network's future and whether it survives.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Transcendental Unifying Values for Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782220
scope_conditions: any network, society, or DAO

claims.claim: Governance design choices must be matched to the network's values, because otherwise the reward structure will dictate the true goals and thereby determine what the network actually values.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Transcendental Unifying Values for Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782220
scope_conditions: networks with explicit governance and reward structures

claims.claim: A long-term successful network requires a dynamic and responsive governance system that keeps the organization in the decentralized democratic realm and prevents it from moving to the next natural stage of centralized governance with a static hierarchy.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Transcendental Unifying Values for Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782220
scope_conditions: long-term network survival

claims.claim: The drift into static power relationships is a universal temptation because centralization is efficient, yet centralized governance is provably flawed.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Transcendental Unifying Values for Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782220
scope_conditions: organizations facing the choice between centralized and decentralized governance

claims.claim: Committing too completely to a global centralized manmade hierarchy, and letting its bureaucracy become too rigid and impersonal, risks a predictable fall that could be the final collapse, because for the first time the structure encompasses the entire planet.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Transcendental Unifying Values for Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782220
scope_conditions: planet-spanning centralized organization

claims.claim: A centralized hierarchy becomes too rigid when those policing the rules gain more power than the members who honor the transcendental value that originally founded the organization, and the spirit of the law should always reign above the letter of the law.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Transcendental Unifying Values for Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782220
scope_conditions: centralized hierarchies with rule enforcement roles

claims.claim: As an organization loses touch with its transcendental values, members use the rules to jockey for position in the hierarchy and corruption erodes the organization's effectiveness.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Transcendental Unifying Values for Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782220
scope_conditions: organizations that have lost contact with their founding values

claims.claim: The same ability to learn from others' behavior that unleashes the efficiency of cooperation also gives people untold power to trick others, imagining how to manipulate them and corrupt the organization for individual benefit at the group's expense.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Transcendental Unifying Values for Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782220
scope_conditions: organizations composed of mind-modeling agents

claims.claim: Science is politically decentralized because no person, university, institution, or nation controls whether a theory becomes established fact, yet this global Science DAO is highly protocol centralized around objective universal truth.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Transcendental Unifying Values for Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782220
scope_conditions: science as a globally open discipline

claims.claim: Scientists do not deserve and can never earn the authority to rule on whether we should ask what meaning or values lie behind the rules guiding the universe; on that subject they have less authority than those who study spirituality, theology, morality, or poetry.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Transcendental Unifying Values for Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782220
scope_conditions: questions of meaning and value rather than physical law

claims.claim: Unlike scientific laws, transcendental values cannot be stated formally and explicitly, so they must be authored by people in touch with transcendental beauty, true poets, who are nevertheless grounded in concrete understanding of the universe and its laws.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Transcendental Unifying Values for Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782220
scope_conditions: construction of unifying values for a network

claims.claim: Decentralization requires every member to participate in constructing the organization's values, since a decentralized network is only as strong as its members and the environment it exists in.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Transcendental Unifying Values for Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782220
scope_conditions: decentralized networks

claims.claim: Because a decentralized organization does not coerce its members as centralized organizations do, its power is determined by how devoted its members are to its values, and its power is its power to unite in service to the goal of shared values.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Transcendental Unifying Values for Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782220
scope_conditions: non-coercive decentralized organizations

claims.claim: The strength of a decentralized organization is measured by summing the power of each member in their individual autonomy, modified by the group's ability to organize and effect its goals in the larger society.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Transcendental Unifying Values for Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782220
scope_conditions: decentralized organizations

claims.claim: Decentralized organizations demand more from their members and return more autonomous power and profit, whereas centralized organizations shelter members in a niche and limit and stultify their power in exchange for security.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Transcendental Unifying Values for Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782220

claims.claim: Decentralized organizations are only as stable as their autonomous members' adherence to their ideals, and that same autonomy makes members individually responsible for constructing, nourishing, and revitalizing those unifying ideals continually.
claims.citation: Craig Calcaterra, Wulf A. Kaal, The Importance of Transcendental Unifying Values for Decentralization (2021). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=3782220
scope_conditions: decentralized organizations

claims.claim: At their worst, DAOs produce ponzi schemes and rug pulls, and these failures damage the credibility and future of web3 as a whole, not just the individual project.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Fallacies (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4067783

claims.claim: Poorly executed DAOs exhibit a recognizable cluster of pathologies, including siphoned coins, distracted and robo voters, centralization, DAO washing by founders, and absent decentralized governance, and these pathologies drive mid-term and long-term DAO failure.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Fallacies (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4067783

claims.claim: Rug pulls grew sharply as a share of crypto crime: of the $7.7 billion in total illicit crypto revenue in 2021, 37 percent came from rug pulls, up from 1 percent of illicit revenue in 2020.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Fallacies (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4067783
scope_conditions: 2021 data
measured as a share of total illicit crypto revenue

claims.claim: Fundraiser DAOs are structurally fragile because they typically lack incentives for meaningful community engagement, so they dissipate once the hype that created them fades.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Fallacies (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4067783
scope_conditions: DAOs formed primarily to raise funds

claims.claim: Governance by fungible tokens lets whales control a fundraiser DAO, which is antithetical to decentralized governance, and selling purchasable voting power via fungible tokens creates the risk of hostile takeover or looting.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Fallacies (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4067783
scope_conditions: governance rights attached to fungible, purchasable tokens

claims.claim: The author contests the myth that DAOs are generally run by scammers: many DAOs and users have indeed fallen victim to rug pulls, but most of those rug pulls trace to the absence of decentralized governance in fundraiser DAOs rather than to DAOs as such.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Fallacies (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4067783
scope_conditions: applies to fundraiser DAOs lacking decentralized governance

claims.claim: DAO projects accounted for a material share of the largest crypto frauds of the year: two of the top six crypto rug pulls in 2021 were DAO projects.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Fallacies (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4067783
scope_conditions: top six crypto rug pulls by size

claims.claim: A DAO token sale can be drained at the moment of closing: in the Anubis DAO sale 13597 ETH was removed from the token sale pool and sent to another address as the sale was about to close, and because the launch platform had not been compromised the loss was attributed to an inside rug pull.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Fallacies (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4067783
scope_conditions: Anubis DAO token sale on the Copper platform, October 2021

claims.claim: Most DAOs that suffer unethical behavior and rug pulls are abused by insiders, and this is possible because insiders are not properly governed and hold too much control over the DAO; true decentralized community governance removes insider and council control over keys and code.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Fallacies (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4067783
scope_conditions: DAOs where councils or privileged insiders retain key and code control

claims.claim: Insider knowledge of contract internals is itself an attack surface: at Snowdog DAO an insider who knew a challenge key embedded in the DAO contract backran the anticipated buyback and sold tokens ahead of it.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Fallacies (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4067783
scope_conditions: Snowdog DAO on the Avalanche protocol
insider holding a contract challenge key

claims.claim: Insider rug pulls are not the only exploit path: a DAO can also be attacked from the outside whenever its governance grants voting power through fungible tokens.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Fallacies (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4067783
scope_conditions: governance voting power is denominated in fungible tokens

claims.claim: The absence of proper decentralized governance built on non-fungible tokens is a key common denominator across DAO failures and rug pulls.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Fallacies (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4067783

claims.claim: Dispersed, passive token holders cannot defend a DAO: because power in Build Finance DAO was not decentralized, the silent majority of token holders lacked the voting power to block the takeover, after which the attacker minted and sold tokens by draining liquidity pools.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Fallacies (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4067783
scope_conditions: low participation among dispersed token holders

claims.claim: Defending a DAO against attackers and looters, and punishing self-dealing, requires sustainable decentralized governance built on non-fungible tokens rather than tradable voting power.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Fallacies (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4067783

claims.claim: Governance in most DAOs is severely underdeveloped, which leaves a minority of stakeholders defining governance, and that minority control in turn produces mediocre and poorly developed proposals.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Fallacies (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4067783
scope_conditions: DAOs still in early governance experimentation

claims.claim: The author rejects the claim that DAOs are ungovernable: the shortcomings are real, but ongoing experimentation with DAO governance designs is gradually identifying workable decentralized governance solutions.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Fallacies (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4067783

claims.claim: Workable DAO governance should account for reputation with non-fungible tokens or weighted keys rather than fungible tokens, so that voting weight tracks reputation instead of purchasing power.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Fallacies (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4067783

claims.claim: DAO governance should use a two vote model that distinguishes a loosely coupled vote, where no reputation is at stake, from a tightly coupled vote, where the voter's reputation is at stake.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Fallacies (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4067783

claims.claim: Reputation in a DAO should be generated only for long term valuable work and for the policing of work, and never for business development work.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Fallacies (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4067783

claims.claim: Smart contracts that govern fungible currency exchanges are engineered for irreversible, unreviewable, programmed self execution, and that design makes the business structure of web3 more rigid.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Fallacies (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4067783
scope_conditions: smart contracts involving fungible currency exchange

claims.claim: Code is law fails as a complete business ordering because business ventures very rarely proceed exactly as written in smart contract code: real business relationships are far messier and more multivalent than a series of smart contracts can predict.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Fallacies (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4067783

claims.claim: Effective business dealing requires that counterparties have confidence a fair resolution will occur when transactions do not develop as planned, which purely self executing code cannot supply.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Fallacies (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4067783

claims.claim: Effective human-centric DAO governance is the remedy for rigid smart contract rules that undermine business activities requiring more flexibility in web3 and the metaverse.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Fallacies (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4067783
scope_conditions: business activities that require flexibility in web3 and the metaverse

claims.claim: Anonymous decentralized networks can encourage troll behavior because participants feel safe attacking others without retribution, and in a DAO that trolling destabilizes the organization and creates friction between members and the DAO.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Fallacies (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4067783
scope_conditions: anonymous participation without reputational stake

claims.claim: The friction generated by anonymous trolling can be mitigated through incentivized reputational architecture governed by protocols the community itself decides on, so anonymity does not have to corrupt DAO governance.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Fallacies (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4067783
scope_conditions: reputational architecture is implemented correctly and community governed

claims.claim: Properly implemented anonymity strengthens decentralized governance because it lets individuals relate without the inherited biases of predecessor generations and a lifetime inside centralized power structures.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Fallacies (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4067783
scope_conditions: anonymity is properly implemented

claims.claim: Anonymity lets information flow from the edges of the system, from individuals who would have no agency in centralized structures, and such inputs are much less likely to materialize if DAO participants know each other.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Fallacies (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4067783
scope_conditions: anonymity is preserved among DAO participants

claims.claim: True anonymity remains eternally difficult to attain with existing web3 technology, yet anonymity in DAO governance is the holy grail of decentralized web3 business and society.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Fallacies (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4067783
scope_conditions: given existing web3 technology

claims.claim: A meaningful reputation governance and accounting mechanism for motivating business and governance participation is what encourages mutually beneficial contributions to a DAO community.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Fallacies (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4067783
scope_conditions: a meaningful reputation governance and accounting mechanism is in place

claims.claim: Traditional work in centralized structures is prone to extrinsically motivated engagement, which intensifies principal agent problems and produces suboptimal outcomes because a principal dictates where, what, and when workers perform.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Fallacies (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4067783
scope_conditions: centralized employment structures with a directing principal

claims.claim: In a DAO, a member's influence and outcomes are determined by the value that member's contributions add to the shared work product, rather than by position in a hierarchy.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Fallacies (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4067783
scope_conditions: contribution value is measurable and governs influence

claims.claim: High value contribution is self-amplifying in a DAO: when a member adds substantial value, other token holders want to add their skills to the same work product through a policing engagement, which focuses all members' joint efforts on the highest possible value proposition.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Fallacies (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4067783
scope_conditions: members can observe and join high value work products

claims.claim: Braintrust demonstrates that innovation in work structure does not cure governance design: despite redefining work outcomes, it uses a suboptimal one token, one vote model that grants proportional control over network governance.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Fallacies (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4067783
scope_conditions: governance by one token, one vote

claims.claim: Work-to-earn DAOs must leave it entirely to each member how much time they contribute; DAOs that impose quotas and participation requirements may not be sustainable long-term in a value-to-efforts workflow environment.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Fallacies (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4067783
scope_conditions: work-to-earn DAOs seeking to attract long-term talent

claims.claim: Proof of personhood projects such as Proof of Humanity and UBI DAO fail because they rest on web-of-trust theory, which has been proven not to work long-term given the sockpuppet attacks that are inevitable in that design.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Fallacies (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4067783
scope_conditions: identity systems built on web-of-trust vouching

claims.claim: Microdemocracy combined with proper incentive design can reverse the decreasing voter participation that undermines representative democracies.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Fallacies (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4067783
scope_conditions: decentralized voting infrastructure is in place

claims.claim: Centralization and monopolies are a threat to market liquidity because they can carry too much mass or too much velocity, and an imbalance in either direction, too much mass and too little velocity or too little mass, damages the market.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Fallacies (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4067783

claims.claim: Decentralized structures outperform centralized ones on liquidity because in them market mass and velocity are uncorrelated, which yields more stable and predictable liquidity.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Fallacies (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4067783

claims.claim: Diversity of viewpoints is severely diminished when power is centralized, whereas information technology allows a global network open to members of diverse values and backgrounds to form.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Fallacies (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4067783

claims.claim: Flatter markets with more diverse interests and talents are more effective and efficient at truth discovery, including price discovery and the identification of ideal solutions to new problems, and decentralization promotes that diversity by improving member autonomy and freedom.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Fallacies (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4067783

claims.claim: Valuation metrics developed for legacy assets apply only in a limited way to digital assets, so importing them wholesale produces unreliable digital asset valuations.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Hayley Howe, Digital Asset Valuation (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4033886
scope_conditions: digital assets as of 2022

claims.claim: Digital asset valuation uncertainty is produced by the combination of an immature digital asset market and a valuation infrastructure, legal, accounting, finance, technology, and back office, that was not built for these assets.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Hayley Howe, Digital Asset Valuation (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4033886
scope_conditions: current state of the digital asset market

claims.claim: Although many traditional assets also resist full assessment, the absence of established pricing standards for digital assets makes the loss of valuation accuracy for financial reporting worse than in traditional markets.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Hayley Howe, Digital Asset Valuation (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4033886
scope_conditions: financial reporting context

claims.claim: The accounting definition of fair value may not apply to digital assets, with the consequence that correct valuation of digital assets for financial reporting purposes may be impossible.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Hayley Howe, Digital Asset Valuation (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4033886
scope_conditions: under existing accounting terminology such as FASB 157 and IFRS 13

claims.claim: Dual listing narrows bid ask spreads in traditional markets by injecting liquidity, but crypto markets behave differently: price differences between two exchanges can reach upwards of five percent during peak trading times.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Hayley Howe, Digital Asset Valuation (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4033886
scope_conditions: peak trading times
assets listed on multiple crypto exchanges

claims.claim: Digital asset exchanges have no closing prices, so digital asset managers cannot rely on the closing price convention that underpins traditional valuation practice.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Hayley Howe, Digital Asset Valuation (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4033886
scope_conditions: digital asset exchanges

claims.claim: Because digital asset valuation methodologies vary significantly, the tradeoffs among them leave digital asset managers with meaningful valuation discretion.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Hayley Howe, Digital Asset Valuation (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4033886
scope_conditions: absence of uniform valuation standards

claims.claim: Even for the most liquid level one digital assets, managers may choose between the price on a favored exchange and an aggregate across exchanges, so the same asset can be reported at different values by different managers.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Hayley Howe, Digital Asset Valuation (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4033886
scope_conditions: quoting level 1 digital assets

claims.claim: The absence of digital asset valuation standards generates uncertainty and confusion for both investors and managers, and the industry would be better off with uniform standards.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Hayley Howe, Digital Asset Valuation (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4033886

claims.claim: Arbitrage trading emerges in crypto markets because of information asymmetries across exchanges, which arise from imperfect disclosure, and the resulting decline in market efficiency is a key indicator of an inefficient market.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Hayley Howe, Digital Asset Valuation (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4033886
scope_conditions: multiple exchanges trading the same asset

claims.claim: Cross exchange price gaps in crypto do not self correct because of frictions on the arbitrageur side: South Korean investors faced foreign exchange conversion costs and regulatory capital controls that made exploiting the Bithumb premium impractical.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Hayley Howe, Digital Asset Valuation (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4033886
scope_conditions: South Korean investors seeking access to US exchanges
capital controls and foreign exchange frictions in place

claims.claim: Digital asset fund valuation disputes are aggravated by nondisclosure: Polychain Capital told a redeeming investor that the fund's asset valuation policy would not be disclosed.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Hayley Howe, Digital Asset Valuation (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4033886
scope_conditions: private digital asset funds
Polychain Capital redemption dispute

claims.claim: An investor who has been fully redeemed loses the ability to test the fund's valuation of his interest: the court held that Greenhouse retained no equity interest and therefore had no right to inspect the partnership's books and records.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Hayley Howe, Digital Asset Valuation (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4033886
scope_conditions: Delaware limited partnerships under 6 Del. C. section 17-305
investor has already withdrawn and been redeemed

claims.claim: Redemption contracts, the traditional price commitment device for privately issued money, lack credibility, whereas pre programmed smart contracts deliver an enforceable and secure quantity commitment instead.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Hayley Howe, Digital Asset Valuation (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4033886
scope_conditions: issuers of privately issued money

claims.claim: A programmed and enforceable quantity commitment secures a reliably positive value for Bitcoin because the governing source code is fully transparent on the blockchain and continuously verifiable.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Hayley Howe, Digital Asset Valuation (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4033886
scope_conditions: cryptocurrencies with observable open source code

claims.claim: As of 2022 there is no agreed upon reliable valuation method for cryptocurrencies.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Hayley Howe, Digital Asset Valuation (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4033886
scope_conditions: as of 2022

claims.claim: Fair market value is the legal standard for valuation, but it carries real world problems that limit its usefulness in practice.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Hayley Howe, Digital Asset Valuation (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4033886

claims.claim: Stocks and cryptocurrencies look similar enough, both traded on markets at fluctuating prices, to invite similar regulation, but they diverge in their potential for abuse, their nature, their acceptance, and their use.

scope_conditions: comparison of listed equities and cryptocurrencies

claims.claim: The adjusted net asset approach revalues balance sheet items toward current fair value but still fails to capture intangible assets, because intangibles are not represented on the balance sheet.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Hayley Howe, Digital Asset Valuation (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4033886
scope_conditions: asset approach valuations relying on book values

claims.claim: DCF currency translation breaks down for digital assets: no set discount rate or currency exchange forward curve exists for them, because they are not traded in exchange markets where closing prices are readily available and representative of fair value.

scope_conditions: DCF analysis where the projection currency is a digital asset rather than fiat

claims.claim: Principal to principal markets are generally not considered observable because little information about their transactions is publicly available, which pushes assets priced there out of the observable input levels.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Hayley Howe, Digital Asset Valuation (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4033886
scope_conditions: principal to principal markets
fair value input hierarchy

claims.claim: When the bid ask spread grows too wide while trades occur at high volume, the market begins to lose liquidity and the asset's value starts to fall, forcing investors who unload positions to surrender unrealized gains.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Hayley Howe, Digital Asset Valuation (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4033886
scope_conditions: exchange traded context
wide spreads combined with high trading volume

claims.claim: Put option based discount models for lack of marketability have been widely used, but they can be inaccurate because real investors do not possess perfect market timing ability.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Hayley Howe, Digital Asset Valuation (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4033886
scope_conditions: prospective put model and related put option DLOM models

claims.claim: The Longstaff model's assumptions are inconsistent with reality on two fronts: investors do not have perfect timing, and its assumed volatility of ten to thirty percent is far below the volatility exceeding fifty percent typical of small stocks.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Hayley Howe, Digital Asset Valuation (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4033886
scope_conditions: application of the Longstaff model to small or highly volatile securities

claims.claim: A major shortcoming of the QMDM is that no court in any case has accepted it, although it has been mentioned explicitly in three tax cases decided in 2000, 2001, and 2006.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Hayley Howe, Digital Asset Valuation (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4033886
scope_conditions: judicial acceptance in United States tax litigation

claims.claim: The main obstacle to digital asset market liquidity may be that the number of token holders has not continued to expand exponentially year over year; a larger stakeholder base would deepen liquidity and permit seamless entry and exit.

scope_conditions: centralized digital asset exchange markets

claims.claim: Digital assets become less liquid precisely when large amounts are moved at once, because a large sell order floods the exchange and drives the price down.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Hayley Howe, Digital Asset Valuation (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4033886
scope_conditions: large block sales through a single exchange

claims.claim: One design remedy for thin trading volume is supervision of digital asset exchanges by a federal governing authority or a self regulatory organization to assure compliance with existing laws.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Hayley Howe, Digital Asset Valuation (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4033886
scope_conditions: digital asset exchanges operating under legal uncertainty

claims.claim: Legal uncertainty about crypto exchanges exerts a chilling effect on the market, and increased liquidity may follow once the market gains greater clarity on the legal issues surrounding this asset class.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Hayley Howe, Digital Asset Valuation (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4033886
scope_conditions: resolution of broker dealer status and securities law classification questions

claims.claim: Market liquidity in digital assets is not only about exchanging crypto for fiat: allowing crypto to be used as a means of transacting for any good or service may itself increase market liquidity.

scope_conditions: buy in from the business community

claims.claim: Because digital asset exchanges perform both the traditional broker dealer function and the custody function, they face uncertainties and increased liability that traditional exchanges, which never touch custody, do not bear.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Hayley Howe, Digital Asset Valuation (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4033886

claims.claim: When exchanges apply different standards about who may trade on their platform, the market ends up showing different prices for the same asset across exchanges, which is one reason trading arbitrage has become common in crypto.

scope_conditions: exchanges excluding participants by residence or other status

claims.claim: The stablecoin exists as a response to digital asset price volatility: it is pegged to the value of an external asset, frequently a fiat currency.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Hayley Howe, Digital Asset Valuation (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4033886
scope_conditions: stablecoins pegged to external assets

claims.claim: Digital assets resemble high growth companies for valuation purposes, so scenario planning is essential and business leaders must reason backward from the future rather than forward from the present, because the relevant markets may not yet exist.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Hayley Howe, Digital Asset Valuation (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4033886
scope_conditions: assets whose markets have not yet formed

claims.claim: Secondary trade pricing from exchanges is a legitimate market approach input for digital assets only when liquidity is high enough to rely on those prices; where liquidity is lacking or unreliable, a discount for lack of liquidity is required.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Hayley Howe, Digital Asset Valuation (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4033886
scope_conditions: market approach applied to tokens
liquidity and depth differ between token to token and token to fiat trades

claims.claim: DCF appears at first glance unsuited to digital asset valuation because valuation is framed as pricing a token at a point in time, but it becomes applicable where networks return cash flows to token holders or to those who contribute work.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Hayley Howe, Digital Asset Valuation (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4033886
scope_conditions: networks that distribute cash flows to token holders or workers

claims.claim: Under a deflationary token issuance model, which caps the number of tokens ever issued, prices are expected to increase because of the fundamental scarcity of token supply.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Hayley Howe, Digital Asset Valuation (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4033886
scope_conditions: deflationary token models such as Bitcoin

claims.claim: As the cryptocurrency market matures, inflationary token models may become more popular, because they permit stability mechanisms and therefore more experimentation with volatility mitigation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Hayley Howe, Digital Asset Valuation (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4033886
scope_conditions: continued maturation of the cryptocurrency market

claims.claim: Bitcoin's issuance schedule and relative scarcity are not necessarily the only reasons for its rise in value, since thousands of copycats share the same issuance schedule without matching its demand.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Hayley Howe, Digital Asset Valuation (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4033886
scope_conditions: scarcity based valuation models such as stock to flow

claims.claim: Uniform digital asset valuation standards can only evolve over time as the market evolves, because standard setting requires common core practices, and those practices are only slowly emerging.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Samuel Evans, Hayley Howe, Digital Asset Valuation (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4033886
scope_conditions: standard setting for digital asset valuation

claims.claim: Even after the ICO boom of 2017 and 2018, many digital asset projects and token launches are designed with the primary focus on benefiting the founding group, which often finds creative ways to cash out of the project after a successful run.
