scope_conditions: post 2018 crypto market cycle
token launches designed around a founding group

claims.claim: A fair launch is a token distribution in which the launched token is held entirely by the community and founders and their affiliates participate only on equal terms as members of that community.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Fair Token Launch (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4015908

claims.claim: The foundation model for token issuance is a core form of centralized top-down governance, and most ICO projects were governed by a small group of individuals rather than by the community at large or a DAO.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Fair Token Launch (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4015908
scope_conditions: ICO era token issuance

claims.claim: ICOs that allowed their token to trade before the underlying product existed, at least in beta, created significant risk for investors because the product might never go live and the token could lose its value entirely.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Fair Token Launch (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4015908
scope_conditions: token trading opens before a working or beta product exists

claims.claim: Fair launch tokens outperformed centrally distributed projects during the late 2020 and early 2021 rally: the collective crypto average token launch gained 112.41% over 90 days while fair launch projects gained over 296%.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Fair Token Launch (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4015908
scope_conditions: digital asset market rally of late 2020 and early 2021
90 day window after launch

claims.claim: Fair launches shift capital formation from venture capitalism toward altruistic capitalism, because a digital asset startup that can successfully raise capital through a fair launch becomes less reliant on venture capital.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Fair Token Launch (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4015908
scope_conditions: startup can successfully raise capital via fair launch

claims.claim: Fair token launches offer equal opportunity for market participants to acquire tokens over longer periods of time at a comparatively equal price.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Fair Token Launch (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4015908
scope_conditions: token launch claiming the fair launch label

claims.claim: Price equality in a fair launch means that no insider group or person can purchase the token at a significant discount.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Fair Token Launch (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4015908
scope_conditions: token launch claiming the fair launch label

claims.claim: The fairness of a launch can be measured by how many individuals have access to the token at launch, assessed through the number of wallets holding the asset combined with the active participation of the wallet owners.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Fair Token Launch (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4015908
scope_conditions: token functioning as a traditional medium of exchange

claims.claim: Under the fairness to the public definition, a fair token launch requires that the token was launched without a founding team, a foundation, or a founding dev team.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Fair Token Launch (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4015908
scope_conditions: strict fairness to the public definition of fair launch

claims.claim: Under the fairness to the public definition of fair launch, no early investor may hold a pre-allocation of project tokens or a pre-mining program, and any individual claim to a percentage of token supply before public sale falls outside the definition of fair launch.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Fair Token Launch (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4015908
scope_conditions: strict fairness to the public definition of fair launch

claims.claim: Bitcoin is one of the best examples of a fair launch because there was no ICO, no founders reward, no pre-mine, and no block reward for dev teams.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Fair Token Launch (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4015908

claims.claim: Small market cap launches at very cheap initial prices carry the potential for team and whale purchase abuses, which is why equitable treatment of the public requires significant project-controlled liquidity.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Fair Token Launch (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4015908
scope_conditions: small market capitalization
very low initial token price

claims.claim: The larger the market capitalization controlled by the DAO, the less likely it becomes that whales and insiders can purchase inexpensive tokens on the market.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Fair Token Launch (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4015908
scope_conditions: DAO governance over project liquidity

claims.claim: The rule that no tokens may be distributed to insiders such as team, founders, associated whales, core investors, advisors, and marketing teams before or after the token sale is the most important staple of fair launch doctrine and cannot be subject to exceptions; any exception should cost the project the fair token launch designation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Fair Token Launch (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4015908
scope_conditions: projects claiming the fair token launch designation

claims.claim: Because the main mandate of a fair launch is equitable treatment of the public, fair launches typically involve a mandate to distribute any and all revenue and profits of the project to community investors.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Fair Token Launch (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4015908
scope_conditions: project operating under fair launch principles

claims.claim: Open-source code combined with protocol fee flowback to users, as with the Uniswap V2 0.3% swap fee that is automatically distributed to liquidity providers, guarantees transparency, accountability, market confidence in the product, and associated protections for the community.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Fair Token Launch (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4015908
scope_conditions: protocol has a viable product that produces revenue
code is open source

claims.claim: A carve-out for start-up expenses is economically unavoidable in most fair launches because it is not feasible to expect founders operating without funding to keep spending time and resources on the project without payback assurances.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Fair Token Launch (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4015908
scope_conditions: founders operate without outside funding
project cannot raise outside capital in a reasonable timeframe

claims.claim: Because pre-public token allocations to cover start-up costs run against the majority view on fair launches, preserving the spirit of fair launch requires that such allocations be fully transparent, announced to the community, and open to a community audit of the books.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Fair Token Launch (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4015908
scope_conditions: project allocates tokens before the public launch to cover startup costs

claims.claim: Without significant marketing a fair launch token is less likely to reach a diverse set of market participants, and projects reaching only a few hundred investors with small million dollar market caps are much more prone to abuse and manipulation.

scope_conditions: token launches with limited marketing reach

claims.claim: Equal opportunity access points for public marketing incentives cannot be guaranteed and require constant reevaluation, so the public marketing permission for any fair token launch should be restricted to a limited percentage of total token supply.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Fair Token Launch (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4015908
scope_conditions: fair launch project grants public marketing incentives

claims.claim: The more decentralized the governance of a fair launch protocol, the less likely the project will be seen as treating public users unfairly, which makes a decentralized autonomous organization design advisable for fair launch projects.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Fair Token Launch (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4015908
scope_conditions: governance design is transparent and decentralized

claims.claim: If the DAO governing a fair launch is controlled by a handful of people in a foundation setting, decentralized governance metrics are less likely to take hold and the public is correspondingly less likely to benefit from decentralized community governance over the launch.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Fair Token Launch (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4015908
scope_conditions: DAO controlled by a small group in a foundation setting

claims.claim: DAO governance built on fungible governance tokens is disfavored and dangerous because governance rights can be bought on open exchanges, whereas non-fungible reputation governance assures the highest levels of decentralization.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Fair Token Launch (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4015908
scope_conditions: DAO governance rights are tradeable on open exchanges

claims.claim: Community DAO governance makes any form of rug pull much less likely, because rug pulls typically benefit only a few select individuals who retained control over the project code or liquidity.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Fair Token Launch (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4015908
scope_conditions: community DAO oversees project code and liquidity

claims.claim: DAO governance over token launch wallets can assure that no single individual exercises rights over the token launch wallet and becomes a single point of failure or abuse.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Fair Token Launch (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4015908
scope_conditions: token launch wallet is governed by the DAO

claims.claim: Founders may hold significant influence over DAO votes initially depending on the DAO design, but higher levels of governance decentralization mitigate these centralization effects quickly through the onboarding of new DAO members.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Fair Token Launch (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4015908
scope_conditions: early stage of DAO formation
DAO design permits ongoing member onboarding

claims.claim: Whale purchases that soak up token supply at the earliest possible time in a launch are the key problem fair launch platforms address, because they can be the origin of significant centralization that harms the project for the entirety of its active market engagement.

scope_conditions: whales able to buy large amounts at the earliest moment of a launch

claims.claim: Technology platforms can make launch abuses less likely by mandating fair auctions in which tokens are released only in tranches, offering a limited number of tokens for a limited number of days, which makes rug pulls overall less likely.

claims.claim: After half of each auction tranche is deposited into an AMM pair, the other half is allocated to open market purchasers and the remaining liquidity on the AMM is burned to ensure that any incentives for rug pulls are removed.

scope_conditions: auction based fair launch platform
Uniswap V2 compatible AMM

claims.claim: Grin avoided privileging miners who could develop ASICs before launch by gradually scaling up the portion of coins allocated to the ASIC-friendly algorithm over two years, which allowed hobbyist miners to participate.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Fair Token Launch (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4015908
scope_conditions: dual proof of work offered over the first two years

claims.claim: Liquidity mining, one of the dominant mechanisms used for fair launches, undermines fairness because it leads those who already have more liquidity or assets to benefit disproportionally from the protocol.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Fair Token Launch (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4015908
scope_conditions: fair launch distributes rewards through liquidity mining

claims.claim: If the top 10 addresses own a disproportionally large supply of a token, the project or community becomes more centralized, an outcome fair launches seek to avoid.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Fair Token Launch (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4015908
scope_conditions: token supply concentration measured across top holder addresses

claims.claim: Binance implemented a subscription mechanism that gives everyone an equal opportunity to purchase newly released NFTs, responding to drops that sell out in seconds and leave interested users waiting for initial owners to flip.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Fair Token Launch (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4015908
scope_conditions: limited supply and high demand NFT drops

claims.claim: An auction mechanism for fair launch tokens avoids pricing tokens below their underlying market value, which in turn helps remedy the problems that derive from large whale token holders who can later manipulate the market.

scope_conditions: public auction of tokens at launch

claims.claim: No more than 40% of total token supply should be auctioned in a fair launch, with 10% serving as a buffer paired with raised funds as permanently locked DEX liquidity and the other 50% allocated to a DEX pair with the raise proceeds to provide long-term locked liquidity.

scope_conditions: public auction of tokens in a fair launch context

claims.claim: In a lottery fair launch protocol, a user who bids low for a ticket increases the potential secondary market return but decreases the chance of winning the lottery, because more users can afford to participate at a low price.

scope_conditions: lottery based fair launch protocol
price determined by community bids

claims.claim: Non-linear reward structures using weighting, tiers, or logarithmic curves counteract centralization of token supply by decentralizing disproportionate returns so that rewards do not scale linearly with the amount of liquidity a user holds.

claims.claim: A fair launch rewards protocol can measure ethical conduct by whether a user engages with the protocol consistently, invests, and votes over time, while users who merely use the network for yield farming may not qualify because they lack engagement.

scope_conditions: protocol can measure historical on chain user behavior

claims.claim: Through fair launch evolution and continuous practice improvements, the fair launch industry and the underlying digital asset businesses can become the foundation of the emerging decentralized digital asset economy.

scope_conditions: continued evolution and improvement of fair launch practice

claims.claim: Rug pull practices can take the form of a whale guaranteeing an inside developer or business head a percentage participation if that insider changes the code governing the project to produce an outcome that benefits only the whale and its associates.

scope_conditions: insiders retain the ability to change project code

claims.claim: In lottery fair launch protocols the ticket price is determined as the median of all tickets purchased, and users then decide whether to accept that price, paying the difference if it exceeds their bid or withdrawing for a refund.

scope_conditions: lottery based fair launch protocol

claims.claim: Blockchain's distributed consensus model makes fraudulent transactions much less likely to be recorded because individual network nodes verify and validate chain transactions before those transactions execute.

claims.claim: Disintermediation is a key feature of blockchain technology because the technology incentivizes direct transactions between creators and consumers.

claims.claim: The literature on securities tokens converges on two commonalities: that a securities token functions as or is synonymous with traditional security assets, and that securities tokens are subject to traditional securities regulation.

claims.claim: For digital assets the decisive element of the Howey analysis is whether the purchaser of the token has a reasonable expectation of profits derived from the efforts of others, which the SEC divides into reliance on the efforts of others and reasonable expectation of profits.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Securities Versus Utility Tokens (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4021599
scope_conditions: SEC framework for investment contract analysis of digital assets

claims.claim: None of the SEC's listed characteristics bearing on reliance on the efforts of others is individually determinative; the element becomes more likely to be met the stronger the presence of those characteristics.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Securities Versus Utility Tokens (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4021599
scope_conditions: SEC framework for investment contract analysis of digital assets

claims.claim: Utility tokens are tokens with an intrinsic utility for a good or service: they emphasize the uses of the token and typically give users access to a product or service or give rewards that incentivize desirable behavior on the platform.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Securities Versus Utility Tokens (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4021599

claims.claim: Utility tokens operate as an access mechanism: in order to interact with a given platform or use case, users are incentivized to acquire access rights to the product or service by acquiring the utility token.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Securities Versus Utility Tokens (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4021599

claims.claim: Rather than replacing legacy financial services as securities tokens do, utility tokens are designed to give users future access to a product or service that may or may not exist at the time of the utility token issuance.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Securities Versus Utility Tokens (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4021599

claims.claim: Utility tokens are not investment contracts and not investments because they are meant for a good or service, and they are typically exempted from federal securities laws if they are properly set up.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Securities Versus Utility Tokens (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4021599
scope_conditions: the utility token is properly structured at issuance
United States federal securities laws

claims.claim: Utility tokens are not created by their issuers for investment purposes; they are designed to be used for their specific utility in a given context.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Securities Versus Utility Tokens (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4021599

claims.claim: Merely calling a token a utility token, or structuring it so that it provides some utility, does not prevent the token from being characterized as a security.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Securities Versus Utility Tokens (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4021599
scope_conditions: United States regulatory characterization

claims.claim: Under SEC guidance a token sold for use or consumption by purchasers may fall outside classification as a security, and the SEC lists characteristics whose stronger presence makes a token less likely to be considered a security.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Securities Versus Utility Tokens (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4021599
scope_conditions: SEC framework for investment contract analysis of digital assets

claims.claim: Utility tokens can be distinguished from securities tokens along several core factors: the purpose of the token, associated valuation, associated rights, user expectations, and regulatory status.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Securities Versus Utility Tokens (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4021599

claims.claim: A utility token's value depends on its functions and therefore correlates with actual demand for the token, so a scaled up project with a high number of users usually yields increased utility token value, whereas a securities token's value correlates with the value of the issuing company.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Securities Versus Utility Tokens (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4021599

claims.claim: Securities token users typically expect the value of the issuing company to be directly tied to token value, while utility token users typically expect no relation between the issuer's current valuation and the value of the utility token.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Securities Versus Utility Tokens (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4021599

claims.claim: The regulatory status of securities tokens is rather well established, whereas the regulatory status of utility tokens remains unclear.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Securities Versus Utility Tokens (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4021599
scope_conditions: as of 2022

claims.claim: The Howey test operates as the practical sorting device between the two categories: a token that passes the Howey test is deemed a security token, while a token that does not qualify under Howey is often classified as a utility token.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Securities Versus Utility Tokens (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4021599
scope_conditions: United States federal securities law

claims.claim: The term securities token is fairly well defined as of 2022, and additional regulatory guidance will continue to delineate its central features and distinguishing characteristics.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Securities Versus Utility Tokens (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4021599
scope_conditions: as of 2022; assumes continued regulatory guidance

claims.claim: As the digital asset industry matures, the distinguishing features between token categories and the associated case law will likely increase and provide more guidance to market participants.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Securities Versus Utility Tokens (2022). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4021599
scope_conditions: industry maturation over time

claims.claim: The paper's empirical basis is a dataset of DAOs selected by the assets held in their treasuries, drawn from across different industries.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Josh Bykowski, Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAO) – A Market Meta Analysis (2023). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4529715

claims.claim: Each DAO in the dataset was given a score between zero and ten by the analyzing teams on each of six factors: Decentralization, Work to Earn, Attack Resistance, Regulatory Compliance, Governance, and Organizational Communication.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Josh Bykowski, Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAO) – A Market Meta Analysis (2023). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4529715
scope_conditions: scores assigned by the analyzing teams

claims.claim: DAOs in the dataset score well below average on implementing true decentralization, averaging 3.78 out of 10, with the highest score being CRDAO at 8 out of 10 and several DAOs scoring 1 out of 10.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Josh Bykowski, Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAO) – A Market Meta Analysis (2023). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4529715
scope_conditions: dataset of DAOs scored by the authors' teams

claims.claim: The decentralized power structure is supposed to encourage cooperation, free information flow, and decision-making that escapes top-down hierarchy, but with few exceptions the current state of DAOs does not deliver this.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Josh Bykowski, Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAO) – A Market Meta Analysis (2023). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4529715
scope_conditions: current state of the DAO market at time of study

claims.claim: Work to earn is the strongest of the six scored categories, yet it still averages only 4.9 out of 10 across the DAOs studied.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Josh Bykowski, Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAO) – A Market Meta Analysis (2023). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4529715

claims.claim: Attack resistance across the studied DAOs averages 4.05 out of 10, and Charity DAOs perform worst in this category, with the best of them, VitaDAO, scoring 3 out of 10 and the remainder at 2 or less.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Josh Bykowski, Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAO) – A Market Meta Analysis (2023). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4529715

claims.claim: Regulatory compliance is the weakest of all six categories, averaging 3.01 out of 10, and Services DAOs are the only category to outperform that average.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Josh Bykowski, Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAO) – A Market Meta Analysis (2023). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4529715

claims.claim: The absence of clear regulatory direction from the SEC and state governments helps explain why many DAOs take minimal action to establish regulatory compliance within their organizations.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Josh Bykowski, Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAO) – A Market Meta Analysis (2023). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4529715
scope_conditions: United States regulatory context

claims.claim: Governance scores across the studied DAOs average 3.81 out of 10, with only a couple of DAOs scoring 7 or higher and the vast majority scoring 5 or less.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Josh Bykowski, Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAO) – A Market Meta Analysis (2023). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4529715

claims.claim: Organizational communication across the studied DAOs averages 4.29 out of 10.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Josh Bykowski, Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAO) – A Market Meta Analysis (2023). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4529715

claims.claim: Information technology has facilitated and arguably necessitated the DAO in the same way that the printing press, navigational instruments, and reliable maritime shipping necessitated and facilitated the joint stock corporation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Josh Bykowski, Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAO) – A Market Meta Analysis (2023). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4529715

claims.claim: There is no consistent standard for DAO governance, which pushes each DAO to invent its own structure, and because decentralized governance is complex many of those structures fail to become truly decentralized, autonomous, or organized.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Josh Bykowski, Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAO) – A Market Meta Analysis (2023). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4529715
scope_conditions: absence of a governance standard
novelty of decentralized governance

claims.claim: Unlike corporate founders, who inherit a known governance template, DAO founders must build a new form of governance from nothing alongside their technology, mission, and values.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Josh Bykowski, Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAO) – A Market Meta Analysis (2023). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4529715
scope_conditions: comparison to incorporation of a traditional corporation

claims.claim: Some DAO governance platforms create more risk than they mitigate, and DAOs that are not well governed are doomed to fail.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Josh Bykowski, Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAO) – A Market Meta Analysis (2023). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4529715
scope_conditions: platform provided governance templates

claims.claim: The most significant risk of bad DAO governance is centralization, in which a small group holds a disproportionate share of power or influence and thereby undermines the decentralized nature of the organization.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Josh Bykowski, Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAO) – A Market Meta Analysis (2023). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4529715

claims.claim: Without clear and effective governance mechanisms, DAO decision-making becomes slow and inefficient, delaying important changes and the resolution of internal issues.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Josh Bykowski, Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAO) – A Market Meta Analysis (2023). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4529715

claims.claim: DAOs without effective governance structures and policies risk violating local laws and regulations, exposing themselves to legal and regulatory consequences.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Josh Bykowski, Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAO) – A Market Meta Analysis (2023). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4529715

claims.claim: One person one vote governance carries the risk of majority tyranny, in which the majority imposes its will on minority groups, and it is unsuited to decisions requiring specialized knowledge.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Josh Bykowski, Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAO) – A Market Meta Analysis (2023). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4529715
scope_conditions: one person one vote model

claims.claim: Quadratic voting remains open to manipulation and strategic voting, and it depends on a robust and transparent voting system to count votes accurately.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Josh Bykowski, Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAO) – A Market Meta Analysis (2023). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4529715
scope_conditions: quadratic voting model

claims.claim: Fungible governance tokens expose a DAO to vote buying and other forms of manipulation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Josh Bykowski, Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAO) – A Market Meta Analysis (2023). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4529715
scope_conditions: fungible token based governance

claims.claim: True decentralization requires the absence of a primary decision-maker, which is very difficult for a decentralized insurance organization to achieve while it is still in its infancy.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Josh Bykowski, Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAO) – A Market Meta Analysis (2023). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4529715
scope_conditions: early stage decentralized insurance organizations

claims.claim: Decentralized organizations carry inherent risks that require establishing a legal entity, and establishing that legal entity inherently contradicts the notion of decentralization.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Josh Bykowski, Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAO) – A Market Meta Analysis (2023). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4529715
scope_conditions: decentralized insurance organizations

claims.claim: Blockchains cannot access off-chain data, and resolving this by using centralized oracles nullifies the advantages of decentralized systems while creating major security risks such as bribing and intimidation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Josh Bykowski, Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAO) – A Market Meta Analysis (2023). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4529715
scope_conditions: oracle dependent smart contracts

claims.claim: The full potential of DAOs can be realized only if the challenges of standardized governance mechanisms, scalability, and legal frameworks are resolved.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Josh Bykowski, Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAO) – A Market Meta Analysis (2023). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4529715

claims.claim: Web3 may not yet be ready for a truly decentralized organization: across platforms there is always a promise of decentralization, yet tangible measures prevent that promise from becoming true.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Josh Bykowski, Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAO) – A Market Meta Analysis (2023). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4529715
scope_conditions: DAO platforms reviewed in the study

claims.claim: Many DAO platforms accept the idea that they must first build a centralized organization and decentralize later once proper protocols are in place, but this mindset undermines the power and accessibility to ownership that is the foundation of a DAO.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Josh Bykowski, Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAO) – A Market Meta Analysis (2023). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4529715
scope_conditions: platforms that plan phased decentralization

claims.claim: Meaningful accessibility in a DAO is impossible if voting rights and ownership are merely passive purchasable assets, no different from traditional stock.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Josh Bykowski, Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAO) – A Market Meta Analysis (2023). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4529715
scope_conditions: purchasable governance tokens

claims.claim: Where a founder retains access to the smart contract behind the governance token, as with 3OH DAO, an internal attack by that founder would be remarkably easy.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Josh Bykowski, Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAO) – A Market Meta Analysis (2023). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4529715
scope_conditions: founder has not renounced ownership of the token smart contract

claims.claim: Lobby3 was effectively attacked from within: founders maintained heavy control and slowly diverted funds to themselves, producing a very slow rug pull.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Josh Bykowski, Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAO) – A Market Meta Analysis (2023). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4529715
scope_conditions: founder controlled DAO with wallet size voting

claims.claim: VitaDAO's one token one vote structure leaves it susceptible to the 51 percent or whale attack, a vulnerability made worse because the VITA token is primarily purchasable.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Josh Bykowski, Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAO) – A Market Meta Analysis (2023). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4529715
scope_conditions: one token one vote with a purchasable token

claims.claim: Allocating twenty percent of total token supply to the four person founding team, as Angel Protocol does, means the organization can never become fully decentralized.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Josh Bykowski, Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAO) – A Market Meta Analysis (2023). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4529715
scope_conditions: founding team holds 20 percent of supply

claims.claim: A reputation system that rewards voting with the majority, as Bridge Mutual uses, can be manipulated by users who create multiple wallets and always vote with the majority.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Josh Bykowski, Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAO) – A Market Meta Analysis (2023). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4529715
scope_conditions: reputation derived solely from voting outcomes

claims.claim: Locking voted tokens for a period after a vote, as Nexus Mutual does for three days, prevents an attacker from using a flashloan to borrow a large amount of wrapped tokens and swing a vote with significant voting weight.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Josh Bykowski, Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAO) – A Market Meta Analysis (2023). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4529715
scope_conditions: token weighted voting with freely traded wrapped token

claims.claim: Short-term incentives in a decentralized insurance mutual would motivate decision-makers never to pay a claim in order to maximize current profit; incentivizing long-term alignment instead motivates them to pay genuine claims because of the value of the resulting reputation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Josh Bykowski, Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAO) – A Market Meta Analysis (2023). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4529715
scope_conditions: discretionary mutual where members decide claims

claims.claim: Chainlink's white-list response to the 2020 gas fee attack was only a temporary fix: had the attack impacted 50 percent of Chainlink node operators, the price feed would not have updated until enough nodes returned.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Josh Bykowski, Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAO) – A Market Meta Analysis (2023). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4529715
scope_conditions: 2020 attack on Chainlink nodes
oracle networks with limited node counts

claims.claim: Requiring governance tokens to be earned through contribution rather than purchased, as GDN DAO does, leaves only minimal risk of 51 percent and sock puppet attacks even under a one token one vote structure.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Josh Bykowski, Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAO) – A Market Meta Analysis (2023). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4529715
scope_conditions: one token one vote with non purchasable tokens

claims.claim: A DAO built on reputation rather than a fungible token, as CRDAO is, makes the 51 percent attack nearly impossible and renders sock puppet attacks technically possible but of little influence.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Josh Bykowski, Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAO) – A Market Meta Analysis (2023). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4529715
scope_conditions: reputation based governance
no fungible governance token

claims.claim: Kleros has weak attack resistance because juror selection is proportional to staked fungible tokens; staking reputation rather than tokens to select jurors would remedy this.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Josh Bykowski, Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAO) – A Market Meta Analysis (2023). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4529715
scope_conditions: token staked juror selection

claims.claim: Big Green DAO's committee unanimity and closed membership make attacks unlikely, but these same protections come at the expense of the decentralized organization the founders were trying to create.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Josh Bykowski, Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAO) – A Market Meta Analysis (2023). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4529715
scope_conditions: vetted membership and unanimous committee approval

claims.claim: When only a minority of members, such as Audius node operators, can stake or earn weighted votes, the majority of token holders occupy the same powerless position as an ordinary shareholder in a corporation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Josh Bykowski, Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAO) – A Market Meta Analysis (2023). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4529715
scope_conditions: tiered voting where staking is restricted to node operators

claims.claim: Traditional AI governance frameworks fail because they rely on static, predefined rules that cannot adapt quickly enough to the pace of AI development or to the nuanced challenges AI presents.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, AI Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4796714
scope_conditions: applies to conventional rule based governance regimes
holds where AI capability changes faster than the rule revision cycle

claims.claim: Conventional governance methods that are reactive or fixed to ex-post solutions are insufficient for governing technologies whose behavior changes continuously after deployment.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, AI Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4796714
scope_conditions: applies to ex-post regulatory regimes
holds for AI systems that continue to learn after release

claims.claim: At the time of publication no legacy governance system exists that can supply the dynamic governance toolsets required to govern evolving AI models ex-ante and manage deployed solutions ex-post.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, AI Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4796714
scope_conditions: as of the paper's publication in 2024
refers to legacy, non web3 governance infrastructure

claims.claim: Ex-post governance, which applies regulation only after AI systems are developed and deployed or after large language models have been pretrained on existing proprietary datasets, fails to address risks and biases preemptively.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, AI Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4796714
scope_conditions: applies to regulation imposed after model development or pretraining
concerns risk and bias formation during development

claims.claim: Technology has historically outpaced regulation, and the exponential trends in AI development will continue to widen the mismatch between regulation and AI development.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, AI Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4796714
scope_conditions: assumes continued exponential improvement in AI capability

claims.claim: Web3 data attestation supports a governance model that assigns liability for AI misuse to identifiable individuals rather than distributing the burden across the whole community, which is what makes it a workable answer to AI related ethical dilemmas.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, AI Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4796714
scope_conditions: requires cryptographic data attestation and verifiable identity
applies to liability arising from AI misuse and uploaded content

claims.claim: The black box character of deep learning models is a governance failure and not merely a technical inconvenience: opacity obstructs debugging, obscures bias detection and mitigation, and prevents comprehension of how inputs become outputs.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, AI Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4796714
scope_conditions: most pronounced in deep learning models
matters where decisions must be explained or audited

claims.claim: Strict privacy and transparency regulation produces a perverse result: because only large technology companies hold the data resources and infrastructure needed to comply and still build effective AI, such regulation consolidates rather than disperses their power.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, AI Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4796714
scope_conditions: applies to stringent data privacy regimes such as GDPR
holds where compliance cost scales with organizational resources

claims.claim: Federated learning does not eliminate privacy risk, because although the data stays decentralized the exchange of model parameters can still expose sensitive information if those parameters are intercepted or improperly handled.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, AI Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4796714
scope_conditions: applies to practical federated learning deployments
risk arises at the parameter exchange step

claims.claim: Federated learning lacks theoretical guarantees of reliability and robustness, which makes its behavior unpredictable in practical applications.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, AI Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4796714
scope_conditions: applies to federated learning as practiced

claims.claim: Bias in AI systems arises when algorithms incorporate discriminatory practices carried in their training data, and the resulting outputs reveal a profound misalignment between AI operations and societal values, ethics, and norms.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, AI Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4796714
scope_conditions: arises through the training data pathway
observable in deployed systems such as chatbots and screening tools

claims.claim: Recentralization is the central obstacle to using blockchain and distributed ledger technology to govern AI: the recentralizing tendency of these networks interferes with their capacity to deliver effective AI governance.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, AI Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4796714
scope_conditions: applies to blockchain and DLT based AI governance proposals
observed in Layer 1 networks as of 2024

claims.claim: Blockchain can only deliver decentralized AI governance if the blockchain trilemma is first overcome, since decentralization, security, and scalability cannot readily be achieved simultaneously within one network.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, AI Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4796714
scope_conditions: applies to blockchain networks used as governance infrastructure
necessary condition, not sufficient

claims.claim: Proof of Stake consensus centralizes control in proportion to the quantity of tokens held, so governance built on such chains is skewed in favor of the wealthy rather than distributed.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, AI Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4796714
scope_conditions: applies to Proof of Stake chains such as Ethereum
concerns token weighted governance power

claims.claim: When decentralization at the Layer 1 level is compromised, the autonomy of the smart contracts deployed on that chain is compromised by affiliation, so smart contracts are corruptible in the current design and cannot reliably serve as neutral instruments of ethical AI governance.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, AI Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4796714
scope_conditions: applies where a few dominant parties influence the underlying Layer 1
holds under current blockchain design as of 2024

claims.claim: Decentralized governance structures impose their own costs: with no central authority to coordinate diverse stakeholders, consensus is difficult to reach, negotiations are prolonged, and enforcement of agreements is weak because no single entity is responsible for compliance.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, AI Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4796714
scope_conditions: applies to decentralized structures without a coordinating authority
evidenced in the paper by the environmental agreement domain

claims.claim: Using human judgment to uncover unconscious bias in AI can perpetuate the very biases it is meant to remove, because human reviewers carry their own implicit biases and may lack the expertise to identify bias in complex AI systems.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, AI Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4796714
scope_conditions: applies to human in the loop bias mitigation programs
holds where reviewers lack technical expertise or bias awareness

claims.claim: Sector specific AI regulation, though responsive to the distinctive features of each field, produces a patchwork of complex rules that is difficult for developers to navigate and creates barriers to entry for smaller companies lacking compliance resources.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, AI Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4796714
scope_conditions: applies where multiple sector regulators issue separate AI rules
burden falls hardest on resource constrained firms

claims.claim: Mandatory AI use reporting fails as a transparency mechanism because it assumes accurate and complete disclosure, while regulated entities have incentives to underreport or misreport in order to avoid scrutiny and regulatory burdens.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, AI Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4796714
scope_conditions: applies to self reporting mandates such as the White House AI reporting proposals
holds where disclosure is unverified

claims.claim: The gap between regulators' technical understanding and the state of the art in AI drives rules to one of two failure states: too vague to be enforceable, or so prescriptive that they suppress creative and beneficial uses of AI.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, AI Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4796714
scope_conditions: applies where regulators lack current technical expertise
holds for fast moving technical domains

claims.claim: Until the known attack vectors on decentralized autonomous organizations are solved, DAO based AI governance solutions remain suboptimal; these include Sybil attacks, tyranny of the majority, Arrow's impossibility theorem, sockpuppet attacks, and tragedy of the commons.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, AI Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4796714
scope_conditions: describes DAOs as set up and governed in the majority of cases in 2024
conditional on the attack vectors remaining unsolved

claims.claim: AI powered DAOs that autonomously generate revenue are especially hard to regulate or dismantle, because the same blockchain security features that protect the organization also make it difficult to intervene once it is operational.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, AI Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4796714
scope_conditions: applies to autonomously revenue generating AI DAOs
arises from blockchain immutability and security guarantees

claims.claim: Purely preemptive regulation cannot succeed on its own, because it is not possible to anticipate every issue or bias an AI system will exhibit before it is operational and interacting with real world variables.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, AI Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4796714
scope_conditions: applies to ex-ante controls imposed at the model and data levels
concerns emergent behavior that appears only in deployment

claims.claim: Ex-ante regulation is preferable in principle but is neither practical nor sufficient inside legacy systems, precisely because legacy systems, unlike the web3 system proposed here, are not equipped to create dynamic feedback effects.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, AI Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4796714
scope_conditions: comparison is between legacy regulatory infrastructure and web3 based governance
turns on the presence or absence of dynamic feedback effects

claims.claim: Strict legacy regulation built on stable and presumptively optimal rules and enforced at the AI development stage can inadvertently stifle innovation by imposing rigid constraints before a model is fully developed or deployed.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, AI Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4796714
scope_conditions: applies to rigid pre-deployment regulatory constraints in legacy systems
concerns exploratory development that has not yet produced a deployable model
