scope_conditions: dataset of 50 DAOs
work to earn scored on a 1 to 10 scale

claims.claim: The average organizational communication score across the sampled DAOs is 4.32, with a maximum of 10 and a minimum of 1, indicating only moderate communication effectiveness overall.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Market Meta Analysis 2024 (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5254152
scope_conditions: dataset of 50 DAOs
organizational communication scored on a 1 to 10 scale

claims.claim: The analysis reveals significant variability across all six attributes, decentralization, security, governance, regulatory compliance, work incentives, and communication effectiveness, reflecting the divergent developmental stages of DAOs.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Market Meta Analysis 2024 (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5254152
scope_conditions: dataset of 50 DAOs scored on six attributes

claims.claim: DeScience and Data Analysis DAOs generally score higher on overall performance metrics, whereas Investment DAOs and Art and Culture DAOs display idiosyncratic mixes of strengths and weaknesses.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Market Meta Analysis 2024 (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5254152
scope_conditions: dataset of 50 DAOs across market categories

claims.claim: Requiring users to purchase governance tokens in order to vote both centralizes power in majority token holders and leaves the DAO highly vulnerable to 51 percent and sock puppet attacks, as illustrated by Gelato DAO which scored 1 on both decentralization and attack resistance.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Market Meta Analysis 2024 (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5254152
scope_conditions: DAOs where voting requires purchasing fungible governance tokens

claims.claim: A DAO operating without a legal wrapper risks being deemed a partnership by estoppel in legal disputes, exposing its members to liability, as scored for Hop DAO with a regulatory compliance score of 1.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Market Meta Analysis 2024 (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5254152
scope_conditions: DAOs with no legal entity or legal wrapper

claims.claim: A DAO that offers no paid work opportunities for participants stifles engagement, as scored for Hop DAO with a Work to Earn score of 1.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Market Meta Analysis 2024 (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5254152
scope_conditions: DAOs with no compensated contribution channel

claims.claim: A one person, one vote structure raises a DAO's resistance to 51 percent and sock puppet attacks, as reflected in TomiDAO's attack resistance score of 6 against a sample average of 3.65.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Market Meta Analysis 2024 (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5254152
scope_conditions: DAOs implementing one person, one vote rather than token weighted voting

claims.claim: Procedural governance safeguards such as two step voting with temperature checks do not produce genuine decentralization when the governance token remains purchasable; in MakerDAO's case the purchasable token renders true decentralization nominal.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Market Meta Analysis 2024 (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5254152
scope_conditions: DAOs combining multi stage voting with freely purchasable governance tokens

claims.claim: Subjecting every community vote to review by a council that is not democratically elected defeats the governance value of community voting, as scored for Goldfinch DAO with a governance score of 2.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Market Meta Analysis 2024 (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5254152
scope_conditions: DAOs where a non elected council holds final say over community votes

claims.claim: Some DAOs substitute anonymity for legal structure: without any legal registration, Olympus DAO relies on anonymity to avoid legal action, which the author scores as the weakest possible regulatory compliance posture.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Market Meta Analysis 2024 (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5254152
scope_conditions: DAOs with no legal registration in any jurisdiction

claims.claim: Adopting a conventional corporate form in a jurisdiction that does not recognize DAOs yields only partial legal protection; Silo Finance is registered as an LLC in Texas, but Texas does not recognize DAOs.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Market Meta Analysis 2024 (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5254152
scope_conditions: DAOs incorporated in jurisdictions lacking DAO specific recognition

claims.claim: A DAO registered in a jurisdiction without DAO legislation risks default treatment as a partnership under existing law, as recorded for Klima DAO in California.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Market Meta Analysis 2024 (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5254152
scope_conditions: DAOs organized in jurisdictions with no DAO statute

claims.claim: A governance design aimed at democratic balance can still centralize power over time when the token supply is fixed, as recorded for MoonDAO.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Market Meta Analysis 2024 (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5254152
scope_conditions: DAOs with a fixed governance token supply

claims.claim: Tiered membership models that tie governance rights and influence to token holdings introduce imbalance and a centralization element into DAO governance, as scored for Bankless DAO.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Market Meta Analysis 2024 (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5254152
scope_conditions: DAOs with contributor tiers or access levels keyed to token ownership

claims.claim: Reliance on fungible, publicly tradable governance tokens undermines a protocol's resilience by exposing it to risks such as 51 percent attacks, as scored for Push Protocol.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Market Meta Analysis 2024 (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5254152
scope_conditions: DAOs whose governance tokens trade on open markets

claims.claim: A tiered voting system that combines temperature checks with token holder percentage thresholds robustly defends a DAO against common attacks, as reflected in Arbitrum's attack resistance score of 8.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Market Meta Analysis 2024 (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5254152
scope_conditions: DAOs implementing multi stage voting with participation thresholds

claims.claim: The absence of a dedicated discussion platform, combined with poor engagement on third party accounts, hinders meaningful discussion and collaboration within a DAO, as scored for BrainDAO with an organizational communication score of 1 despite high decentralization and attack resistance scores.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, DAO Market Meta Analysis 2024 (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5254152
scope_conditions: DAOs communicating only through external social platforms

claims.claim: Web3 community governance built on Weighted Directed Acyclic Graphs, validation pools with reputation staking, and a federated communications protocol provides an evolutionary approach to optimizing AI models rather than a static compliance layer over them.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How AI Models are Optimized Through Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4855607
scope_conditions: applies to the six AI model families the author examines: deep learning, federated learning, transformer, GNN, RL, and RLHF

claims.claim: The computational cost of improving deep learning performance scales so badly that halving the error rate is estimated to require over five hundred times more computational resources, which raises a sustainability problem for the deep learning paradigm itself.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How AI Models are Optimized Through Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4855607
scope_conditions: scaling driven improvement of deep learning accuracy

claims.claim: Deep learning models inadvertently learn and amplify whatever biases exist in their training data, so the composition of the training corpus, not the architecture, is the source of unfair or discriminatory outcomes.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How AI Models are Optimized Through Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4855607
scope_conditions: depends on the data used for training

claims.claim: Deep learning models adapt to changes in data distribution far less readily than human learning does, which limits their reliability once the operating environment diverges from the training data.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How AI Models are Optimized Through Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4855607
scope_conditions: settings where the data distribution shifts after training

claims.claim: In federated learning the communication cost of many edge devices sending model parameters to a central server frequently exceeds the computation cost, and heterogeneity in the participating devices, including varying computational capabilities and resource constraints, compounds the problem.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How AI Models are Optimized Through Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4855607
scope_conditions: federated learning across numerous heterogeneous edge devices

claims.claim: Federated learning does not eliminate privacy risk: because gradients and partial parameters are transmitted, the system remains vulnerable to attacks that leak data, and this vulnerability together with communication overhead is a significant hurdle to deployment.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How AI Models are Optimized Through Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4855607
scope_conditions: federated learning schemes that share gradients or partial parameters with a server

claims.claim: The self attention mechanism in transformers scales quadratically with input sequence length, which makes transformers expensive and slow to train and use on long sequences and disqualifies them where real time processing or limited compute is required.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How AI Models are Optimized Through Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4855607
scope_conditions: long input sequences
real time or compute constrained deployments

claims.claim: GPT class models are costly to run, and their closed nature and undisclosed algorithmic details raise transparency and accountability concerns that their performance does not offset.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How AI Models are Optimized Through Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4855607
scope_conditions: proprietary, closed weight transformer models

claims.claim: In the legal domain the adoption of transformer based language models is blocked less by capability than by resources and access: training and deployment are resource intensive and large, quality tagged legal datasets are usually restricted.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How AI Models are Optimized Through Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4855607
scope_conditions: legal applications of transformer based language models

claims.claim: GNN scalability on large real world graphs is a genuine trade off rather than an engineering gap: sampling methods lose influential neighbors while clustering methods lose structural patterns, so each remedy sacrifices part of the signal the model needs.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How AI Models are Optimized Through Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4855607
scope_conditions: large real world graphs where full graph processing is infeasible

claims.claim: GNNs are vulnerable to adversarial attacks that target both node features and graph structure, and their lack of interpretability remains a major obstacle to applying them to real world problems.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How AI Models are Optimized Through Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4855607
scope_conditions: real world GNN deployments where adversaries can influence the graph

claims.claim: Most GNN architectures assume homogeneous graph structures, so adapting them to heterogeneous graphs with diverse node and edge types remains an unsolved research challenge, and full batch training on large graphs suffers memory overflow.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How AI Models are Optimized Through Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4855607
scope_conditions: graphs with diverse node and edge types
large graphs trained full batch

claims.claim: Explainable reinforcement learning research has not yet produced usable explanations: the field relies on toy examples, omits user testing, produces explanations that are themselves complex, uses basic visualizations, and rarely open sources its code.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How AI Models are Optimized Through Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4855607
scope_conditions: current explainable RL research as surveyed in the text

claims.claim: Deep reinforcement learning demands large amounts of training data, which suggests its algorithms differ fundamentally from human learning, and learning without supervision becomes particularly hard when rewards are sparse, as they typically are in sequence generation tasks.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How AI Models are Optimized Through Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4855607
scope_conditions: sparse reward settings
sequence generation tasks

claims.claim: Reward modeling learned through interaction with users carries two structural pathologies: majority views disproportionately influence the learned reward function, and the agent may engage in reward hacking.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How AI Models are Optimized Through Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4855607
scope_conditions: reward functions learned from aggregated user interaction

claims.claim: There is a trade off in RLHF between the agent imitating human advice and learning autonomously, and human guidance that is too specific will prevent the agent from discovering novel optimal strategies.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How AI Models are Optimized Through Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4855607
scope_conditions: human in the loop RL where the extent of human involvement is a design choice

claims.claim: Balancing helpfulness against harmlessness is an inherent tension in Safe RLHF rather than a tuning problem that can be resolved once.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How AI Models are Optimized Through Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4855607
scope_conditions: Safe RLHF designs that optimize helpfulness and harmlessness jointly

claims.claim: RLHF fails on several fronts at once: humans can pursue harmful goals either innocently or maliciously, human feedback degrades when examples are hard to evaluate and especially when RLHF is applied to superhuman models, and reward models diverge from humans through misspecification and misgeneralization.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How AI Models are Optimized Through Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4855607
scope_conditions: especially acute when RLHF is applied to models more capable than their human evaluators

claims.claim: In traditional federated learning environments the reliability of updates arriving from various nodes is hard to establish; web3 smart contracts and consensus mechanisms can automate that verification at the point of aggregation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How AI Models are Optimized Through Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4855607
scope_conditions: federated learning with untrusted or unverified participating nodes

claims.claim: Decentralized collective governance without a central authority reduces both single points of failure and the biases that attach to traditional centralized systems, which is the core structural argument for governing AI through web3 rather than through a central body.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How AI Models are Optimized Through Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4855607
scope_conditions: governance arrangements where stakeholders collectively govern

claims.claim: Validation pools evaluate contributions democratically on the basis of staked tokens, and the outcome of that evaluation governs the minting of new reputation tokens, so community consensus on AI decisions is what determines standing in the system.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How AI Models are Optimized Through Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4855607
scope_conditions: the proposed web3 community governance architecture

claims.claim: The acyclic property of WDAGs is load bearing for governance rather than incidental: because loops and cycles are impossible, the progression of governance rules stays unambiguous and the framework cannot accumulate redundancies and contradictions.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How AI Models are Optimized Through Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4855607
scope_conditions: governance rule systems represented as directed acyclic graphs

claims.claim: Assigning weights to the edges of a governance WDAG lets the system prioritize some governance elements over others, which is how stakeholders are guided to the most relevant and impactful information when making decisions.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How AI Models are Optimized Through Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4855607
scope_conditions: WDAG based governance where edge weights encode priority

claims.claim: WDAGs allow new regulatory and ethical standards to be integrated into existing AI systems without overhauling the entire model architecture, which is what makes rapid legal adaptation feasible in sectors such as public safety and healthcare.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How AI Models are Optimized Through Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4855607
scope_conditions: sectors where AI applications must rapidly adapt to new laws and ethical considerations

claims.claim: Traditional governance models lack the real time responsiveness to community sentiment that a decentralized WDAG system supplies, and this latency, not an absence of rules, is what leaves conventional AI governance out of step with community values.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How AI Models are Optimized Through Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4855607
scope_conditions: comparison of centralized governance models against decentralized, continuously updated ones

claims.claim: Requiring community members to stake reputation tokens in order to validate data quality is what produces robust and reliable training datasets, and this participatory validation improves annotation accuracy while reducing bias.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How AI Models are Optimized Through Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4855607
scope_conditions: training data validation carried out by a reputation staking community

claims.claim: Because annotating large datasets is labor intensive and expensive, smart contracts that reward community members with tokens for annotation are needed to sustain a steady flow of high quality labeled data for deep learning.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How AI Models are Optimized Through Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4855607
scope_conditions: supervised deep learning that depends on large labeled datasets

claims.claim: The interaction between transformer models and the web3 community forms an evolutionary feedback loop in which community input shapes model development and the improved models return better service to the community, which is what sustains participation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How AI Models are Optimized Through Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4855607
scope_conditions: communities that both govern and consume the model they govern

claims.claim: In federated learning, validation pools coordinated by smart contracts should dispense rewards pro rata to the reputation a node has accumulated through productive work, so that incentives track a node's actual contribution to the model's learning rather than mere participation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How AI Models are Optimized Through Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4855607
scope_conditions: federated learning where node contribution quality varies and must be motivated

claims.claim: The feedback effects that make community governance of federated learning work will not materialize unless expert community members are selected coherently, making coherent expert selection a precondition of the mechanism rather than an optional refinement.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How AI Models are Optimized Through Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4855607
scope_conditions: community driven governance of federated learning models

claims.claim: A precedent and citation WDAG accounting system documents and traces every adjustment to a federated learning model, and that full accounting is what enables dynamic feedback effects and the rapid integration of new techniques.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How AI Models are Optimized Through Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4855607
scope_conditions: governance of iteratively updated federated learning models

claims.claim: GNNs and web3 systems optimize each other through mutual feedback effects, and it is this bidirectional learning, rather than one system merely serving the other, that produces an evolutionary dynamic optimization process.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How AI Models are Optimized Through Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4855607
scope_conditions: GNNs deployed inside the web3 systems they analyze

claims.claim: The RLHF process is exposed to failure because participants may hold potentially adversarial and misaligned interests, so the vulnerability lies in the incentive structure of feedback provision rather than in the learning algorithm.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How AI Models are Optimized Through Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4855607
scope_conditions: RLHF systems where feedback providers have divergent stakes

claims.claim: Distributing governance across all participants prevents any single entity from dominating decision making, and because model or training changes then require consensus, the resulting decisions reflect collective rather than individual interest.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How AI Models are Optimized Through Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4855607
scope_conditions: governance systems where change requires consensus among distributed participants

claims.claim: Applying decentralized voting and consensus to RLHF permits human feedback to be verified before it is used to calibrate the Reward Model, which raises the integrity and reliability of the feedback data entering the model.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How AI Models are Optimized Through Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4855607
scope_conditions: RLHF pipelines where feedback can be verified prior to reward model training

claims.claim: Web3 systems provide inexpensive community based smart contract dispute resolution, and these mechanisms minimize legal cost while increasing both the certainty of outcomes and the protections available to stakeholders.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How AI Models are Optimized Through Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4855607
scope_conditions: disputes among stakeholders inside a web3 community

claims.claim: Issuing non fungible reputation tokens that represent voting power, access rights, or entitlement to a share of the project's success creates an economic structure in which participants are directly invested in the success of the RLHF process.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How AI Models are Optimized Through Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4855607
scope_conditions: RLHF communities where retention and sustained participation matter

claims.claim: Gathering a wide range of human feedback makes the Reward Model reflect a comprehensive spectrum of human preferences and values, and it is this inclusivity that mitigates bias and captures a richer understanding of what counts as a desirable outcome.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How AI Models are Optimized Through Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4855607
scope_conditions: reward models trained on feedback drawn from a broad participant base

claims.claim: Organizations should adopt web3 governance frameworks incrementally, beginning with less critical applications in order to assess impacts and refine methodologies, because staged adoption is what allows the risks to be managed while the benefits of decentralized AI governance are realized.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How AI Models are Optimized Through Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4855607
scope_conditions: organizations incorporating these optimizations into existing and future AI systems

claims.claim: Governance protocols themselves must be continuously evaluated and adapted, because without that ongoing revision AI models will neither maintain optimal performance nor stay in line with changing regulations and societal expectations.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How AI Models are Optimized Through Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4855607
scope_conditions: AI systems operating under regulations and societal expectations that change over time

claims.claim: Growth in philanthropy is the main driver of impact innovation, and the successive phases of impact innovation from Impact 1.0 to Impact 3.0 are responses to that growth.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Impact Investing Innovation - From Impact 1.0 to 3.0 (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4685567
scope_conditions: global philanthropy since the turn of the century

claims.claim: Kaal stipulates the load bearing definition of the paper: impact certificates are electronic tickets that can be sold to claim a project's impact, functioning analogously to a carbon credit.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Impact Investing Innovation - From Impact 1.0 to 3.0 (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4685567

claims.claim: Impact 1.0 foundations developed plutocratic power structures because their leaders and trustees were never democratically elected, and Impact 3.0 addresses this by adding WEB3 collaborative democratic measures on top of the existing foundation structures.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Impact Investing Innovation - From Impact 1.0 to 3.0 (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4685567
scope_conditions: private foundation governance
Impact 3.0 still relies on foundation structures

claims.claim: Because Impact 1.0 entrusted individual donors rather than donor collectives with identifying which problems to solve, individual philanthropists can reshape underfunded causes according to their own ideals without meaningful checks and balances or crowd wisdom.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Impact Investing Innovation - From Impact 1.0 to 3.0 (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4685567
scope_conditions: Impact 1.0 and 2.0 philanthropic strategies
high net worth individual and corporate donors

claims.claim: Impact 3.0 shortens the lag between donors taking their tax deductions and the donated funds actually reaching impact projects, which is a capital allocation timing failure of Impact 1.0 and 2.0.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Impact Investing Innovation - From Impact 1.0 to 3.0 (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4685567
scope_conditions: donors receiving tax deductions in advance of deployment

claims.claim: Kaal limits the reach of his own proposal: donors motivated by personal or local causes may have no interest in scaling impact at all, so the paper's target audience is only the subgroup of high dollar donors who want technology based improvements in philanthropy.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Impact Investing Innovation - From Impact 1.0 to 3.0 (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4685567
scope_conditions: donors motivated by personal experience or institutional loyalty

claims.claim: Because Impact 1.0 lacks a liquid and efficient funding marketplace, donors protect their interest by overinvesting in process rather than in impact outcomes directly.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Impact Investing Innovation - From Impact 1.0 to 3.0 (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4685567
scope_conditions: absence of a liquid impact funding marketplace

claims.claim: Without a full view of the impact market, Impact 1.0 donors end up funding projects run by people already in their existing networks rather than the most qualified projects judged by objective standards.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Impact Investing Innovation - From Impact 1.0 to 3.0 (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4685567
scope_conditions: no central impact marketplace
funding sources that are not well known

claims.claim: The absence of an efficient marketplace lets big dollar donors hijack the priorities of impact intermediaries such as foundations, donor advised funds, NGOs and fiscal sponsors, producing a feast or famine pattern for fundable projects.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Impact Investing Innovation - From Impact 1.0 to 3.0 (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4685567
scope_conditions: intermediated philanthropy without a central marketplace

claims.claim: Credential tracking is a necessary condition for Impact 3.0: any Impact 3.0 platform built without WEB3 credential tracking systems will encounter significant disruption over time, as foreshadowed by the failure to enforce and monitor net zero commitments in Impact 1.0.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Impact Investing Innovation - From Impact 1.0 to 3.0 (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4685567
scope_conditions: Impact 3.0 platforms
stakes higher than in Impact 1.0 carbon markets

claims.claim: In an impact certificate system the rules of the game are set by demand: altruists define what counts by deciding which minted certificates they are willing to pay for.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Impact Investing Innovation - From Impact 1.0 to 3.0 (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4685567
scope_conditions: impact teams can mint and publicly declare ownership of certificates

claims.claim: Kaal concedes that at their worst Impact 1.0 carbon credits are non transparent, fraudulent and fail to mitigate climate change, but contests the inference drawn from that record: operational shortcomings do not necessarily invalidate the underlying theory.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Impact Investing Innovation - From Impact 1.0 to 3.0 (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4685567
scope_conditions: distinguishes operational execution from underlying theory

claims.claim: Impact markets that promote retrospective funding and resale of impact carry an inherent risk of incentivizing net negative ventures, because individuals can capture the benefit of positive impacts without bearing the cost when their actions produce negative impacts.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Impact Investing Innovation - From Impact 1.0 to 3.0 (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4685567
scope_conditions: retrospective funding
resale of impact permitted

claims.claim: Impact 1.0 impact markets fail on the demand side: they have more sellers than buyers, and many potential buyers would have funded those projects anyway, which removes the need for a secondary market and significantly reduces resale value.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Impact Investing Innovation - From Impact 1.0 to 3.0 (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4685567
scope_conditions: Impact 1.0 secondary markets for social impact credits

claims.claim: Participatory grantmaking in Impact 2.0 trades efficiency for inclusivity: balancing the two is complex and potentially leads to longer decision making processes and increased resource allocation for facilitation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Impact Investing Innovation - From Impact 1.0 to 3.0 (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4685567
scope_conditions: participatory grantmaking models in Impact 2.0

claims.claim: Impact measurement in Impact 2.0 has no settled standard: consensus on measurement methodologies and metrics remains elusive, which produces divergent approaches and hinders comparability across programs and sectors.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Impact Investing Innovation - From Impact 1.0 to 3.0 (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4685567
scope_conditions: Impact 2.0 measurement practice

claims.claim: The impact measurement consulting business follows a distinctly centralized approach, and without the crowd wisdom and community audit that WEB3 Impact 3.0 supplies, such consulting practices are subject to single points of failure.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Impact Investing Innovation - From Impact 1.0 to 3.0 (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4685567
scope_conditions: centralized consulting model for impact measurement

claims.claim: Impact 3.0 makes verification a precondition of funding: unlike Impact 1.0 and 2.0, where projects could receive funding without impact verification, Impact 3.0 only allows funding where projects are verified and demonstrate impact via milestones.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Impact Investing Innovation - From Impact 1.0 to 3.0 (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4685567
scope_conditions: listing requires either winning a competition or an expert community upvote

claims.claim: Firm commitment underwriting of impact certificate listings gives the project team and the investing community an assurance that the entire listing, including all certificate fractions, will be purchased provided the corresponding impact milestone deliverables are upvoted by the WEB3 expert community.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Impact Investing Innovation - From Impact 1.0 to 3.0 (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4685567
scope_conditions: an underwriting donor community exists

claims.claim: Decentralized governance models such as DAOs answer the criticism that micro level quantum properties do not scale to the macro level, because DAOs demonstrate participatory governance structures that operate effectively in large, complex economies.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Quantum Economy and Tokenomics (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4900878
scope_conditions: large scale decentralized economies with DAO governance

claims.claim: Programmable tokens and smart contracts give quantum economics an experimental testbed, so contested phenomena such as preference reversal can be modeled with quantum decision theory and then empirically validated and refined rather than argued in the abstract.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Quantum Economy and Tokenomics (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4900878
scope_conditions: phenomena that can be instantiated in programmable token systems

claims.claim: DeFi protocols automate financial transactions through smart contracts, cutting out intermediaries and increasing transparency, and those same features let quantum economics build models that are self executing and adaptable to real time data, overcoming implementation problems that defeat traditional economic models.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Quantum Economy and Tokenomics (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4900878
scope_conditions: DeFi platforms operating on smart contract infrastructure

claims.claim: The zero space structure of smart contracts produces a form of quantum transaction entanglement, in which transactions execute instantaneously and uniformly across the network regardless of the physical distance between the wallets involved.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Quantum Economy and Tokenomics (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4900878
scope_conditions: blockchain networks where contract execution is replicated across all nodes

claims.claim: In blockchain transactions the signing function, performed by wallets holding cryptographic keys, is separate from execution, which occurs inside the smart contract, so tokens are never physically held in the same locality as the keys and the smart contract acts as the intermediary executing predefined rules.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Quantum Economy and Tokenomics (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4900878
scope_conditions: smart contract based blockchain transactions

claims.claim: Because the blockchain is a distributed ledger existing simultaneously across all nodes, physical space is effectively eliminated within the network, and a triggered smart contract executes its code across the entire network instantaneously without regard to where wallets or keys are located.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Quantum Economy and Tokenomics (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4900878
scope_conditions: distributed ledgers replicated across all network nodes

claims.claim: Distributing validation and execution across many nodes mitigates central point of failure risk and makes the network more resilient to attacks and disruptions, which is the security payoff of decentralization.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Quantum Economy and Tokenomics (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4900878
scope_conditions: decentralized networks where no single node controls the system

claims.claim: Quantum computing cuts both ways for blockchain: it can raise the efficiency and security of blockchain networks, but safeguarding those systems against the threats it also creates depends on research into quantum resistant cryptographic algorithms.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Quantum Economy and Tokenomics (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4900878
scope_conditions: as quantum computing capability advances

claims.claim: Integrating stablecoins pegged to fiat currencies gives a token ecosystem a stable transactional medium and mitigates the volatility that otherwise attaches to cryptocurrencies, alongside DeFi services that let users earn returns and access credit outside the banking system.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Quantum Economy and Tokenomics (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4900878
scope_conditions: the VOW ecosystem as a case study

claims.claim: A reputation governance layer that awards reputation tokens for contributions and behavior fosters trust and drives positive engagement within a token community, complementing DAO based token holder voting.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Quantum Economy and Tokenomics (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4900878
scope_conditions: the VOW ecosystem as a case study

claims.claim: Tokenizing physical and digital assets enables fractional ownership and supplies liquidity, which broadens access to investment opportunities that were previously out of reach.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Quantum Economy and Tokenomics (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4900878
scope_conditions: the VOW ecosystem as a case study

claims.claim: Guaranteeing users full ownership and control over their digital assets protects them from asset confiscation and from loss of purchasing power through currency devaluation, which matters most to individuals in regions with unstable financial systems.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Quantum Economy and Tokenomics (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4900878
scope_conditions: regions with unstable financial systems
requires the user to retain full ownership and control of the assets

claims.claim: An operating token ecosystem such as VOW can function as empirical evidence for quantum economics, since a working decentralized system that manages complex economic phenomena supports the validity and utility of the abstract framework it instantiates.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Quantum Economy and Tokenomics (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4900878
scope_conditions: conditional on the continued practical success of the ecosystem

claims.claim: Tokenomics supplies the practical mechanisms that operationalize the abstract concepts of quantum economics, and this synthesis both advances quantum economics and promotes the growth and sustainability of decentralized digital economies.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Quantum Economy and Tokenomics (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4900878

claims.claim: Legal accumulation is produced by a specific legislative practice: new regulations are layered over existing ones without repealing outdated provisions. The resulting corpus is more complex and less transparent, which raises compliance costs for individuals and businesses.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Future of Law - Dynamic Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4957318
scope_conditions: modern legislative systems that enact new law faster than they repeal old law

claims.claim: Overlapping or contradictory regulation raises the risk of selective enforcement and legal arbitrage, because entities that cannot be expected to comply with everything can instead exploit the gaps and inconsistencies to their advantage.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Future of Law - Dynamic Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4957318
scope_conditions: where regulated parties cannot readily understand the full body of applicable rules

claims.claim: Codification is self defeating at scale: although a specific statute is individually cheaper to understand than a vague standard, the sheer volume of statutory law generates information costs that make the legal landscape more complex rather than simpler.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Future of Law - Dynamic Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4957318
scope_conditions: systems that have shifted from common law adjudication to comprehensive codification
where the volume of new legislation grows continuously

claims.claim: Expanding regulatory oversight across sectors produces regulatory accretion, the cumulative growth of rules, which yields a complex and sometimes contradictory legal environment and burdens the very agencies charged with enforcement and oversight.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Future of Law - Dynamic Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4957318
scope_conditions: administrative states with broad sectoral regulatory mandates

claims.claim: Inconsistent application of a proliferating body of law by different judges and regulatory bodies produces unpredictable legal outcomes, which increases litigation as parties seek judicial clarification and in turn undermines public confidence in the legal system.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Future of Law - Dynamic Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4957318
scope_conditions: where statutes and regulations multiply faster than interpretive doctrine consolidates

claims.claim: As law becomes more detailed and specialized it becomes less accessible to the general public, which complicates citizens' ability to understand the rules governing them and discourages engagement and participation in democratic processes.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Future of Law - Dynamic Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4957318
scope_conditions: where legal complexity outpaces lay comprehension

claims.claim: Web2 platform architecture is a causal contributor to distrust in legal institutions: centralized models driven by engagement metrics prioritize sensationalism over nuanced discourse, which accelerates misinformation and echo chambers and magnifies public distrust.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Future of Law - Dynamic Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4957318
scope_conditions: centralized, engagement optimized social media platforms
where citizens use social media as a substitute for formal legal channels

claims.claim: Sunset provisions are legislative tools that impose automatic expiration dates on laws or regulations, and their function is to compel periodic review and reassessment rather than to repeal directly.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Future of Law - Dynamic Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4957318

claims.claim: Sunset regulation has fallen out of wide use, and the author attributes this primarily to the administrative burden and political inertia of regularly reviewing and repealing laws, not to any defect in the concept itself.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Future of Law - Dynamic Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4957318
scope_conditions: legislatures without dedicated review capacity

claims.claim: Sunset provisions fail on their own terms when the mandated reviews are not conducted thoroughly, because laws then either expire or continue without proper scrutiny, which defeats the purpose of the mechanism.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Future of Law - Dynamic Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4957318
scope_conditions: where legislative review capacity or attention is insufficient

claims.claim: Sunset provisions likely increase rents extracted by interest groups and entrench current majoritarian preferences, and they can create planning problems for both public and private actors.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Future of Law - Dynamic Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4957318
scope_conditions: politically salient statutes subject to periodic renewal

claims.claim: Because renewal deadlines create recurring windows for legislative action, sunset clauses become instruments of political maneuvering in which lawmakers cater to interest groups or shifting political winds instead of pursuing long term policy solutions.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Future of Law - Dynamic Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4957318
scope_conditions: where renewal is politically contested

claims.claim: The possibility that a law will expire without guaranteed renewal creates a climate of uncertainty that discourages the investment and long term planning which depend on consistent regulatory frameworks.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Future of Law - Dynamic Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4957318
scope_conditions: capital intensive or long horizon business decisions
regulated markets where entry depends on rule stability

claims.claim: Sunset provisions endanger politically contentious institutions rather than ineffective ones, because agencies that face opposition or controversy can be dissolved through expiration regardless of their ongoing relevance or necessity.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Future of Law - Dynamic Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4957318
scope_conditions: agencies that are subjects of intense political debate

claims.claim: Deadline pressure inverts the intended effect of sunset provisions: the need to reassess and renew by a fixed date produces hasty decisions or the continuation of flawed policies because there is insufficient time for proper evaluation.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Future of Law - Dynamic Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4957318
scope_conditions: where expiration dates arrive faster than deliberative review can be completed

claims.claim: Sunset provisions in tax law do not deliver fiscal restraint, because shifting baselines, exceptions to budget rules, and the difficulty of accurately costing temporary legislation undermine their theoretical benefits.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Future of Law - Dynamic Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4957318
scope_conditions: tax legislation subject to budget scoring rules

claims.claim: Sunsetting performs best in crisis driven financial legislation, where it supplies a built in mechanism for reviewing and potentially repealing laws enacted under emergency conditions and thereby mitigates the harms of legislating under pressure.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Future of Law - Dynamic Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4957318
scope_conditions: legislation enacted in response to acute financial crisis
where the enacting conditions are expected to subside

claims.claim: Legal garbage collection is stipulated as the systematic review and removal of outdated, redundant, or otherwise unnecessary laws from the legal code, by analogy to garbage collection in computer science.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Future of Law - Dynamic Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4957318

claims.claim: Legal garbage collection is blocked by politics rather than by analysis: outdated or redundant laws remain contentious when they carry symbolic importance for particular constituencies or when repeal would be read as weakening the regulatory framework.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Future of Law - Dynamic Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4957318
scope_conditions: statutes with symbolic or ideological significance
where repeal is publicly visible

claims.claim: Determining genuine obsolescence is hard because statutes are interconnected: an apparently redundant law may be a foundational element of another statute or regulatory framework, so repeal produces a ripple effect through the broader legal ecosystem.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Future of Law - Dynamic Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4957318
scope_conditions: dense statutory systems with cross referencing provisions

claims.claim: The cost of comprehensive legal review deters governments from committing the necessary resources, which prevents legal garbage collection from being applied consistently and effectively.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Future of Law - Dynamic Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4957318
scope_conditions: jurisdictions with budget constraints or competing policy priorities

claims.claim: Removing laws without fully understanding their current applications or interdependencies creates legal gaps and unintended policy outcomes, so the act of cleanup can itself weaken regulatory or protective frameworks.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Future of Law - Dynamic Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4957318
scope_conditions: where repeal proceeds without mapping of downstream dependencies

claims.claim: Legal garbage collection faces an unavoidable tradeoff: streamlining the legal framework by removing outdated laws must be balanced against preserving legal history, since historical statutes record the evolution of legal principles and societal values.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Future of Law - Dynamic Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4957318
scope_conditions: where removal is implemented as deletion rather than archiving

claims.claim: Experimental rules impose a cost on the regulated: because the rules are temporary and subject to change, they complicate compliance efforts, disrupt long term planning, and create ambiguity that can produce resistance or unintended non compliance.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Future of Law - Dynamic Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4957318
scope_conditions: where the experimental rule substantially modifies an existing regulatory framework

claims.claim: Automatic adjustment mechanisms are pre established legislative components that let laws self update in response to changing circumstances, and their purpose is to counter policy drift, the divergence of policy from its original intent as conditions change.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Future of Law - Dynamic Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4957318
scope_conditions: policy domains with observable triggering indicators such as inflation or unemployment

claims.claim: Automatic adjustment mechanisms trade democratic input for responsiveness: by removing policy changes from the legislative agenda they limit opportunities for public debate and scrutiny, which raises accountability and transparency concerns.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Future of Law - Dynamic Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4957318
scope_conditions: where adjustment is triggered automatically without legislative revisiting

claims.claim: War functions as a catalyst for legal reform because it compels legislators to focus on laws immediately relevant to wartime and post war objectives, which enables rapid removal of outdated, inefficient, or irrelevant provisions that would otherwise persist.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Future of Law - Dynamic Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4957318
scope_conditions: wartime and immediate post war periods
where extraordinary powers to reorganize legal frameworks are available

claims.claim: The speed of post war Japanese legal reform demonstrates that large scale legal change is possible when strong political will and adequate resources are present, which locates the binding constraint on legal cleanup in will and resources rather than in feasibility.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Future of Law - Dynamic Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4957318
scope_conditions: post World War II Japan under Allied occupation
where external actors supplied impetus and expertise

claims.claim: Web3 systems answer the web2 pathology at the architectural level rather than the content level: decentralized, transparent, community governed designs eliminate the centralized control that drives misinformation and echo chambers, and substitute transparency, decentralization, and user control.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Future of Law - Dynamic Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4957318
scope_conditions: decentralized and community governed platform architectures

claims.claim: The proposed system stipulates a forum as an on chain collection of uniquely identified posts that may cite prior contributions, and this citation structure is what constitutes the Weighted Directed Acyclic Graph.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Future of Law - Dynamic Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4957318
scope_conditions: on chain forums where posts and citations are recorded immutably

claims.claim: Validation pools are the consensus mechanism of the proposed system: author stakes are pooled to evaluate specific forum posts, and the outcome can mint new reputation tokens that record the community's consensus on a contribution.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Future of Law - Dynamic Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4957318
scope_conditions: where participants stake reputation on the evaluation of specific posts

claims.claim: Unlike traditional governance that relies on periodic reviews and updates, the WDAG system taps a continuous stream of data from a wide range of stakeholders, which is what makes real time rather than cyclical legal adjustment possible.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Future of Law - Dynamic Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4957318
scope_conditions: where a decentralized network can supply continuous stakeholder sentiment data

claims.claim: In the WDAG system a legal precedent or rule that gains favor because it is effective automatically receives a higher weight, and that weight is set by user preferences and citations rather than by any legislative act.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Future of Law - Dynamic Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4957318
scope_conditions: where citation and user preference data are recorded on chain
where effectiveness is revealed through use

claims.claim: Because weights adjust continuously with use, the WDAG system eliminates the need for periodic external review altogether; the system evolves toward the most relevant and effective legal norms without a scheduled reassessment step.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Future of Law - Dynamic Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4957318
scope_conditions: where citation activity is sufficient to reveal relative relevance

claims.claim: The WDAG system suppresses rent seeking by internalizing advocacy: there are no external costs or lobbying pressures because any advocacy occurs transparently within the system's forums, where all user actions and preferences are recorded.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Future of Law - Dynamic Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4957318
scope_conditions: where all stakeholder action occurs inside the on chain forum
where user actions and preferences are fully observable

claims.claim: The WDAG system never repeals: all precedents and rules are retained on the blockchain, so no legal principle is ever permanently discarded even when it ceases to be applied.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Future of Law - Dynamic Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4957318
scope_conditions: blockchain based retention of all precedents

claims.claim: Obsolescence in the WDAG system is expressed as gradual loss of weight rather than deletion, which keeps rules revisitable if circumstances change and avoids hasty or ill considered removal decisions.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Future of Law - Dynamic Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4957318
scope_conditions: where relevance is a continuous weight rather than a binary in force status

claims.claim: Political resistance to repeal dissolves under the WDAG model because a rule that loses substantial backing simply diminishes in relevance through the citation mechanism, with no external legislative act of repeal to contest.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Future of Law - Dynamic Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4957318
scope_conditions: where support and opposition are expressed through citation behavior

claims.claim: The WDAG system preserves legal history as a byproduct of its architecture: all legal precedents are retained within a blockchain based framework in a transparent and immutable format, so historical access does not trade off against current relevance.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Future of Law - Dynamic Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4957318
scope_conditions: blockchain based immutable record keeping

claims.claim: A shift toward WDAG based dynamic solutions is not merely attractive but necessary for a legal system that is both efficient and equitable in addressing the complexities of contemporary governance.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, The Future of Law - Dynamic Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4957318
scope_conditions: contemporary governance under rapid technological and societal change

claims.claim: The accessible reserves of publicly available human-created text usable for training large language models could be exhausted by 2028 at current usage trajectories.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Artificial Intelligence The Final Frontier (2025). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5095633
scope_conditions: current growth trajectories in training set size continue
restricted to publicly available human-created text

claims.claim: Data exhaustion is caused primarily by the exponential growth in the size of datasets needed to build increasingly sophisticated AI models, not by any sudden loss of existing text.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Artificial Intelligence The Final Frontier (2025). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5095633

claims.claim: The total effective stock of human-generated text is estimated at roughly 300 trillion tokens, with a plausible range from 100 trillion to 1 quadrillion tokens.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Artificial Intelligence The Final Frontier (2025). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5095633
scope_conditions: estimate of effective stock, not raw internet volume

claims.claim: The apparent abundance of internet text overstates the usable supply, because much of it fails quality thresholds for model training due to redundancy, noise, or irrelevance.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Artificial Intelligence The Final Frontier (2025). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5095633
scope_conditions: applies to internet-sourced text used for model training

claims.claim: The current data production market cannot scale or sustain a high-quality text supply because content creators face limited incentives and no direct compensation structures.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Artificial Intelligence The Final Frontier (2025). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5095633
scope_conditions: market as currently structured around platforms and content aggregators

claims.claim: Privacy rules, copyright, and the uneven global distribution of digital connectivity independently reduce both the availability and the diversity of human-generated text for AI training.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Artificial Intelligence The Final Frontier (2025). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5095633

claims.claim: The author proposes a decentralized, Mechanical Turk style data production model in which individual contributors are directly compensated for generating, refining, or annotating text data.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Artificial Intelligence The Final Frontier (2025). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5095633

claims.claim: Decentralized data production will succeed only if it solves fraudulent submissions, content moderation, and alignment with ethical and legal frameworks; these are necessary conditions, not incidental risks.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Artificial Intelligence The Final Frontier (2025). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5095633

claims.claim: The high cost of processing colossal datasets confines frontier AI innovation to a small number of well-resourced institutions.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Artificial Intelligence The Final Frontier (2025). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5095633
scope_conditions: applies where model development requires processing very large datasets

claims.claim: When a training dataset disproportionately represents one region or demographic group, the resulting model produces skewed and sometimes inappropriate outputs once deployed in unfamiliar settings.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Artificial Intelligence The Final Frontier (2025). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5095633
scope_conditions: deployment context differs from the demographic composition of the training data

claims.claim: As AI-generated content proliferates online it dilutes the diversity and originality of the text pool available for later training, producing performance degradation across successive model generations.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Artificial Intelligence The Final Frontier (2025). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5095633
scope_conditions: repeated training generations drawing on an increasingly synthetic web

claims.claim: The governance protocols required for GDPR and AI Act compliance, including anonymization, data minimization, and explicit consent, themselves complicate the assembly of robust AI training datasets.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Artificial Intelligence The Final Frontier (2025). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5095633
scope_conditions: jurisdictions with GDPR-style data protection mandates

claims.claim: Latency, throughput limits, and the absence of fully automated continuous training and validation together defeat the timeliness advantage that real-time data is supposed to deliver.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Artificial Intelligence The Final Frontier (2025). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5095633
scope_conditions: AI pipelines ingesting live, high-velocity data streams

claims.claim: In fast-moving fields such as technology, law, and public policy, models trained on obsolete datasets fail to capture new trends, behaviors, or regulatory changes, which reduces their predictive and explanatory power.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Artificial Intelligence The Final Frontier (2025). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5095633
scope_conditions: domains with rapid regulatory or behavioral change

claims.claim: In healthcare, biased or stale training data produces algorithms that misdiagnose underrepresented populations and thereby reinforce existing health disparities instead of reducing them.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Artificial Intelligence The Final Frontier (2025). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5095633
scope_conditions: clinical deployment on populations underrepresented in training data

claims.claim: Data protection compliance carried out in a way that overly constrains researcher access converts a privacy gain into a net social loss, because the societal benefits of AI are offset by a stunted innovation ecosystem.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Artificial Intelligence The Final Frontier (2025). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5095633
scope_conditions: where compliance is implemented without counterbalancing privacy-preserving techniques

claims.claim: Decentralizing data processing across secure nodes, using techniques such as federated learning and homomorphic encryption, circumvents the privacy and security exposure of centralized data management and lowers breach risk.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Artificial Intelligence The Final Frontier (2025). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5095633
scope_conditions: privacy-preserving computation techniques are actually deployed

claims.claim: The centralized frameworks used by the leading annotation companies, including Scale AI, Appen, Hive, V7 Labs, CloudFactory, and Sama, carry theoretical and practical shortcomings around bias, ethical sourcing, and data diversity that undermine the equitability and generalizability of the resulting AI models.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Artificial Intelligence The Final Frontier (2025). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5095633
scope_conditions: centralized data annotation providers as currently structured

claims.claim: Biases held by human annotators or embedded in automated annotation systems are propagated into the models trained on their output, producing AI that performs inequitably across demographic groups.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Artificial Intelligence The Final Frontier (2025). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5095633
scope_conditions: applies even to providers that emphasize high-quality data such as Scale AI and Appen

claims.claim: Automating annotation to gain speed and cost savings produces less nuanced labeling that misses the complex human judgments and context certain AI applications require.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Artificial Intelligence The Final Frontier (2025). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5095633
scope_conditions: automation-heavy annotation workflows such as those of Hive and V7 Labs

claims.claim: Human-in-the-loop annotation, including under ethical labor models, imposes financial and time costs large enough to slow the pace at which AI models can be upgraded.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Artificial Intelligence The Final Frontier (2025). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5095633
scope_conditions: pipelines that depend on human annotators

claims.claim: Centralizing annotation data inside a small number of vendor firms creates a standing risk of breach or misuse that can produce legal liability and loss of trust in AI technologies.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Artificial Intelligence The Final Frontier (2025). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5095633
scope_conditions: data aggregated and held by centralized annotation vendors

claims.claim: Maintaining consistent annotation quality across many annotators and automated systems is unsolved at scale, and small labeling errors translate into significant degradation of model performance in critical applications.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Artificial Intelligence The Final Frontier (2025). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5095633
scope_conditions: large-scale annotation operations
safety-critical applications such as autonomous driving

claims.claim: Smart contracts that release payment automatically once preset quality thresholds are met reduce human error, cut administrative overhead, and accelerate data-labeling cycles relative to intermediated payment processes.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Artificial Intelligence The Final Frontier (2025). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5095633
scope_conditions: quality thresholds can be specified in advance and verified on-chain

claims.claim: Transparent DAO governance lets platforms compensate contributors according to demonstrated expertise and reputation, which mitigates the exploitative labor practices associated with centralized annotation services.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Artificial Intelligence The Final Frontier (2025). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5095633
scope_conditions: governance is genuinely transparent and reputation is verifiable

claims.claim: High transaction costs in centralized payment systems make micro-payments for small tasks uneconomic, whereas blockchain ledgers process tiny transfers efficiently and thereby widen the pool of contributors willing to do micro-tasks.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Artificial Intelligence The Final Frontier (2025). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5095633
scope_conditions: ledger transaction fees are low enough to support micro-payments

claims.claim: Adoption of decentralized data platforms is blocked by an expertise barrier: prospective contributors must manage tokens, maintain secure wallets, and understand the underlying technology, which deters users unaccustomed to digital assets.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Artificial Intelligence The Final Frontier (2025). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5095633
scope_conditions: current blockchain user experience

claims.claim: Decentralized data annotation at scale is not operationally feasible without advances in consensus algorithms or layer-two scaling, because existing blockchain infrastructures cap transaction speed and network capacity.
claims.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Artificial Intelligence The Final Frontier (2025). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5095633
